Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 1: Toolkit and First Arrays

How to teach the first session of Python Data Science. Welcome a room of people who can already write Python functions, loops and small programs; prove that every machine has a working environment and the course data; find out what they remember; then get real work out of the toolkit (a first look at 20,302 orders) and meet the structure everything else in the course is built on, the NumPy array. Learners leave having loaded real files, read three tracebacks from the bottom, measured for themselves why an array beats a list for numbers, and been surprised, once and safely, by a view.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 0.1–1.1 Session 1 of 21

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (the goal and one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (a kit lab, new practice on the lesson's skills) → start the lesson's own project. The lesson exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Type, do not paste. Every code block in a demo script below was run to produce the output printed under it. Type it live, ask for a prediction before you run it, and read errors from the last line up, out loud.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep getting_started.html and numpy_arrays_vs_lists.html open in browser tabs for the diagrams (the setup map, the list-versus-array memory picture, the view and copy picture). Labs live in labs/module-01/: _starter.py files are handouts, _solution.py files are yours.
  • Session 1 is different in one way: it opens with 30 minutes of welcome, environment check and diagnostic instead of the usual 10-minute retrieval warm-up. Lesson 0.1's installation steps are done before the session from the setup guide; the room spends its 0.1 time using the toolkit, not installing it.
  • Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs. Lesson codes (0.1, 1.1) match the course site.
The #1 risk of Session 1: installation eats the session

Lesson 0.1 is an install lesson, and installs go wrong in ways that are different on every laptop. If you let the room install together on venue Wi-Fi, you will still be fixing machines at the break and Lesson 1.1 will not happen. Three things prevent it. Before: send the setup guide a week ahead and ask every learner to reply with the last line of check_environment.py; chase the ones who do not reply. In the room: the check gets 12 minutes and no more; a machine that is not ready gets a partner, not your attention. After: the NOT READY output is a numbered list the learner can follow at home, and you check it again at the start of Session 2. The second risk is quieter: a learner whose notebook kernel is not the course environment, who gets through today on an old pandas and then sees different output from the lesson pages for weeks. The version lines in the check are there to catch exactly that.

Before the Session

  • ☐ A week before: email the setup guide (the kit's Setup Guide, which follows Lesson 0.1: Python 3.12 or newer, a pinecrest-analysis folder, .venv, python -m pip install -r requirements.txt, pinecrest-data.zip unzipped into it). Attach labs/module-01/l0_1-orientation/check_environment.py and ask learners to run it and reply with its last line. No reply means an install risk: chase it.
  • ☐ Files to hand out (shared folder or USB stick, in case the network fails): requirements.txt, pinecrest-data.zip, the whole labs/ folder without the *_solution.py files (keep labs_paths.py in it: every lab imports it), and the workbook. Learners put labs/ inside pinecrest-analysis, next to data/, so the labs find the data on their own.
  • ☐ Run the kit check once: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-01 from the instructor-kit folder. Every line should say PASS (8 files). Run python labs/module-01/l0_1-orientation/check_environment.py on the projector machine so you can show what READY looks like.
  • ☐ Servers to start: none. Internet is needed only by learners who still have to install; the session itself runs offline.
  • ☐ Projector machine: a terminal with (.venv) active in your own pinecrest-analysis, JupyterLab (or VS Code) started from that folder, font size 18 pt or more, two empty notebooks ready: lesson_0_1 and lesson_1_1. Browser tabs: the course home page, getting_started.html, numpy_arrays_vs_lists.html.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the five-step routine (terminal → cd pinecrest-analysis → activate, see (.venv) → start JupyterLab or VS Code here → kernel is .venv), and space for the three array rules you will add after the break.
  • ☐ Print or share: the workbook (its Start Here page has the diagnostic), and sticky notes for help flags and the exit ticket.
Known environment traps
SymptomCauseFix
python is not recognized, or typing python opens the Microsoft Store (Windows)No environment is active yet, and Windows only provides pyUse py -m venv .venv to create the environment. Once it is active, plain python works.
Activate.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this systemPowerShell's default execution policyOnce per user: Set-ExecutionPolicy -Scope CurrentUser RemoteSigned, answer Y, activate again.
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas' in a terminalThe environment is not active in this windowActivate it; look for (.venv). Activation is per terminal window.
ModuleNotFoundError in a notebook although the terminal works; or pandas 2.x in the version checkThe notebook kernel is a different PythonJupyterLab: start it from the activated terminal. VS Code: Select Kernel ▸ the entry that mentions .venv.
FileNotFoundError: ... 'data/orders.csv'Python is working in another folder, or the zip was extracted into a nested folder such as pinecrest-data/dataprint(Path.cwd()). Start JupyterLab from pinecrest-analysis; move data so that pinecrest-analysis/data/orders.csv exists.
ERROR: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement ... during the installPython older than 3.12 (or much newer than the pins)python --version. Install 3.12 or newer, delete .venv, create it again, reinstall.
The virtual environment was not created successfully because ensurepip is not available (Debian, Ubuntu)The venv module is a separate system packagesudo apt install python3-venv python3-pip, then create the environment again.
jupyter lab starts but no browser opensNo default browser, or a remote or WSL sessionCopy the http://localhost:8888/lab?token=... line from the terminal into a browser.
The install is very slow or fails halfway (venue Wi-Fi)Several hundred megabytes of downloadsDo not install in the room. This is why the setup guide goes out a week ahead. Today: pair up; install at home.
A locked work laptop: nothing can be installedNo administrator rightsPair today. Before Session 2: the python.org installer's per-user option usually needs no admin rights; otherwise their IT team. A hosted notebook service works only if they upload the data folder and match the versions.

In the room. The lesson pages estimate 90 + 80 = 170 minutes for a solo learner, and after the 30-minute opening, the break and the wrap-up the room has 130. So the room does, for each lesson: the mental model, the live demo, one guided kit lab, and the first two steps of the lesson project. Lesson 0.1's installation sections (Install Python, the virtual environment, the packages, downloading the data) are prework, verified by the environment check, and are not repeated in the room.

Goes home (2 to 3 hours). first_look.py Steps 3 to 6 and the benchmark report Steps 3 to 6; each lesson's Hands-on Exercises (three, plus a stretch); both Quick Quizzes; both journal entries; and Lesson 1.1's "Before the Next Lesson" list. Anyone whose check said NOT READY also fixes their machine.

Protect, in this order: the environment check (nobody leaves without knowing whether their machine is ready and what to do if not); the views and copies step of the 1.1 demo and Lab B; reading three tracebacks from the bottom in the 0.1 demo. Cut first: the four-line script and help(len) in the 0.1 demo (Steps 11 and 12), then the 0.1 project start (send all of first_look.py home), then the speed measurement in the 1.1 demo (Step 6; the project measures it anyway).

Opening Segment

0:00

Welcome, Environment Check and Diagnostic

30 min
Timing
5mWelcome and introductions
5mHow the course runs: 21 sessions, two lessons each, the room and home split, the journal
12mEnvironment check: check_environment.py ends with READY on every machine (or the machine gets a helper)
8mDiagnostic: six predict-the-output questions, not graded
Sequence and talking points
  1. Welcome (5m). One minute on yourself, including a question you once answered with data that changed someone's mind. Then a fast round: name, where you learned your Python, and one thing you would like to be able to find out from data by the end of the course. Write three or four of those on the board; they come back in today's first journal entry. Housekeeping in one breath: break at 1:25, where the lab files are, and "if you are stuck, put a sticky note on your laptop lid and keep trying while I get to you."
  2. How the course runs (5m). Show the course home page. Say: "Twenty-one sessions of three hours, two lessons a session. NumPy first, then pandas, charts, statistics, SQL, data from the web, interactive dashboards, and a capstone you choose. Every lesson uses the same made-up company, Pinecrest Outfitters, so by the end you will know its data well." Then the deal: "Each lesson was written for someone working alone for 75 to 110 minutes, so two do not fit in three hours. In this room we do the parts that are hard to do alone: the mental model, a live demo, a guided lab, and the first steps of each lesson's project. At home you finish the projects and do the lesson's exercises, quiz and journal: plan on two to three hours a week." Open getting_started.html and scroll once through the pattern: objectives, sections with code and its real output, common mistakes, a project in steps, exercises with hidden solutions, a quiz, a journal prompt.
  3. Environment check (12m). Say: "Before any new ideas, we prove that every machine is ready." On the projector, then theirs: 1 open a terminal; 2 cd pinecrest-analysis; 3 activate and look for (.venv); 4 python check_environment.py (the file is in labs/module-01/l0_1-orientation/; they copy it into the project folder, or run it by its path). Done = the last line says READY for Python Data Science. Anyone who ran it at home and saw READY runs it once more and becomes a helper. A NOT READY machine prints a numbered fix list: activation and the data folder you fix now (one minute each); a missing Python 3.12 or a full package install you do not start on venue Wi-Fi: pair that learner with a ready neighbor for today and fix it at the break or at home.
  4. Diagnostic (8m). Say: "Six quick questions from the Intro and Intermediate courses. This is not a test and nobody collects it. It tells you what to reread and tells me what to slow down for." Learners answer D1 to D6 on the workbook's Start Here page (about four minutes), then show fingers (1 to 4 for A to D) as you reveal each on the slide. Settle any argument by running the code. Keep a tally of wrong answers per question on a sticky note.
Diagnostic answers and how to read the tally

Answers: D1 A) ['Sat', 'Sun'] ['Tue', 'Wed']; D2 C) [1, 2, 3, 4] [1, 2, 3]; D3 B) 3 2; D4 D) 54.0 55.0; D5 A) 2 434.9; D6 B) 5962.05962.0.

  • D1 (slicing) and D2 (names and copies) feed straight into Lesson 1.1 today. If a third of the room misses D2, slow down at the views step of the 1.1 demo and connect it explicitly: "b = a gave two names for one list; an array slice does the same thing for part of an array."
  • D3 (dictionaries) and D5 (comprehensions) are the loop-and-count habits that NumPy and pandas replace. Misses here are not urgent: say so.
  • D4 (functions, defaults, return) matters every time a library call takes keyword arguments. Two or more misses: narrate the arguments of read_csv and genfromtxt out loud in the demos ("skip_header=1: a keyword argument, like rate=0.10").
  • D6 (text from files) predicts trouble with dtypes. Misses here: make a point of printing .dtype in every demo step.
  • Anyone with three or more wrong: not a problem to announce. Pair them with a strong neighbor today, and at the wrap-up hand them labs/module-01/l0_1-orientation/diagnostic_starter.py as extra homework: six small functions with a checker, one per skill (diagnostic_solution.py is your reference). The workbook's Start Here page names what to review for each question.
Watch-outs
  • Do not debug one machine in front of the room. Two minutes per machine, then pair them and move on. The trap table in Before the Session covers nearly everything you will see.
  • Mixed backgrounds. Some learners finished Intermediate Python last week; some learned Python at work years ago. The diagnostic is for them as much as for you.
  • "I already use pandas." Welcome them and give them a job: helper during the environment check, and the stretch tasks in each lab. Ask them to let Module 1 build the array model before reaching for DataFrame shortcuts.
  • Versions. The lessons print output from Python 3.12, NumPy 2.5, pandas 3.0. A learner on older versions will see different output (pandas 3 changed how text columns and copies behave). The check prints every version: compare there first.

Lesson Plans

0.1

Your Data Science Toolkit

55 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Install Python 3.12 or newer and create a virtual environment for the course on Windows, macOS or Linux
  • Install the course packages from a requirements.txt file and confirm they work
  • Run code both in a notebook and as a script, and say when each one suits the job
  • Download the course data and load a file from it with a relative path
  • Read a Python traceback from the bottom up and take a sensible next step when you are stuck
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the workshop model, the five things you repeat every time you sit down, notebook or script
20mLive demo: version check, where am I, first look at the orders, three errors on purpose, a four-line script
15mGuided lab: payment_methods_starter.py (how do Pinecrest customers pay?)
10mStart the lesson project: first_look.py, Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

Say it while you draw four nested boxes on the board: "Python is the building. A virtual environment is one workshop inside it with its own tool wall: the tools hanging there are for this project only. The packages are the tools. A notebook is the workbench where you try things, and the data folder is the lumber."

Then the routine, written on the board and left there all session: 1 open a terminal, 2 cd pinecrest-analysis, 3 activate (look for (.venv)), 4 start JupyterLab or VS Code from that folder, 5 check that the notebook's kernel is the .venv one. "Almost every problem in week one is one of these five being skipped."

One sentence for the data: "Every file belongs to Pinecrest Outfitters, a made-up outdoor-gear shop with a website and four stores. It is fictional, so you can dig into customer records freely, and it was built with real things to find."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

The environment check in the opening already proved that every machine works, so this demo is about using the toolkit, not installing it. Work in a new notebook called lesson_0_1 in your own pinecrest-analysis folder; learners type along in theirs. Steps 7 to 9 are errors you cause on purpose: read the last line out loud each time before you fix anything.

  1. Prove which Python is running (2m). Say: "First cell of any new project: ask the tools who they are. If these three lines print, the workshop is stocked." 
    import sys
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

print("Python", sys.version.split()[0])
print("NumPy ", np.__version__)
print("pandas", pd.__version__)
    Python 3.12.14
NumPy  2.5.4
pandas 3.0.6
    Last digits may differ in the room; the first two numbers should match. Anyone with pandas 2.x has the wrong kernel or an old environment: send them to the trap table.
  2. Where is Python working? (1m). Say: "A relative path starts from the folder Python is working in. Before I open a file I ask whether Python can see it." 
    from pathlib import Path

print(Path("data/orders.csv").exists())
    True
    If anyone gets False: print(Path.cwd()) shows where they really are. Close JupyterLab, cd into the project folder, start it again.
  3. Load the orders (2m). Say: "One line reads the file into a table. pandas calls it a DataFrame; Module 2 teaches it properly. Today we need three moves." Use .T so three rows fit the projector. 
    orders = pd.read_csv("data/orders.csv", parse_dates=["order_date"])
print(orders.shape)
print(orders.head(3).T)
    (20302, 11)
                                  0                    1                    2
order_id                     100001               100002               100003
customer_id                   12673                10034                12448
order_date      2024-01-01 00:00:00  2024-01-01 00:00:00  2024-01-01 00:00:00
channel                       store                store               online
store                     Flagstaff            Asheville               Online
status                    completed            completed            completed
payment_method                 cash                 card                 card
promo_code                      NaN                  NaN                  NaN
discount_pct                      0                    0                    0
shipping_cost                   0.0                  0.0                14.95
order_total                   434.9                278.9                 75.9
    Ask: "What is one row of this file?" (One order.) "How many?" (20,302.) Point at NaN in promo_code: no value, not zero.
  4. Pick one column and summarize it (2m). Say: "Square brackets with a column name give one column. describe() is the fastest first look at a number." 
    print(orders["order_total"].describe())
    count    20302.000000
mean       194.596663
std        178.760964
min          6.380000
25%         78.850000
50%        146.850000
75%        264.950000
max       4893.000000
Name: order_total, dtype: float64
    Ask before you explain: "The mean is about $195 but the 50% row is $147. What does that tell you?" (A few large orders pull the mean up.) "And the max?" Leave $4,893 as an open question: it is Exercise 3.
  5. Count the categories (2m). Say: "value_counts() counts how often each value appears. It is the first thing to run on any text column." 
    print(orders["status"].value_counts())
    status
completed    18762
returned      1143
cancelled      397
Name: count, dtype: int64
    Ask: "If I add up every order_total, is that Pinecrest's revenue?" (No: 1,143 returned and 397 cancelled orders are in there.)
  6. Filter the rows, then total (2m). Say: "The expression in the brackets is a filter: keep the rows where it is true. Read it as 'orders where status equals completed'." 
    completed = orders[orders["status"] == "completed"]

print(len(completed))
print(f"Completed revenue: ${completed['order_total'].sum():,.2f}")
    18762
Completed revenue: $3,624,306.27
    This is the pattern the lab repeats with a different column.
  7. Error 1: the wrong path (2m). Say: "Now I break it on purpose. Do not look at the top. Scroll to the last line." In the notebook the traceback is about 30 lines; the last one is all you need. 
    orders = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")
    FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'orders.csv'
    Read it aloud: "No such file: orders.csv." Then find the arrow at your own line. Say: "The lines in the middle are inside pandas. They are how it got there, not where the mistake is."
  8. Error 2: a column name that is almost right (2m). Say: "A KeyError from a table means there is no column with exactly this name." 
    orders["Order Date"]
    KeyError: 'Order Date'
    Do not guess the fix. Ask the table:
  9. Ask the table for its names. 
    print(orders.columns.tolist())
    ['order_id', 'customer_id', 'order_date', 'channel', 'store', 'status', 'payment_method', 'promo_code', 'discount_pct', 'shipping_cost', 'order_total']
    Say: "Copy the name from here. Lowercase, underscore."
  10. Error 3: a name that does not exist (1m). Say: "A typo, or a cell that has not been run since the kernel started. Python even offers a guess in the full traceback: Did you mean 'orders'?" 
    print(ordres.shape)
    NameError: name 'ordres' is not defined
    Now demonstrate the notebook trap: Kernel ▸ Restart Kernel, run only the describe() cell, and get the same NameError for orders. Fix: Run ▸ Run All Cells from the top.
  11. The same work as a script (3m). Say: "A notebook is where I work it out. A script is how I keep it." Create count_orders.py in the project folder with these lines, then run python count_orders.py in the terminal (check for (.venv) first). 
    """count_orders.py: how many orders, and how many were completed?"""
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.read_csv("data/orders.csv")
completed = orders[orders["status"] == "completed"]
print("Orders:", len(orders), "| completed:", len(completed))
    Orders: 20302 | completed: 18762
    Say: "It starts fresh every time and prints only what I print. That is why the lessons always use print(): the output is the same in both places."
  12. Ask the documentation (1m). Say: "Python can describe its own tools. In a notebook, pd.read_csv? opens the same help in a panel." 
    help(len)
    Help on built-in function len in module builtins:

len(obj, /)
    Return the number of items in a container.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • The kernel or the terminal is not the course environment. Symptom: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas', or a pandas version that starts with 2. Coach with a question, not a fix: "What does your prompt start with?" and, in a notebook, "Which kernel does the top-right corner name?" Then have them run import sys; print(sys.executable): the path should contain .venv.
  • Python is working in a different folder. Symptom: FileNotFoundError for a file they can see in the file browser, usually because JupyterLab was started from the home folder or the zip was extracted into pinecrest-data/data. Coach: "Ask Python where it is: print(Path.cwd()). Is there a data folder inside that folder?" Do not let them paste an absolute path: it works today and breaks the lesson code tomorrow.
  • Cells run out of order, or a name that is almost right. Symptom: NameError for a variable that is plainly on the screen, or KeyError: 'Status'. Coach: "Read me the last line." Then: "When did the cell that creates it last run?" (Restart and run all.) For a KeyError: "Print orders.columns and copy the name." Praise reading the error before asking for help; that habit is objective five.
Guided lab

File: learners open labs/module-01/l0_1-orientation/payment_methods_starter.py; your reference is labs/module-01/l0_1-orientation/payment_methods_solution.py. It practices the lesson's three moves (read a file, pick a column, count and filter) on a question the lesson does not ask: how do customers pay?

Run it first, as shipped (1m). Everyone runs the starter untouched and sees five TODO lines. That proves the lab can find the data. If a learner sees "The Pinecrest course data was not found", their labs folder is not next to a data folder: the message names both fixes.

TODO 1 to 2 together (5m), TODO 3 to 5 in pairs (8m). Circulate for orders["payment_method"] typed with a capital or a space, and for = where == is meant inside the filter.

Expected: shape (20302, 11); card 12,392, digital_wallet 4,794, cash 1,614, gift_card 1,502; digital wallet share 23.6%; 1,502 gift-card orders averaging $193.22; all 1,614 cash orders have channel store.

Debrief (1m): "Cash is never used online. Is that a finding or a check?" (A check: the data behaves the way the business works. When a check like this fails, you have found a data problem.)

Fast finishers: labs/module-01/l0_1-orientation/debug_traceback.py, a script with three bugs to fix one traceback at a time (a wrong file name, a wrong column name, a misspelled variable). Fixed, it prints 20302 orders, 1143 returned, largest returned order $1,168.75.

Start the lesson project

The lesson project is first_look.py: a summary of the orders file and a chart of completed revenue by month. In the room, do Steps 1 and 2 only (10 minutes), in a notebook.

Open the lesson page at "Project: First Look at Pinecrest" and read the brief aloud. Everyone types Step 1 (load, count, first and last date) and Step 2 (value_counts() on channel and status). Done in the room = Orders: 20302, first order 2024-01-01, last order 2025-12-31, online 12,854 and store 7,448.

Goes home: Step 3 (completed revenue $3,624,306.27), Step 4 (best month 2025-06, slowest 2024-02), Step 5 (the bar chart monthly_revenue.png with 24 bars) and Step 6 (assemble the script and run it from the terminal). Tell them the three numbers to expect so they can check themselves.

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold-call gently, or think-pair-share):

  1. You open a new terminal tomorrow and python first_look.py says there is no module named pandas. What did you skip? Answer: Activating the environment in that terminal. Nothing was uninstalled.
  2. Why does the lesson say python -m pip and not just pip? Answer: It guarantees the pip that belongs to the Python you are running, which is the environment's when it is active.
  3. A traceback is thirty lines long. Which line do you read first, and which do you look for second? Answer: The last line (error type and message), then the line that points into your own file.
  4. When would you choose a notebook, and when a script? Answer: A notebook to explore and look at each result; a script for finished work that must run the same way every time.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q1 B) This terminal will use the project's own Python and the packages installed for it; Q2 D) python -m pip install -r requirements.txt; Q3 1143; Q4 A) Print orders.columns and copy the exact column name from there; Q5 C) A NameError: the name orders is not defined; Q6 True False. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: Pair anyone whose check said NOT READY with a ready neighbor for the demo and the lab (one keyboard, two heads) and fix the machine at the break, not in front of the room. For learners who froze on the diagnostic, sit them where you can see their screen and give them the typing role in the pair. Keep the five-step routine on the board and point to it instead of fixing things for them.

Stretch: debug_traceback.py; then the lesson's Bonus Challenge (load daily_sales.csv and explain why the store totals are so much larger than the store rows in orders.csv: the answer is in data/README.md). Ask experienced learners to hold back on pandas tricks they already know: Module 2 gets there.

1.1

Arrays vs Lists

75 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Explain how a NumPy array stores numbers differently from a Python list, and why that makes it smaller and faster
  • Create arrays from lists, from scratch, and from a CSV file, and read their dtype, shape, ndim and size
  • Select elements, rows and columns with indexing and slicing in one and two dimensions
  • Predict whether an operation gives you a view or a copy, and make a copy when you need one
  • Measure memory and speed yourself and choose between a list and an array for a task
Timing in the room
10mFrame: two containers, two jobs; the parking lot and the starting grid; why pandas sits on arrays
30mLive demo: first array, four facts, * 2, one type only, memory, speed, a CSV column with nan, rows and columns, views and copies
20mGuided lab: transactions_week_starter.py, then what_if_copy_starter.py in pairs
15mStart the lesson project: the benchmark report, Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

Say: "A list is a public parking lot. Motorcycles, sedans and delivery trucks all park there, each in its own space, and the attendant keeps a clipboard saying which vehicle is where. An array is the starting grid of a race: every car the same class, bumper to bumper in numbered positions. Nobody needs a clipboard, and because the grid is uniform the whole field can move as one."

Turn the picture into the three rules you will repeat all session, and write them on the board: one type (the dtype), fixed size (arrays do not grow), whole-array operations (no loop). Add a fourth line under them for the second half: a slice is a window, not a photocopy.

Why it matters, in one breath: "pandas stores every column as an array. Matplotlib plots arrays. SciPy computes on arrays. Understand this one container and the rest of the course stops looking like magic spells."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

New notebook, lesson_1_1, same project folder. Ask for a prediction before every run: the lesson is built on small surprises (* 2, the silent text conversion, the nan mean, the view), and a surprise only teaches if the learner committed to a guess first. Steps 5 and 6 measure; the timing in Step 6 will differ on every machine and that is the point.

  1. A first array (2m). Say: "These are Boise's revenue figures for the first week of January 2024, Monday to Sunday. np.array takes a list and lines the values up on the grid." 
    import numpy as np

week_list = [5962.00, 6583.13, 3866.59, 7667.88, 9570.46, 12388.57, 9361.59]
week = np.array(week_list)

print(week)
print(type(week))
    [ 5962.    6583.13  3866.59  7667.88  9570.46 12388.57  9361.59]
<class 'numpy.ndarray'>
    Point at the screen: no commas. That is how you tell an array from a list at a glance.
  2. Four facts every array knows (2m). Say: "When something surprises you, print these. They answer most questions." 
    print(week.dtype, week.shape, week.ndim, week.size)
    float64 (7,) 1 7
    (7,) is a tuple with one entry: one dimension, seven long. Ask: "How many bytes is a float64?" (8.)
  3. The same operator, two meanings (2m). Ask first: "What is week_list * 2? What is week * 2?" Take two guesses for each, then run. 
    print(len(week_list * 2))
print(week * 2)
    14
[11924.   13166.26  7733.18 15335.76 19140.92 24777.14 18723.18]
    Say: "For a list, star means repeat: fourteen items. For an array, it is arithmetic on every element. No loop."
  4. One type only (2m). Ask: "What happens if one value is text?" 
    mixed = np.array([42, "tent", 3.5])
print(mixed)
print(mixed.dtype)
    ['42' 'tent' '3.5']
<U32
    Say: "No error. NumPy quietly turned all three into text, because text is the only type that can hold them all. One stray word in a column of numbers and the whole array is strings. When an array misbehaves, check .dtype first."
  5. Measure the memory (3m). Say: "Do not take my word for it that arrays are small. Measure." Type it slowly; the two list lines are the address book and the houses. 
    import sys

n = 1_000_000
numbers_list = list(range(n))
numbers = np.arange(n)

list_bytes = sys.getsizeof(numbers_list) + sum(sys.getsizeof(x) for x in numbers_list)
print(f"list : {list_bytes:>12,} bytes")
print(f"array: {numbers.nbytes:>12,} bytes")
print(f"ratio: {list_bytes / numbers.nbytes:.1f}x")
    list :   36,000,056 bytes
array:    8,000,000 bytes
ratio: 4.5x
    Say: "The list keeps an 8-byte address for every number, and every number is a full Python object of 28 bytes. The array stores the type once and then only values."
  6. Measure the speed (3m). Say: "Same job both ways: raise a million prices by 8%. Best of five runs." Your numbers will differ from this page and from each other; write three learners' speedups on the board. 
    import timeit

prices_list = [float(x) for x in range(n)]
prices = np.array(prices_list)

t_list = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: [p * 1.08 for p in prices_list], number=1, repeat=5))
t_array = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: prices * 1.08, number=1, repeat=5))
print(f"speedup: {t_list / t_array:.0f}x")
    speedup: 53x
    (The figure above is from the machine that built this kit. Anything from about 10x to 100x is normal.) Say: "The list version asks 'what are you?' a million times. The array version makes one call into compiled code that already knows." Name it: vectorization. Session 2 is all about it.
  7. Converting chops, it does not round (2m). Ask: "What is 2.9 as an integer? And minus 2.9?" 
    print(np.array([2.9, -2.9, 7.5]).astype(np.int64))
    [ 2 -2  7]
    Say: "The decimal part is dropped. If you want rounding, call .round() first."
  8. A real column, and a nan (3m). Say: "Column 5 of the daily sales file is revenue. One line loads it." Ask for a prediction of the mean before running: "somewhere around what?" 
    revenue = np.genfromtxt("data/daily_sales.csv", delimiter=",", skip_header=1, usecols=5)

print(revenue.shape, revenue.dtype)
print(revenue.mean())
    (2903,) float64
nan
    Let the nan sit for a second. Say: "Not a bug in your code. Six store-days have no revenue recorded, and any arithmetic that touches a missing value gives a missing value."
  9. Count the gaps, then skip them. 
    print(np.isnan(revenue).sum())
print(np.nanmean(revenue).round(2))
    6
7435.04
    Say: "An average store-day is about $7,435. Remember the symptom: a nan result means a missing value got into the calculation."
  10. Two dimensions: rows, comma, columns (4m). Say: "Units sold on the first three days of 2024. Rows are days; columns are Asheville, Bend, Boise, Flagstaff." Have the room say "rows, comma, columns" out loud for each line before you run it. 
    units = np.array([[110, 105, 148,  69],
                  [ 88,  84, 152,  82],
                  [103, 133,  90,  92]])

print(units.shape)
print(units[0, 2])       # row 0, column 2
print(units[1])          # all of row 1
print(units[:, 2])       # every row, column 2
print(units[0:2, 1:3])   # rows 0-1, columns 1-2
    (3, 4)
148
[ 88  84 152  82]
[148 152  90]
[[105 148]
 [ 84 152]]
    Ask: "How would you get Boise's column out of a list of lists?" (A loop or a comprehension.) "Here it is one expression."
  11. A slice is a window (4m). The most important two minutes of the lesson. Ask for a show of hands: "After I change window[0], has a changed?" Count the hands, then run. 
    a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
window = a[1:4]
window[0] = 999

print(a)
print(np.shares_memory(a, window))
    [ 10 999  30  40  50]
True
    Say: "A list slice is a photocopy. An array slice is a window cut into the wall of the same room: reach through and move the furniture, and it has moved for everyone. NumPy does this because copying a 2 GB array every time you slice it would be a disaster." Tie it to diagnostic D2.
  12. Ask for a copy when you need one (1m). 
    a = np.array([10, 20, 30, 40, 50])
safe = a[1:4].copy()
safe[0] = 999

print(a)
print(np.shares_memory(a, safe))
    [10 20 30 40 50]
False
    Rule for the board: "If you will change a slice and still need the original, copy first."
  13. One True or False, please (2m). Say: "One more error worth meeting on purpose. Read the last line." 
    if week > 6000:
    print("A good week")
    ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous. Use a.any() or a.all()
    Say: "week > 6000 is seven answers and if needs one. Say which question you are asking:"
  14. any or all. 
    print(week > 6000)
print((week > 6000).any(), (week > 6000).all())
    [False  True False  True  True  True  True]
True False
    Close the demo by pointing at the board's three rules and asking the room to name where each one showed up.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Expecting a slice to be a copy. Symptom: "my original numbers changed and I never touched them." There is no error message, which is what makes it hard. Coach: "Run np.shares_memory(original, piece). What does True mean?" Then: "Where should the .copy() go?" In the lab this is the whole of Lab B, so let pairs find it before you explain it again.
  • Rows and columns the wrong way round. Symptom: week2[1] when they want Bend's column (it gives Tuesday's row), or IndexError: index 5 is out of bounds for axis 1 with size 4. Coach: "Say it out loud: rows, comma, columns. Print .shape. Which number is the stores?" Have them point at the row and the column on the printed table with a finger before typing.
  • A silent type change. Symptom: 102.9 stored in an integer array comes back as 102; a column that prints with quotes and refuses .mean(); a result of nan. None of these raise an error. Coach: "What does .dtype say?" and for nan: "What does np.isnan(x).sum() say?" The habit to build is asking the array before asking the instructor.
Guided lab

Lab A (10m, everyone): labs/module-01/l1_1-arrays-vs-lists/transactions_week_starter.py; reference labs/module-01/l1_1-arrays-vs-lists/transactions_week_solution.py. A different column from the lesson's (transactions, column 3): describe the array, slice rows 28 to 55 (the second week of January 2024) and reshape to 7 days by 4 stores, then pull out a row, a column and one cell, and convert to int16.

Expected, Lab A: shape (2903,), float64, ndim 1, size 2903; 0 missing; Saturday's row [93. 59. 151. 71.]; Bend's column [49. 42. 39. 46. 66. 59. 73.]; Boise on Saturday 151, which is also the week's maximum; 224 bytes as float64 against 56 as int16; np.array_equal is True.

Circulate in Lab A for: transactions[28:55] (27 values: cannot reshape array of size 27 into shape (7,4), a perfect moment to say "the stop is left out"); week2[1] for Bend; reshape(4, 7), which runs without an error and scrambles the days (ask: "is row 0 one day or one store? Check against the first four values of the file").

Lab B (10m, pairs): labs/module-01/l1_1-arrays-vs-lists/what_if_copy_starter.py; reference labs/module-01/l1_1-arrays-vs-lists/what_if_copy_solution.py. A manager's what-if ("10 more units a day at Bend") that must not change the real week. One learner types, the other predicts each np.shares_memory answer before it runs; swap at Step 5.

Expected, Lab B: Bend's real total 868 printed three times and never changed; what-if total 938; a column slice shares memory (True), the .copy() does not (False); storing 97.6 in the int64 array gives 97, and 97.6 in the float64 version.

Circulate in Lab B for: what_if = week1 (a second name, not a copy: the real total becomes 938 and the last line gives it away); what_if = week1[:, :] (a view of everything: same result). Do not fix it for them. Ask: "Which printed line tells you the real data changed?"

Fast finishers: labs/module-01/l1_1-arrays-vs-lists/debug_silent_traps.py: three blocks that run without an error and print wrong answers (text in a numeric array, an int8 overflow, a view). Correct answers: average price 48.5, total stock 260, Monday still 148.

Start the lesson project

The lesson project is the benchmark report: the same analysis of two years of store data with lists and with arrays, written up from the learner's own measurements. In the room, do Steps 1 and 2 (15 minutes).

Step 1 together: load visitors (column 2) and revenue (column 5) with genfromtxt; both should print (2903,) float64. Ask why the visitor counts print as 201. with a dot (genfromtxt reads everything as float64 unless told otherwise).

Step 2 on their own: .tolist() twins and the memory comparison. Done in the room = list : 92,952 bytes, array: 23,224 bytes, ratio: 4.0x. Anyone who gets 23,280 for the list counted only the container: point at the sum(sys.getsizeof(x) ...) half.

Goes home: Step 3 (time spend per visitor both ways), Step 4 (6 missing days; mean spend per visitor $20.87 by two methods), Step 5 (week1 as a 7 by 4 view; Boise's column totals $55,400.22) and Step 6 (the printed report). They must keep this notebook: Lesson 1.2 picks up revenue and visitors again next session.

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold-call gently, or think-pair-share):

  1. An array of one million int64 values: how many bytes of data? Answer: 8,000,000. Eight bytes each, and nothing else per element.
  2. sales has shape (3, 4): days by stores. What is the shape of sales[:, 1], and what does it hold? Answer: (3,): one store's value on each of the three days.
  3. I slice first = revenue[:28] and set first[0] = 0. What happened to revenue? Answer: Its first value is now 0 too: a slice is a view. revenue[:28].copy() would have protected it.
  4. You are reading values one at a time and do not know how many are coming. List or array? Answer: Collect in a list, convert once with np.array(the_list), compute on the array.
  5. The mean of a column prints nan. What do you check, and what do you use instead? Answer: np.isnan(x).sum() to count the missing values, then np.nanmean(x).

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q7 A) [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3] [2 4 6]; Q8 6 [0 4 8]; Q9 B) [5 6 7 8]; Q10 D) float64; Q11 nan 20.0; Q12 C) Collecting sensor readings one at a time when you do not know how many there will be. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: Give anyone lost in two dimensions the paper version: print (or draw) the 7 by 4 table from Lab A, label the rows Mon to Sun and the columns with the four stores, and have them circle what week2[5], week2[:, 1] and week2[5, 2] select before typing anything. For views, the lesson's window example with five numbers is easier to hold in the head than the lab's table: rerun it with them and change one number at a time.

Stretch: debug_silent_traps.py, then the lesson's Exercise 4 second half (time np.cumsum against a running-total loop and explain why the speedup is smaller) or the Bonus Challenge (speedup by size from 10 to 1,000,000 elements: at which size does the array start to win, and why might a list win for ten?).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Put the three questions on the slide. Learners answer on a sticky note or in the workbook's Exit Ticket box and leave it on the way out. Sort the notes into "got it" and "not yet" before Session 2: the pile for question 2 decides how much of the Session 2 warm-up goes to views and copies.

  1. Your prompt does not start with (.venv). What will probably go wrong, and what do you type to fix it? Answer: Python will not find the course packages (ModuleNotFoundError). Activate the environment: .venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1 on Windows, source .venv/bin/activate on macOS and Linux, from the project folder.
  2. a = np.array([1, 2, 3]), then b = a[:2] and b[0] = 9. What is a now, and what one change would have protected it? Answer: [9 2 3]: a slice is a view of the same memory. b = a[:2].copy() makes an independent array.
  3. The mean of a revenue array prints nan. What does that tell you, and what do you use instead? Answer: At least one value is missing, and arithmetic with a missing value gives a missing value. np.nanmean(revenue) skips them (np.isnan(revenue).sum() counts them).
Homework (about 2 to 3 hours)
  • Finish both lesson projects. first_look.py (Steps 3 to 6: completed revenue $3,624,306.27, best month 2025-06, monthly_revenue.png with 24 bars, then run the script from a terminal) and the benchmark report (Steps 3 to 6: 6 missing days, mean spend per visitor $20.87, Boise's week-1 column $55,400.22, the printed report).
  • Lesson exercises. 0.1: Exercises 1 to 3 (store counts, promo codes, the $4,893 order); Exercise 4 is a stretch. 1.1: Exercises 1 to 3 (inspect and convert, the grid, shrink a column safely); Exercise 4 is a stretch.
  • Both Quick Quizzes on the lesson pages (five questions each; answers are in the Answer Key).
  • Journal: start journal.md in the project folder and write both entries. The 0.1 prompt asks for the exact commands they need each time they sit down: this is the most useful paragraph they will write all week.
  • Before the Next Lesson (from 1.1): keep the project notebook; load one more column (transactions, column 3) and print its shape, dtype, minimum and maximum; predict np.array([1, 2, 3]) + np.array([10, 20, 30]) before running it.
  • If the environment check said NOT READY: follow its numbered list, then run it again. Email you the last line.
  • Optional, for anyone who missed two or more diagnostic questions: labs/module-01/l0_1-orientation/diagnostic_starter.py.
Bring list for Session 2
  • A laptop on which check_environment.py ends with READY (same environment as today: nothing new to install).
  • The pinecrest-analysis folder with data/ unzipped and the labs/ folder inside it. Session 2's starters are in labs/module-02/.
  • The finished Lesson 1.1 project notebook: Lesson 1.2 picks up the revenue and visitors arrays.
  • The workbook and the journal. No servers, no accounts, no internet needed.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: the environment check result for every learner; the 1.1 views and copies steps and Lab B; at least Steps 7 to 9 (the three errors) of the 0.1 demo.
  • Cut first (saves 4m): 0.1 demo Steps 11 and 12 (the script and help). Say the one sentence, "a notebook to work it out, a script to keep it", and point at Step 6 of the lesson project.
  • Cut second (saves 10m): the 0.1 project start. Read the brief, give the three check numbers, send all six steps home.
  • Cut third (saves 3m): the speed measurement in the 1.1 demo. Keep the memory measurement; the project times things anyway.
  • If the opening runs to 40 minutes (a room with many NOT READY machines): take the 10 from the 0.1 project start, never from Lesson 1.1.
  • Never cut: the exit ticket. It takes four minutes and it is your only evidence of what landed.
Running short: what to add
  • Run debug_traceback.py as a whole-room race in pairs: first pair to print the three correct lines explains their routine.
  • Do Lesson 1.1's Exercise 2 (the 3 by 4 grid) on the board: learners call out the index expression for (a) to (d) before you type it.
  • Start Step 3 of the benchmark report together and compare speedups across the room: why are they different? (Different processors; the pattern holds everywhere.)
  • Give five quiet minutes for the first journal entry in the room. Learners who start it here are far more likely to keep the habit.
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 2: Vectorized Operations and Broadcasting

How to teach the session where learners stop writing loops over numbers. In the first half they describe what they want done to a whole array: arithmetic between parallel arrays, boolean masks that count, filter and combine, np.where, and summaries along an axis. In the second half they learn the two short rules that let NumPy combine a table with a row, a column or a single number, and the habit, checking shapes, that catches the mistakes NumPy will not report. By the end they have compared four stores of very different sizes fairly, in one line.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 1.2–1.3 Session 2 of 21

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (one mental model, the rules on the board) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (two kit labs per lesson: new questions on the same data) → start the lesson's own project. The lesson exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Predict before every run. Both lessons are about being able to say what will come out: how many values, what shape, error or no error. In 1.3, write the two shapes on the board, right-aligned, before every operation, and take the room's call.
  • Every code block below was run to produce the output printed under it, on the course data with NumPy 2.5. Type it live; read errors from the last line.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep numpy_vectorized_operations.html and numpy_broadcasting.html open for the diagrams (the mask as punched cardboard, the axis picture, the stamp, the right-aligned shape examples). Labs live in labs/module-02/.
  • Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs. Lesson codes (1.2, 1.3) match the course site.
The #1 risk of Session 2: wrong answers that raise no error

Until now a mistake produced a traceback. Today's important mistakes do not. Aggregating along the wrong axis gives numbers that answer a different question. A missing value drops silently out of both halves of a comparison. A row meeting a column builds a grid of sixteen plausible-looking numbers where four were wanted. A learner who has not built the habit of checking will leave thinking everything worked. So make checking the visible routine of the session: before a run, say the expected shape or count out loud; after it, print .shape or add the pieces up. Praise a learner who catches a wrong shape more than one who types fast. The second risk is pace: Lesson 1.2 is the longest in the module and it is easy to spend the whole first half on masks. Hold the 1.2 demo to 30 minutes; the lab is where masks stick.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Run the kit check: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-02 from the instructor-kit folder (8 files, all PASS).
  • ☐ Files to hand out: labs/module-02/ without the *_solution.py files (learners already have labs_paths.py from Session 1). Six files: four starters and the handouts debug_masks.py and debug_shapes.py.
  • ☐ Servers to start: none. No internet needed.
  • ☐ Projector machine: (.venv) active in pinecrest-analysis, JupyterLab or VS Code started from that folder, two empty notebooks lesson_1_2 and lesson_1_3, font 18 pt or more. Browser tabs: both lesson pages.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: space on the left for the three 1.2 rules; on the right, a hand-drawn 7 by 4 table (rows Mon to Sun, columns Asheville, Bend, Boise, Flagstaff) that you will point at all session.
  • ☐ Sort last session's exit tickets. If more than a third missed the view question, give warm-up question 3 an extra minute and rerun the five-number window example.
  • ☐ Optional paper: a half-sheet of shape pairs for the 1.3 support activity (six pairs, two right-aligned boxes each).
Known environment traps
SymptomCauseFix
A learner's revenue.mean() is a number, not nanThey are running an old notebook where revenue was already cleaned, or loaded a different columnRestart the kernel and run the load helper cell again. Column 5 is revenue.
RuntimeWarning: Mean of empty slice (or invalid value encountered in divide)NumPy stores nan and carries on instead of stoppingNot a crash. Ask what was empty or missing. The project's Step 5 prints this warning on purpose.
load(1) returns an array of nan instead of store namesThe default dtype=float cannot read text, and genfromtxt stores nan without complainingload(1, dtype=str); for dates, load(0, dtype="datetime64[D]").
FileNotFoundError: data/daily_sales.csv not foundThe notebook was started from another folder (Session 1's trap)print(Path.cwd()); start JupyterLab from pinecrest-analysis.
Different output from the page for string arrays or printingNumPy older than 2.x in a kernel that is not the course environmentRun check_environment.py again; choose the .venv kernel.

In the room. The lesson pages estimate 85 + 75 = 160 minutes for a solo learner, and after the warm-up, the break and the wrap-up the room has 150. The room does, for each lesson: the mental model, the live demo, two guided kit labs, and the first two steps of the lesson project.

Goes home (2 to 3 hours).
