Warm-up

0:00

Warm-up: Retrieval from Session 1

10 min
How to run it
  • Slide up, notes closed, three minutes of silent writing in the workbook's Warm-up box, then answers out loud: cold-call gently, one question per learner.
  • Question 3 (views) is the one to watch. If the room is shaky, rerun last session's five-number window example before moving on: Lesson 1.2 contrasts it with masks, which return copies.
  • Questions 2 and 5 lead straight into today: whole-array arithmetic, and rows, comma, columns.
Five questions (answers for you)
  1. Name the three rules that are true of every NumPy array and not of a Python list. Answer: One type for the whole array (the dtype), a fixed size, and operations that act on every element at once.
  2. What does [1, 2, 3] * 2 give? What does np.array([1, 2, 3]) * 2 give? Answer: [1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3] (a list repeats) and [2 4 6] (an array does arithmetic).
  3. b = a[1:4], then b[0] = 0. What happened to a, and how do you prevent it? Answer: a[1] is now 0, because a slice is a view. b = a[1:4].copy() makes an independent array.
  4. The mean of the revenue array printed nan. Why, and what did you use instead? Answer: Six values are missing and arithmetic with a missing value gives nan. np.nanmean(revenue) skips them.
  5. t has shape (7, 4): days by stores. What does t[:, 2] select, and what is its shape? Answer: Every row of column 2: one store's value on each of the seven days. Shape (7,).
Homework check
  • Show of hands: who ran first_look.py from a terminal? Who has a benchmark report? Write three learners' speedups on the board and ask why they differ.
  • Ask for the prediction from 1.1's "Before the Next Lesson": np.array([1, 2, 3]) + np.array([10, 20, 30]) (it is [11 22 33]: first with first, second with second). That is the first idea of Lesson 1.2.
  • Anyone whose environment check said NOT READY last time runs it again now. Still not ready: pair them, and fix it at the break.
  • Do not re-teach the homework. Two minutes for the single most common question, and the rest go on sticky notes for the break.

Lesson Plans

1.2

Vectorized Operations

75 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Combine arrays element by element with arithmetic and with universal functions such as np.sqrt, np.log10 and np.maximum
  • Build boolean masks with comparisons, combine them with &, | and ~, and use them to count, filter and assign
  • Choose values by condition with np.where and np.select
  • Summarize a two-dimensional array along rows or columns with axis=, and predict the shape of the result
  • Rewrite a Python loop over numbers as an array expression and check that both give the same answer
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the workbench and the assembly line; parallel arrays; the three board rules
30mLive demo: array-with-array arithmetic, ufuncs, masks (count, filter, combine), np.where and np.select, axis=, positions, the nan trap
25mGuided lab: staffing_load_starter.py, then eight_weeks_axis_starter.py
10mStart the lesson project: the store scorecard, Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

Say: "A Python loop is a craftsperson at a workbench: pick up one item, inspect it, work on it, put it down, pick up the next. Careful, flexible, slow. A vectorized operation is an assembly line. You set the machine up once, 'multiply by 1.08', and the whole batch flows through. The machine can be fast because every item on the belt is the same kind of thing: that is the one-dtype rule from last session."

Then the goal for today, in the lesson's words: "By the end, when someone asks 'which days beat $15,000, and what was the average on sale weekends?', your first thought is an array expression and not a for statement."

Write three lines on the board and leave them up: The sum of a mask counts; its mean is a fraction. · **&, |, ~, with parentheses around every comparison. · The axis you name is the axis that disappears.**

Live demo (you type, they follow)

New notebook, lesson_1_2. Learners who finished the Lesson 1.1 project already have revenue and visitors; everyone reloads them with the helper in Step 1 so the room is in the same place. Ask for a prediction before every run. Step 10 is two errors on purpose: read the last line of each out loud, because learners will meet both within ten minutes in the lab.

  1. A loading helper and four parallel arrays (3m). Say: "Every column of the daily sales file is useful today, so wrap last session's genfromtxt call in a small function." 
    import numpy as np

def load(col, dtype=float):
    """Read one column of daily_sales.csv into an array."""
    return np.genfromtxt("data/daily_sales.csv", delimiter=",",
                         skip_header=1, usecols=col, dtype=dtype)

visitors = load(2)
transactions = load(3)
units = load(4)
revenue = load(5)

print(visitors.shape, transactions.shape, revenue.shape)
print(visitors[:4], transactions[:4])
    (2903,) (2903,) (2903,)
[201. 200. 333. 144.] [51. 52. 68. 33.]
    Say: "Position 0 in every array is the same store-day: Asheville on January 1, 2024. Arrays that line up like this are parallel arrays. Everything today depends on that."
  2. Array with array: pair by position (2m). Ask: "What does dividing one array by another do?" Then: "Two retail measures in two lines, for all 2,903 store-days." 
    conversion = transactions / visitors     # share of visitors who bought something
basket = revenue / transactions          # dollars per purchase

print(conversion[:4].round(3))
print(basket[:4].round(2))
    [0.254 0.26  0.204 0.229]
[98.37 79.48 87.68 92.78]
    Read the first pair as a sentence: "51 of 201 visitors bought something, 25.4%, and the average purchase was $98.37."
  3. Universal functions (2m). Say: "Operators cover arithmetic. For everything else there are ufuncs: functions that apply themselves to every element." Boise's first week again, to keep the output small. 
    week = np.array([5962.00, 6583.13, 3866.59, 7667.88, 9570.46, 12388.57, 9361.59])

print(np.round(week, -2))                      # nearest hundred
print(np.abs(week - week.mean()).round(0))     # distance from the weekly average
    [ 6000.  6600.  3900.  7700.  9600. 12400.  9400.]
[1952. 1331. 4048.  246. 1656. 4474. 1447.]
    Read the last line slowly: week.mean() is one number; subtracting it touches every day; np.abs removes the signs. Three vectorized steps, no loop. Mention math.sqrt(week) fails with TypeError: only 0-dimensional arrays can be converted to Python scalars: use the np. function of the same name.
  4. A ufunc of two inputs (1m). Say: "Boise's daily target is $8,000. How far short was each day, counting days that beat it as zero?" 
    print(np.maximum(8000 - week, 0))
    [2038.   1416.87 4133.41  332.12    0.      0.      0.  ]
    np.maximum(x, y) compares pair by pair and returns an array. week.max() collapses one array to one number. Different jobs, similar names.
  5. A comparison makes a mask (2m). Ask: "What do you get when you compare an array with a number?" 
    busy = week > 9000
print(busy)
print(busy.dtype)
    [False False False False  True  True  True]
bool
    Say: "A sheet of cardboard with holes punched where the answer is True. It is useful three ways: count, filter, assign."
  6. Count and measure (3m). Point at board rule one. Ask for the two numbers before running. 
    print(busy.sum(), busy.mean().round(3))

big = revenue > 15000
print(big.sum(), "store-days above $15,000")
print(f"{big.mean():.1%} of all store-days")
    3 0.429
101 store-days above $15,000
3.5% of all store-days
    Say: "True counts as 1. The sum is how many; the mean is what fraction." This is the single most reused idea of the session.
  7. Filter: the mask goes in the brackets (2m). Say: "Lay the cardboard over the data and read what shows through the holes." 
    print(week[busy])
print(revenue[big][:5])
print(revenue[big].mean().round(2))
    [ 9570.46 12388.57  9361.59]
[16262.39 15993.3  19117.36 17442.78 22093.08]
17683.61
    Ask: "Is week[busy] a view or a copy?" (A copy: the chosen elements can be scattered anywhere, so NumPy gathers them into a new array. A slice was a view; a mask is not.)
  8. A mask from one column, used on another (3m). Say: "The mask and the array must have the same shape. They do not have to be the same array." 
    stores = load(1, dtype=str)
promo = load(7)

is_boise = stores == "Boise"
print(is_boise.sum(), "Boise rows")
print(np.nanmean(revenue[is_boise]).round(2))     # mean revenue on Boise days
print(visitors[is_boise].mean().round(1))         # mean visitors on Boise days
    727 Boise rows
10144.21
485.2
    Ask: "Why np.nanmean for revenue and plain .mean() for visitors?" (Six revenues are missing; no visitor counts are.)
  9. Combine masks (3m). Point at board rule two. Say: "Real questions have two parts: Boise AND a sale day." 
    is_promo = promo == 1

print((is_boise & is_promo).sum())     # Boise sale days
print((~is_promo).sum())               # ordinary days, all stores
print(np.nanmean(revenue[is_promo]).round(2))
print(np.nanmean(revenue[~is_promo]).round(2))
    24
2807
13950.46
7211.74
    There is a finding here: an average sale day brings in $13,950 against $7,212. Say: "Did the sale cause all of that? Sale weekends are also holiday weekends. Module 4 gives you tools for that question. Counting and comparing is where it starts."
  10. Two errors on purpose (3m). Say: "Now the two mistakes everyone makes this week. First, the word and." Read the last line. 
    both = (revenue > 10000) and (promo == 1)
    ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous. Use a.any() or a.all()
    Say: "and wants one true-or-false value and each side is 2,903 answers. Same message as if week > 6000 last session." Now drop the parentheses:
  11. The missing parentheses. 
    both = revenue > 10000 & promo == 1
    TypeError: ufunc 'bitwise_and' not supported for the input types, and the inputs could not be safely coerced to any supported types according to the casting rule ''safe''
    Say: "Cryptic, but learn the keyword: when an error says bitwise_and, look for missing parentheses. Python tried 10000 & promo first." Fix it on screen: (revenue > 10000) & (promo == 1).
  12. An if/else for every element (3m). Say: "A mask answers 'which ones?'. np.where answers 'this value where it holds, that value where it does not'. For three or more outcomes, np.select: first true condition wins, like if/elif." 
    print(np.where(week > 9000, "strong", "normal"))

conditions = [np.isnan(revenue), revenue >= 12000, revenue >= 6000]
tier = np.select(conditions, ["missing", "high", "medium"], default="low")
names, counts = np.unique(tier, return_counts=True)
print(names)
print(counts)
    ['normal' 'normal' 'normal' 'normal' 'strong' 'strong' 'strong']
['high' 'low' 'medium' 'missing']
[ 260 1120 1517    6]
    Ask: "Why is the isnan condition first?" (First match wins; a missing value fails both comparisons and would fall through to "low".) np.unique(..., return_counts=True) is the quickest tally in NumPy.
  13. Which way to collapse? (3m). Point at board rule three. Draw the 3 by 4 table on the board and physically squash it flat downward for axis=0. Ask for each shape before running. 
    units3 = np.array([[110, 105, 148,  69],
                   [ 88,  84, 152,  82],
                   [103, 133,  90,  92]])

print(units3.sum())           # everything
print(units3.sum(axis=0))     # collapse the rows: one total per store
print(units3.sum(axis=1))     # collapse the columns: one total per day
    1256
[301 322 390 243]
[432 406 418]
    Say: "Shape (3, 4). axis=0 squashes the 3 away and leaves 4 numbers. If you cannot remember which is which, print the shape of the result: it tells you what survived."
  14. Positions and parallel arrays (2m). Say: "argmax does not return the largest value. It returns WHERE it is. A position can look something up in a parallel array." 
    days = np.array(["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"])

print(week.argmax(), days[week.argmax()], week.max())
print(days[np.argsort(week)][::-1][:3])      # the top three days
    5 Sat 12388.57
['Sat' 'Fri' 'Sun']
    np.argsort gives the positions that would sort the array; reversed and cut to three, they index the day names.
  15. The quiet one: nan fails every comparison (2m). Ask: "Every store-day is either above zero or it is not. So these two counts add up to 2,903. Yes?" 
    print(revenue.size)
print((revenue > 0).sum() + (revenue <= 0).sum())
print((revenue == np.nan).sum(), np.isnan(revenue).sum())
    2903
2897
0 6
    Say: "Six rows are in neither group, and nothing equals nan, not even nan. 'The rest' is not the same as 'not the first group'. Test for missing values on purpose with np.isnan."
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • **and / or, or no parentheses.** Symptoms: ValueError: The truth value of an array with more than one element is ambiguous, or TypeError: ufunc 'bitwise_and' not supported for the input types. Coach: "Read me the last line. Which word in your line wants a single True or False?" For the second: "What does Python do first here, the & or the >? Put a pair of parentheses around each question." Do not type the fix for them; point at board rule two.
  • The wrong axis, with no error. Symptom: 56 numbers where 4 were expected (or the reverse), or a plausible answer to a different question. Coach: "How many answers should there be: one per store or one per day? Print .shape of what you got." Then: "Which axis has to disappear to leave that many?" In Lab B make every learner say the expected shape before running each aggregation.
  • **Forgetting that nan is in neither group.** Symptom: counts that do not add up to 2,903; a mean of nan after filtering revenue; (revenue == np.nan).sum() giving 0. Coach: "How many store-days are there? How many are in your two groups? Where are the other six?" The habit: any time revenue is involved, ask what happens to the six missing values, and use np.isnan and the nan-aware functions on purpose.
Guided lab

Lab A (13m, everyone): labs/module-02/l1_2-vectorized-operations/staffing_load_starter.py; reference labs/module-02/l1_2-vectorized-operations/staffing_load_solution.py. A question the lesson does not ask: how many visitors does each staff member look after, and when is a store stretched? One division, one mask, two combined masks, np.select, argmax with parallel arrays.

Expected, Lab A: visitors per staff member: mean 55.3, min 28.2, max 116.5; 814 stretched store-days (60 or more), 28.0%; stretched AND sale day 26; stretched OR sale day 884; labels quiet 361, steady 1,728, stretched 814; most stretched day 2025-02-26 at Bend (233 visitors, 2 staff).

Circulate in Lab A for: stretched and is_promo; per_staff >= 60 & promo == 1 (the bitwise_and error); np.select conditions in the wrong order (>= 45 first labels everything from 45 up as steady and the stretched count comes out 0: ask "which condition does a value of 80 meet first?"); per_staff.max() printed where the date and store are wanted (ask "that is the value: where is it?").

Debrief Lab A (2m): show the solution's last block: visitors per staff is 52 to 58 at all four stores. Ask why (staff are scheduled from expected demand, so a bigger store simply has more people on duty). That idea returns in Module 4 as a confound.

Lab B (10m, pairs): labs/module-02/l1_2-vectorized-operations/eight_weeks_axis_starter.py; reference labs/module-02/l1_2-vectorized-operations/eight_weeks_axis_solution.py. A 56-day by 4-store table of transactions; every answer is one aggregation with the right axis. The rule for pairs: the partner who is not typing says the expected shape out loud before each run.

Expected, Lab B: total 13,255; per store [2935. 3312. 4347. 2661.]; first five day totals [204. 196. 196. 234. 287.]; busiest day per store 2024-02-24, 2024-02-24, 2024-01-13, 2024-01-27; three busiest days 2024-02-24 (392), 2024-01-13 (374), 2024-01-20 (360); days won: Asheville 1, Bend 8, Boise 45, Flagstaff 2.

Circulate in Lab B for: table.argmax(axis=1) used for "each store's busiest day" (56 positions, all 0 to 3: ask "can a row number be 3 at most when there are 56 rows?"); day[top3] forgotten, so positions 54, 12, 19 are reported as if they were answers; np.argsort(day_total)[:3] (the three QUIETEST days).

Fast finishers: labs/module-02/l1_2-vectorized-operations/debug_masks.py: two bugs that raise errors (and; missing parentheses) and two that do not (the six nan rows in neither group; a "copy" that is a second name, so capping it changes the real data). Fixed answers: 15, 15, 6, and 101 capped values with revenue untouched.

Start the lesson project

The lesson project is the store scorecard: conversion, basket value and sale-weekend lift for all four stores, with no loop over the 2,903 rows. In the room, do Steps 1 and 2 (10 minutes).

Step 1 together: load seven arrays, including dates with dtype="datetime64[D]" and stores with dtype=str. Check: 2903 store-days, 6 with no revenue. Step 2 on their own: conversion, basket value and units per sale, one array expression each. Done in the room = 23.5%, $88.64, 2.11.

Goes home: Step 3 (one line per store; the only loop runs four times), Step 4 (sale-day lift 1.93x, weekend mean $10,073.19, the weekday trick with date subtraction), Step 5 (np.select labels: the four counts add up to 2,903) and Step 6 (the five biggest days, all Boise sale days, found with argsort). Tell them the headline before they leave so they know where it is going: conversion and basket value are nearly identical at every store; Boise's extra revenue is almost all foot traffic.

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold-call gently, or think-pair-share):

  1. big = revenue > 15000. What is big.sum()? What is revenue[big].sum()? Answer: The first counts the store-days above $15,000 (101). The second adds up their revenue.
  2. How do I write "Flagstaff or Bend" as a mask? Answer: (stores == "Flagstaff") | (stores == "Bend"), or np.isin(stores, ["Flagstaff", "Bend"]).
  3. A table has shape (56, 4). What is the shape of table.mean(axis=0), and what does it hold? Answer: (4,): one average per store. The 56 days were collapsed.
  4. picked = week[week > 9000], then picked[0] = 0. Did week change? Answer: No. Selecting with a mask builds a new array. Assigning through the mask, week[week > 9000] = 0, would change it.
  5. When is a Python loop still fine? Answer: Over a handful of groups (four stores, twelve months), or when each step truly depends on the previous result. Not over the rows.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q1 A) 3 0.75; Q2 C) ((stores == "Bend") & (visitors > 500)).sum(); Q3 [3 6] (3,); Q4 B) 2; Q5 ['retry' 'pass' 'pass']; Q6 D) Boise 3. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: For learners who write the loop in their head first: let them. Have them say the loop in words ("for each day, if it is above 9,000, count it") and then find each phrase in the lesson's loop-to-array table, which is printed in the workbook's key ideas. For the axis, use fingers on the printed table: "squash it this way: how many numbers are left?" Pair anyone who missed Session 1's views question with a partner for Lab A.

Stretch: debug_masks.py; then the lesson's Exercise 4 (retire the shipping loop with np.select and check it with np.allclose) or the Bonus Challenge (a 7 by 4 table of mean revenue by weekday and store built from 28 masks, which Lesson 1.3 then standardizes in one line).

1.3

Broadcasting

75 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • State the broadcasting rules and use them to predict the shape of a result, or that an operation will fail
  • Combine a 2-D table with a row of values and with a column of values
  • Reshape an array for broadcasting with np.newaxis, reshape and keepdims=True
  • Build a grid of every combination from two 1-D arrays
  • Recognize the broadcasting mistakes that raise no error, and catch them by checking shapes
Timing in the room
10mFrame: the rubber stamp; the two rules; shapes written right-aligned
25mLive demo: table and row, table and column (the error, then keepdims), np.broadcast_shapes, three ways to add an axis, a grid, z-scores, two silent mistakes
25mGuided lab: fair_visitors_starter.py, then target_grid_starter.py
15mStart the lesson project: the weekday index, Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

Say: "Picture a paper form with seven lines and a rubber stamp that prints one line of four numbers. To stamp the whole form you press it on line 1, then line 2, down the page. The stamp does not get longer. It is reused. Broadcasting is NumPy doing the stamping: when one array is missing a dimension, or has length 1 along it, NumPy reuses it along that dimension."

The two rules, written on the board as a procedure learners will do on paper all session: 1. Write the shapes one above the other, lined up on the RIGHT. A missing entry counts as 1. 2. Each pair must be equal, or one of them is 1. The result takes the larger of each pair. Any pair that fails: the "could not be broadcast together" error.

And the pattern to remember, under the rules: **per column (per store): a table and a row, it just works. Per row (per day): a table and a column, so keepdims=True.**

Live demo (you type, they follow)

New notebook, lesson_1_3. Before every operation in this demo, write the two shapes on the board one above the other, right-aligned, and have the room call the result or "error". That paper habit is the skill; the code is short. Steps 11 and 12 are mistakes that raise no error: let the wrong number sit on the screen and ask whether anyone would have caught it.

  1. The week as a table (2m). Say: "The first week of revenue again: 7 days by 4 stores, Asheville, Bend, Boise, Flagstaff. And the broadcast you already know: a table and one number." 
    import numpy as np

def load(col, dtype=float):
    """Read one column of daily_sales.csv into an array."""
    return np.genfromtxt("data/daily_sales.csv", delimiter=",",
                         skip_header=1, usecols=col, dtype=dtype)

revenue = load(5)
week1 = revenue[:28].reshape(7, 4)
print(week1.shape)
print((week1 / 1000).round(1)[:2])        # revenue in thousands: first two days
    (7, 4)
[[5.  4.1 6.  3.1]
 [3.6 3.7 6.6 3.6]]
  2. A table and a row (3m). Board: (7, 4) over (4,). Ask: "4 meets 4. 7 meets nothing. Result?" Then run. 
    store_mean = week1.mean(axis=0)
print(store_mean.round(2), store_mean.shape)

diff = week1 - store_mean
print(diff.shape)
print(diff.round(0)[-2:])                 # Saturday and Sunday
    [5099.55 5446.93 7914.32 4681.29] (4,)
(7, 4)
[[1703. 1636. 4474. 1576.]
 [-985. 1272. 1447. 1283.]]
    Say: "The row of four averages was stamped onto each of the seven rows. Every cell now reads 'dollars above or below this store's own average'."
  3. A ratio reads better across stores (2m). Say: "Boise is nearly twice Asheville's size, so raw dollars only say 'Boise is bigger'. Divide by each store's own average instead." 
    print((week1 / store_mean).round(2)[-3:])    # Friday, Saturday, Sunday
    [[1.44 0.87 1.21 1.2 ]
 [1.33 1.3  1.57 1.34]
 [0.81 1.23 1.18 1.27]]
    Read one cell: "Boise's Saturday at 1.57 is 57% above Boise's weekly average." Every store's best day now stands out on the same scale.
  4. A table and a column: the error (3m). Say: "Next question: what share of each day's total did each store take? Every row divided by its own total." Board: (7, 4) over (7,). Ask the room to apply the rules before you run it. 
    day_total = week1.sum(axis=1)
print(day_total.shape)
share = week1 / day_total
    (7,)
ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (7,4) (7,)
    Read the shapes in the message from the right: "4 meets 7. Not equal, neither is 1." Say: "A flat array can only be a row, and a row of seven does not fit a table four wide. We need seven numbers standing as a column."
  5. keepdims keeps the axis (3m). Say: "Ask the aggregation to keep the axis it collapsed." Board: (7, 4) over (7, 1). 
    day_total = week1.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)
print(day_total.shape)

share = week1 / day_total
print(share.round(3)[:2])
print(share.sum(axis=1))          # every row should add up to 1
    (7, 1)
[[0.276 0.227 0.328 0.168]
 [0.207 0.211 0.377 0.205]]
[1. 1. 1. 1. 1. 1. 1.]
    The last line is a check worth making every time: shares of a whole must add up to 1.
  6. Let NumPy apply the rules (2m). Say: "You can ask for the result shape without doing any arithmetic." Have the room predict each line. 
    print(np.broadcast_shapes((7, 4), (4,)))
print(np.broadcast_shapes((7, 4), (7, 1)))
print(np.broadcast_shapes((3, 1), (1, 5)))
    (7, 4)
(7, 4)
(3, 5)
    The last one is new: both arrays have a 1, in different places, and both are stretched. A column of 3 meets a row of 5: a 3 by 5 table.
  7. Three ways to make a column (2m). Say: "Most broadcasting work is one move: turn n flat values into a column of shape (n, 1). You will meet all three spellings in other people's code." 
    totals = week1.sum(axis=1)                 # flat: shape (7,)

col_a = totals[:, np.newaxis]              # index with a new axis
col_b = totals.reshape(-1, 1)              # -1 means "work this out for me"
col_c = week1.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)   # never flatten in the first place
print(totals.shape, col_a.shape, col_b.shape, col_c.shape)
    (7,) (7, 1) (7, 1) (7, 1)
    Advice to give: if the small array comes from an aggregation of the big one, use keepdims=True. It is right for every shape.
  8. Column meets row: a grid (3m). Say: "Four tent prices, three possible discounts. Every combination, with no loop inside a loop." Board: (4, 1) over (3,). 
    prices = np.array([299.95, 217.95, 449.00, 129.50])     # four products
discounts = np.array([0.10, 0.15, 0.20])                # three scenarios

sale_price = prices[:, np.newaxis] * (1 - discounts)
print(sale_price.shape)
print(sale_price.round(2))
    (4, 3)
[[269.96 254.96 239.96]
 [196.16 185.26 174.36]
 [404.1  381.65 359.2 ]
 [116.55 110.08 103.6 ]]
    Rows are products, columns are discount levels. Ask: "What would prices * (1 - discounts) do, without the new axis?" ((4,) with (3,): an error.)
  9. Standardize every column in one line (2m). Say: "Subtract each column's mean, divide by its standard deviation: a z-score. Two broadcasts in one expression, both a table and a row." 
    z = (week1 - week1.mean(axis=0)) / week1.std(axis=0)
print(z.round(2)[-2:])
print(z.std(axis=0))
    [[ 1.29  1.35  1.73  1.36]
 [-0.75  1.05  0.56  1.1 ]]
[1. 1. 1. 1.]
    Say: "Boise's Saturday is 1.73 standard deviations above Boise's own average. You can now compare stores of different sizes directly. This one line comes back in Module 4 and in Lesson 2.9."
  10. The accidental grid (3m). Say: "Four actual values, four predictions, and I want the four errors. One array arrived as a column." Run it and say nothing for a moment. 
    actual = np.array([100.0, 200.0, 300.0, 400.0])
predicted = np.array([[110.0], [190.0], [330.0], [380.0]])    # shape (4, 1)

errors = actual - predicted
print(errors.shape)
print(np.abs(errors).mean())      # the average size of an error
    (4, 4)
126.25
    Ask: "Is 126.25 right?" Board: (4,) over (4, 1): a row meets a column, so NumPy built all sixteen combinations. No error, and a plausible number that means nothing. Fix:
  11. Four in, four out. 
    errors = actual - predicted.ravel()
print(errors.shape, errors, np.abs(errors).mean())
    (4,) [-10.  10. -30.  20.] 17.5
    Say: "The habit that catches it: four values in should mean four values out. Print the shape."
  12. The square table that hides a wrong axis (2m). Say: "With seven rows, forgetting keepdims gave an error. With four rows and four columns it does not." 
    square = week1[:4]                               # 4 days x 4 stores
wrong = square - square.mean(axis=1)             # flat array of 4 day-means
right = square - square.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)

print(np.abs(wrong.sum(axis=1)).round(2))        # should be zeros if the rows were centered
print(np.abs(right.sum(axis=1)).round(2))
    [ 829.24 1563.14  620.76 3013.13]
[0. 0. 0. 0.]
    Say: "The four day-means happened to fit as a row, so day 1's mean came off column 1, day 2's off column 2. Wrong answer, no complaint. Use keepdims=True whenever you aggregate along axis=1 and combine with the table: then the code is right for every shape."
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • A flat array where a column was needed. Symptom: ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (224,4) (224,). This is the friendly one. Coach: "The message gives you both shapes. Write them one above the other, right-aligned. Which pair fails?" Then: "What shape would work? Which keyword keeps that axis?" Resist saying keepdims first.
  • The accidental grid. Symptom: no error; a result with far more values than expected, or a summary number that is wildly off (an average error of 1,753 when every forecast was within about 250). Coach: "How many answers should there be? Print .shape." Then the board procedure on (4,) and (4, 1). Lab B Step 4 is built to produce this; let pairs be puzzled for a minute before you step in.
  • The square table that hides a wrong axis. Symptom: no error and a right-shaped result that is simply wrong, only when rows and columns happen to be equal in number. Coach: "Check it: if each row was centered on its own mean, what should each row add up to?" The durable fix is a habit, not a patch: keepdims=True on every axis=1 aggregation that is combined with its table, and a check line such as share.sum(axis=1).
Guided lab

Lab A (13m, everyone): labs/module-02/l1_3-broadcasting/fair_visitors_starter.py; reference labs/module-02/l1_3-broadcasting/fair_visitors_solution.py. Visitors (not the project's revenue) for 224 days by 4 stores. A table and a row to compare each store with its own normal; a table and a column for each store's share of the day. Learners write the two shapes and a prediction in the starter's comments before each operation.

Expected, Lab A: store averages [281.4 323.4 440.9 281.6]; ratio shape (224, 4); busiest day at 2.51, 2.45, 2.30 and 2.40 times normal, all four on 2024-05-25; rows of the share table add up to 1; average share [0.213 0.244 0.332 0.211]; Boise's largest share 0.406 on 2024-04-20 and smallest 0.243 on 2024-02-10.

Circulate in Lab A for: skipping the written prediction (insist: it is the skill); table.mean(axis=1) for the store averages (224 numbers: ask how many stores there are); the keepdims error in Step 4, which the starter asks them to cause on purpose and read from the right.

Debrief Lab A (2m): "All four stores had their busiest day, relative to normal, on the same date. What is special about Saturday May 25, 2024?" (The Memorial Day sale weekend. The project finds the same weekend with z-scores on revenue.)

Lab B (10m, pairs): labs/module-02/l1_3-broadcasting/target_grid_starter.py; reference labs/module-02/l1_3-broadcasting/target_grid_solution.py. Four shape predictions checked with np.broadcast_shapes, a 4 by 3 grid of revenue targets (stores by growth scenarios), a mask on the grid, then a forecast check that silently builds a 4 by 4 grid.

Expected, Lab B: (4,) with (3,) fails; (4, 1) with (3,) gives (4, 3); (224, 4) with (4,) gives (224, 4); (4,) with (4, 1) gives (4, 4). Targets: Asheville 5875, 5989, 6274; Bend 7208, 7348, 7698; Boise 10449, 10651, 11159; Flagstaff 7096, 7234, 7579. Five of twelve above $7,500; per store [0 1 3 1]. Step 4 as shipped: shape (4, 4), average size 1753.02. Fixed: errors [-196.17 197.87 -255.79 189.75], average size 209.9.

Circulate in Lab B for: current * (1 + growth) with no new axis (the (4,) (3,) error: perfect, ask them to draw it); above.sum(axis=0) for "per store" (three numbers, one per scenario); pairs who "fix" Step 4 by taking errors[0] or the diagonal instead of fixing the shape.

Fast finishers: labs/module-02/l1_3-broadcasting/debug_shapes.py: one loud bug and two silent ones (a flat array where a column was needed; a (7,) minus (7, 1) grid of 49 "gaps"; the square-table trap). Fixed answers: seven zeros; 7 gaps with a largest gap of 6131.55; four zeros.

Start the lesson project

The lesson project is the weekday index: how much is a Saturday worth at each store, on a scale where 1.00 means "an average day for this store", plus the days that were unusual for their own store. In the room, do Steps 1 and 2 (15 minutes).

Step 1 together, slowly, because the reshape only works when no rows are missing: the first 896 rows are exactly 224 days of 4 stores (January 1 to August 11, 2024; Bend's export fails the next day). Check the store order by printing three rows of the reshaped names. Done = table.shape is (224, 4) and missing values per store are [1 1 0 1].

Step 2 on their own: store_mean = np.nanmean(table, axis=0) and ratio = table / store_mean. Done in the room = store means [5697.45 6650.89 9108.3 5895.63] and a ratio table of shape (224, 4). Ask: "Why does this broadcast as it stands?" (A table and a row.)

Goes home: Step 3 (reshape to (32, 7, 4) and average over the weeks: Saturday is about 1.5 at every store), Step 4 (the line chart: four lines that nearly overlap), Step 5 (z-scores above 3: 13 store-days, eight of them on the Memorial Day sale weekend) and Step 6 (shares with keepdims=True: Boise takes about a third).

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold-call gently, or think-pair-share):

  1. Shapes (5, 3) and (5,). Does it broadcast? Answer: No. From the right, 3 meets 5: not equal, neither is 1. The five values need to be a column, (5, 1).
  2. I want each store's column minus that store's mean. Do I need keepdims? Answer: No. Per-column values are a row of shape (4,), which lines up with the table's last axis as it stands.
  3. What does a column of shape (3, 1) times a row of shape (5,) give? Answer: A (3, 5) table of every combination.
  4. Name the three ways to turn a flat array of n values into a column. Answer: arr[:, np.newaxis], arr.reshape(-1, 1), or keepdims=True on the aggregation that made it.
  5. Does broadcasting copy the small array seven times before subtracting? Answer: No. The small array is reused from the same memory. Only the result is full size.

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (learners do them at the end of the block or at home).

Answers: Q7 B) An array of shape (6, 3); Q8 C) t - t.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True); Q9 (2, 3) 60; Q10 D) (8, 5) and (8,); Q11 (4, 3); Q12 A) An array of shape (12, 12): every sales value minus every plan value, with no error. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: Hand out a half-sheet with six pairs of shapes and two empty right-aligned boxes for each; learners fill in the result or "error" on paper before touching a keyboard (the lesson's Exercise 2 pairs work well). For anyone who is lost in axis=, stay with the 7 by 4 week and the two questions "per store or per day?" and "row or column?" until both come quickly; the 224-day table adds nothing new.

Stretch: debug_shapes.py; then the lesson's Exercise 4 (a 4 by 4 table of how alike the stores' weekly profiles are, built with two new axes and no loop) or the Bonus Challenge (the 32 by 7 by 4 array: each store's share of its own week, and the week when Saturday's share was highest at Boise).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, no notes, 4 minutes)

Three questions on the slide, answered on a sticky note or in the workbook's Exit Ticket box. Question 3 is the one to sort by: a learner who writes keepdims=True and can say why has the session.

  1. revenue and promo are parallel arrays. Write one line that counts the sale days (promo equal to 1) with revenue above 10,000. Answer: ((revenue > 10000) & (promo == 1)).sum(): &, parentheses around each comparison, and the sum of the mask counts.
  2. A table has shape (224, 4): days by stores. What is the shape of table.mean(axis=0), and what does each value mean? Answer: (4,): one mean per store. The axis you name (the 224 days) is the one that disappears.
  3. You want every row of that table divided by its own row total. Write the expression, and say what goes wrong if you leave out the keyword. Answer: table / table.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True). Without keepdims=True the totals have shape (224,); from the right, 4 meets 224 and NumPy raises "could not be broadcast together".

The store scorecard (Steps 3 to 6: four store rows, sale-day lift 1.93x, weekend mean $10,073.19, labels that add up to 2,903, the five biggest days) and the weekday index (Steps 3 to 6: Saturday near 1.5 at every store, the chart, 13 store-days with z above 3, Boise's share about a third).
  • Read in full the two 1.2 sections the room only touched: "Sorting and Picking by Position" and "From Loop to Array Expression".
  • Lesson exercises. 1.2: Exercises 1 to 3 (units per visitor, two conditions, along each axis); Exercise 4 (retire a loop) is a stretch. 1.3: Exercises 1 to 3 (row then column, predict the shape, scale every store from 0 to 1); Exercise 4 is a stretch.
  • Both Quick Quizzes on the lesson pages, and both journal entries.
  • Before the Next Lesson (from 1.3): keep the project notebook; predict what (8, 1, 3) and (5, 1) give, then check with np.broadcast_shapes; and write down a guess: if you picked 30 days at random from Boise's revenue and added them up, then did it again with a different 30, how different would the two totals be?
  • If Lab B of either lesson was not finished in class, finish it: the starter says what to expect.
Bring list for Session 3
  • The same working environment (READY). Nothing new to install: numpy and matplotlib are already there.
  • The pinecrest-analysis folder with data/ and labs/. Session 3's starters are in labs/module-03/.
  • The finished Lesson 1.3 project notebook: the 224-day by 4-store table is used again.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long: what to protect and what to cut first
  • Protect: 1.3 demo Steps 4, 5 and 10 to 12; Lab A of each lesson; the exit ticket.
  • Cut first (saves 3m): 1.2 demo Steps 3 and 4 (ufuncs). Point at the lesson's ufunc table instead.
  • Cut second (saves 10m): 1.2 Lab B (eight_weeks_axis). Do its fill-in from the workbook on the board in two minutes and assign the file as homework.
  • Cut third (saves 4m): 1.3 demo Steps 7 and 9 (three ways to add an axis; z-scores). The project teaches z-scores at home.
  • Cut fourth (saves 10m): the 1.2 project start. Read the brief, give the three check numbers (23.5%, $88.64, 2.11), send all six steps home.
  • Do not cut the 1.3 project's Step 1 walk-through: the "is this reshape safe?" check is hard to do alone the first time.
Running short: what to add
  • Run debug_masks.py or debug_shapes.py as a pairs race; the first pair explains each bug at the projector.
  • Do 1.3's Exercise 2 (predict the shape for five pairs) as a show of fingers: 1 for "works", 2 for "error", then call the shape.
  • Do 1.2's Exercise 3 (along each axis) on the board with the hand-drawn 7 by 4 table: learners call axis=0 or axis=1 and the shape before you type.
  • Start Step 3 of the weekday index together: the reshape to (32, 7, 4) and averaging over the weeks is the first three-dimensional array of the course, and it is easier with a picture.
Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 3: Randomness and Linear Algebra

How to teach the session that closes the NumPy module. In the first half learners make their own numbers: random draws they can reproduce exactly, fair samples and shuffles of real rows, and small simulations that answer "what could happen?", with the discipline of checking a model against reality. In the second half they meet the working parts of linear algebra with no proofs: the dot product as a receipt, the @ operator, solving for unknowns, and least squares, which is linear regression. They leave having fitted a model to real store data with a matrix they built themselves, and having questioned what its coefficients mean.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 1.4–1.5 Session 3 of 21

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm for both lessons: frame (one mental model) → live demo (you type, they type along) → guided lab (two kit labs per lesson: new questions on the course data) → start the lesson's own project. The lesson exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Two different kinds of checking today. In 1.4 the check is "does my simulation agree with the real data?". In 1.5 it is last session's shape check, plus "put the answer back in" (np.allclose(A @ x, b)) and "what else could explain this coefficient?".
  • Every code block below was run to produce the output printed under it. The 1.4 outputs depend on drawing in the order shown from a fresh generator: type the steps in order, each cell once.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep numpy_random_generation.html and numpy_linear_algebra.html open for the figures: the three distribution histograms, the estimate settling as simulations accumulate, the receipt, the shape rule, and the scatter plot with its least-squares line. Labs live in labs/module-03/.
  • This session ends Module 1. The wrap-up names what carries over to pandas (everything) and hands over to Session 4. Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs.
The #1 risk of Session 3: a confident number that nobody questions

Both lessons produce impressive output very easily: a probability to three decimals from one line of simulation, a regression coefficient from one call to lstsq. The danger is that learners leave trusting whatever comes out. Each lesson carries its own antidote, and both are the parts most easily cut when time is short, so protect them. In 1.4 it is the second gift-bag model (the answer moves from about 4% to about 28% when one assumption changes) and Lab B's reality check. In 1.5 it is reading a slope as "goes with" and quoting a forecast with its typical miss; the staffing trap (Exercise 4) is the homework that makes it stick. The second risk is the title of 1.5. "Linear algebra" frightens people who had a bad time with it in school. Say early and plainly that there are no proofs, that a vector is a 1-D array and a matrix a 2-D array, and keep the receipt on the board.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Run the kit check: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-03 from the instructor-kit folder (8 files, all PASS).
  • ☐ Files to hand out: labs/module-03/ without the *_solution.py files: four starters and the handouts debug_random.py and debug_linalg.py.
  • ☐ Servers to start: none. No internet needed.
  • ☐ Projector machine: (.venv) active in pinecrest-analysis, two empty notebooks lesson_1_4 and lesson_1_5, font 18 pt or more. Browser tabs: both lesson pages, scrolled to the distribution histograms (1.4) and the Boise scatter plot (1.5).
  • ☐ Rehearse the 1.4 demo once from a restarted kernel, in order, so the numbers on your screen match this guide. One accidental rerun of a cell changes everything after it.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: a blank column headed "Two random 30-day totals: how different?" for the homework guesses. Space for model → repeat → count. For the second half: the receipt's four sides and the shape rule.
  • ☐ Sort last session's exit tickets. If many missed keepdims, give warm-up question 5 an extra minute: 1.5 leans on shapes from its first matrix product.
Known environment traps
SymptomCauseFix
A learner's random numbers do not match yours or the lesson pageA cell was run twice or out of order; or a different seed; or draws made in a different orderRestart the kernel and run from the top. If it still differs from the lesson page after the dice in Step 2, that is expected: the lesson draws more in between.
AttributeError: module 'numpy.random' has no attribute 'default_rng'A very old NumPy in a kernel that is not the course environmentRun check_environment.py; select the .venv kernel.
A chart window does not appear, or plt.show() prints nothing, in a scriptA script run in a terminal without a display; or the figure was closedWork in a notebook for the project's charts, or save with fig.savefig("months.png"). Charts are taught in Module 3; today they are typed as given.
LinAlgError: Singular matrix from np.linalg.solveTwo rows (or columns) of the matrix carry the same informationPrint the matrix. One equation repeats another: a different slip, or lstsq, is needed.
lstsq returns [nan nan]A missing value in the dataOne mask, & ~np.isnan(revenue), applied to every array before building the matrix.
FutureWarning about rcond from np.linalg.lstsqNumPy older than 2.0Harmless; rcond=None silences it. Check the environment: the course uses NumPy 2.5.
