The lesson pages estimate 75 + 85 = 160 minutes for a solo learner, and the room has 150 after the warm-up, break and wrap-up, of which 45 go to the kit labs. So the room runs each lesson's frame, a compressed demo of its main thread, the guided lab and the first step of each lesson project. Done in the room: the mental models, saving and verifying a figure, the tiny-text demonstration, presets and the closing loop, mean against median on the order totals, a variance by hand, ddof, the IQR, both pixel_budget and orders_per_buyer labs. Goes home: the rest of both projects (Chart Pack Steps 2 to 4, Typical Order Memo Steps 2 to 5), the unfinished lab steps, the lessons' exercises, the Quick Quizzes, both journals, and the reading-only parts: the raster zoom figure, rasterized=True for heavy scatter plots, the dark-style chart, PdfPages, the n - 1 simulation and the FAQs.

Five retrieval questions (no notes, pairs, 60 seconds each)
  1. fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2): what kind of object is axs, and what loop visits every panel whatever the grid shape? Answer: A 2-D NumPy array of Axes. for ax, group in zip(axs.flat, groups): works for every grid shape.
  2. What does sharey=True buy you in a grid of panels, and what does it cost? Answer: Heights become comparable across panels. The cost: small series are flattened, so shape is harder to see. Choose on purpose and tell the reader.
  3. Why is a twin-axis chart with two different measures risky, and what should you draw instead? Answer: The two scales are arbitrary, so the chart can be made to say almost anything. Use stacked panels with a shared x axis, or plot a ratio.
  4. What should a finished chart's title say? And the subtitle? Answer: The title states the finding. The subtitle says what is plotted, the units and the period.
  5. You have a dictionary of style settings. How do you apply it to one block of plotting code without changing the rest of the session? Answer: with plt.rc_context(style_dict): around the block.

Lesson Plans

3.4

Saving Figures

65 min
Timing
10mFrame: the last step is part of the work; the sheet of paper and the scanner
25mLive demo: 10 short steps, learners type along in a new notebook
20mGuided lab: pixel_budget, then the start of category_price_pack
10mStart the lesson project: the Pinecrest Chart Pack, Step 1
Objectives (the lesson's own)
  • Save a figure with fig.savefig() and predict its size in pixels from figsize and dpi
  • Choose between raster formats (PNG) and vector formats (SVG, PDF) for a given destination
  • Explain why text looks tiny or huge in a saved chart, and fix it with the figure size
  • Control the saved area and background with bbox_inches, facecolor and transparent
  • Write one function that applies a house style and saves for web, slides or print, then use it in a loop that closes each figure
Mental model to say

Say: "A Matplotlib Figure is a sheet of paper with a size in inches. Everything on it, including the text, is laid out on that sheet. Saving to an image is like scanning the sheet: the scanner's resolution, in dots per inch, decides how many pixels you get. A bigger sheet and a finer scan both give more pixels, but they are not the same thing. A finer scan makes everything sharper. A bigger sheet makes the text smaller relative to the page."

Hold up a sheet of paper with one word written on it, then a sheet twice the size with the same word at the same handwriting size. "Same pen. Which page looks empty?" Write on the board and leave it up all session: pixels = inches x dpi and under it figsize sets how big the text looks; dpi sets how many pixels you get. The lesson's decision chart (printed or resized: PDF or SVG; a slide: PNG at slide size; web or email: PNG at about 110 dpi) is worth showing from the lesson page once.

Live demo (you type, they follow)

New notebook session10_saving.ipynb in the course project folder (so that data/ is next to it). Everything is saved into a charts folder that the code creates. Do not call plt.show() in the demo: in a notebook the figure appears under the cell, and the habit to build today is judge the saved file, not the notebook preview. Keep a file explorer or image viewer open on the charts folder.

  1. Set the stage (3m). This first cell is the lesson's own setup: the one cell today that learners may copy from the lesson page instead of typing. Say: "Nothing new here. It is the monthly table from Lesson 3.1 and a chart function in the style of Lesson 3.3. Today is about what happens after the chart is drawn." 
    from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from matplotlib.ticker import FuncFormatter

daily = pd.read_csv("data/daily_sales.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
daily["month"] = daily["date"].dt.to_period("M").dt.to_timestamp()
monthly = daily.pivot_table(index="month", columns="store",
                            values="revenue", aggfunc="sum")
stores = list(monthly.columns)

def thousands(x, pos):
    return f"${x / 1000:,.0f}K"

def revenue_chart(store, figsize=(8, 4)):
    """Draw one store's monthly revenue. Returns the figure and its Axes."""
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize, layout="constrained")
    ax.plot(monthly.index, monthly[store], color="#667eea",
            marker="o", markersize=3)
    ax.set_title(f"{store}: monthly in-store revenue",
                 loc="left", fontweight="bold")
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(thousands))
    ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    return fig, ax

fig, ax = revenue_chart("Boise")
print(monthly.shape, stores)
    (24, 4) ['Asheville', 'Bend', 'Boise', 'Flagstaff']
    24 months by 4 stores. In a notebook the Boise chart appears under the cell.
  2. Save it, then prove it (3m). Say: "Saving is one method call on the figure. Then we do not trust, we check: read the file back." Ask before running the last line: "8 by 4 inches. How many pixels?" 
    out = Path("charts")
out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

fig.savefig(out / "boise.png")

saved = out / "boise.png"
print(saved.exists(), f"{saved.stat().st_size / 1024:.0f} KB")
print(plt.imread(saved).shape)
    True 35 KB
(400, 800, 4)
    Point at the shape: rows first (400 high), then columns (800 wide), then 4 channels (red, green, blue, alpha). The default dpi is 100. The size in KB can differ a little on other machines.
  3. One multiplication (3m). Write pixels = inches x dpi on the board. Have the room predict all three lines before you run. 
    for dpi in (72, 150, 300):
    path = out / f"boise_{dpi}dpi.png"
    fig.savefig(path, dpi=dpi)
    height, width, channels = plt.imread(path).shape
    kb = path.stat().st_size / 1024
    print(f"dpi={dpi:>3}: {width} x {height} pixels, {kb:>4.0f} KB")
    dpi= 72: 576 x 288 pixels,   24 KB
dpi=150: 1200 x 600 pixels,   57 KB
dpi=300: 2400 x 1200 pixels,  128 KB
    Say: "Same sheet of paper, scanned at three resolutions. The picture is identical. Only the number of pixels describing it changes."
  4. The tiny-text problem (4m). The most important two minutes of the lesson. Say: "I need 1,200 pixels wide. Twelve inches at 100, or six inches at 200. Same pixels. Same chart?" Take a show of hands, then run and open both files side by side in the file explorer or an image viewer. 
    big_canvas, _ = revenue_chart("Boise", figsize=(12, 6))
big_canvas.savefig(out / "canvas_12in.png", dpi=100)

small_canvas, _ = revenue_chart("Boise", figsize=(6, 3))
small_canvas.savefig(out / "canvas_6in.png", dpi=200)

for name in ("canvas_12in.png", "canvas_6in.png"):
    print(name, plt.imread(out / name).shape[:2])
plt.close(big_canvas)
plt.close(small_canvas)
    canvas_12in.png (600, 1200)
canvas_6in.png (600, 1200)
    Say: "Font sizes are in points, and a point is 1/72 of an inch: a physical length on the sheet. On the 6-inch sheet the same title is twice as prominent. figsize controls how big the text looks. dpi controls how many pixels you get." Leave the two files on screen for the break.
  5. Raster or vector (3m). Say: "A PNG is a grid of colored squares. An SVG or a PDF is a list of drawing instructions, sharp at any size." The format comes from the extension. 
    for extension in ("png", "svg", "pdf"):
    path = out / f"boise_formats.{extension}"
    fig.savefig(path)
    print(f"{path.name:<20} {path.stat().st_size / 1024:>5.1f} KB")
    boise_formats.png     35.0 KB
boise_formats.svg     31.6 KB
boise_formats.pdf     13.3 KB
    Open the PDF and zoom to 800%: still sharp, and the title can be selected as text. Then zoom the PNG. Rule of thumb for the board: PNG for screens and slides, PDF or SVG for print and anything that will be resized, never JPEG for charts.
  6. The tight bounding box changes the size (2m). Say: "You will see bbox_inches="tight" in every tutorial. Watch what it does to the size we asked for." 
    fig.savefig(out / "boise_default.png", dpi=100)
fig.savefig(out / "boise_tight.png", dpi=100, bbox_inches="tight")

for name in ("boise_default.png", "boise_tight.png"):
    rows, cols = plt.imread(out / name).shape[:2]
    print(f"{name:<20} {cols} x {rows}")
    boise_default.png    800 x 400
boise_tight.png      811 x 411
    Say: "It guarantees nothing is cut off and gives up the exact size. Our figures use layout="constrained", so everything already fits. When a slide needs exactly 1,920 by 1,080, leave it off."
  7. Backgrounds (2m). Say: "Transparent sounds perfect for slides. Look at the corner pixel." 
    fig.savefig(out / "boise_transparent.png", transparent=True)
corner = plt.imread(out / "boise_transparent.png")[0, 0]
print("top-left pixel (red, green, blue, alpha):", corner)
    top-left pixel (red, green, blue, alpha): [1. 1. 1. 0.]
    Alpha 0 means fully see-through. Say: "The background is gone. The title is still black. On a dark slide it disappears." The safe default is fig.savefig(path, facecolor="white"); for a dark slide, draw in a dark style (the lesson shows it; do not type it now).
  8. Put the decisions in one place (4m). Say: "I know the settings now. Typing them correctly every time is how mistakes creep in. One table, two small functions." Type the table slowly and say each pixel size out loud as you type the row. 
    PRESETS = {
    "web":   {"figsize": (9, 4.5),   "dpi": 110, "extension": "png"},
    "slide": {"figsize": (9.6, 5.4), "dpi": 200, "extension": "png"},
    "print": {"figsize": (6.5, 3.5), "dpi": 300, "extension": "pdf"},
}

def new_figure(kind="web"):
    """Create a figure sized for 'web', 'slide' or 'print'."""
    size = PRESETS[kind]["figsize"]
    return plt.subplots(figsize=size, layout="constrained")

def save_chart(fig, name, kind="web", folder="charts"):
    """Save fig as folder/name_kind.ext. Returns the path."""
    preset = PRESETS[kind]
    folder = Path(folder)
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    path = folder / f"{name}_{kind}.{preset['extension']}"
    fig.savefig(path, dpi=preset["dpi"], facecolor="white")
    return path

def draw_revenue(ax, store):
    ax.plot(monthly.index, monthly[store], color="#667eea",
            marker="o", markersize=3)
    ax.set_title(f"{store}: monthly in-store revenue",
                 loc="left", fontweight="bold")
    ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(thousands))
    ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)

for kind, preset in PRESETS.items():
    width, height = preset["figsize"]
    dpi = preset["dpi"]
    print(kind, round(width * dpi), "x", round(height * dpi))
    web 990 x 495
slide 1920 x 1080
print 1950 x 1050
    The figure is created at the right size before drawing, because the size decides how the text relates to the chart. (The lesson also wraps the loop in the pinecrest_style dictionary from Lesson 3.3; learners who have it should use it.)
  9. Many charts: create, draw, save, close (3m). Say: "pyplot keeps every figure alive until you close it. A notebook hides that. A loop does not." Run the loop, then ask what the last line will print. 
    plt.close("all")
for store in stores:
    chart, ax = new_figure("web")
    draw_revenue(ax, store)
    path = save_chart(chart, store.lower())
    plt.close(chart)
    rows, cols = plt.imread(path).shape[:2]
    print(path, f"{cols} x {rows}")

print("open figures:", len(plt.get_fignums()))
    charts/asheville_web.png 990 x 495
charts/bend_web.png 990 x 495
charts/boise_web.png 990 x 495
charts/flagstaff_web.png 990 x 495
open figures: 0
    Comment out plt.close(chart), run again and show open figures: 4. Say: "Four is harmless. Four hundred is a memory problem." Put the line back.
  10. Make the classic mistake on purpose (2m). Say: "Here is the bug that reaches the meeting." Type it exactly, with plt.savefig. 
    chart, ax = revenue_chart("Bend")     # the chart you care about
scratch = plt.figure()                # later, another figure is created
plt.savefig(out / "bend_oops.png")    # saves the *current* figure

image = plt.imread(out / "bend_oops.png")
print("every pixel is white:", bool((image[..., :3] == 1).all()))
plt.close("all")
    every pixel is white: True
    No error, and a blank file. Say: "plt.savefig() saves whatever pyplot thinks is current. You are holding the figure in a variable, so say which one: chart.savefig(...)."
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Raising dpi to fix small text. The slide's labels are tiny, so the learner saves again at dpi=600: a file many times larger with text exactly as small. Coach with the board rule: "Which knob changes how big the text is on the sheet?" Then have them halve the figsize and double the dpi, and compare plt.imread(path).shape before and after: same pixels, bigger text.
  • plt.savefig() instead of fig.savefig() (often after plt.show() in a script, or after another figure was created). No error, a blank or wrong file. Coach: "Which figure did you ask to be saved? Show me its name in that line." The check that catches it is the lesson's: bool((plt.imread(path)[..., :3] == 1).all()).
  • Reading imread().shape as (width, height), or expecting an exact size with bbox_inches="tight". Coach the first with "rows first, like a DataFrame: shape is (rows, columns)". For the second, ask them to print the shape with and without the argument (800 x 400 against 811 x 411 in the demo) and decide whether their destination needs an exact size.
Guided lab

First 12 minutes, everyone: labs/module-10/l3_4-saving-figures/pixel_budget_starter.py (reference: labs/module-10/l3_4-saving-figures/pixel_budget_solution.py). Before anyone types, have them write the Step 1 prediction in the comment: 7 x 3.5 inches at 100 dpi. Walk the room during TODO 2; the usual stall is realizing the big sheet needs dpi 100 and the small one dpi 200. Stop the room after TODO 3 and take three answers to "which is easier to read, and why?" Expected by the end: email: (700, 350), two (1400, 700) lines, 5 files, open figures: 0.

Last 8 minutes: labs/module-10/l3_4-saving-figures/category_price_pack_starter.py, TODO 1 and TODO 2 only (the two presets and the one-line save). TODO 3 to 4 finish at home; the manifest at the bottom tells them when they are done (7 files, web 960 x 480, slides 1920 x 1080, 0 open figures). Labs write into an output folder next to the lab file and never call plt.show(): learners open the saved files, which is the point.

Early finishers: labs/module-10/l3_4-saving-figures/debug_blank_slide.py, a script that runs without an error and gets three things wrong.

Start the lesson project

The lesson's project is The Pinecrest Chart Pack (about 30 minutes alone): one chart per store, saved for web and print, plus a four-page PDF, verified by a manifest. In the room do Step 1 only: learners continue in the demo notebook (the project reuses PRESETS, new_figure() and save_chart()), type the yearly pivot and growth, and print it. Everyone should see Asheville -5.0, Bend 3.8, Boise 9.3, Flagstaff 19.7 before the break. Read the completion checklist out loud so they know what "done" means at home: 9 files, every web PNG exactly 990 by 495, 4 pages, 0 open figures. Steps 2 to 4 are homework.

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold call, then pair-share):

  1. "I need an image 1,000 pixels wide. Give me two different figsize and dpi pairs. How will the two files differ?" Answer: For example 10 inches at 100 dpi and 5 inches at 200 dpi. Same pixels; in the 5-inch version the text and lines are twice as large relative to the chart.
  2. "The designer will resize my chart for the annual report. Which format, and why?" Answer: PDF or SVG: vector files are redrawn sharply at any size. A PNG only has the pixels it was saved with.
  3. "My loop saves 300 charts and the kernel dies. What is missing?" Answer: plt.close(fig) after each save. pyplot keeps every figure alive until it is closed.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (do two in the room if time allows; the rest is homework):

Answers: Q1 B) 1,080 wide by 600 high; Q2 (150, 200); Q3 D) In B the text, lines and markers are twice as large relative to the chart; Q4 A) Pass rasterized=True to the scatter layer and keep saving as PDF; Q5 C) Only the background became transparent; the text is still black, on a dark slide; Q6 1. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: give learners the PRESETS table on paper and have them fill in a fourth column, the pixel size, by hand before running anything. Pair anyone who was absent for Lesson 3.3 with a neighbor for the setup cell; they do not need pinecrest_style to follow today. If typing is slow, let them copy the save_chart() cell from the lesson page and spend the time on the loop.

Stretch: lesson Exercise 2 (add a "square" preset of 1,080 by 1,080 and choose the inches so the text is comfortable), or Exercise 4 (write PNG metadata and read it back with Pillow). Strong learners can start the bonus challenge: move the presets and both functions into charting.py and import them.

4.1

Descriptive Statistics I: Center and Spread

85 min
Timing
15mFrame: two questions about any column; the restaurant review; why this module exists
30mLive demo: 11 short steps on order totals, weather and five days of tent sales
25mGuided lab: orders_per_buyer, then Steps 1 to 3 of visitor_spread
15mStart the lesson project: the Typical Order Memo, Step 1
Objectives (the lesson's own)
  • Compute the mean, median and mode of a column with pandas and say what each one measures
  • Recognize when the mean misleads, and choose the median instead, using Pinecrest's skewed order totals
  • Compute range, variance, standard deviation and interquartile range (IQR), and explain each in the units of the data
  • Explain the difference between dividing by n and by n - 1, and predict which one NumPy and pandas use by default
  • Pair the right measure of center with the right measure of spread for a given column
Mental model to say

Say: "Nobody reads 1,000 reviews before choosing a restaurant. You look at the average rating, and then, if you are careful, at how much the reviews disagree. A 4.2 where everyone gave a 4 is a different restaurant from a 4.2 made of fives and ones. Two numbers, what is typical and how much it varies, are the least you need to describe anything honestly."

Name the two questions and write them as column headings on the board: Center: what is typical? (mean, median, mode) and Spread: how much does it vary? (range, variance, SD, IQR). Fill the columns in as the demo goes. Open Module 4 in one sentence: "Modules 1 to 3 gave you tables and charts. This module turns them into claims you can defend." Then the hook: "'Our average order is $195' is true. And most orders are nowhere near $195. By the break after next you will be able to say why."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

New notebook session10_center_spread.ipynb. The numbers in the demo are the lesson's own, so learners can find every step again on the lesson page tonight. Ask for a prediction before every cell that prints a comparison. Step 4 draws a histogram: save it with fig.savefig as practiced before the break.

  1. The mean is a balance point (3m). New notebook. Say: "The marketing lead wants the average order value for a slide. Easy: add them up, divide by how many." 
    import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.read_csv("data/orders.csv", parse_dates=["order_date"])
totals = orders["order_total"]

print(orders.shape)
print(totals.sum(), len(totals))
print(totals.sum() / len(totals))
print(totals.mean())
    (20302, 11)
3950701.45 20302
194.59666289035565
194.59666289035565
    Say: "About $3.95 million over 20,302 orders: $194.60. Picture every order as a weight on a ruler. The mean is where the ruler balances."
  2. One far-away weight (3m). Say: "Five ordinary orders. Then the same five plus one of Pinecrest's real bulk orders." Have learners predict the second mean. 
    five = np.array([42.50, 88.00, 150.00, 163.25, 271.00])
six = np.append(five, 4893.00)

print("five orders: mean", five.mean(), " median", np.median(five))
print("six orders : mean", six.mean(), " median", np.median(six))
    five orders: mean 142.95  median 150.0
six orders : mean 934.625  median 156.625
    Say: "One order moved the mean from about $143 to about $935, a number that describes none of the six. The median moved by $6.63. A statistic that barely reacts to extremes is called robust."
  3. The real column (3m). Ask first: "What share of orders is below the average order? Half?" Write the guesses on the board. 
    print("mean  :", round(totals.mean(), 2))
print("median:", totals.median())
below = totals < totals.mean()
print("share of orders below the mean:", round(below.mean(), 3))
    mean  : 194.6
median: 146.85
share of orders below the mean: 0.626
    Say: "63% of orders are smaller than the average order. Neither number is wrong; they answer different questions." Dwell on the last line: a comparison gives True/False, True counts as 1, so the mean of a boolean column is a proportion. They will use that all module.
  4. See the tail (3m). Say: "A picture explains the $50 gap faster than a formula." Type the histogram; in a notebook it appears under the cell. 
    from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4), layout="constrained")
ax.hist(totals[totals <= 1000], bins=50, color="#667eea", edgecolor="white")
ax.axvline(totals.median(), color="#15803d", linewidth=2.5,
           label=f"median ${totals.median():,.2f}")
ax.axvline(totals.mean(), color="#b91c1c", linewidth=2.5, linestyle="--",
           label=f"mean ${totals.mean():,.2f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Order total ($)")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of orders")
ax.legend()
Path("charts").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
fig.savefig("charts/order_totals.png", dpi=110)

print("orders above $1,000 (not drawn):", (totals > 1000).sum())
    orders above $1,000 (not drawn): 37
    Name the shape: right-skewed, the normal shape of anything about money. The tail has leverage on the balance point, so the mean sits to the right of the median. (This is also the Session's first half in action: the chart is saved for the web.)
  5. Check the tempting explanation (3m). Say: "Someone will say it is just the twelve bulk orders. Check before you believe it." 
    is_bulk = totals > 2000
print("bulk orders:", is_bulk.sum())
print("mean without them  :", round(totals[~is_bulk].mean(), 2))
print("median without them:", totals[~is_bulk].median())

big = totals > 500
print("orders above $500:", big.sum(), f"({big.mean():.1%} of all orders)")
    bulk orders: 12
mean without them  : 192.63
median without them: 146.85
orders above $500: 1131 (5.6% of all orders)
    Say: "Removing them moves the mean by about $2. The gap comes from the whole tail: 1,131 ordinary orders above $500, a tent and a sleeping bag." The honest conclusion for the board: mean for totals, median for a typical order, report both and say which is which.
  6. The mode (2m). Say: "The only center that works for categories." 
    print(orders["payment_method"].mode())
print(pd.Series([1, 1, 2, 2, 3]).mode().tolist())
top = totals.mode()[0]
print(top, "appears", (totals == top).sum(), "times out of", len(totals))
    0    card
Name: payment_method, dtype: str
[1, 2]
53.9 appears 114 times out of 20302
    Three points: .mode() returns a Series because ties happen (take [0] for one value); pandas 3 prints dtype: str (older versions say object); and the mode of a measured quantity is mostly an accident ($53.90 is mostly one popular $46.95 item plus $6.95 shipping).
  7. Same center, different spread (3m). Say: "Center is half the story. Two store cities, daily high temperature." 
    weather = pd.read_csv("data/store_weather.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
boise = weather.loc[weather["city"] == "Boise", "high_f"]
asheville = weather.loc[weather["city"] == "Asheville", "high_f"]

for name, city in [("Boise", boise), ("Asheville", asheville)]:
    print(f"{name:<10} mean {city.mean():5.1f}  median {city.median():5.1f}"
          f"  range {city.max() - city.min():3d}  SD {city.std():5.1f}")
    Boise      mean  62.4  median  63.0  range 102  SD  22.5
Asheville  mean  66.5  median  66.0  range  79  SD  15.5
    Say: "Four degrees apart on average. Nobody who has lived in both would call the climates alike. The range uses just two days, the two strangest ones. The SD uses all 731."
  8. A variance by hand (4m). Do this one on the board first, then in code. Five days of tent sales: 4, 7, 5, 10, 4. 
    tents = np.array([4, 7, 5, 10, 4])
deviations = tents - tents.mean()

print("mean              :", tents.mean())
print("deviations        :", deviations, " sum:", deviations.sum())
squared = deviations ** 2
print("squared deviations:", squared, " sum:", squared.sum())
print("divide by n       :", squared.sum() / 5)
print("divide by n - 1   :", squared.sum() / 4)
print("square root of 6.5:", round(np.sqrt(6.5), 2))
    mean              : 6.0
deviations        : [-2.  1. -1.  4. -2.]  sum: 0.0
squared deviations: [ 4.  1.  1. 16.  4.]  sum: 26.0
divide by n       : 5.2
divide by n - 1   : 6.5
square root of 6.5: 2.55
    Say: "Plain deviations cancel to zero: the balance point again. Squaring makes them positive and counts big misses more. The variance is in tents squared, so take the square root to get back to tents: the standard deviation. Six tents a day, give or take about 2.5."
  9. Two libraries, two answers (3m). Ask the room to predict which of the three lines will match. 
    print("NumPy  np.std(tents)          :", round(np.std(tents), 4))
print("pandas pd.Series(tents).std() :", round(pd.Series(tents).std(), 4))
print("NumPy  np.std(tents, ddof=1)  :", round(np.std(tents, ddof=1), 4))
    NumPy  np.std(tents)          : 2.2804
pandas pd.Series(tents).std() : 2.5495
NumPy  np.std(tents, ddof=1)  : 2.5495
    Say: "NumPy divides by n: ddof=0. pandas divides by n - 1: ddof=1. Population, when the data is the whole group you care about; sample, when it stands in for something bigger. If unsure, ddof=1. With 20,302 rows the two differ by less than half a cent, so it is a small-sample question." Why n - 1 at all: a sample is measured against its own mean, the point it is closest to, so its deviations come out a little too small. The lesson proves it with 100,000 simulated samples; that simulation is homework reading.
  10. Spread that shrugs off extremes (3m). Say: "An SD of $179 around a mean of $195 suggests some orders are below zero. For skewed data the SD is inflated by the same tail as the mean. The robust partner of the median is the IQR." 
    q1 = totals.quantile(0.25)
q3 = totals.quantile(0.75)
print("Q1:", q1, " Q3:", q3, " IQR:", round(q3 - q1, 2))

with_typo = pd.concat([totals, pd.Series([1_000_000.0])], ignore_index=True)
typo_iqr = with_typo.quantile(0.75) - with_typo.quantile(0.25)
print("mean  :", round(totals.mean(), 2), "->", round(with_typo.mean(), 2))
print("median:", totals.median(), "->", with_typo.median())
print("SD    :", round(totals.std(), 2), "->", round(with_typo.std(), 2))
print("IQR   :", round(q3 - q1, 2), "->", round(typo_iqr, 2))
    Q1: 78.85  Q3: 264.95  IQR: 186.1
mean  : 194.6 -> 243.84
median: 146.85 -> 146.85
SD    : 178.76 -> 7019.02
IQR   : 186.1 -> 186.13
    Say it as a sentence: "The middle half of Pinecrest's orders are between $78.85 and $264.95." Then the stress test: one bad row out of 20,303 multiplied the SD by 39 and did not move the IQR. Two standard pairs for the board: mean with SD for symmetric data, median with IQR for skewed data.
  11. Missing values (2m). Say: "One practical matter. Six store-days have no revenue recorded." 
    daily = pd.read_csv("data/daily_sales.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
revenue = daily["revenue"]

print("rows:", len(revenue), " values present:", revenue.count())
print("pandas mean:", round(revenue.mean(), 2))
print("NumPy mean :", np.mean(revenue.to_numpy()))
print("np.nanmean :", round(np.nanmean(revenue.to_numpy()), 2))
    rows: 2903  values present: 2897
pandas mean: 7435.04
NumPy mean : nan
np.nanmean : 7435.04
    Say: "pandas skips missing values without telling you. NumPy returns nan without an error. Two habits: print .count() next to len(), and ask whether the missing rows could be different from the rest." Next session's survey data is where that question bites.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Two libraries, two standard deviations. A learner's SD does not match a neighbor's or the lesson's, because one used np.std (divide by n) and the other .std() on a Series (divide by n - 1). Coach: "When your number does not match someone else's, check ddof first." Have them write the choice into the code, np.std(x, ddof=1), so it stops being an accident.
  • Averaging averages. To get an overall mean they average the group means from a groupby (the lesson's example gives $182.66 instead of $194.60). Coach: "Does Asheville's 1,413 orders count as much as Online's 12,854 in your number?" Fix: compute from the original rows, or np.average(means, weights=counts).
  • Mean and SD for skewed data out of habit. "Orders average $195 plus or minus $179" is arithmetic that paints a symmetric hump that does not exist. There is no error message, so it is the most common. Coach with one question every time a mean is reported: "What is the median? Show me the histogram." If mean and median disagree noticeably, lead with median and IQR.
Guided lab

First 12 minutes, everyone: labs/module-10/l4_1-center-and-spread/orders_per_buyer_starter.py (reference: labs/module-10/l4_1-center-and-spread/orders_per_buyer_solution.py). The loyalty team says "our customers order about five times". Have learners write a guess for the order of mean, median and mode before TODO 1. Expected: mean 5.15, median 4.0, mode 1; 65.1% of buyers below the mean; mean x buyers = 20302 but median x buyers = 15768. Debrief with one question: "Which number goes in which sentence?"

Next 13 minutes: labs/module-10/l4_1-center-and-spread/visitor_spread_starter.py, Steps 1 to 3 (variance by hand on five days, matching NumPy and pandas, the four-store table). Expected in Step 1: 510.96 dividing by n and 638.7 dividing by n - 1. Steps 4 and 5 (relative spread, the stress test) go home. Watch for spread() still returning the np.nan placeholders: the table prints all NaN and the starter says so.

Early finishers: labs/module-10/l4_1-center-and-spread/debug_average_of_averages.py: three findings that run without an error and are wrong (an average of averages, a silent nan, two ddof defaults).

Start the lesson project

The lesson's project is The Typical Order Memo (about 35 minutes alone, in a new notebook lesson_4_1_project). In the room do Step 1: everyone types center_and_spread(values), which returns a dictionary of six numbers, and runs it on orders["order_total"]. They should see n 20,302.00, mean 194.60, median 146.85, sd 178.76, iqr 186.10 and mean_vs_median_pct 32.51. Say the rule of thumb from the lesson: when the mean is more than about 10% above the median, look at a histogram before reporting a mean. If minutes remain, start Step 2 (the three-row table). Steps 2 to 5 are homework; the memo must be generated from variables, with no number typed by hand.

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold call, then pair-share):

  1. "The mean order is $194.60 and the median is $146.85. Which one is wrong?" Answer: Neither. The mean is the balance point and is pulled up by the long right tail; the median is the middle order. Mean for totals, median for a typical order.
  2. "np.std(x) gave 2.28 and pd.Series(x).std() gave 2.55 on the same five numbers. Why?" Answer: NumPy divides by n (ddof=0), pandas by n - 1 (ddof=1). For a sample standing in for something bigger, use ddof=1.
  3. "Your column is delivery times in days, strongly right-skewed, maybe with typing errors. Which two numbers do you report?" Answer: Median and IQR: both ignore the extremes. Add the mean only if someone needs a total.

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (do two in the room if time allows; the rest is homework):

Answers: Q7 B) 30.0; Q8 C) The mode; Q9 2.0 2.5; Q10 A) The mean, $194.60; Q11 D) Median and interquartile range; Q12 A) 200.0 nan 2. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: keep the board's two columns (center, spread) visible and have learners copy them into the workbook's notes box as each term appears. For the variance, do the five-number table by hand on paper (value, deviation, squared deviation) before touching code. Learners who are anxious about statistics should hear early that today has no formulas to memorize: every number is one method call, and the skill is choosing which to report.

Stretch: lesson Exercise 4 (break the catalog: one price loses its decimal point; compare mean, median, SD, IQR and the 5% trimmed mean from scipy.stats.trim_mean), or the bonus challenge (rerun the n - 1 simulation for sample sizes 2, 5, 10, 30, 100 and compare with (n - 1) / n).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, on paper or sticky notes, no notes)
  1. A figure has figsize=(6, 4) and is saved with dpi=150. How many pixels wide and high is the PNG? Answer: 900 wide by 600 high (6 x 150 and 4 x 150).
  2. A column of order totals is strongly right-skewed. Which measure of center and which measure of spread do you report for a typical order? Answer: The median and the IQR. (The mean is for totals.)
  3. np.std(x) and pd.Series(x).std() give different answers for the same small list. Why? Answer: NumPy divides by n (ddof=0); pandas divides by n - 1 (ddof=1).

Read the slips before Session 11. If more than a quarter miss question 1, open Session 11 with one more pixel prediction. If question 3 is weak, the 4.2 demo's z-score step (which uses the SD) is the place to revisit ddof.

  • Lesson 4.1 practice: Exercises 1 to 3 (Exercise 4 is a stretch), the Quick Quiz, and the journal prompt. Read the section "Sample or Population? The n - 1 Question" and run its simulation once.

Bring list for Session 11

If You Run Long or Short

Protect: the tiny-text demonstration (demo step 4) with both files opened side by side, the pixel_budget lab, mean against median on the real order totals (demo steps 3 to 5), the variance by hand, and the first step of each lesson project.

Running long, cut in this order: (1) the backgrounds step of the 3.4 demo (say the rule, show the lesson's three-panel figure); (2) the bbox_inches step (one sentence: "it changes the size"); (3) category_price_pack in the room (all of it goes home); (4) the missing-values step of the 4.1 demo (it returns in Session 11); (5) visitor_spread in the room. Do not cut either project start: two minutes of "your first cell runs" saves twenty at home.

Running short: run the debug handouts as a whole-room hunt (one on the projector, pairs call out the faults), do the two Predict items per lesson from the workbook together, then let learners continue the Chart Pack to Step 2 or the Memo to Step 2.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 11: Shape, Outliers and Distributions

How to teach the session that finishes describing data and starts reasoning about data not yet seen. Before the break learners measure the shape of a column, locate values in it with percentiles and z-scores, run two outlier rules that disagree, and learn that a flag is a question, not a verdict. After the break they meet four workhorse distributions through scipy.stats, watch the central limit theorem turn a skew of 5.3 into a bell, and build their first confidence interval.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 4.2–4.3 Session 11 of 21

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm as every session: Frame (the goal and a mental model) → Live demo (you type, they type along) → Guided lab (the kit's lab files) → Start the lesson project. The lesson's exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Type, do not paste. Every code block in the demo scripts is what to type, one notebook cell per step, in the course project folder. Every output shown was produced by running that code with the course environment (pandas 3.0, SciPy 1.18).
  • Ask for a prediction before you run. Rank the columns by skew, guess the share of days above $12,000, guess whether two outlier rules agree, guess the shape of 20,000 sample means. The surprise only teaches if they committed first.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep statistics_descriptive.html and statistics_probability_distributions.html open in browser tabs for the figures (the labeled box plot, the stacked survey bars, the normal curve over the spend histogram, the four-panel central limit figure, the fifty intervals) and the tables (skewness cutoffs, what to do with an outlier, the four methods, which distribution when).
  • Teal = hands-on, amber = watch-outs. Labs for this session live in labs/module-11/: starters for learners, solutions for you.
The risk of Session 11: the densest three hours of Module 4

Lesson 4.2 has eight ideas and Lesson 4.3 has more: four distributions, four methods, simulation, the central limit theorem, the standard error and a confidence interval. Nobody holds all of that after one pass. Decide in advance what must land in the room: before the break, a flag is a question, not a verdict, and every grouped number carries its n; after the break, freeze a distribution, ask it a question, check it against data, and the 95% describes the method. The rest is exposure that the lesson pages and the homework will consolidate. Say so to the room: "You will not remember all four distributions tonight. You will remember how to ask one a question." The second risk is random numbers: a learner who runs a cell twice gets different results from yours and thinks they made an error. Tell them in advance that the conclusions will match even when the digits do not.

Before Session 11

  • ☐ Run the lab check from the kit folder: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-11. Eight lines should say PASS.
  • ☐ Copy the starters and the two debug handouts (*_starter.py, debug_*.py) from labs/module-11/ to the shared folder. Keep every *_solution.py on your machine.
  • ☐ Projector machine: Jupyter (or VS Code notebooks) opened in the course project folder; font size at least 18 pt.
  • ☐ Files used today: data/orders.csv, data/order_items.csv, data/daily_sales.csv, data/products.csv, data/survey.csv, data/store_weather.csv. No servers to start, no accounts, nothing new to install: scipy is already in the course environment (check once with python -c "import scipy; print(scipy.__version__)").
  • ☐ Run the 4.3 demo once, top to bottom, on the projector machine and confirm your outputs match this guide (they will, with default_rng(42) and the cells run once each in order). Then restart the kernel so the generator is fresh for class.
  • ☐ Whiteboard, written before learners arrive: on the left center · spread · shape · position and A flag is a question, not a verdict.; on the right an empty four-row table headed cdf · sf · ppf · pmf.
  • ☐ Optional, for the central limit theorem: a handful of dice (three per learner).
  • ☐ Known environment traps. (1) Random results depend on the order in which cells are run; restart and run all to get back in step. (2) ax.boxplot() on a column with missing values draws an empty frame with no error: dropna() first. (3) Matplotlib 3.9 and later use orientation="horizontal" and tick_labels= in boxplot; a learner on an older Matplotlib needs vert=False and labels=. (4) pandas .quantile() wants 0 to 1 and raises a ValueError for 25; np.percentile() wants 0 to 100 and raises nothing for 0.25. (5) scipy.stats.zscore divides by n (ddof=0) unless told otherwise; the lesson computes z-scores by hand with the pandas SD. (6) stats.skew() (NumPy-style, used on arrays in the CLT step) and pandas .skew() use slightly different formulas; on 20,302 rows both print 5.48.
  • ☐ Skim the Session 10 homework: the Chart Pack manifest (9 files) and the Typical Order Memo. Two "before the next lesson" tasks feed today's opening: which line of describe() could they not name, and is visitors skewed (its mean is 355.9 and its median 322, so yes, to the right).
  • ☐ Sticky notes or slips of paper for the exit ticket.

The lesson pages estimate 90 + 100 = 190 minutes for a solo learner, and the room has 150 after the warm-up, break and wrap-up, of which 45 go to the kit labs. So this session leans on homework more than most. Done in the room: both mental models; skewness and the log trick; quantiles and z-scores; both outlier rules and the investigation of the bulk orders; describe() and the box plot; the survey table with its n; simulation with one generator; the normal model and the four methods; one binomial and one Poisson example with its mean-against-variance check; the central limit theorem table; one confidence interval and its coverage; the catalog_weights and conversion_model labs; the first step or two of each lesson project. Goes home: the rest of both projects (Store Profile Sheet Steps 2 to 6, Returns Forecast Steps 3 to 6), the unfinished lab steps, the lessons' exercises, Quick Quizzes and journals, and the reading-only parts: quantile interpolation, histogram bins, named aggregation with q1 and q3, the full survey section (the distribution table, the stacked bar chart), the binomial check against 507 real batches, the fifty-interval figure and the six common mistakes of 4.3.
