Five retrieval questions (no notes, pairs, 60 seconds each)
  1. A figure with figsize=(10, 5) is saved with dpi=200. How many pixels wide and high is the PNG? Answer: 2,000 wide by 1,000 high: pixels = inches x dpi.
  2. The labels on your slide image are too small. Which two settings do you change, and what stays the same? Answer: A smaller figsize and a higher dpi, so the pixel size stays the same. Raising the dpi alone does not make text bigger.
  3. Pinecrest's mean order is $194.60 and the median is $146.85. Why do they differ, and which describes a typical order? Answer: The totals are right-skewed: a long tail of large orders pulls the mean up. The median describes a typical order; the mean is for totals.
  4. np.std(x) and pd.Series(x).std(): which divides by n and which by n - 1? Answer: NumPy divides by n (ddof=0); pandas divides by n - 1 (ddof=1).
  5. What is the IQR, and why prefer it to the SD for a skewed column? Answer: Q3 minus Q1, the width of the middle half of the data. It is robust: extreme values cannot inflate it.
Homework check

Show of hands: whose Chart Pack manifest showed 9 files with every web PNG at 990 x 495? Whose memo was generated entirely from variables? Then the two tasks from the end of Lesson 4.1. "You ran orders["order_total"].describe(). Which line could you not name?" (Most say std or the percent lines; all of them are explained in today's first demo.) "Is visitors skewed?" Take a guess, then the numbers: mean 355.9, median 322, so the mean is about 10% above the median: a right skew.

Bridge to today

Say: "Last session we described a column with a center and a spread, and we kept saying 'it depends on the shape'. Today we measure the shape, locate single values inside it, and decide what to do with the ones that stand apart. After the break the subject changes from data you have to data you have not seen yet."

Lesson Plans

4.2

Descriptive Statistics II: Shape, Position and Outliers

65 min
Timing
10mFrame: the pile of sand; shape is the first thing to check
25mLive demo: 11 short steps on order totals, daily revenue and the survey
20mGuided lab: catalog_weights, then the start of price_satisfaction
10mStart the lesson project: the Store Profile Sheet, Step 1
Objectives (the lesson's own)
  • Describe the shape of a distribution with a histogram and a skewness value, and say what the shape implies for your choice of summary
  • Locate a value within its column using percentiles, quantiles and z-scores
  • Apply the IQR and z-score outlier rules, explain why they disagree, and choose a defensible action for flagged values
  • Read every line of describe() and every part of a box plot
  • Summarize by group with groupby().agg(), and summarize 1-to-5 survey answers as the ordered categories they are
Mental model to say

Say: "Pour every value of a column onto a number line, like sand. The pile that forms is the distribution, and a histogram is a photograph of it. Center says where the pile sits. Spread says how wide it is. Shape says whether it is one even mound, a mound with a long ramp on one side, or two mounds. Every other summary is an attempt to describe that pile without showing the photograph."

Draw three piles on the board: an even mound, a mound with a ramp to the right, two mounds. Under them write the four words of the module so far: center, spread, shape, position. Last session covered the first two; today adds the other two and the question that follows from them: what do you do with the values that stand apart? Give the answer away early and repeat it all session: a flag is a question, not a verdict.

Live demo (you type, they follow)

New notebook session11_shape.ipynb. The numbers are the lesson's own, so learners can find every step again on the lesson page tonight. The demo saves one figure with fig.savefig (in a notebook it also appears under the cell). Ask for a prediction before each comparison. If time is short, say steps 4 and 8 instead of typing them.

  1. Put a number on shape (3m). New notebook. Say: "Last session we judged shape by eye and by mean against median. Skewness is the number: zero for a symmetric pile, positive when the long tail is on the right." Have the room rank the four columns from most symmetric to most skewed before you run. 
    import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

orders = pd.read_csv("data/orders.csv", parse_dates=["order_date"])
daily = pd.read_csv("data/daily_sales.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
products = pd.read_csv("data/products.csv")
totals = orders["order_total"]
daily["spend_per_visitor"] = daily["revenue"] / daily["visitors"]
spend = daily["spend_per_visitor"].dropna()

print("product ratings   :", round(products["rating"].skew(), 2))
print("spend per visitor :", round(spend.skew(), 2))
print("daily revenue     :", round(daily["revenue"].skew(), 2))
print("order totals      :", round(totals.skew(), 2))
no_bulk = totals[totals <= 2000]
print("  without the 12 bulk orders:", round(no_bulk.skew(), 2))
print("  log(order totals)         :", round(np.log(totals).skew(), 2))
    product ratings   : -0.02
spend per visitor : 0.27
daily revenue     : 1.51
order totals      : 5.48
  without the 12 bulk orders: 1.64
  log(order totals)         : -0.41
    Write the convention on the board: between -0.5 and 0.5 roughly symmetric (mean and SD are fair), beyond 1 strongly skewed (median and IQR). Two cautions from the output: skewness is not robust (twelve orders move it from 1.64 to 5.48), and it says nothing about the number of humps. The last line is the log trick: 5.48 becomes -0.41.
  2. Position by rank (3m). Say: "Center, spread and shape describe the whole pile. Position describes one value's place in it. 'This order was $517' says little. 'Larger than 95% of orders' says a lot." 
    cuts = [0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 0.90, 0.95, 0.99]
print(totals.quantile(cuts).to_string())

print("share of orders at or below $500:", round((totals <= 500).mean(), 4))
    0.10     41.9500
0.25     78.8500
0.50    146.8500
0.75    264.9500
0.90    405.3950
0.95    516.7975
0.99    737.4430
share of orders at or below $500: 0.9443
    Read down the list out loud: one order in ten is under $42, half are under $147, one in a hundred is over $737. Then the reverse question, with last session's tool: the mean of a boolean is a proportion, so a $500 order sits at about the 94th percentile. Warn now: pandas .quantile() takes 0 to 1, NumPy's np.percentile() takes 0 to 100.
  3. Position by distance: the z-score (3m). Write z = (value - mean) / SD on the board. Ask: "Is a $12,000 day a big deal?" Let them argue, then run. 
    for store in ["Asheville", "Boise"]:
    revenue = daily.loc[daily["store"] == store, "revenue"]
    z = (12000 - revenue.mean()) / revenue.std()
    share = (revenue >= 12000).mean()
    print(f"{store:<9} mean {revenue.mean():7,.0f} SD {revenue.std():5,.0f}"
          f"  z = {z:5.2f}  days at or above: {share:.1%}")
    Asheville mean   5,704 SD 2,064  z =  3.05  days at or above: 1.5%
Boise     mean  10,144 SD 3,715  z =  0.50  days at or above: 24.3%
    Say: "The same $12,000 is three standard deviations above Asheville's average and half a standard deviation above Boise's. The raw number cannot tell you that."
  4. Standardizing does not change the shape (2m). Say: "Convert the whole column." Ask what the mean and SD of a z-scored column must be. 
    z_totals = (totals - totals.mean()) / totals.std()
print("mean of z:", abs(round(z_totals.mean(), 6)),
      "  SD of z:", round(z_totals.std(), 6))
print("largest z:", round(z_totals.max(), 1),
      "  smallest z:", round(z_totals.min(), 2))
    mean of z: 0.0   SD of z: 1.0
largest z: 26.3   smallest z: -1.05
    Mean 0 and SD 1, always. But the largest order is 26 SDs above the mean and the smallest barely 1 below: the pile is as lopsided as before. "95% within 2 SDs" belongs to one bell-shaped distribution, which is the second half of today.
  5. Outlier rule 1: the IQR fences (3m). Say: "An outlier is a value far from the rest. 'Far' needs a definition. Rule one: a fence 1.5 IQRs beyond each quartile. This is the rule box plots use." 
    q1, q3 = totals.quantile(0.25), totals.quantile(0.75)
iqr = q3 - q1
lower_fence = q1 - 1.5 * iqr
upper_fence = q3 + 1.5 * iqr
flag_iqr = (totals < lower_fence) | (totals > upper_fence)

print("fences:", round(lower_fence, 2), "to", round(upper_fence, 2))
print("flagged:", flag_iqr.sum(), f"({flag_iqr.mean():.1%} of orders)")
    fences: -200.3 to 544.1
flagged: 848 (4.2% of orders)
    Point at the lower fence: minus $200.30. No order can ever be flagged as too small, and 4% are flagged as too large.
  6. Outlier rule 2 disagrees (3m). Say: "Rule two: z beyond 3. Same data. Same answer?" 
    flag_z = z_totals.abs() > 3
print("flagged:", flag_z.sum(), f"({flag_z.mean():.1%} of orders)")
print("smallest flagged order:", totals[flag_z].min())

print(f"IQR-flagged orders: {flag_iqr.mean():.1%} of orders, "
      f"{totals[flag_iqr].sum() / totals.sum():.1%} of revenue")
    flagged: 217 (1.1% of orders)
smallest flagged order: 731.85
IQR-flagged orders: 4.2% of orders, 15.4% of revenue
    848 or 217. Ask why. (The mean and SD are inflated by the very values being judged; the quartiles are not.) Then the last line: deleting what the IQR rule flags would throw away 4% of the orders and over 15% of the money. Say the sentence of the lesson: "A flag is a question, not a verdict."
  7. Investigate before you remove (3m). Say: "So ask the question. Are the twelve largest orders errors? Look them up." 
    items = pd.read_csv("data/order_items.csv")
bulk_ids = orders.loc[totals > 2000, "order_id"]
bulk_lines = items[items["order_id"].isin(bulk_ids)]
largest = bulk_lines.groupby("order_id")["quantity"].max()

print("orders above $2,000:", len(bulk_ids))
print("largest quantity on each:", sorted(largest.tolist()))
print(orders.loc[totals > 2000, ["channel", "status"]].value_counts())
    orders above $2,000: 12
largest quantity on each: [25, 26, 27, 28, 30, 30, 30, 32, 35, 38, 39, 39]
channel  status   
online   completed    12
Name: count, dtype: int64
    Every one is a completed online order with one line of 25 to 39 units: outfitters buying in bulk. Real sales. Walk the lesson's decision chart on the board: provable error? fix or remove it. Not an error but not part of your question? analyze separately and say so. Otherwise keep it and stay robust (median, IQR).
  8. Read describe() properly (2m). Say: "You have run this since the first lesson. You can now read every line." 
    print(totals.describe().round(2).to_string())
    count    20302.00
mean       194.60
std        178.76
min          6.38
25%         78.85
50%        146.85
75%        264.95
max       4893.00
    Three checks to do in your head every time: is count lower than the number of rows; are mean and 50% far apart; are the two halves of the box unequal (264.95 - 146.85 against 146.85 - 78.85)? std is the sample SD (ddof=1).
  9. A box plot is the IQR rule, drawn (3m). Say: "A box plot shows the median, the quartiles, and the fence rule in one shape." Type it with dropna() and say why: with a missing value Matplotlib draws an empty frame and raises nothing. 
    asheville = daily.loc[daily["store"] == "Asheville", "revenue"].dropna()
a_q1, a_med, a_q3 = asheville.quantile([0.25, 0.5, 0.75])
a_iqr = a_q3 - a_q1
whisker_hi = asheville[asheville <= a_q3 + 1.5 * a_iqr].max()
whisker_lo = asheville[asheville >= a_q1 - 1.5 * a_iqr].min()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 2.6), layout="constrained")
ax.boxplot(asheville, orientation="horizontal", widths=0.5)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xlabel("Asheville daily revenue ($)")
fig.savefig("asheville_box.png", dpi=110)

print("Q1, median, Q3:", round(a_q1), round(a_med), round(a_q3))
print("whiskers end at:", round(whisker_lo), "and", round(whisker_hi))
print("points beyond the upper fence:",
      (asheville > a_q3 + 1.5 * a_iqr).sum())
    Q1, median, Q3: 4263 5208 6652
whiskers end at: 2268 and 10229
points beyond the upper fence: 23
    Point at the picture: the line in the box is the median, not the mean; the box is the middle half; each whisker ends at the last real data point inside the fence, not at the fence and not at the maximum; separate points are what the rule flags. A box plot compares groups well and hides humps.
  10. Summaries by group carry their n (2m). Say: "Most real questions are comparisons, so most real summaries are grouped." 
    by_store = daily.groupby("store")["revenue"].agg(
    ["count", "mean", "median", "std"])
print(by_store.round(0))
               count     mean  median     std
store                                    
Asheville    726   5704.0  5208.0  2064.0
Bend         721   6998.0  6456.0  2546.0
Boise        726  10144.0  9360.0  3715.0
Flagstaff    724   6890.0  6405.0  2686.0
    Say: "A mean with no n beside it cannot be judged: is that group 700 days or 7?" The counts differ by the six missing revenue values. The lesson goes on to named aggregation with q1 and q3 functions; that is the project's Step 1.
  11. Survey answers are ordered categories (4m). Say: "Pinecrest surveyed 1,800 customers on a 1-to-5 scale. That looks like numeric data. It is not, quite: 4 is more satisfied than 3, but nothing says the steps are equal. The word is ordinal." 
    survey = pd.read_csv("data/survey.csv")

def top_two(values):
    return (values.dropna() >= 4).mean() * 100

def bottom_two(values):
    return (values.dropna() <= 2).mean() * 100

staff = survey.groupby("store")["sat_staff"].agg(
    n="count", rows="size", median="median",
    satisfied_pct=top_two, dissatisfied_pct=bottom_two)
print(staff.round(1))
                 n  rows  median  satisfied_pct  dissatisfied_pct
store                                                        
Asheville  193   202     4.0           57.5              14.0
Bend       228   232     4.0           78.9               4.4
Boise      320   329     4.0           76.9               2.2
Flagstaff  206   213     4.0           74.8               4.4
Online     248   824     4.0           74.6               2.8
    Two findings in one table. First: the median is 4 in every store and tells you nothing, while the shares do: Asheville has 57.5% satisfied against 75 to 79% elsewhere, and 14% dissatisfied. Second: compare n with rows for Online: 248 answers from 824 respondents. Most online shoppers never met the staff, so the answers are not missing at random. Whether Asheville's gap could be a fluke is a question for Session 12; describing it clearly, with counts, comes first.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Passing a percentage where a fraction is wanted, or the reverse. totals.quantile(25) raises ValueError: percentiles should all be in the interval [0, 1]; the dangerous twin raises nothing: np.percentile(totals, 0.9) quietly returns the 0.9th percentile. Coach: "Which function, and which scale does it take? pandas .quantile(): 0 to 1. NumPy np.percentile(): 0 to 100." Have them check a result against describe().
  • Deleting whatever the rule flags. "The IQR rule says they are outliers, so I removed them." Coach with two questions from the lesson's chart: "Is it a provable error? Is it part of your question?" Then make it concrete: the 848 flagged orders are 15.4% of revenue. Remove only provable errors, write down what was removed, and use the median and IQR so the rest cannot distort the summary.
  • A grouped statistic without its n, or a Likert mean on its own. A table of group means looks finished. Coach: "How many answers is each mean based on? Add count and size." For 1-to-5 answers: "Show me the distribution, or the share satisfied, next to that mean." A related silent failure worth naming: ax.boxplot() on a column with missing values draws an empty frame; dropna() first.
Guided lab

First 12 minutes, everyone: labs/module-11/l4_2-shape-position-outliers/catalog_weights_starter.py (reference: labs/module-11/l4_2-shape-position-outliers/catalog_weights_solution.py). The shipping team asked to "remove the outlier weights first". Learners run the whole workflow on weight_kg: shape, position, both rules, then look at what was flagged. Expected: skew 3.46 (0.18 after a log); 26 products flagged by the IQR rule and 4 by the z-score rule; 11 of the 26 are tents; nothing removed. Watch Step 2: 14 products have no weight, and comparing a missing value with 2 gives False, so the share needs dropna() (89.9%, not 84.7%). Debrief with one question: "What do you send back to the shipping team?"

Last 8 minutes: labs/module-11/l4_2-shape-position-outliers/price_satisfaction_starter.py, TODO 1 to 3 (the distribution table, bottom_two(), the grouped table). The grouped table is the payoff: ages 18 to 24 are 19.4% satisfied and 38.2% dissatisfied with prices, against about 44% and 15% for everyone else, and the medians hide it. TODO 4 to 6 (who skipped, saving the chart, the sentence) go home. The chart is saved to OUTPUT; the lab never calls plt.show().

Early finishers: labs/module-11/l4_2-shape-position-outliers/debug_summary_report.py: four results that run without an error and are wrong.

Start the lesson project

The lesson's project is The Store Profile Sheet (about 40 minutes alone, in a new notebook lesson_4_2_project). The operations manager wants a profile of daily revenue at the four stores and has asked to "take out the weird days first". In the room do Step 1: drop the six store-days with no revenue (2,903 rows become 2,897), add the weekday name, and build the grouped profile with q1 and q3 functions and named aggregation. Everyone should see four rows: Asheville's median 5,208, Bend's 6,456, Boise's 9,360, Flagstaff's 6,405, and Boise's maximum of 27,677 far beyond its 95th percentile of 16,834. Do not give away the ending (all 91 flagged days turn out to be weekends, promotions or December days). Steps 2 to 6 are homework.

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold call, then pair-share):

  1. "Daily revenue has a skewness of 1.51. Which center and spread do you report, and what would you draw first?" Answer: Median and IQR (beyond 1 is strongly skewed), and a histogram first: skewness does not show how many humps there are.
  2. "A value is flagged by the IQR rule. What are the two questions you ask before doing anything?" Answer: Is it a provable error? Is it part of the question I am answering? Remove only provable errors; otherwise keep it (and stay robust) or analyze it separately and say so.
  3. "On a box plot, where does the upper whisker end?" Answer: At the largest data value that is still within 1.5 IQRs above Q3. Not at the fence itself, and not at the maximum unless nothing is flagged.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (do two in the room if time allows; the rest is homework):

Answers: Q1 C) On the log scale the pile is roughly symmetric, so methods that prefer symmetric data will behave better there; Q2 25.0; Q3 A) The day is far above Asheville's own average, measured in Asheville's SDs, and only a little above Boise's; Q4 D) The mean and SD are inflated by the same large orders being judged, which pushes the z-score line outward; the quartiles are not; Q5 14.5 1; Q6 B) Report it with its n and say who answered: 70% of Online shoppers skipped the question, so it describes the minority who dealt with staff. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: keep the lesson's outlier decision chart on screen during the lab and have learners trace it with a finger for one flagged product. For z-scores, do one by hand on the board with round numbers (a store with mean 300 and SD 100: what is the z of a 500-visitor day?) before any code. Give anyone lost in named aggregation the pattern on paper: agg(new_name="function").

Stretch: lesson Exercise 4 (the outlier rule on the log scale), or extend the lab: z-scores of weight within each category with groupby().transform(), the technique the project's Step 2 uses. Does a 6-person tent still look unusual among tents?

4.3

Probability Distributions

85 min
Timing
15mFrame: the vending machine; discrete or continuous; why the rest of the module needs this
30mLive demo: 12 short steps, one seeded generator, run in order
25mGuided lab: conversion_model, then Steps 1 to 4 of lines_per_order_ci
15mStart the lesson project: the Returns Forecast, Steps 1 and 2
Objectives (the lesson's own)
  • Explain what a random variable and a probability distribution are, and tell discrete from continuous
  • Choose between the uniform, normal, binomial and Poisson distributions for a situation, and check the choice against data
  • Answer probability questions with scipy.stats using pmf/pdf, cdf, sf and ppf
  • Simulate random outcomes reproducibly with np.random.default_rng and use simulation to check a calculation
  • Demonstrate the central limit theorem by simulation, compute a standard error, and build and correctly interpret a 95% confidence interval for a mean
Mental model to say

Say: "Picture a vending machine that drops a random snack each time you press the button. You cannot say what the next press will give you. But if someone tells you the machine is stocked with 50% chips, 30% candy and 20% cookies, you know a great deal: what to expect most often, how surprised to be by three cookies in a row, and roughly what 100 presses will produce. That stocking list is a probability distribution: every possible outcome, with its probability."

Then the two kinds, as two columns on the board: discrete (counted: returns in a day; binomial, Poisson; one exact value has a real probability) and continuous (measured: spend per visitor; uniform, normal; only ranges have probability). Finish the frame with why this lesson exists: "Every tool in the rest of this module, tests, A/B tests, confidence intervals, is built by asking 'what would chance alone produce?' Distributions are how that question gets an answer."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

New notebook session11_distributions.ipynb. Create the generator once, in the first cell, and run every cell once, in order. A generator hands out its numbers in sequence: run a cell twice or skip one and every random result after it changes a little (the conclusions do not). The outputs below come from running these cells top to bottom with default_rng(42). The lesson page runs a longer sequence of cells, so its random results (the auditor's sample, the coverage percentage) differ slightly from the ones here: same method, different draws. That difference is itself a teaching point.

  1. One generator, and the law of large numbers (3m). New notebook. Say: "Until now we described data that exists. A business also plans for data that does not exist yet. We cannot know tomorrow's number. We can know how it behaves." Create the generator once and say so. 
    import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

orders = pd.read_csv("data/orders.csv", parse_dates=["order_date"])
daily = pd.read_csv("data/daily_sales.csv", parse_dates=["date"])

many = rng.integers(1, 7, size=100_000)      # 100,000 rolls of a die
shares = pd.Series(many).value_counts(normalize=True).sort_index()
print(shares.round(3).tolist())
print("mean of the rolls:", round(many.mean(), 3))
    [0.167, 0.167, 0.165, 0.167, 0.168, 0.166]
mean of the rolls: 3.5
    Each face comes up very close to 1/6, and the average roll settles on 3.5, the expected value: no single roll is ever 3.5. Say: "That is why simulation works. If you can simulate a process, you can estimate any probability about it by counting." Tell learners their random numbers will match yours only if they run the same cells in the same order, once each.
  2. Two routes to one answer (2m). Say: "A customer is equally likely to walk in at any moment of an hour. Chance they arrive in the first 15 minutes?" 
    arrivals = rng.uniform(0, 60, size=100_000)       # minutes past the hour
print("simulated:", round((arrivals < 15).mean(), 3))

arrival = stats.uniform(loc=0, scale=60)          # a frozen distribution
print("exact    :", arrival.cdf(15))
    simulated: 0.25
exact    : 0.25
    The simulation counted; the scipy object calculated. Name the object: a frozen distribution, parameters fixed, ready to answer questions. For the uniform, scale is the width, not the end.
  3. Freeze a normal with the data's own mean and SD (3m). Say: "Last lesson's even mound: revenue per visitor. A normal distribution is completely described by two numbers." 
    spend = (daily["revenue"] / daily["visitors"]).dropna()
mu, sigma = spend.mean(), spend.std()
spend_model = stats.norm(loc=mu, scale=sigma)
print("mean:", round(mu, 2), " SD:", round(sigma, 2), " n:", len(spend))

for k in (1, 2, 3):
    in_data = ((spend - mu).abs() < k * sigma).mean()
    in_theory = stats.norm.cdf(k) - stats.norm.cdf(-k)
    print(f"within {k} SD:  data {in_data:.1%}   normal {in_theory:.1%}")
    mean: 20.87  SD: 3.0  n: 2897
within 1 SD:  data 68.6%   normal 68.3%
within 2 SD:  data 95.1%   normal 95.4%
within 3 SD:  data 99.6%   normal 99.7%
    The 68-95-99.7 rule, and its fine print: it is a property of the normal shape. The spend data follows it to within a fraction of a percentage point; order totals would not. Show the lesson's histogram with the curve laid over it from the lesson page.
  4. Four questions, four methods (4m). Draw the lesson's table on the board as you go: cdf(x) this or less; sf(x) more than this; ppf(q) which value has q below it; pmf(k) exactly k (discrete). Have learners say the method before you type each line. 
    print("P(spend below $15): model", round(spend_model.cdf(15), 3),
      " data", round((spend < 15).mean(), 3))
print("P(spend above $25): model", round(spend_model.sf(25), 3),
      " data", round((spend > 25).mean(), 3))
print("P($18 to $24)     : model",
      round(spend_model.cdf(24) - spend_model.cdf(18), 3),
      " data", round(((spend >= 18) & (spend <= 24)).mean(), 3))
print("95th percentile   : model", round(spend_model.ppf(0.95), 2),
      " data", round(spend.quantile(0.95), 2))
    P(spend below $15): model 0.025  data 0.019
P(spend above $25): model 0.084  data 0.087
P($18 to $24)     : model 0.683  data 0.686
95th percentile   : model 25.8  data 26.01
    Say: "A model summarizes 2,897 numbers with two. It buys the ability to ask about values you have never seen, at the cost of small errors you can measure." It is close in the middle and a little off in the tails. One warning: for a continuous variable pdf is the height of the curve, not a probability. Probabilities are areas: differences of cdf.
  5. Binomial: successes out of n tries (3m). Say: "A counting question. Out of the next 40 orders, how many will come back?" Fixed number of tries, independent, same probability each time. 
    is_returned = orders["status"] == "returned"
p_return = is_returned.mean()
returns_in_40 = stats.binom(n=40, p=p_return)
print("return rate:", round(p_return, 4),
      " expected in 40:", round(returns_in_40.mean(), 2))

for k in range(4):
    print(f"P(exactly {k} returns) = {returns_in_40.pmf(k):.3f}")
print(f"P(5 or more)        = {returns_in_40.sf(4):.3f}")
    return rate: 0.0563  expected in 40: 2.25
P(exactly 0 returns) = 0.098
P(exactly 1 returns) = 0.235
P(exactly 2 returns) = 0.273
P(exactly 3 returns) = 0.207
P(5 or more)        = 0.072
    Circle sf(4): "more than 4" is "5 or more" for a count. Off-by-one slips here are the most common binomial error. Mention the assumption that matters at Pinecrest: online orders come back about twice as often as store orders (6.9% against 3.4%), so an all-online batch is not this model.
  6. Check it by simulation (1m). Say: "Do not take the formula on faith. Count." 
    sim = rng.binomial(n=40, p=p_return, size=100_000)
print("simulated P(5 or more):", round((sim >= 5).mean(), 3))
    simulated P(5 or more): 0.073
    Formula (0.072) and simulation agree to within a thousandth. The lesson adds a third check, against 507 real batches.
  7. Poisson: events in an interval (4m). Say: "A different counting question. How many returned orders does a day produce? There is no fixed number of tries, just events scattered through time. One parameter: the average rate." 
    all_days = pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2025-12-31")
returns_per_day = (orders[is_returned].groupby("order_date").size()
                   .reindex(all_days, fill_value=0))
lam = returns_per_day.mean()
print("days:", len(returns_per_day), " mean:", round(lam, 3),
      " variance:", round(returns_per_day.var(), 3))

returns_model = stats.poisson(mu=lam)
observed = returns_per_day.value_counts().sort_index()
expected = returns_model.pmf(observed.index) * len(returns_per_day)
print(pd.DataFrame({"days observed": observed,
                    "Poisson expects": expected.round(1)}))
    days: 731  mean: 1.564  variance: 1.526
   days observed  Poisson expects
0            151            153.1
1            239            239.3
2            190            187.1
3             98             97.5
4             39             38.1
5             11             11.9
6              2              3.1
7              1              0.7
    Two things to stress. The reindex(..., fill_value=0) puts the zero-return days back; without it the mean is wrong. And the check: mean about equal to variance is the fingerprint of a Poisson. The fit is striking: 151 zero-return days observed against 153 expected.
  8. A count that is not Poisson (2m). Say: "Do not assume every count is Poisson. Total orders per day." 
    orders_per_day = orders.groupby("order_date").size()
print("mean    :", round(orders_per_day.mean(), 1))
print("variance:", round(orders_per_day.var(), 1))

print("count covering 95% of days:", returns_model.ppf(0.95))
print("P(5 or more returns)      :", round(returns_model.sf(4), 3))
    mean    : 27.8
variance: 64.4
count covering 95% of days: 4.0
P(5 or more returns)      : 0.022
    The variance is more than twice the mean: weekends, seasons and sale days move the rate. The word is overdispersion, and a Poisson model there would be far too confident. The last two lines are the planning questions the returns model can answer; they are the heart of the lesson project.
  9. The central limit theorem, watched (4m). The big idea of the lesson. Say: "Order totals are about as far from a bell as data gets: skew 5.5. Draw a sample of n orders, take its mean. Do that 20,000 times. What does the pile of means look like?" 
    population = orders["order_total"].to_numpy()
sd = population.std()
print("    n  mean of means  SD of means  sigma/sqrt(n)   skew")
for n in (5, 30, 200):
    means = rng.choice(population, size=(20_000, n)).mean(axis=1)
    print(f"{n:>5} {means.mean():>14.2f} {means.std():>12.2f} "
          f"{sd / np.sqrt(n):>14.2f} {stats.skew(means):>6.2f}")
        n  mean of means  SD of means  sigma/sqrt(n)   skew
    5         194.58        79.08          79.94   2.21
   30         194.70        32.42          32.64   0.93
  200         194.43        12.49          12.64   0.39
    Three things, one per column: the means center on the true mean ($194.60); their spread shrinks like sigma over root n (to halve it you need four times the data); their shape approaches the normal (skew falls toward 0). Then what the CLT does not say: it does not make the data normal. A million orders are exactly as skewed as before. Show the lesson's four-panel figure.
  10. One sample, a standard error, an interval (4m). Say: "In real work you get one sample and never see the population. An auditor pulls 200 orders." 
    sample = rng.choice(population, size=200, replace=False)
x_bar, s = sample.mean(), sample.std(ddof=1)
se = s / np.sqrt(len(sample))
low, high = stats.t.interval(0.95, df=len(sample) - 1, loc=x_bar, scale=se)

print("sample mean:", round(x_bar, 2), " sample SD:", round(s, 2))
print("standard error:", round(se, 2),
      " scipy.stats.sem:", round(stats.sem(sample), 2))
print(f"95% CI: {low:.2f} to {high:.2f}")
print("true mean:", round(population.mean(), 2))
    sample mean: 182.93  sample SD: 147.89
standard error: 10.46  scipy.stats.sem: 10.46
95% CI: 162.31 to 203.55
true mean: 194.6
    Write SE = s / sqrt(n) and mean plus or minus about 2 SE on the board. SD against SE: the SD (about $148 here) says how much single orders vary and does not shrink with more data; the SE (about $10) says how much the sample mean would vary from sample to sample. This auditor's sample mean is $12 below the truth, and the interval still contains $194.60. (The lesson page's sample differs, because its generator had been used for different draws: same method, different 200 orders.)
  11. What "95% confident" means (2m). Say: "The 95% describes the method, not this one interval. We own the population, so we can check: 10,000 samples, 10,000 intervals." 
    n = 200
big = rng.choice(population, size=(10_000, n))
m = big.mean(axis=1)
e = big.std(axis=1, ddof=1) / np.sqrt(n)
t_mult = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df=n - 1)
covered = ((m - t_mult * e <= population.mean())
           & (population.mean() <= m + t_mult * e))
print(f"{covered.mean():.1%} of 10,000 intervals contain the true mean")
    93.9% of 10,000 intervals contain the true mean
    Close to 95%, a little short because the data is so skewed. Say exactly this: "If we repeated the whole procedure many times, about 95% of the intervals would contain the true mean. Any single interval either contains it or does not." And what an interval is not: it is not a range that holds 95% of the orders.
  12. Make the classic mistake on purpose (1m). Say: "scipy rarely complains. Watch." 
    wrong = stats.norm(loc=mu, scale=sigma ** 2)     # variance passed as scale
right = stats.norm(loc=mu, scale=sigma)
print(round(wrong.cdf(15), 3), round(right.cdf(15), 3))
    0.257 0.025
    scale is the standard deviation. Passing the variance makes the bell three times too wide, with no error: 25.7% instead of 2.5%. Textbooks write N(mean, variance), which is where the habit comes from.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Giving scipy the wrong meaning for an argument. scale=sigma ** 2 (the variance where the SD is wanted), or stats.uniform(10, 20) read as low and high when the second argument is the width (the range is 10 to 30). No error either way. Coach: "Name the arguments, loc= and scale=, and print model.ppf([0.025, 0.975]) to see whether the range is believable."
  • Off by one with sf on a count, or cdf and ppf swapped. "5 or more" is sf(4), not sf(5). And ppf(15) returns nan because ppf takes a probability and returns a value. Coach: "Say the question in words first: this or less, more than this, or which value has this much below it? Then pick the method."
  • Misreading a confidence interval. Two versions: "95% of orders are between $162 and $204" (it is a statement about the mean, not about single orders: only about a tenth of orders fall in such a range), and "there is a 95% probability the true mean is in this interval" (the 95% describes the method: about 95 of 100 intervals built this way contain the true mean). Coach by rerunning the coverage cell and asking: "What is the 95% a percentage of?"
Guided lab

First 13 minutes, everyone: labs/module-11/l4_3-probability-distributions/conversion_model_starter.py (reference: labs/module-11/l4_3-probability-distributions/conversion_model_solution.py). Conversion is transactions divided by visitors. Learners describe it, freeze stats.norm, check the 68-95-99.7 rule against the data, then answer three managers' questions. Have them write the method name next to each question before coding it (the starter has blanks for this). Expected: mean 0.2354, SD 0.0271, skew 0.05; within 1, 2 and 3 SD the data has 69.4%, 95.6%, 99.5%; P(below 20%) model 0.096 against 0.090 in the data; a bad day (5th percentile) is about 19.1%.

Next 12 minutes: labs/module-11/l4_3-probability-distributions/lines_per_order_ci_starter.py, Steps 1 to 4: an intern's sample of 150 orders, the standard error two ways, a 95% t interval, and the prediction in Step 4 (what share of individual orders lies inside the interval?). Expected: sample mean 2.093, SE 0.0821, interval 1.931 to 2.256, which contains the true mean of 2.241. Steps 5 and 6 (coverage over 5,000 repeats; four times the sample) go home. The file is seeded: run top to bottom, everyone gets the same numbers.

Early finishers: labs/module-11/l4_3-probability-distributions/debug_delivery_model.py: four model answers that run without an error, all wrong.

Start the lesson project

The lesson's project is The Returns Forecast (about 40 minutes alone, in a new notebook lesson_4_3_project): a checked Poisson model of daily returns, with capacity numbers and a confidence interval. In the room do Steps 1 and 2. Step 1 builds the daily series including the zero days (reindex(days, fill_value=0)): 731 days, 1,143 returned orders, busiest day 7, 151 days with none. Step 2 checks the model before trusting it: mean 1.564 against variance 1.526, then the observed-against-expected table, where no count is off by more than about three days. Say what the remaining steps answer so nobody opens them cold: how much capacity covers 95% of days, what a simulated year looks like, and a margin of error on the rate. Steps 3 to 6 are homework.

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold call, then pair-share):

  1. "A warehouse checks 60 parcels, each with the same 2% chance of damage, independently. Which distribution, and which parameters?" Answer: Binomial with n = 60 and p = 0.02: a fixed number of independent tries with the same probability.
  2. "I have model = stats.norm(loc=20.87, scale=3.0). Which method tells me the spend that only 5% of days fall below?" Answer: model.ppf(0.05): ppf takes a probability and returns a value (about $15.94).
  3. "The standard deviation of my sample is $148 and the standard error is $10. Which one shrinks if I collect four times as much data, and by how much?" Answer: The standard error: it halves (it divides by the square root of n). The SD describes single orders and stays about the same.

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (do two in the room if time allows; the rest is homework):

Answers: Q7 D) Poisson; check that the mean and the variance are about equal; Q8 0.5; Q9 A) batch.sf(2); Q10 B) About $8.94; Q11 C) 800; Q12 A) They are identical: each pass builds a new generator from the same seed, which replays the same numbers. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: give learners the lesson's four-methods table on paper and have them tick the method for each question before typing. For the CLT, do it physically if you can: three dice per person, each person reports the mean of their three, and you tally the means on the board; the tally is a mound even though one die is flat. Learners who are shaky on simulation should rerun the dice cell with 10, 1,000 and 100,000 rolls and watch the shares settle.

Stretch: lesson Exercise 4 (how the interval's width depends on n, for 50, 200, 800 and 3,200), or extend the lab: is conversion more variable than a binomial model allows? For a store-day with 330 visitors and p = 0.235, the binomial SD of the rate is sqrt(p(1 - p) / 330); compare it with the observed SD (0.0271) and explain the gap.

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, on paper or sticky notes, no notes)
  1. The IQR rule flags 91 store-days as unusually high. What do you do before removing any of them? Answer: Investigate them: are they provable errors, and are they part of the question? (In the lesson's project all 91 are weekends, promotions or December days: real, and kept.)
  2. You have a frozen distribution called model. Which method returns the value that 95% of the distribution lies below? Answer: model.ppf(0.95). (cdf goes from a value to a probability; ppf goes back.)
  3. A 95% confidence interval for the mean order total is $162 to $204. Does that mean 95% of orders are between $162 and $204? If not, what does the 95% describe? Answer: No. It is a statement about the mean, not about single orders. The 95% describes the method: about 95 of 100 intervals built this way contain the true mean.

Read the slips before Session 12. Question 3 matters most: Session 12's hypothesis tests are built on the same standard error and the same "what would chance alone produce" logic. If more than a quarter answer "yes, 95% of orders", open Session 12 with the coverage simulation again.

Homework (about 2 to 3 hours)
  • Lesson 4.2 project: finish the Store Profile Sheet (Steps 2 to 6): z-scores within each store, the flagged days and what they turn out to be, the box plot saved as store_profile.png, the written profile.
  • Lesson 4.2 practice: Exercises 1 to 3 (Exercise 4 is a stretch), the five-question Quick Quiz, and the journal prompt. Read the survey section in full, including "Who Did Not Answer?"
  • Lesson 4.3 project: finish the Returns Forecast (Steps 3 to 6): planning questions with pmf, sf and ppf, a simulated year, a week, a confidence interval for the rate.
  • Lesson 4.3 practice: Exercises 1 to 3 (Exercise 4 is a stretch), the Quick Quiz, and the journal prompt. Read "Common Mistakes" in full: all six are silent.
  • Kit labs: finish price_satisfaction (TODO 4 to 6) and lines_per_order_ci (Steps 5 and 6).
  • Workbook: the 12 self-check items and anything left in Predict, then run.
  • Before Lesson 4.4 (from the lesson page): make a scatter plot of visitors against revenue from daily_sales.csv and describe the pattern in one sentence. Then predict: do stores take more revenue on days when more staff are on duty? Why might that be true even if adding staff did nothing?
Bring list for Session 12
  • Their notes on the pattern mean plus or minus t x s / sqrt(n): the t-test in Lesson 4.5 is built on the same standard error.
  • The scatter plot of visitors against revenue and their written prediction about staffing: Session 12 opens with it.
  • Data files for Session 12: daily_sales.csv, store_weather.csv, products.csv, order_items.csv, survey.csv, orders.csv, customers.csv (all already in data/).
  • Installs: none new. Session 12 uses scipy.stats and, for two cells, statsmodels; both are in the course environment. Anyone unsure runs python -c "import statsmodels; print(statsmodels.__version__)" at home.
  • Servers to start: none. Accounts: none needed.
  • This workbook, with the Session 11 self-check done.

If You Run Long or Short

Protect: the two outlier rules disagreeing and the bulk-order investigation (4.2 demo steps 5 to 7), the survey table with n beside rows (step 11), the catalog_weights lab, freezing a normal and asking it questions (4.3 demo steps 3 and 4), the central limit theorem table (step 9), one confidence interval with its coverage check (steps 10 and 11), and the first step of each lesson project.

Running long, cut in this order: (1) 4.2 demo step 4 (standardizing: one sentence) and step 8 (describe(): point at the lesson's table); (2) price_satisfaction in the room (all of it goes home; show the solution's table for one minute instead); (3) 4.3 demo step 6 (the simulation check) and step 8 (overdispersion: say it, show the two numbers from the lesson); (4) the binomial step shortened to the frozen object and sf(4); (5) lines_per_order_ci in the room. Never cut the central limit theorem or the coverage check: Session 12 stands on them.

Running short: do the dice version of the central limit theorem physically, run a debug handout as a whole-room hunt, do the Predict items together, then let learners continue the Store Profile Sheet to Step 3 (the flagged days) and ask them to guess what the flagged days are before Step 4.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 12: Correlation and Hypothesis Tests

How to teach the session that turns description into claims. Before the break learners measure how two columns move together, choose between Pearson and Spearman, and take apart a correlation of 0.88 between staffing and revenue that points to exactly the wrong decision. After the break they ask whether a difference could be chance: they build a test by shuffling, read a p-value correctly, and report every test with an effect size and a confidence interval. Lesson 4.4 contains no hypothesis tests; they begin after the break.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 4.4–4.5 Session 12 of 21

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm as every session: Frame → Live demo (you type, they type along) → Guided lab (the kit's lab files) → Start the lesson project. The lesson's exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • Type, do not paste. Every code block in the demo scripts is what to type, one notebook cell per step, in the course project folder. Every output shown was produced by running that code with the course environment (pandas 3.0, SciPy 1.18, statsmodels 0.15).
  • Keep the halves apart. Lesson 4.4 describes association and never tests it: if a learner asks "is 0.46 significant?" before the break, write the question on the board and answer it after. In 4.5, never let a p-value appear without an effect size and an interval, in your own speech included.
  • Words matter more than code today. Write the definition of the p-value on the board before class and point at it every time someone reads a p-value out loud.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep statistics_correlation_analysis.html and statistics_hypothesis_testing.html open for the figures (the four scatter panels, the heatmap, the staffing diagram, the pooled and like-with-like scatters, the shuffle histogram, the power curve) and the tables (choosing Pearson or Spearman, the five explanations, what a p-value is not, the test chooser).
  • Teal = hands-on, amber = watch-outs. Labs for this session live in labs/module-12/: starters for learners, solutions for you.
The risk of Session 12: confident misreadings

Nothing in today's code is hard. The danger is in the sentences: "r = 0.88, so more staff sell more", "p = 0.03, so there is a 3% chance the stores are the same", "p = 0.57, so they are the same", "p = 0.003, so it is a big problem". Each one sounds right, and learners will hear all four in their working lives. Spend the session on the sentences. Two board rules carry it: every correlation gets the question "how did this data come to be?", and every p-value travels with an effect size and a confidence interval. Never phrase a p-value as the probability that a hypothesis is true, including in passing; learners copy the instructor's wording. Second risk: the session ends Module 4's teaching, and Session 13 opens with a checkpoint. Announce it clearly at the wrap-up so nobody is surprised.

Before Session 12

  • ☐ Run the lab check from the kit folder: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-12. Eight lines should say PASS.
  • ☐ Copy the starters and the two debug handouts (*_starter.py, debug_*.py) from labs/module-12/ to the shared folder. Keep every *_solution.py on your machine.
  • ☐ Projector machine: Jupyter (or VS Code notebooks) opened in the course project folder; font size at least 18 pt.
  • ☐ Files used today: data/daily_sales.csv, data/store_weather.csv, data/products.csv, data/order_items.csv, data/survey.csv, data/orders.csv (and data/customers.csv for the lesson's null-result example). No servers to start, no accounts, nothing new to install: scipy and statsmodels are in the course environment. Check once: python -c "import scipy, statsmodels; print(scipy.__version__, statsmodels.__version__)".
  • ☐ Whiteboard, written before learners arrive: on the left plot first · direction, form, strength · how did this data come to be?; on the right the definition p-value = the probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed.
  • ☐ Read the Session 13 plan from its author (lessons 4.6 A/B Testing and 4.7 the EDA workflow, with Checkpoint 1) so your wrap-up announcement matches: a short open-notebook checkpoint on Modules 1 to 4.
  • ☐ Known environment traps. (1) daily.corr() on a table with text raises a ValueError: select numeric columns or pass numeric_only=True. (2) np.corrcoef returns nan with missing values; pandas .corr() drops missing pairs silently, so print the n. (3) SciPy tests return nan with missing values. (4) stats.ttest_ind defaults to Student's test; always type equal_var=False. (5) Result objects print NumPy wrappers (np.float64(...)): format with f-strings. (6) permutation_test takes a few seconds; rng= is the keyword in current SciPy (older versions used random_state=). (7) A pearsonr result carries a .pvalue; in 4.4 use only .statistic.
  • ☐ Skim the Session 11 homework: the Store Profile Sheet (all 91 flagged days were weekends, promotions or December) and the Returns Forecast (capacity 4 a day; rate 1.56 with a CI of 1.47 to 1.65). Collect the "before the next lesson" predictions about staffing: they are the bridge into the staffing puzzle.
  • ☐ Sticky notes or slips of paper for the exit ticket.

The lesson pages estimate 95 + 110 = 205 minutes for a solo learner, the longest pair in the course, and the room has 150 after the warm-up, break and wrap-up. So this session protects the two ideas everything after it depends on (the confound, and the correct reading of a test) and sends the breadth home. Done in the room: the scatter-first habit, r from z-scores, Spearman, a correlation matrix, the staffing confound tested three ways, a first regression line, a permutation test built by hand, the p-value and what it is not, Welch with its interval and Cohen's d, significance against importance, one paired test, one chi-square test, one Mann-Whitney test, false alarms by simulation, the reviews_and_sales and returned_order_size labs, and the first steps of both projects. Goes home: the rest of both projects (Rain Check Steps 2 to 6; Does Rain Keep Shoppers Away? Steps 3 to 7), the unfinished labs, the exercises, Quick Quizzes and journals, and the reading-only parts: the heatmap code, Simpson's paradox (a simulated example), the regression cautions in full, permutation_test, the null chi-square result on loyalty tiers, the power curve and solve_power, the 30-test scan, and the assumption checks.
