Warm-up

0:00

Warm-up: Retrieval from Session 11

10 min
Timing
6mFive questions, no notes: answer alone on paper, compare with a neighbor, then one answer per question out loud
3mHomework check: the Store Profile Sheet, the Returns Forecast, the staffing prediction
1mBridge to today
Five retrieval questions (no notes, pairs, 60 seconds each)
  1. A column has a skewness of 1.5. Which center and spread do you report, and what do you draw first? Answer: Median and IQR (strongly skewed, long right tail), and a histogram first: skewness does not show humps.
  2. An outlier rule flags 4% of your rows. Which two questions do you ask before removing anything? Answer: Is it a provable error? Is it part of the question I am answering? Remove only provable errors, and say what you removed.
  3. You have a frozen distribution model. Which method gives P(X at most x), and which gives P(X more than x)? Answer: model.cdf(x) and model.sf(x).
  4. In one sentence: what does the central limit theorem say becomes normal? Answer: The distribution of the sample mean (not the data): centered on the population mean, with SD sigma / sqrt(n).
  5. A 95% confidence interval for the mean order total is $165 to $209. What does the 95% describe? Answer: The method: about 95 of 100 intervals built this way contain the true mean. It is not a range for 95% of orders.
Homework check

Show of hands: who found out what the 91 "weird days" in the Store Profile Sheet were? (All weekends, promotions or December days: kept.) Who has a capacity number from the Returns Forecast? (4 a day, exceeded on about 2% of days.) Then the bridge: "You were asked to predict whether stores take more revenue on days with more staff, and why that might be true even if adding staff did nothing. What did you write?" Collect two or three answers; somebody will say "busy days get more staff". Write it on the board and leave it: the 4.4 demo proves them right.

Bridge to today

Say: "Until now we described one column at a time. Today, two columns, and two of the most useful and most misused ideas in statistics. Before the break: do two things move together, and does that mean what it seems? After the break: could a difference be nothing but chance?"

Lesson Plans

4.4

Correlation Analysis

60 min
Timing
10mFrame: two dancers; plot first; direction, form, strength
25mLive demo: 11 short steps, ending with the staffing verdict and a regression line
20mGuided lab: reviews_and_sales, then the start of staffing_rule
5mStart the lesson project: the Rain Check, Step 1 (the merge)
Objectives (the lesson's own)
  • Read direction, form and strength from a scatter plot, and explain why the plot comes before the number
  • Compute Pearson and Spearman correlations with pandas and scipy, and choose between them
  • Build a correlation matrix and draw it as an annotated heatmap with Matplotlib
  • Identify a confounding variable and test for it by comparing like with like
  • Fit and interpret a simple regression line, and state what it does and does not tell you
Mental model to say

Say: "Watch two people on a dance floor. If they step forward and back together, they are positively correlated. If one steps forward whenever the other steps back, negatively. If each moves with no regard for the other, uncorrelated. Correlation measures how well their movements are synchronized. It says nothing about why: one may be leading, or both may be following the same music."

Write plot first on the board, and under it the three things to read from any scatter plot: direction, form, strength. Then the question that follows every correlation, which is the whole lesson: how did this data come to be? Tell the room up front that today's lesson has no p-values; "could this be chance?" is the second half of the session.

Live demo (you type, they follow)

New notebook session12_correlation.ipynb. The numbers are the lesson's own. Two steps are said, not typed (the list of explanations, and the heatmap, which the lab practices). If time runs short, cut step 4 to the printed matrix and step 6 to one sentence. Do not cut steps 5, 7 and 8: the staffing verdict is the lesson.

  1. Plot first (3m). New notebook. Say: "Every lesson so far looked at one column. Most real questions involve two. The first move with two numeric columns is always the same: a scatter plot." Read three things from it out loud: direction, form, strength. 
    import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import stats

daily = pd.read_csv("data/daily_sales.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
sales = daily.dropna(subset=["revenue"]).copy()
products = pd.read_csv("data/products.csv")
items = pd.read_csv("data/order_items.csv")
units_sold = items.groupby("sku")["quantity"].sum().rename("units_sold")
catalog = products.merge(units_sold, on="sku")   # products that sold
print(sales.shape, catalog.shape)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4), layout="constrained")
ax.scatter(sales["visitors"], sales["revenue"], s=6, alpha=0.3)
ax.set_xlabel("Visitors")
ax.set_ylabel("Revenue ($)")
fig.savefig("visitors_revenue.png", dpi=110)
    (2897, 8) (234, 14)
    A rising, straight, tight band. Then show the lesson's four-panel figure (visitors and revenue; price and units; price and rating; a perfect curve scored as 0) and say: "Two of these four are warnings. The number measures one specific thing, and you need the picture to know whether that is what your data is doing."
  2. What r is made of (3m). Say: "You already have the ingredients: z-scores. Multiply them row by row and average." Have the room predict whether the four routes agree. 
    x, y = sales["visitors"], sales["revenue"]
zx = (x - x.mean()) / x.std()
zy = (y - y.mean()) / y.std()
print("by hand        :", round((zx * zy).sum() / (len(x) - 1), 4))
print("pandas .corr() :", round(x.corr(y), 4))
print("np.corrcoef    :", round(np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1], 4))
print("scipy pearsonr :", round(stats.pearsonr(x, y).statistic, 4))
    by hand        : 0.9435
pandas .corr() : 0.9435
np.corrcoef    : 0.9435
scipy pearsonr : 0.9435
    Three properties follow: no units (try revenue in cents), symmetric, and not robust. Then the warning for the board: r is not a slope and not a percentage. 0.94 does not mean 94 cents per visitor. (pearsonr also carries a .pvalue; say "that is the next lesson's question" and move on.)
  3. Spearman: correlation of ranks (3m). Say: "Price against units sold. Obviously related, and it scores a feeble -0.32. It is just not straight." 
    price, units = catalog["price"], catalog["units_sold"]
print("Pearson         :", round(price.corr(units), 3))
print("Spearman        :", round(price.corr(units, method="spearman"), 3))
print("Pearson on ranks:", round(price.rank().corr(units.rank()), 3))
print("Pearson of logs :", round(np.log(price).corr(np.log(units)), 3))
    Pearson         : -0.319
Spearman        : -0.6
Pearson on ranks: -0.6
Pearson of logs : -0.628
    Spearman is Pearson on the ranks: it measures whether one goes consistently up as the other goes down, straight or not. When the two disagree, there is a curve or an influential point. Spearman's other home is ordinal data: overall satisfaction and the recommend score give 0.63 in the lesson. Habit for the board: compute both.
  4. Many pairs at once (2m). Say: "With more than two columns, compute every pair." 
    columns = ["visitors", "transactions", "units", "revenue",
           "staff_on_duty", "promo_day"]
corr = sales[columns].corr().round(2)
print(corr.rename(columns=lambda name: name[:6]))
                   visito  transa  units  revenu  staff_  promo_
visitors         1.00    0.97   0.96    0.94    0.93    0.32
transactions     0.97    1.00   0.99    0.98    0.90    0.37
units            0.96    0.99   1.00    0.99    0.89    0.36
revenue          0.94    0.98   0.99    1.00    0.88    0.37
staff_on_duty    0.93    0.90   0.89    0.88    1.00    0.32
promo_day        0.32    0.37   0.36    0.37    0.32    1.00
    Read it: diagonal of 1s, mirror image, so only one triangle matters. Then the important sentence: "A solid block of very high correlations is not five discoveries. It is one fact seen five ways: some days are busier. Look for the common driver." The lesson draws it as an annotated heatmap (imshow, a diverging colormap, scale fixed at -1 to 1); the lab has learners draw one.
  5. The staffing puzzle (3m). Say: "One cell deserves a closer look: staff and revenue, 0.88. Imagine it arriving on an executive's desk." 
    staff, revenue = sales["staff_on_duty"], sales["revenue"]
line = stats.linregress(staff, revenue)
print("r:", round(staff.corr(revenue), 3))
print("revenue with 4 staff:", round(revenue[staff == 4].mean()))
print("revenue with 8 staff:", round(revenue[staff == 8].mean()))
print("slope:", round(line.slope), "dollars per extra staff member")
    r: 0.882
revenue with 4 staff: 4759
revenue with 8 staff: 9109
slope: 1154 dollars per extra staff member
    Let the proposal write itself ("schedule more staff, sell more"), then ask the question that follows every correlation: how did this data come to be? The data dictionary: staff are "scheduled in advance". Draw the lesson's diagram: expected demand drives both staffing and visitors. A third variable that drives both is a confounder.
  6. The calendar moves both (2m). Say: "Check the story before you believe it." 
    sales["weekday"] = sales["date"].dt.day_name()
by_day = sales.groupby("weekday")[["staff_on_duty", "revenue"]].mean()
print(by_day.loc[["Tuesday", "Saturday"]].round(1))
print(sales.groupby("promo_day")[["staff_on_duty", "revenue"]]
      .mean().round(1))
              staff_on_duty  revenue
weekday                         
Tuesday             5.0   5716.1
Saturday            9.6  10932.9
           staff_on_duty  revenue
promo_day                        
0                    6.3   7211.7
1                   10.8  13950.5
    Saturdays have the most staff and the most revenue, Tuesdays the least of both; promotion days have 10.8 staff against 6.3. The schedule and the sales both follow the calendar.
  7. Test 1: compare like with like (3m). Say: "If staff raise revenue, then among days expected to be equally busy, the days with an extra person should still sell more." Explain transform as "the group's mean, written on every row". 
    sales["month"] = sales["date"].dt.to_period("M")
alike = sales.groupby(["store", "month", "weekday", "promo_day"])
sales["staff_dev"] = (sales["staff_on_duty"]
                      - alike["staff_on_duty"].transform("mean"))
sales["revenue_dev"] = sales["revenue"] - alike["revenue"].transform("mean")
print("groups:", alike.ngroups)
print("r, all days pooled       :", round(staff.corr(revenue), 3))
print("r, within comparable days:",
      round(sales["staff_dev"].corr(sales["revenue_dev"]), 3))
    groups: 768
r, all days pooled       : 0.882
r, within comparable days: 0.143
    From 0.88 to 0.14. Among comparable days, more staff than usual tells you very little about revenue.
  8. Tests 2 and 3 (3m). Say: "Two more angles. Hold visitors constant. And ask whether each visitor spends more on well-staffed days." 
    def residuals(target, predictor):
    fit = stats.linregress(predictor, target)
    return target - (fit.intercept + fit.slope * predictor)

staff_left = residuals(staff, sales["visitors"])
revenue_left = residuals(revenue, sales["visitors"])
print("partial r, controlling for visitors:",
      round(staff_left.corr(revenue_left), 3))
print("r, staff and spend per visitor     :",
      round(staff.corr(revenue / sales["visitors"]), 3))
    partial r, controlling for visitors: 0.068
r, staff and spend per visitor     : 0.032
    Put the verdict table on the board: 0.88 pooled, 0.14 like with like, 0.07 holding visitors constant, 0.03 with spend per visitor. Three checks agree. Then the honest limit: this does not prove staffing has no effect (no day in the data is badly understaffed). Observational data can rule a simple story out; to rule one in you need an experiment, which is Lesson 4.6.
  9. Correlation is not causation, in a list (1m). Write the lesson's five explanations for any correlation on the board without code: A causes B; B causes A; a confounder causes both; selection; chance. Ask which ones apply to staffing. Reverse arrow (expected revenue causes the schedule) and confounder (the calendar). Chance is ruled out by 2,897 days; selection by how the file was built.
  10. A first regression line (3m). Say: "Correlation tells you how tightly points follow a line. Regression tells you which line." 
    fit = stats.linregress(sales["visitors"], sales["revenue"])
print("slope    :", round(fit.slope, 2))
print("intercept:", round(fit.intercept, 2))
print("r squared:", round(fit.rvalue ** 2, 3))

predicted = fit.intercept + fit.slope * sales["visitors"]
leftover = sales["revenue"] - predicted
print("predicted for 400 visitors:", round(fit.intercept + fit.slope * 400))
print("typical miss:", round(leftover.std()))
    slope    : 21.19
intercept: -107.93
r squared: 0.89
predicted for 400 visitors: 8367
typical miss: 1081
    Read every number in units: about $21 more revenue per extra visitor, on average; the intercept only positions the line (no day is near zero visitors); visitors account for 89% of the variance. Three cautions: do not extrapolate beyond 125 to 1,164 visitors; the line from revenue to visitors is a different line; a slope is not a causal effect (the $1,154 per staff member was a correct slope and almost entirely confound).
  11. Two mistakes on purpose (2m). Say: "Two that give a clean-looking answer." 
    print(np.corrcoef(daily["visitors"], daily["revenue"])[0, 1])

u = pd.Series(np.arange(-5, 6))
print(u.corr(u ** 2))
    nan
0.0
    First: six missing revenues and NumPy returns nan; pandas drops missing pairs. Second: a perfect curve scores 0. r near zero means no linear relationship; only the scatter plot can say there is none.
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Reading r as a slope or a percentage. "r = 0.94, so 94 cents a visitor" or "r = 0.5, half related". Coach: "r measures how tightly the points hug a line, not how steep it is. For the slope, fit the line. For 'how much does it account for', square r." Have them print r ** 2 for 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9.
  • Reading a correlation as a cause. The staffing proposal is the example everyone will make in real life. Coach with the five explanations on the board and one question: "Was either variable decided by someone using information related to the other?" Then: "Does it survive comparing like with like?"
  • Trusting r without the picture. r = 0 for a curve, nan from np.corrcoef with a missing value, or a ValueError from daily.corr() on a table with text. Coach: "Show me the scatter plot." For the errors: use pandas .corr() (which drops missing pairs and says nothing, so print the n), and select numeric columns or pass numeric_only=True.
Guided lab

First 12 minutes, everyone: labs/module-12/l4_4-correlation-analysis/reviews_and_sales_starter.py (reference: labs/module-12/l4_4-correlation-analysis/reviews_and_sales_solution.py). Marketing claims "products with more reviews sell more". Learners plot first (the starter asks for one sentence per panel before any number), then Pearson and Spearman, a Spearman matrix and heatmap saved to OUTPUT, and a partial correlation holding price constant. Expected: reviews and units 0.456 and 0.442; rating and units about 0; price -0.319 and -0.600; partial 0.424. Debrief with the direction question: "Which way could the arrow run?" (Sales produce reviews.)

Last 8 minutes: labs/module-12/l4_4-correlation-analysis/staffing_rule_starter.py, Steps 1 and 2: a regression line that recovers the managers' scheduling rule (1.59 staff per 100 visitors, r 0.925) and its typical miss. Steps 3 to 5 go home; Step 4's prediction (is the reversed line just 1 / slope?) is a good opener for Session 13.

Early finishers: labs/module-12/l4_4-correlation-analysis/debug_correlation_claims.py: four claims about r, all wrong.

Start the lesson project

The lesson's project is The Rain Check (about 40 minutes alone, in lesson_4_4_project): does rain keep shoppers away, once you compare like with like? In the room do Step 1 only: merge the weather into the sales with left_on=["date", "store"], right_on=["date", "city"], how="left" and check the row count: 2,903 before, 2,903 after, 0 missing weather. Tell them where it goes: the pooled correlation looks weak (about -0.19), and comparing like with like doubles it. The same merged table starts the 4.5 project after the break, so everyone should leave this step with it working. Steps 2 to 6 are homework.

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold call, then pair-share):

  1. "Pearson says -0.32 and Spearman says -0.60 for the same two columns. What do you suspect, and what do you look at?" Answer: A consistent relationship that is curved (or an influential point). Look at the scatter plot, perhaps on log axes.
  2. "r = 0.88 between staff and revenue. Name two explanations other than 'staff cause revenue'." Answer: A confounder (expected demand, the calendar, drives both) and the reverse arrow (expected revenue decides the schedule).
  3. "The line says $21 of revenue per extra visitor and the intercept is -$108. Does a store with no visitors lose $108?" Answer: No. No day is anywhere near zero visitors; the intercept only positions the line. Do not interpret it, and do not extrapolate.

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6 (do two in the room if time allows; the rest is homework):

Answers: Q1 B) Products with more reviews tend to have sold more; the arrow may run from sales to reviews, and the data alone cannot say; Q2 -1.0; Q3 C) Subtract each group's mean (same store, month, weekday and promotion status) from both columns with groupby().transform("mean"), then correlate the deviations; Q4 D) 1-to-5 overall satisfaction and the 0-to-10 recommend score; Q5 the line accounts for 25% of the variance; Q6 A) A slope describes how revenue differs across days with different staffing, not what changing the staffing would do; here it is mostly the calendar acting on both. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: give learners the five explanations for a correlation on a card and have them sort each example from the demo onto it. For like-with-like, do it first with four rows on the board (two Saturdays, two Tuesdays): subtract each group's mean by hand, then correlate. transform("mean") is then just "the group mean written on every row".

Stretch: lesson Exercise 4 (a reusable partial_corr function: staff and revenue controlling for visitors, and the reverse), or the lab extension: the reviews-units link within each category (groupby("category")). Does it hold everywhere?

4.5

Hypothesis Testing

90 min
Timing
15mFrame: the courtroom; the Asheville question; the four steps of every test
35mLive demo: 12 short steps from a test built by hand to false alarms and power
25mGuided lab: returned_order_size, then Step 1 of footwear_returns
15mStart the lesson project: Does Rain Keep Shoppers Away?, Steps 1 and 2
Objectives (the lesson's own)
  • Explain the logic of a hypothesis test in plain words, and say what a p-value is and what it is not
  • Build a permutation test by simulation and match it to SciPy's ready-made tests
  • Choose and run a one-sample, Welch two-sample or paired t-test, a chi-square test, or a rank-based test for the data in front of you
  • Report every test with an effect size and a confidence interval, and check its assumptions on the data
  • Describe Type I and Type II errors and power, and correct for multiple comparisons
Mental model to say

Say: "A court starts from 'innocent until proven guilty'. It does not ask the defendant to prove innocence. It asks whether the evidence would be surprising if the defendant were innocent. If it would be very surprising, the court rejects innocence. If not, the verdict is 'not guilty', which is not the same as 'proven innocent'. A hypothesis test works the same way. The starting assumption, the null hypothesis, is 'nothing is going on: any difference is chance'. Then you ask how surprising your data would be if that were true."

Write the two verdicts on the board: reject the null and fail to reject the null (never "accept"). Then say why this lesson matters more than any other in the module: "The p-value is the most misread number in statistics. By the end of today you will read it correctly, and you will never report one alone."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

New notebook session12_tests.ipynb. The numbers are the lesson's own; the two simulations use default_rng(42) created inside their cells, so they reproduce on every machine. Step 4 is said, not typed. If time runs short, say step 7 in one sentence and show step 10's numbers from the lesson page; never cut steps 2 to 6 (the test built by hand, the p-value, Welch with its interval and effect size).

  1. The question (3m). New notebook. Say: "Head office noticed that Asheville shoppers give a lower recommend score. Before anyone schedules a meeting about Asheville: could that gap be luck?" 
    import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats

survey = pd.read_csv("data/survey.csv")
in_store = survey[survey["store"] != "Online"]
is_ash = in_store["store"] == "Asheville"
asheville = in_store.loc[is_ash, "recommend"].dropna()
others = in_store.loc[~is_ash, "recommend"].dropna()

for name, g in [("Asheville", asheville), ("Other stores", others)]:
    print(f"{name:<12} n = {len(g)}  mean = {g.mean():.2f}"
          f"  sd = {g.std():.2f}")
observed = asheville.mean() - others.mean()
print(f"Observed difference: {observed:.3f}")
    Asheville    n = 197  mean = 6.98  sd = 2.05
Other stores n = 752  mean = 7.34  sd = 2.04
Observed difference: -0.357
    About a third of a point on an eleven-point scale, with answers spread about 2 points either side. Is 0.36 a lot? Looking will not tell you. You need to know how big a gap chance alone produces with groups of this size.
  2. Build chance yourself: shuffle the labels (4m). Say: "If the store makes no difference, the 'Asheville' label is a sticker that could have landed on anyone. Peel off all 949 stickers, shuffle, stick them back, measure the gap. Ten thousand times." 
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
pooled = np.concatenate([asheville, others])
n_ash = len(asheville)
shuffled_diffs = np.empty(10_000)
for i in range(10_000):
    shuffled = rng.permutation(pooled)
    shuffled_diffs[i] = shuffled[:n_ash].mean() - shuffled[n_ash:].mean()

print(shuffled_diffs[:5].round(3))
print(f"typical chance gap (SD): {shuffled_diffs.std():.3f}")
    [-0.03   0.034 -0.216  0.277  0.124]
typical chance gap (SD): 0.165
    Each number is a gap between two groups that cannot truly differ. Their spread, about 0.165, is a standard error measured by simulation: Session 11's idea, for a difference. The real gap is a little more than two of those from zero. Show the lesson's histogram with the real gap marked in the tail.
  3. Count: the p-value (3m). Say: "How often did chance produce a gap at least this large, in either direction?" 
    as_extreme = np.abs(shuffled_diffs) >= abs(observed)
print(as_extreme.sum(), "of 10,000 shuffles gave a gap at least this large")
print(f"p-value = {as_extreme.mean():.3f}")
    300 of 10,000 shuffles gave a gap at least this large
p-value = 0.030
    Write the definition on the board and leave it there all session: the p-value is the probability, if the null hypothesis were true, of a result at least as extreme as the one observed. Then the four steps of every test: state what "nothing going on" means; work out what that produces; see where the real result falls; report how rare it is. Vocabulary: H0, H1, alpha = 0.05 chosen before looking, "reject" or "fail to reject" (never "accept").
  4. What a p-value is not (2m). Read the lesson's table aloud, no code. Have learners say "no" out loud to each. "There is a 3% chance the null is true": no, p is computed assuming the null. "97% chance Asheville is worse": no, same mistake turned around. "The gap is large": no, p mixes effect size with sample size. "p = 0.20 means the stores are the same": no, not detected is not absent. And 0.049 against 0.051 is the same evidence: report the number.
  5. The shortcut: Welch's t-test (3m). Say: "For a difference in means there is a classic shortcut: the difference divided by its standard error, read off the t distribution. Welch's version does not assume equal variances. SciPy's default does, so type equal_var=False every time." 
    res = stats.ttest_ind(asheville, others, equal_var=False)
ci = res.confidence_interval(confidence_level=0.95)
print(f"t = {res.statistic:.2f}, df = {res.df:.0f}, p = {res.pvalue:.3f}")
print(f"95% CI for the difference: {ci.low:.2f} to {ci.high:.2f}")
    t = -2.17, df = 305, p = 0.030
95% CI for the difference: -0.68 to -0.03
    The same p as the shuffle: one by simulation, one by theory. The interval is the more useful half: Asheville is between 0.68 and 0.03 points lower. It excludes 0, which is the same fact as p below 0.05, and it shows what p cannot: the true gap might be meaningful or almost nothing.
  6. How big? Cohen's d (2m). Say: "A p-value never travels alone. It comes with an effect size and an interval." 
    def cohens_d(x, y):
    nx, ny = len(x), len(y)
    pooled = (((nx - 1) * np.var(x, ddof=1) + (ny - 1) * np.var(y, ddof=1))
              / (nx + ny - 2))
    return (np.mean(x) - np.mean(y)) / np.sqrt(pooled)

print(f"Cohen's d = {cohens_d(asheville, others):.2f}")
    Cohen's d = -0.17
    Near 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large: this is small. Say the honest sentence: "Asheville shoppers rated Pinecrest 0.36 points lower on average (95% CI 0.03 to 0.68 lower; Welch p = 0.030; d = -0.17, small)." Evidence worth following up, nowhere near a crisis.
  7. Significant is not the same as important (2m). Say: "Now the opposite case. Target score 7.5, all 1,746 answers." 
    everyone = survey["recommend"].dropna()
res1 = stats.ttest_1samp(everyone, popmean=7.5)
ci1 = res1.confidence_interval()
print(f"n = {len(everyone)}, mean = {everyone.mean():.2f}")
print(f"p = {res1.pvalue:.4f}")
print(f"95% CI {ci1.low:.2f} to {ci1.high:.2f}, "
      f"d = {(everyone.mean() - 7.5) / everyone.std():.2f}")
    n = 1746, mean = 7.36
p = 0.0028
95% CI 7.27 to 7.45, d = -0.07
    A smaller p than Asheville's and a tiny shortfall (d = -0.07). With 1,746 answers even a small miss is detectable. Write on the board: statistically significant = unlikely to be chance alone; practically significant = big enough to matter. The first is a calculation, the second a judgment.
  8. Pairs: the same days, two stores (3m). Say: "Bend against Flagstaff, visitors, on the same dates. Watch the verdict change with the test." 
    daily = pd.read_csv("data/daily_sales.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
visitors = daily.pivot(index="date", columns="store", values="visitors")
pair = visitors[["Bend", "Flagstaff"]].dropna()
wrong = stats.ttest_ind(pair["Bend"], pair["Flagstaff"], equal_var=False)
right = stats.ttest_rel(pair["Bend"], pair["Flagstaff"])
print(len(pair), "days; mean difference",
      round((pair["Bend"] - pair["Flagstaff"]).mean(), 1))
print(f"as independent groups: p = {wrong.pvalue:.3f}")
print(f"as pairs             : p = {right.pvalue:.4f}")
    722 days; mean difference 6.5
as independent groups: p = 0.274
as pairs             : p = 0.0024
    Traffic swings from a February Tuesday to an August Saturday in both stores together. The independent test sees all that swing as noise; pairing by date subtracts it out. Real and small: about 6.5 visitors a day. Caveat to say once: consecutive days are not fully independent, so daily-data p-values are approximate.
  9. Categories: chi-square (3m). Say: "Means are for numbers. When both variables are categories, compare counts." 
    orders = pd.read_csv("data/orders.csv")
orders["returned"] = orders["status"] == "returned"
table = pd.crosstab(orders["channel"], orders["returned"])
chi = stats.chi2_contingency(table)
print(table)
print(f"chi-square = {chi.statistic:.1f}, df = {chi.dof}")
print(f"p = {chi.pvalue:.1e}")
print("smallest expected count:", round(chi.expected_freq.min(), 1))
rates = orders.groupby("channel")["returned"].mean()
print(f"online {rates['online']:.1%}, store {rates['store']:.1%}")
    returned  False  True 
channel               
online    11964    890
store      7195    253
chi-square = 109.7, df = 1
p = 1.1e-25
smallest expected count: 419.3
online 6.9%, store 3.4%
    The null: channel and returning are unrelated. The expected counts are the assumption check (about 5 or more in every cell; the smallest is 419). The effect: online orders come back twice as often (6.9% against 3.4%). Cramér's V is only 0.07 here, so for a 2 x 2 table report the rates and their ratio: that is what a reader can act on.
  10. Ratings: Mann-Whitney (3m). Say: "A t-test compares means, and a mean assumes equal steps between 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. For ratings, use ranks." 
    staff_ash = in_store.loc[is_ash, "sat_staff"].dropna()
staff_oth = in_store.loc[~is_ash, "sat_staff"].dropna()
mw = stats.mannwhitneyu(staff_ash, staff_oth)
print(f"n = {len(staff_ash)} and {len(staff_oth)}, p = {mw.pvalue:.1e}")
print("probability of superiority:",
      round(mw.statistic / (len(staff_ash) * len(staff_oth)), 2))
    n = 193 and 754, p = 3.0e-09
probability of superiority: 0.37
    This is the gap learners described in Session 11 (57.5% satisfied against 75 to 79%). Now it has a test: p about 3 in a billion. The effect size: pick one Asheville shopper and one other-store shopper at random; the Asheville rating is the higher one 37% of the time (50% would be no difference).
  11. False alarms, watched (3m). Say: "A test can be wrong two ways. Here is the first one, happening." Draw two groups from the same pool, so the null is true by construction. 
    rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
pool = in_store["recommend"].dropna().to_numpy()
p_null = np.array([
    stats.ttest_ind(rng.choice(pool, 197), rng.choice(pool, 752),
                    equal_var=False).pvalue
    for _ in range(2_000)])
share = (p_null < 0.05).mean()
print(f"{share:.1%} of 2,000 tests of a true null were significant")
    5.3% of 2,000 tests of a true null were significant
    About 5%, as alpha promises: one test in twenty rings the alarm when nothing is going on (a Type I error). The other way to be wrong is a miss (Type II); the chance of catching a real effect is power, and it depends on sample size: with 50 per group a small real effect (d = 0.2) is caught only 17% of the time. Then multiple comparisons in one line: 30 tests of true nulls give a 79% chance of at least one false alarm. The lesson's scan of 6 age groups x 5 items finds 6 "significant" results, 3 after Holm's correction. Count every test you ran.
  12. A mistake on purpose (1m). Say: "SciPy does not skip missing values." 
    raw = in_store.loc[in_store["store"] == "Asheville", "recommend"]
print(stats.ttest_ind(raw, others, equal_var=False).pvalue)
print(round(stats.ttest_ind(raw, others, equal_var=False,
                            nan_policy="omit").pvalue, 3))
    nan
0.03
    nan with no error. Fix: .dropna() first, or nan_policy="omit". Close with the reporting template from the lesson, on the board: what was compared (and n) · the estimate · its 95% CI · the test and p · the effect size in words · caveats (how the data were collected, how many tests).
Three mistakes to expect, and how to coach each
  • Reading the p-value as the probability that the null is true ("a 3% chance the stores are the same", "97% sure Asheville is worse"). Coach with one question every time: "What was assumed when p was computed?" Then have them rewrite the sentence starting with "If there were no difference, ...". The board definition stays up all session.
  • "Not significant" read as "no difference", and "significant" read as "big". Coach both with the effect size and the interval: "What does the confidence interval allow?" For a small sample show the lesson's pilot (10 answers, p = 0.82 for a real gap). For a huge sample show the target test (p = 0.003, d = -0.07). Two separate questions: is it chance? does it matter?
  • Silent mechanical errors. nan from a missing value (SciPy does not skip: .dropna() or nan_policy="omit"); stats.ttest_ind(x, y) without equal_var=False (Student's test, no warning); chi2_contingency on raw columns instead of a crosstab table; a paired test on two columns dropped separately (misaligned days); alternative="less" chosen after looking. Coach: "Read your call out loud and say what each argument means."

Expected: difference $25.54 (95% CI $15.29 to $35.79), p = 1.1e-06, d = 0.14, permutation p 0.0002; online only $23.85. The debrief is the point of the lab: real, and small. Ask a volunteer to read their report and the room to find any sentence that misreads p.

Last 10 minutes: labs/module-12/l4_5-hypothesis-testing/footwear_returns_starter.py, Step 1: the online table, the rates (14.4% against 4.8%) and the chi-square test with its expected counts. Steps 2 to 4 (stores, where nothing is detected; Holm; the report) go home.

Early finishers: labs/module-12/l4_5-hypothesis-testing/debug_test_report.py: five conclusions, five misreadings.

Start the lesson project

The lesson's project is Does Rain Keep Shoppers Away? (about 40 minutes alone, in lesson_4_5_project). In the room do Steps 1 and 2: the same merge as the Rain Check plus days["rainy"] = days["precip_in"] >= 0.10 (rainy-day shares: Asheville 0.24, Bend 0.07, Boise 0.09, Flagstaff 0.14), then the table of visitors by store and rain. Before anyone runs a test, everyone writes the hypotheses and alpha as a comment, exactly as the lesson shows; walk the room and read them. Steps 3 to 7 (one store completely, a permutation check, all four stores with Holm, the seasonal challenge, the written finding) are homework.

Checks for understanding

Ask these out loud during the demo and the lab (cold call, then pair-share):

  1. "Finish the sentence: a p-value of 0.03 means that, if ..." Answer: "... there were no real difference, a result at least this extreme would turn up in about 3% of samples." Not the probability that the null is true.
  2. "Bend and Flagstaff visitor counts on the same 722 dates. Which test, and why?" Answer: A paired t-test (ttest_rel): the days pair one to one, and pairing removes the shared swing of the calendar.
  3. "You ran 30 tests and 6 came out below 0.05. What do you do before reporting any of them?" Answer: Correct for multiple comparisons (Holm), report how many tests were run, and label scanned findings as exploratory.

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12 (do two in the room if time allows; the rest is homework):

Answers: Q7 A) In a world where the store makes no difference, about 3% of shuffles produced a gap at least as large as the real one; Q8 D) A Mann-Whitney U test; Q9 nan; Q10 C) It is below 0.05; Q11 B) We could not detect a difference with this sample; it is too small to say much; Q12 23%. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: keep the four steps of a test and the definition of the p-value on the board, and have learners say the four steps for each test in the demo. Give anyone overwhelmed by the menu of tests the lesson's decision chart on paper (category outcome? rating? one group against a target? the same units twice? otherwise Welch). Reassure the room that the permutation test is always available: if a formula feels like magic, shuffle.

Stretch: lesson Exercise 5 (simulate the power of a Mann-Whitney test at 25, 50, 100 and 200 answers per group), or extend Lab 4.5-B: in the store result, how large a difference could the data have missed? (A confidence interval for a difference in proportions, or a power calculation.)

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, on paper or sticky notes, no notes)
  1. Staff on duty and revenue correlate at r = 0.88. Give two explanations other than "more staff cause more revenue". Answer: A confounder (expected demand, the calendar, drives both) and the reverse arrow (expected revenue decides the schedule). Selection and chance also count as explanations in general.
  2. Complete the sentence: "A p-value is the probability of ______, assuming ______." Answer: "... a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true." It is not the probability that the null is true.
  3. Besides the p-value, which two numbers belong in every test report? Answer: An effect size (how big?) and a confidence interval (how sure, and how big it could be).

Read the slips before Session 13. Question 2 is the one to watch: any answer that turns the p-value into the probability of a hypothesis means the learner needs the "What a p-value Is Not" table again before the A/B-testing lesson, which leans on it. Session 13's author can open with it if several miss it; pass on the count.

Homework (about 2 to 3 hours)
  • Lesson 4.4 project: finish the Rain Check (Steps 2 to 6): look, measure two ways, compare like with like, the effect in visitors, the finding with its limits.
  • Lesson 4.4 practice: Exercises 1 to 3 (Exercise 4 is a stretch), the Quick Quiz, and the journal prompt.
  • Lesson 4.5 project: finish Does Rain Keep Shoppers Away? (Steps 3 to 7), ending with a written finding in the reporting template.
  • Lesson 4.5 practice: Exercises 1 to 4 (Exercise 5 is a stretch), the Quick Quiz, and the journal prompt. Reread the "What a p-value Is Not" table tomorrow.
  • Kit labs: finish staffing_rule (Steps 3 to 5) and footwear_returns (Steps 2 to 4).
  • Workbook: the 12 self-check items and anything left in Predict, then run.

  • Prepare for the Session 13 checkpoint: a short open-notebook task on Modules 1 to 4 (NumPy, pandas, Matplotlib, statistics). Tidy your lesson notebooks so you can find things, and skim the key ideas pages of this workbook from Session 1 on. No memorizing needed: it is open-notebook.
Bring list for Session 13
  • Session 13 includes Checkpoint 1: a short open-notebook analysis task on Modules 1 to 4 (about 30 minutes inside the session). Learners bring their lesson notebooks from Modules 1 to 4 and this workbook; they may use them, the lesson pages and the documentation. Not graded on speed.
  • Their cohens_d function and the reporting template (Lesson 4.6 uses both), and their note on which test they would use for ab_test.csv.

If You Run Long or Short

Protect: the staffing confound tested like with like (4.4 demo steps 5 to 8), the permutation test and the definition of the p-value (4.5 steps 2 to 4), Welch with its interval and effect size and the significant-is-not-important contrast (steps 5 to 7), the returned_order_size lab with its "real and small" debrief, the merge that starts both projects, and the Session 13 checkpoint announcement.

Running long, cut in this order: (1) 4.4 step 4 (the matrix: show the lesson's heatmap instead) and step 11 (the two mistakes: one sentence each); (2) staffing_rule in the room; (3) 4.5 step 8 (the paired test: show the two p-values from the lesson and say why they differ); (4) 4.5 step 10 (Mann-Whitney: one sentence and the result, since learners know the gap from Session 11); (5) footwear_returns in the room. Never cut the p-value definition, the effect size, or the exit ticket.

Running short: run both debug handouts as whole-room hunts (one sentence per conclusion, the room votes on what is wrong), then let learners continue the 4.5 project to Step 3 (Asheville in full) and read their reports aloud against the template.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 13: A/B Testing and the EDA Workflow

How to teach the session that closes Module 4: one real experiment from the plan written before launch to the ship decision, a seven-step routine for data nobody has explained to you, and a 30-minute checkpoint in which learners run that routine alone.

2 lessons + checkpoint 3 hrs session Lessons 4.6–4.7 Session 13 of 21

How to Use This Guide

  • This is the last session of Module 4 and the fullest of the course: two lessons and Checkpoint 1 in 180 minutes. The lesson blocks are 60 and 55 minutes instead of the usual 75 to 80. The guide says exactly what is typed in the room, what is shown from the lesson page, and what goes home.
  • Same rhythm as every session, compressed: Frame (goal and mental model) → Live demo (you type, they follow) → Guided lab (new practice from the kit) → Start the project (five minutes: the brief and the first cell). Then the checkpoint.
  • Type, don't paste, with one stated exception (the 55-test scan in the 4.7 demo). Every code block below was run on the course data; the gray block under it is the real output.
  • Labs for this session live in labs/module-13/: starters for learners, solutions for you. Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs.
  • Keep statistics_ab_testing.html and statistics_eda_workflow.html open in browser tabs for the diagrams and the three charts you show but do not type (the daily p-value chart, the six bar panels, the heatmap of gaps).
The #1 risk of Session 13: the clock

The lesson pages estimate 100 + 110 = 210 minutes for a solo learner. After the warm-up, the break, the checkpoint and the wrap-up the room has 115. The checkpoint is fixed at 2:15: do not let the EDA lab run into it. If you are behind at the break, shorten the 4.7 demo (see "If You Run Long"), never the checkpoint. The second risk is tone: a checkpoint in the last hour makes some learners tense from 0:00. Say in the first minute that it is practice for the capstone, that it is open notebook, and that it is not graded.

Before the Session

  • ☐ From the instructor-kit/ folder run python3 labs/check_labs.py module-13. Expect 14 passed, 0 failed (six lab pairs and the checkpoint pair).
  • ☐ Copy the starter files only to the shared folder: labs/module-13/l4_6-ab-testing/*_starter.py, labs/module-13/l4_7-eda-workflow/*_starter.py and labs/module-13/checkpoint-1/checkpoint1_starter.py. Keep every *_solution.py on your machine; checkpoint1_solution.py is the checkpoint's model answer.
  • ☐ Files used today, all in data/: ab_test.csv, survey.csv, customers.csv, orders.csv, order_items.csv, products.csv, daily_sales.csv. No servers, no internet, no accounts.
  • ☐ Projector machine: two empty notebooks, session13_ab.ipynb and session13_eda.ipynb, in the folder that holds data/. Font 18 pt or larger. Run the statsmodels import cell once before class: the first import takes several seconds.
  • ☐ Board, before learners arrive: the six plan lines (unit, primary metric, guardrail, hypotheses, sample size, decision rule) on the left; the seven EDA steps on the right; between them "A failed health check means STOP" and "Missing for WHOM?".
  • ☐ Print or share the Checkpoint 1 task sheet (it is in the workbook) and decide how files are handed in. Have a visible 30-minute timer ready.
  • ☐ Read the model answer and the seven weak answers in the Answer Key before class. Five minutes now saves twenty when marking.
  • ☐ Skim the Session 12 homework: the Rain Check and "Does Rain Keep Shoppers Away?" projects, and the Lesson 4.5 note that asked which test fits ab_test.csv. The warm-up uses it.
Known environment traps

statsmodels missing or old. from statsmodels.stats.proportion import confint_proportions_2indep fails on a very old statsmodels. The course pins 0.15: python -m pip install -r requirements.txt inside the course environment fixes it. Wrong working folder. FileNotFoundError: data/ab_test.csv means the notebook is not next to the data/ folder; the labs do not have this problem (they find the data through labs_paths). A chart window that blocks. In a plain terminal plt.show() waits for the window to close; in the checkpoint tell terminal users to savefig instead. NaN from SciPy. stats.ttest_ind returns nan if either input contains a missing value: today that is a learning moment in the checkpoint, not an environment fault. Do not fix it for them.

Warm-up

0:00

Warm-up: Retrieval from Session 12

10 min
Timing
6mFive retrieval questions on paper, no notes, then answers by show of hands
3mHomework check and the bridge to today
1mToday's roadmap and the checkpoint, said plainly
Five retrieval questions (Lessons 4.4 and 4.5)
  1. Across store-days, staff on duty and revenue correlate at r = 0.88. Give one reason this does not mean "add staff, sell more". Answer: Staff are scheduled from expected demand (weekday, season, promotions), and expected demand also drives revenue: a confounder. Comparing like with like (same store, month, weekday, promo status) the correlation falls to 0.14.
  2. For the same two columns Pearson's r is -0.32 and Spearman's is -0.61. What does the gap tell you? Answer: The relationship is consistent in direction but curved (or one influential point is distorting Pearson). Spearman works on ranks, so it measures any monotonic trend. Plot it.
  3. Finish the sentence: "A p-value is the probability of ... assuming ..." Answer: ...a result at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true. It is not the probability that the null is true, and it says nothing about the size of the effect.
  4. Which test: (a) the mean of two independent groups of different sizes; (b) whether two categorical columns are related? Answer: (a) Welch's t-test, stats.ttest_ind(x, y, equal_var=False). (b) Chi-square on a table of counts, stats.chi2_contingency(pd.crosstab(a, b)). Hold on to (b): today's first test is the same test in another form.
  5. You run 20 tests at alpha = 0.05 and one comes back with p = 0.04. What do you say about it? Answer: About one false alarm is expected from 20 tests when nothing is going on. Count every test, correct (Holm), and call a scanned result exploratory.
Homework check and bridge

Ask who finished the two rain projects and what number they would give a store manager (rainy days have about 20% fewer visitors: -18% to -26% by store). Then the Lesson 4.5 note: "You were asked to look at ab_test.csv and write down which test compares conversion between the two variants. What did you write?" (Chi-square on the two-by-two table, or a two-proportion test: the same test. Today's first half is that test with everything that has to happen around it.)

Roadmap, said plainly: "Two lessons and one checkpoint. Before the break, an experiment from plan to decision. After the break, a routine for data you have never seen. At 2:15, thirty minutes on your own with a small question: open notebook, not graded, practice for the capstone."

Watch-outs
  • Question 3 is the one most rooms get wrong ("the probability the null is true"). Do not move on until someone has said "assuming the null is true" aloud. Today's peeking and scanning both depend on it.
  • Someone missed Session 12: pair them now. They need p-values, Welch's t-test and the idea of multiple comparisons; point them at Lesson 4.5's "A Template for Reporting Any Test" and do not re-teach.

Lesson Plans

4.6

A/B Testing

60 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Write an experiment plan that names the metric, the unit, the sample size and the decision rule before any data are collected
  • Calculate the sample size for a conversion test with statsmodels power functions
  • Check that randomization worked, then run a two-proportion test and report the difference with its confidence interval
  • Explain why peeking inflates false alarms and why segment results are exploratory
  • Use a guardrail metric and practical significance to turn a result into a written recommendation
Timing inside the block (60 minutes)
10mFrame and mental model
25mLive demo, steps 1 to 12
20mGuided lab: novelty check
5mStart the Decision Memo project
Mental model to say

"Imagine sorting a crowd into two rooms by flipping a coin for each person. Tall people, impatient people, people on phones, people who were going to buy anyway: every kind ends up split about evenly, including kinds you never thought to measure. The rooms are alike in everything except what you do to them next. So if they behave differently afterward, either the treatment did it or chance did, and last session taught you how to judge chance."

Bridge from Session 12: "Last time rain and visitors: we had to work hard to argue that rain itself was responsible, because rain comes with seasons. An experiment removes that weakness by design. It does not make the statistics optional. Most of what goes wrong in A/B testing goes wrong AROUND the test."

Then put the six-line plan on the board and leave it there all session: Unit (a visitor who reaches checkout) · Primary metric (conversion per visitor) · Guardrail (order value, revenue per visitor) · Hypotheses (two-sided, alpha 0.05) · Sample size and duration (computed, then fixed) · Decision rule (ship if conversion is significantly higher and the guardrail holds). Ask: "Why two-sided when everyone hopes the page is better?" (A new page can be worse, and you would need to know.)

Live demo (you type, they follow): the checkout experiment, plan to decision

One notebook, session13_ab.ipynb, in the folder that holds data/. Twelve short cells. The clock is tight: the marked minutes add up to 25. If you are two minutes behind at step 6, say steps 2 and 9 instead of typing them.

  1. Imports and the sample size (3m). Say: "Before any data exists, four ingredients: the baseline, the smallest lift worth catching, alpha and power. statsmodels wants the two rates as ONE number, Cohen's h." Type the imports once; they serve the whole demo. 
    import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
from statsmodels.stats.power import NormalIndPower
from statsmodels.stats.proportion import (proportion_effectsize, proportions_ztest,
                                          confint_proportions_2indep)

baseline, target = 0.089, 0.100
h = proportion_effectsize(target, baseline)
n_per_arm = NormalIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=h, alpha=0.05, power=0.80)
print(f"Cohen's h = {h:.4f}")
print(f"Visitors needed per arm: {n_per_arm:,.0f}")
    Cohen's h = 0.0376
Visitors needed per arm: 11,092

    Ask before running: "More or fewer than 2,000 per arm?" Most rooms guess far too low. "Conversion is yes-or-no. Each visitor carries very little information."

  2. Small lifts cost time (1m). Say: "The checkout page gets about 1,000 visitors a day. Watch the days column." 
    for goal in [0.094, 0.100, 0.109]:
    h_goal = proportion_effectsize(goal, baseline)
    n = NormalIndPower().solve_power(effect_size=h_goal, alpha=0.05, power=0.80)
    print(f"detect 8.9% -> {goal:.1%}: {n:>7,.0f} per arm, "
          f"about {2 * n / 1000:>4.0f} days")
    detect 8.9% -> 9.4%:  52,187 per arm, about  104 days
detect 8.9% -> 10.0%:  11,092 per arm, about   22 days
detect 8.9% -> 10.9%:   3,492 per arm, about    7 days

    "Half a point takes three and a half months. The team planned for 1.1 points and rounded 22 days up to 28: four complete weeks, so every weekday is counted four times."

  3. Load and check the unit (2m). Say: "The test has run. Before a single conversion: is this the experiment the plan describes?" 
    ab = pd.read_csv("data/ab_test.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
print("Rows:", len(ab), " unique visitors:", ab["visitor_id"].nunique())
print("Dates:", ab["date"].min().date(), "to", ab["date"].max().date(),
      f"({ab['date'].nunique()} days)")
print(ab["variant"].value_counts().to_string())
    Rows: 28000  unique visitors: 28000
Dates: 2025-09-08 to 2025-10-05 (28 days)
variant
treatment    14079
control      13921

    One row per visitor, 28 days. The arms are not equal: 14,079 against 13,921. "Is that a problem?" Let them argue for ten seconds.

  4. Health check 1: the split (2m). Say: "A fair coin rarely lands exactly half and half. binomtest asks whether THIS imbalance is more than a coin produces." 
    n_treat = int((ab["variant"] == "treatment").sum())
srm = stats.binomtest(n_treat, n=len(ab), p=0.5)
print(f"Treatment share: {n_treat / len(ab):.2%}")
print(f"p-value against a 50/50 split: {srm.pvalue:.3f}")
    Treatment share: 50.28%
p-value against a 50/50 split: 0.348

    "One of the rare places where you hope for a LARGE p-value." Write on the board: a failed check means stop, not adjust.

  5. Health check 2: balance (2m). Say: "Both arms should have the same mix of anything fixed before the visitor saw a page." 
    for col in ["device", "returning"]:
    mix = pd.crosstab(ab["variant"], ab[col], normalize="index").round(3)
    p_mix = stats.chi2_contingency(pd.crosstab(ab["variant"], ab[col])).pvalue
    print(mix.to_string())
    print(f"chi-square p = {p_mix:.2f}\n")
    device     desktop  mobile  tablet
variant                           
control      0.376   0.551   0.073
treatment    0.379   0.554   0.067
chi-square p = 0.11

returning  False  True 
variant                
control    0.652  0.348
treatment  0.646  0.354
chi-square p = 0.27

    About 55% mobile and 35% returning in both arms. "The experiment is healthy, so its results can be read."

  6. The primary result: counts first (2m). Say: "Now the planned analysis, run once. Counts before rates." 
    summary = ab.groupby("variant")["converted"].agg(
    conversions="sum", visitors="count", rate="mean")
print(summary.round(4))
c_c, n_c = summary.loc["control", ["conversions", "visitors"]]
c_t, n_t = summary.loc["treatment", ["conversions", "visitors"]]
rate_c, rate_t = c_c / n_c, c_t / n_t
print(f"\nDifference: {(rate_t - rate_c) * 100:+.2f} percentage points")
print(f"Relative lift: {rate_t / rate_c - 1:+.1%}")
               conversions  visitors    rate
variant                                 
control           1233     13921  0.0886
treatment         1412     14079  0.1003

Difference: +1.17 percentage points
Relative lift: +13.2%

    Stop here. "1.17 points AND 13.2%. Both true. Which will the head of e-commerce hear if you say 'conversion improved 13%'?" (From 9% to 22%.)

  7. The test and its interval (3m). Say: "Same pattern as last session: difference, divided by its standard error. proportions_ztest takes COUNTS, treatment first." 
    z, p = proportions_ztest([c_t, c_c], [n_t, n_c])
low, high = confint_proportions_2indep(c_t, n_t, c_c, n_c, compare="diff")
print(f"z = {z:.2f}, p = {p:.4f}")
print(f"95% CI for the difference: {low * 100:+.2f} to {high * 100:+.2f} points")
    z = 3.35, p = 0.0008
95% CI for the difference: +0.49 to +1.86 points

    "If the pages converted equally, a gap this large would turn up in fewer than 1 experiment in 1,000." Then break it on purpose: pass the rates [0.1003, 0.0886] instead of counts and show p = 0.98. "No error. A wrong number that looks fine."

  8. Wrap it in a function (2m). Say: "We will run this comparison on slices all afternoon. One function, one dictionary of everything worth reporting." Type it carefully; the lab and the project reuse it. 
    def compare_rates(df):
    """Treatment vs control conversion for the rows in df."""
    s = df.groupby("variant")["converted"].agg(["sum", "count"])
    c_c, n_c = s.loc["control"]
    c_t, n_t = s.loc["treatment"]
    r_c, r_t = c_c / n_c, c_t / n_t
    ci = confint_proportions_2indep(c_t, n_t, c_c, n_c, compare="diff")
    return {"visitors": int(n_c + n_t), "control": r_c, "treatment": r_t,
            "diff": r_t - r_c, "ci_low": ci[0], "ci_high": ci[1],
            "se": np.sqrt(r_c * (1 - r_c) / n_c + r_t * (1 - r_t) / n_t),
            "p": proportions_ztest([c_t, c_c], [n_t, n_c])[1]}

overall = compare_rates(ab)
for name in ["control", "treatment", "diff", "ci_low", "ci_high", "p"]:
    print(f"{name:<10}{overall[name]:.4f}")
    control   0.0886
treatment 0.1003
diff      0.0117
ci_low    0.0049
ci_high   0.0186
p         0.0008
  9. Statistical against practical (1m). Say: "The product team said half a point is the least worth having. Lay the interval next to that." 
    worthwhile = 0.005      # half a percentage point, from the plan
print("Whole interval above zero:", overall["ci_low"] > 0)
print("Whole interval above the worthwhile lift:", overall["ci_low"] > worthwhile)
    Whole interval above zero: True
Whole interval above the worthwhile lift: False

    "Real effect, probably worthwhile, size still uncertain. That sentence goes in the memo as a caveat."

  10. What a weekly peeker would have seen (3m). Say: "The plan said: analyze once, after day 28. Someone opens the dashboard every Monday. Predict: is the p-value below 0.05 after week 1?" 
    ab["week"] = (ab["date"] - ab["date"].min()).dt.days // 7 + 1
for wk in [1, 2, 3, 4]:
    r = compare_rates(ab[ab["week"] <= wk])
    print(f"after week {wk}: {r['visitors']:>6,} visitors   "
          f"control {r['control']:.2%}   treatment {r['treatment']:.2%}   "
          f"p = {r['p']:.4f}")
    after week 1:  7,018 visitors   control 8.20%   treatment 9.25%   p = 0.1188
after week 2: 14,083 visitors   control 8.82%   treatment 9.73%   p = 0.0622
after week 3: 21,043 visitors   control 9.12%   treatment 9.99%   p = 0.0308
after week 4: 28,000 visitors   control 8.86%   treatment 10.03%   p = 0.0008

    "After week 1 an impatient team abandons a page that works. Stopping at the first p below 0.05 is stopping at a lucky moment by construction." Quote the lesson's simulation, do not run it: 4.4% false alarms with one look, 12.2% with four looks, about 27% with daily looks. The day-by-day chart and the simulation are homework reading.

  11. Segments: handle with care (3m). Say: "Did it work for everyone? Same function, three slices." 
    by_device = pd.DataFrame({dev: compare_rates(g)
                          for dev, g in ab.groupby("device")}).T
show = ["control", "treatment", "diff", "ci_low", "ci_high"]
print((by_device[show] * 100).round(2))
print(by_device["p"].round(5).to_string())
mob, desk = by_device.loc["mobile"], by_device.loc["desktop"]
gap = mob["diff"] - desk["diff"]
gap_se = np.sqrt(mob["se"] ** 2 + desk["se"] ** 2)
p_gap = 2 * stats.norm.sf(abs(gap / gap_se))
print(f"\nDifference between the lifts: {gap * 100:.2f} points, p = {p_gap:.3f}")
             control  treatment  diff  ci_low  ci_high
desktop    11.73      12.00  0.27   -0.97     1.50
mobile      6.82       8.58  1.76    0.92     2.60
tablet      9.40      10.83  1.43   -1.24     4.13
desktop    0.67236
mobile     0.00004
tablet     0.29476

Difference between the lifts: 1.49 points, p = 0.049

    Let the room write the tempting headline first ("works on mobile, not on desktop"). Then three objections: nobody planned it; desktop's interval still contains +1.17; and the claim is about a DIFFERENCE, which needs its own test: p = 0.049, on the line, unplanned. "A lead, not a finding. The word for the memo is exploratory."

  12. The guardrail, on every visitor (1m). Say: "More orders that are each much smaller would not be a win. Buyers are not a randomized group, visitors are: count a non-buyer as $0." 
    ab["revenue"] = ab["order_value"].fillna(0)
rev_c = ab.loc[ab["variant"] == "control", "revenue"]
rev_t = ab.loc[ab["variant"] == "treatment", "revenue"]
res = stats.ttest_ind(rev_t, rev_c, equal_var=False)
print(f"Revenue per visitor: control ${rev_c.mean():.2f}, "
      f"treatment ${rev_t.mean():.2f}")
print(f"Welch p = {res.pvalue:.4f}")
    Revenue per visitor: control $7.90, treatment $8.94
Welch p = 0.0045

    "Conversion up, revenue per visitor up, guardrail holds: ship it. You write that memo in the project."

Three mistakes to expect
  • The raw difference as the effect size. Someone types solve_power(effect_size=0.011, ...) and gets 129,733 per arm. No error. Coach: "What does the documentation call that argument? Which function turns two rates into it?" (proportion_effectsize(target, baseline); the right answer is 11,092.) In the lab this shows up as a follow-up test that would take a year.
  • Rates instead of counts into the z-test. proportions_ztest([0.1003, 0.0886], [14079, 13921]) prints z = 0.024, p = 0.98. Coach: "Does your result reproduce the rates you printed a cell ago? What would 'a tenth of one conversion' mean?" The habit to teach: counts in, and check the output against the summary table.
  • Two p-values compared to declare a difference. "Week 4 is significant and weeks 1 to 3 are not, so it only worked in week 4." Coach: "Read me the four lifts, not the four p-values. Does any weekly interval exclude +1.17?" Then: "A claim about a difference needs a test of the difference." The lab is built on exactly this.
Guided lab (20 min)

Learners open labs/module-13/l4_6-ab-testing/novelty_check_starter.py; your reference is labs/module-13/l4_6-ab-testing/novelty_check_solution.py. The question is new: a product manager fears a novelty effect (a lift that was big in week 1 and has been shrinking), and a colleague reads the weekly table as "it only worked in week 4". compare_rates and describe are given.

  • Minutes 0 to 5, TODO 1 and 2. Walk the room. The week column is the demo's line; the trap is using <= (cumulative, the peeking table) instead of == (each week by itself). Expected weekly lifts: +1.05, +0.76, +0.80, +2.08 points; only week 4 has p below 0.05 (0.0026).
  • Minutes 5 to 12, TODO 3. Halves: +0.91 points (weeks 1 to 2) and +1.43 (weeks 3 to 4). Difference +0.52 points, standard error 0.70, p = 0.46. If someone subtracts the p-values, send them back to the demo's device cell.
  • Minutes 12 to 17, TODO 4. Everyone writes the sentence. Ask two learners to read theirs aloud. A good one: "Every week shows a positive lift and every weekly interval contains the overall +1.17. The late lift is not smaller than the early one (p = 0.46 for the difference), so there is no sign of a novelty effect. One week alone is too small to be significant."
  • Minutes 17 to 20, debrief. Two questions: "Why is week 4 significant alone and week 2 not?" (Chance plus 7,000 visitors per week: a week has little power.) "Was this check in the plan?" (No: exploratory, and say so.)
  • Fast finishers start labs/module-13/l4_6-ab-testing/followup_test_plan_starter.py (size a mobile-only confirmation test: 7,458 per arm, about 27 days, for 6.8% to 8.0%). It goes home for everyone else, with labs/module-13/l4_6-ab-testing/aa_test_starter.py as the stretch.
Start the lesson project (5 min)

Open the lesson page at "Project: The Decision Memo". Read the brief aloud (one notebook, one new segment question, a one-page memo to the head of e-commerce). Everyone creates lesson_4_6_project.ipynb and runs the Step 1 health-check cell: four printed lines ending Balance on returning: p = 0.27. Say what they will meet at home in Step 3: a colleague who reads two p-values (0.008 and 0.051) on opposite sides of 0.05. "You have just done the same thing with weeks." Steps 2 to 5 are homework; the memo is the point.

Checks for understanding

Workbook self-check, Q1 to Q6 (learners do them at home; use two as cold calls if time allows). Good cold calls: Q4 (the broken split) and Q6 (the memo sentence).

Answers: Q1 C) Groups that are alike in everything except the page, including things nobody measured; Q2 A) effect_size expects Cohen's h from proportion_effectsize(0.100, 0.089), not the raw difference in rates; Q3 1.17 0.132; Q4 D) Stop and find where the control visitors went: the experiment did not run as planned, so its results cannot be read; Q5 B) About 12%, because each look is another chance to cross the line by luck; Q6 C) The gain appears concentrated on mobile; the evidence that devices differ is borderline and exploratory, and worth a follow-up test. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: pair anyone who was shaky on p-values last session with a confident neighbor for the lab, and give them the sentence frame for TODO 4: "Every week ... The difference between the halves is ... so ...". They may skip step 2 of the demo notebook (the days table) and copy compare_rates from the lesson page instead of typing it. Stretch: followup_test_plan then aa_test; or the lesson's bonus challenge (find the per-look threshold that brings four looks back to 5%). Ask stretch learners: "Your follow-up plan uses the observed 8.6% as the target. Why is that optimistic?" (A test that crossed the line tends to overstate its effect.)

Break (1:10 to 1:20)

Leave the weekly peeking table on the projector. Over the break, open the second notebook and the Lesson 4.7 page, and tick nothing on the board yet.

4.7

An EDA Workflow

55 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Follow a seven-step exploratory data analysis (EDA) routine on an unfamiliar dataset, starting from written questions
  • Establish what one row means, which columns are keys, and which values are missing and why
  • Summarize single variables, pairs of variables and segments with the right table, chart or test for each
  • Tell a finding from a lead: correct for scanning many comparisons and check an obvious competing explanation
  • Write up findings, caveats and next questions so that someone else can act on them
Timing inside the block (55 minutes)
10mFrame and mental model
20mLive demo, steps 1 to 10
20mGuided lab: who pays for shipping?
5mStart the returns project
Mental model to say

"A good detective does not walk in and arrest the first person who looks nervous. They ask what they are trying to find out, secure the scene, note what is there and what is missing, examine each piece of evidence, look for connections, and write a report that separates what is established from what is suspected. Same order every time, because the routine is what stops them from overlooking the obvious."

Write the seven steps on the board, numbered, and leave room beside each for a tick: 1 Questions · 2 Structure · 3 Quality · 4 One variable · 5 Two variables · 6 Segments · 7 Findings and caveats. Draw the arrow from 7 back to 1. Say: "There is very little new syntax in this lesson. What is new is the order, and the judgment about what each result means. And in forty minutes you will do it alone, on the clock." (The checkpoint is a small run of this routine; saying so focuses the room.)

Connect to the first half: "Plan first, separate confirmed from exploratory, write it down. Same habits, without the luxury of a coin flip."

Live demo (you type, they follow): the customer survey in ten cells

A second notebook, session13_eda.ipynb. Tick each step on the board as you reach it. The marked minutes add up to 20. The lesson's two charts (six bar panels, the heatmap of gaps) are shown from the lesson page, not typed.

  1. Questions first (1m). Say: "The head of customer experience has budget for one or two projects. Before the file is open, what do we want to know?" Type the four questions as a comment (or have them on the board): 
    # 1. Which parts of the experience do customers rate lowest?
# 2. Which part is most closely tied to overall satisfaction and recommending?
# 3. Is any store or age group noticeably less satisfied, and with what?
# 4. Who answered? Can these responses speak for Pinecrest's customers in general?
  2. Structure: one function for every new table (3m). Say: "The most important fact about a table is its grain: what one row is. I want the same first look at every table, so I write it once." 
    import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats
pd.set_option("display.width", 150)

survey = pd.read_csv("data/survey.csv", parse_dates=["survey_date"])

def overview(df):
    """One row per column: type, missing values, distinct values and an example."""
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "dtype": df.dtypes.astype(str),
        "missing": df.isna().sum(),
        "missing_pct": (df.isna().mean() * 100).round(1),
        "unique": df.nunique(),
        "example": df.apply(lambda col: str(col.dropna().iloc[0])[:22]),
    })

print(survey.shape)
print(overview(survey))

store                     str        0  ...       5               Asheville

sat_selection         float64       53  ...       5                     5.0

sat_website           float64      472  ...       5                     3.0
recommend             float64       54  ...      11                     6.0
comment                   str      977  ...      26  Love this store. Will 

[12 rows x 5 columns]

    Read it aloud with them: response_id and customer_id have 1,800 distinct values in 1,800 rows (grain: one response per customer). Ratings are float only because of the gaps. Then point: "sat_staff 33.6% missing, sat_website 26.2%. Too many to be carelessness. Park it for one minute."

  3. Quality: impossible values, duplicates (1m). Say: "Quick checks first: anything outside its scale, any repeated row?" 
    items = ["sat_overall", "sat_selection", "sat_price", "sat_staff", "sat_website"]
print(survey[items + ["recommend"]].agg(["min", "max"]))
print("Fully duplicated rows:", survey.duplicated().sum())

  4. Quality: missing for whom? (3m). Say: "The useful question is never only 'how many are missing?' It is 'missing for WHOM?' Predict: who skipped the staff question?" 
    survey["shops"] = np.where(survey["store"] == "Online", "online", "in store")
missing_share = survey.groupby("shops")[items].agg(lambda col: col.isna().mean())
print(missing_share.round(2))

    "70% of online shoppers skipped the staff question. People left out the part of Pinecrest they do not use. So sat_staff is really 'what store shoppers think of the staff'. Fill those gaps with the average and you change who the analysis is about." Then the two silent mistakes, one line each: len(survey.dropna()) (295 of 1,800 left) and survey['sat_staff'].fillna(0).mean() (2.67 instead of 4.02).

  5. Quality: who is in the data? (2m). Say: "Question 4. The customer table can tell us who answered. validate makes pandas prove the relationship I believe in." 
    customers = pd.read_csv("data/customers.csv")
joined = survey.merge(customers[["customer_id", "loyalty_tier"]], on="customer_id",
                      how="left", validate="one_to_one")
who = pd.DataFrame({

    "all_customers": customers["loyalty_tier"].value_counts(normalize=True),

    "Silver and Gold are 54% of respondents and 42% of customers. Engaged customers answer surveys. That is a caveat for every sentence we write from here on."

  6. One variable at a time (2m). Say: "Ratings are ordinal: median and the share at each end, the mean as a convenient extra. Divide by the number who ANSWERED."

    "median": survey[items].median(),
    "mean": survey[items].mean().round(2),

})

    They will find Asheville staff (3.62), 18-24 price (2.80) and 65+ website (3.04). "You just ran 55 comparisons with your eyes. That is multiple testing, whether or not you call it that."

  9. Discipline 1: count the comparisons and correct (3m). Say: "Each group against everyone else, on each item, Mann-Whitney for ratings, then Holm." This is the one block today you may paste from the lesson page; read it line by line instead of typing it. 
    from statsmodels.stats.multitest import multipletests

rows = []
for seg in ["store", "age_group"]:
    for level in sorted(survey[seg].unique()):
        inside = survey[seg] == level
        for item in items:
            x = survey.loc[inside, item].dropna()
            y = survey.loc[~inside, item].dropna()
            rows.append({"group": level, "item": item, "n": len(x),
                         "gap": x.mean() - y.mean(),
                         "p": stats.mannwhitneyu(x, y).pvalue})
scan = pd.DataFrame(rows)
scan["p_holm"] = multipletests(scan["p"], method="holm")[1]
print(f"{len(scan)} tests, {(scan['p'] < 0.05).sum()} below 0.05 before "
      f"correction, {(scan['p_holm'] < 0.05).sum()} after")
top = scan.sort_values("p").head(4).round({"gap": 2, "p": 6, "p_holm": 4})
print(top.to_string(index=False))
    55 tests, 9 below 0.05 before correction, 4 after
    group        item   n   gap        p  p_holm
      65+ sat_website 291 -0.64 0.000000  0.0000
    18-24   sat_price 186 -0.57 0.000000  0.0000
Asheville   sat_staff 193 -0.47 0.000000  0.0000
    55-64 sat_website 210  0.21 0.000919  0.0478

    Nine before, four after. Three are the dark cells. The fourth: 55-64 year olds rate the website +0.21 higher. "Look at the size and at the cause: 'everyone else' includes the unhappy 65+ group. A side effect of how I built the scan. It does not go in the findings."

  10. Discipline 2: could something else explain it? (2m). Say: "Asheville's staff rating is the result most likely to lead to action, so challenge it. Maybe Asheville just has a different age mix." 
    in_store = survey[survey["store"] != "Online"]
staff_table = in_store.pivot_table(index="store", columns="age_group",
                                   values="sat_staff", aggfunc="mean")
print(staff_table.round(2))
