Boise       4.18   4.13   4.10   4.15   4.02  4.11
Flagstaff   3.85   4.11   4.05   4.05   3.94  4.09

    "Asheville is the lowest store in every age group. Age mix does not explain it. That does not prove the staff are the cause: it removes one competing explanation and leaves the finding standing." Close by showing the lesson's findings note on the projector: findings with numbers, caveats, next questions. Step 7 is what they do in the lab.

Three mistakes to expect
  • dropna() on the whole table. In the lab or the checkpoint someone drops every row with any gap. On the survey that leaves 295 of 1,800 responses. Coach: "How many rows did you have before and after that line? Which column does THIS question need?" (dropna(subset=[...]).)
  • A merge that multiplies rows. survey.merge(orders, on='customer_id') turns 1,800 rows into 9,230 and no message appears. Coach: "What is one row now? Say it out loud." Then: "What relationship did you expect? Put it in validate= and let pandas check." Summarize to one row per customer first, then merge.
  • The best of many comparisons reported as if it were planned. Learners will scan a table, find the biggest gap and write it up with its raw p-value. Coach: "How many groups did you look at before you chose that one?" The three-part fix: count, correct, call it exploratory, and look at the size of the gap, not only its p-value.
Guided lab (20 min)

Learners open labs/module-13/l4_7-eda-workflow/shipping_rules_starter.py; your reference is labs/module-13/l4_7-eda-workflow/shipping_rules_solution.py. Nobody at Pinecrest can find the shipping policy: the learners work the rule out of the data by running steps 1 to 7 on one column. Questions and the structure cell are given.

  • Minutes 0 to 4, TODO 1 (quality). The crosstab of channel by charge shows store orders never pay shipping (7,448 at 0.00). "So which rows are the question about?" Online only.
  • Minutes 4 to 7, TODO 2 (one variable). Online: 71.4% ship free, 21.4% pay 6.95, 7.2% pay 14.95.
  • Minutes 7 to 13, TODO 3 and 4 (two variables). The key move is goods = order_total - shipping_cost. If someone groups by order_total the threshold is blurred by the shipping itself: ask "What is included in order_total?" (It is in the data dictionary.) The min/max table gives it away: free orders start at exactly 75.00, the 6.95 orders stop at 74.96. The two-by-three table has zeros where a rule with no exceptions should.
  • Minutes 13 to 16, TODO 5 (segments). The 14.95 charge sits at 6% to 9% of orders in every size band: not tied to order size. "What could it be?" (Faster delivery, chosen by the customer: a hypothesis. No column records it.)
  • Minutes 16 to 20, TODO 6 (the note). Everyone writes findings and at least one caveat. Push on the caveat: "Did you READ the rule or INFER it?" Take one note on the projector and mark each sentence F (finding), C (caveat) or N (next question).
  • Goes home: labs/module-13/l4_7-eda-workflow/order_size_scan_starter.py (a 22-test scan with one survivor and a competing explanation; the best preparation for the capstone) and labs/module-13/l4_7-eda-workflow/customer_overview_starter.py (stretch).
Start the lesson project (5 min)

Open the lesson page at "Project: Why Do Orders Come Back?". Read the brief. Everyone creates lesson_4_7_project.ipynb, writes their own four questions in a Markdown cell before scrolling to the lesson's list, and runs the Step 2 cell (three tables, three grains: one row per order, per order line, per product). Tell them the project is 45 minutes at home and that Step 6 is where the finding is. Do not reveal it.

Checks for understanding

Workbook self-check, Q7 to Q12. Good cold calls: Q9 (who answered?) and Q12 (finding or caveat?).

Answers: Q7 B) Its grain: what one row represents, and which column identifies a row; Q8 0 2; Q9 D) Customers who answered, mostly online shoppers, rate the website 3.54; Q10 4 5; Q11 A) The one that survived, with the size of its gap, the number of comparisons, and the result of checking an obvious competing explanation; the other two are leads; Q12 B) Every respondent has placed an order, so customers who never ordered are not heard. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: in the lab, give the goods line to anyone stuck at minute 9 and let them spend their time on the tables and the note. For the scan in the demo, they follow on the lesson page instead of typing. Stretch: order_size_scan in the room, then the lab's next question ("do customers add items to reach $75.00?": look at the distribution of goods between 60 and 90). Ask stretch learners to say what an inner merge of orders and customers silently does (drops 739 orders from 150 closed accounts; customer_overview shows it).

Checkpoint 1

2:15

Checkpoint 1: analysis task on Modules 1 to 4

30 + 5 min
What it is

A 30-minute, individual, open-notebook analysis task on Modules 1 to 4: one small question on the course data that no lesson has worked, answered with the routine the learners have just practiced. It is formative. Nothing rides on the score; it tells each learner, and you, where they stand before the course turns to databases and the web, and it is a rehearsal for the capstone at one-tenth the size. The rubric uses the same four levels and the same row names as the capstone rubric in Lesson 8.1 (without the Reproducibility row), so the feedback carries forward.

The question (also on the task sheet in the workbook):

Checkpoint 1 question

Pinecrest's store buyers believe that December shoppers buy more expensive things. Finance wants a number before it plans next December's stock. Using data/daily_sales.csv: is the average price per unit sold (revenue ÷ units) higher in December than in the rest of the year? By how much, how sure are you, and is it the same in all four stores?

Why this question: it needs a derived column, a check for missing values, a fair comparison of two groups, a segment check, one chart and an honest note, and it has a second layer for strong learners (December is the peak of a winter plateau, so "December against the rest" understates the gap). It is not one of the four capstone questions and no lesson, project or exercise computes revenue per unit by month.

Run it in the room
  1. Before 2:15. Close the returns project notebooks. Each learner opens a NEW notebook (or the scaffold labs/module-13/checkpoint-1/checkpoint1_starter.py, which has the question, the load line and six empty headings). Workbooks open at the Checkpoint 1 task sheet.
  2. Rules, said once (1 minute). "Thirty minutes. Your own work. Open notebook means: your notes, your earlier notebooks, your helper functions, the lesson pages and the library documentation are all allowed. Your neighbor and AI assistants are not. I will answer questions about what the question means and about a crashing environment, not about method. A finished small answer beats an unfinished big one."
  3. 2:15 start. Put the clock and the question on the projector (the deck has a slide for it). Say: "The first three minutes are for the plan. No code yet."
  4. Time calls. At 3 minutes: "Plan written? Start coding." At 12: "You should have your column and your checks." At 20: "You should have your comparison. Make the figure." At 25: "Write the note now, even if the analysis is not finished. Say what you would do next." At 30: "Stop. Save."
  5. While they work. Walk once at minute 8 and once at minute 18 and write down, per learner, one thing you see (plan written or not; NaN handled or not; interval present or not). Those notes make the marking fast. Do not coach method. If someone is frozen at minute 10, say only: "What is one row? What would you compute for each row?"
  6. 2:45 hand-in. Learners save the notebook as checkpoint1_&lt;name&gt;.ipynb (or .py) and hand it in the way your course collects work (shared folder, email, USB stick). The note inside the notebook is the part you mark first. On paper is fine for the note if machines misbehave.
  7. 2:47 two-minute debrief. Show ONE thing from the model answer: the twelve monthly means (or the saved figure). Ask: "Who compared December with all other months? Look at January and February. What is hiding in 'the rest'?" Do not show the numbers of the full model answer if another group sits the checkpoint later; otherwise post the model answer after marking.
Mark it

Use the 5-row rubric in the Answer Key (4 levels, 20 points; Proficient in every row is 15). Budget five minutes per learner: read the note first, then scan the notebook for the plan, the missing-value handling, the interval and the figure. The Answer Key has the full model answer from a real run and seven common weak answers with what each reveals.

  • Marking in the room is realistic only for the Question-and-plan row (your walk at minute 8) and the Data-handling row (your walk at minute 18). Mark the rest afterward and return it at the start of Session 14, before the warm-up.
  • The numbers a correct answer contains: 2,897 usable store-days (6 dropped for missing revenue); December $44.95 against $41.65; difference $3.31 (+7.9%), 95% CI $2.97 to $3.65; Cohen's d = 1.33; gaps of $2.86 to $3.79 in the four stores. Mann-Whitney instead of Welch is equally acceptable; so is the ratio of sums ($45.06 against $41.53).
  • Return the rubric, not a grade. Circle one cell per row and write one sentence: the single change that would move the lowest row up a level. Anyone with a row at Beginning gets a two-minute conversation at the next break.
  • What to do with the results. If more than a third of the room has no interval or effect size, open Session 14's warm-up with a three-minute redo of the Welch cell from the model answer. If more than a third skipped the plan, start the Session 14 lab with "write the question first" as an explicit step. Note learners at Beginning in two or more rows: they are the ones to pair for support through Module 5 and to check on at the capstone's first milestone.

Accommodations: extra time is fine (let the learner finish during the wrap-up and hand in at 3:00); a learner who missed Session 12 may do the task with the Lesson 4.5 page open at "A Template for Reporting Any Test". A learner who is absent today does it at home on the honor system before reading any answers.

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, on a sticky note or in the chat; answers)
  1. Name two things you check about an A/B test before you look at a single conversion. Answer: Any two of: one row per unit (visitor_id is unique); the split is consistent with the design (stats.binomtest against 50/50: here p = 0.35); the arms are balanced on things fixed before the page was shown (device, returning). If a check fails: stop, do not adjust.
  2. "Significant on mobile, not significant on desktop." What is the right next step, and what word goes in the memo? Answer: Test the difference between the two lifts directly (here 1.49 points, p = 0.049) and correct for the slices. The word is "exploratory": the comparison was not planned.
  3. Write the first three steps of the EDA routine and say what "grain" means. Answer: Questions, structure, quality (then one variable, two variables, segments, findings and caveats). Grain: what one row of the table represents.
Homework (about 3.5 hours; the two projects first)
  • Lesson 4.6: finish the Decision Memo (Steps 2 to 5; write your own memo before reading the lesson's), Exercises 1 to 4 (5 is a stretch), the quiz and the journal. Read "The Peeking Problem" from the daily chart to the end, and "Common Mistakes".
  • Lesson 4.7: the returns project, all seven steps (about 45 minutes), Exercises 1 to 3 (4 is a stretch), the quiz and the journal. Read Step 7 of the lesson and compare your note with the lesson's only after writing yours.
  • Kit labs: labs/module-13/l4_6-ab-testing/followup_test_plan_starter.py and labs/module-13/l4_7-eda-workflow/order_size_scan_starter.py. Stretch: aa_test and customer_overview.
  • Keep: save compare_rates, overview and rate_by in a file of your own helpers. The capstone reuses them.
  • Workbook: self-check Q1 to Q12.
Bring list for Session 14 (Lessons 5.1 and 5.2: SQL from Python)

☐ data/pinecrest.db in your data folder (it came in the same zip as the CSV files; check with python -c "import sqlite3; print(sqlite3.connect('data/pinecrest.db').execute('SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders').fetchone())", which should print (20302,)). ☐ SQLAlchemy installed (it is in requirements.txt; check with python -c "import sqlalchemy; print(sqlalchemy.__version__)", which should print a 2.1 version). ☐ Your sketch, on paper, of how customers, orders, order_items and products connect: which column links each pair and which side is "one" (Lesson 4.7, "Before the Next Lesson"). ☐ Your helpers file. ☐ No SQL is assumed, no server to install, no account needed: SQLite ships with Python.

If You Run Long or Short

Long. The checkpoint starts at 2:15 whatever happens. Cut in this order: (1) 4.6 demo step 2 (the days table) and step 9 (the threshold): say them. (2) 4.7 demo step 7 (the correlation columns): say "0.43 to 0.58, nothing dominates". (3) 4.7 demo step 5 (who answered): show the output from the lesson page. (4) "Start the project" for 4.7 becomes one sentence and homework. (5) The 4.6 lab's TODO 4 sentence is written at home. (6) Last resort: the shipping lab stops after TODO 4 (the rule is found) and the note is homework. Never cut: the health checks, the interval, "missing for whom", the corrected scan, the checkpoint.

Short (a small or fast group). In 4.6 run followup_test_plan in the room and ask for the one-paragraph plan aloud. In 4.7 run order_size_scan after the shipping lab: its Step 3 (is June about tents?) is the best ten minutes of capstone preparation in the kit. If the checkpoint itself finishes early for some learners, their stretch is on the task sheet (is it the mix? use order_items and products). Do not start the debrief before 2:45.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 14: SQL from Python: Queries and Joins

How to teach the first SQL session: connect to a database from Python, ask one table for exactly what you need, pass values safely, then combine tables with joins, CTEs and CASE without losing or inventing a single row.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 5.1–5.2 Session 14 of 21

How to Use This Guide

  • Module 5 starts here. For most learners this is their first SQL, and both lessons are dense. Every idea has a pandas twin they already own: say the pandas version aloud whenever a query looks foreign.
  • Same rhythm as every session: Frame → Live demo (you type, they follow) → Guided lab (new practice from the kit) → Start the project. The lesson projects are finished at home.
  • Type SQL one clause per line and run it after each clause. Every code block below was run on the course data; the gray block under it is the real output.
  • Labs live in labs/module-14/: starters for learners, solutions for you. Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs.
  • Keep sql_database_connections.html and sql_complex_queries.html open in browser tabs for the flow diagrams, the join table and the recursion diagram.
The #1 risk of Session 14: results that are wrong and look right

In pandas a bad merge at least changes .shape in front of you. In SQL an inner join drops 739 orders, a fan-out triples revenue and a comparison with NULL skips 18,154 rows, all without a word. The habit to build all session: say the row count you expect before you run the query, then count. The second risk is safety: one learner will build SQL with an f-string out of habit. Stop the room when you see it.

Before the Session

  • ☐ From the instructor-kit/ folder run python3 labs/check_labs.py module-14. Expect 12 passed, 0 failed.
  • ☐ Copy the starter files only to the shared folder: labs/module-14/l5_1-database-connections/*_starter.py and labs/module-14/l5_2-complex-queries/*_starter.py. Keep every *_solution.py on your machine.
  • ☐ Files used today: data/pinecrest.db (3.5 MB, six tables) and, for the project checks at home, orders.csv, order_items.csv, products.csv. No server, no internet, no accounts: SQLite ships inside Python.
  • ☐ On the projector machine, and on any learner machine you can reach, run python -c "import sqlite3; print(sqlite3.sqlite_version)" and python -c "import sqlalchemy; print(sqlalchemy.__version__)". You need SQLAlchemy 2.x.
  • ☐ Projector: one empty notebook, session14_sql.ipynb, in the folder that holds data/. Font 18 pt or larger. Delete any old pinecrest_work.db in that folder so step 1 starts clean.
  • ☐ Board: on the left the running order FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT; on the right, covered until after the break, 739 · 1,058 · 609 · 8; across the top, "Say the row count before you run it."
  • ☐ Checkpoint 1 rubrics, marked, one sentence of advice each. They go back in the first two minutes.
  • ☐ Skim the Session 13 homework: the Decision Memo, the returns project (its finding, online footwear, is today's 5.2 project in SQL) and the paper sketch of the four tables.
Known environment traps

An old SQLite. RIGHT JOIN and FULL OUTER JOIN need SQLite 3.39 or later (Lesson 5.2 shows a rewrite that works everywhere); nothing in the demo or the labs needs them. A version below 3.25 means Session 15's window functions will not run: note the learner and get them a newer Python before then. A typo in the file name creates a new, empty database and the error arrives one line later as OperationalError: no such table: orders. Look for a stray small .db file and delete it. The wrong working folder gives the same message for the same reason. The labs avoid both (they find the data through labs_paths and open it read-only). database is locked: two notebooks hold the same working copy and one has an uncommitted write; commit or restart one kernel. Windows will not overwrite pinecrest_work.db while a connection to it is open (PermissionError on the shutil.copy line when rerunning): restart the kernel first. SQLAlchemy 2 refuses bare strings (ObjectNotExecutableError): wrap SQL in text(...).

Warm-up

0:00

Warm-up: Retrieval from Session 13

10 min
Timing
2mCheckpoint 1 rubrics back, one sentence to the room
6mFive retrieval questions on paper, no notes, then answers
2mHomework check and today's roadmap
Checkpoint 1 rubrics

Hand the rubrics back face down. One sentence to the room, chosen from what you saw when marking, for example: "Most of you had the right answer; fewer of you said how sure you were. An estimate without an interval is half an answer." If more than a third of the room had no interval or effect size, spend three warm-up minutes re-running the Welch cell from the model answer instead of questions 1 and 2. Individual conversations happen at the break.

Five retrieval questions (Lessons 4.6 and 4.7)
  1. Name three of the six lines of an experiment plan. Answer: Any three of: unit, primary metric, guardrail metric, hypotheses (two-sided, alpha), sample size and duration, decision rule.
  2. Conversion went from 8.86% to 10.03%. Say the lift two ways. Answer: +1.17 percentage points (absolute) and +13% (relative). Both are correct; always say which.
  3. Why is "stop the test the first time p is below 0.05" a problem? Answer: Each look is another chance to cross the line by luck. With weekly looks the false-alarm rate was about 12% instead of 5%; with daily looks about 27%.
  4. What does "grain" mean, and what is the grain of order_items? Answer: What one row represents. One product line on an order (45,490 rows for 20,302 orders). Today's joins live or die on this.
  5. Merging 1,800 survey rows with orders on customer_id gave 9,230 rows. What happened, and what guards against it? Answer: Each response was repeated once per order of that customer. Guard: summarize to one row per customer first, and state the relationship with validate=. In SQL the same trap is called fan-out, and you will see it turn $3.7 million into $10.3 million after the break.
Homework check and roadmap

Ask what the returns project found (online orders containing footwear are returned 14.4% of the time against 4.8%; in stores footwear makes no difference). "Keep that number. You will find it again today, in a different language." Ask one learner to describe the link between orders and order_items from their sketch.

Roadmap: "Every dataset so far arrived as a file. In most organizations the data lives in a database. Before the break: ask one table for what you need, safely. After the break: combine tables without losing or inventing rows."

Watch-outs
  • Questions 4 and 5 are the bridge to today. If the room is unsure about "grain", spend the extra minute now.
  • A learner who missed Session 13 does Checkpoint 1 at home on the honor system (task sheet in the Session 13 workbook). Nothing today depends on it.

Lesson Plans

5.1

Database Connections

75 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Open a SQLite database from Python, run a query through a cursor, and close the connection cleanly
  • Write SELECT queries that filter, sort, aggregate and group rows, and say which pandas operation each clause matches
  • Pass values into a query with parameters, and explain why building SQL with f-strings is dangerous
  • Use a SQLAlchemy engine with text(), and move data both ways with pd.read_sql and DataFrame.to_sql
  • Name the main things that change when the database is PostgreSQL instead of SQLite
Timing inside the block (75 minutes)
10mFrame and mental model
30mLive demo, steps 1 to 13
25mGuided lab: the staff report, then a safe stock lookup
10mStart the Store Scorecard: Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

"A CSV file is a photocopied binder. To find last March's returned orders you carry the whole binder to your desk and flip through every page yourself. A database is a library with a librarian at the desk. You hand over a request slip, 'returned orders, March, Boise store, sorted by total', and the librarian brings back only those pages. The request slip is written in SQL, and the librarian is the database engine."

Then the reassurance: "You already know the ideas. Filtering, sorting, grouping and merging are what you did in Module 2. Today you learn to say the same things in a second language. When a query feels foreign, translate it into pandas in your head." Put the SQL-to-pandas table (it is in the workbook) on the projector and leave it up through the break.

One line on the engine: "SQLite is a complete SQL database in a single file, with no server and no password, and it ships inside Python. Nearly everything you write today runs unchanged on PostgreSQL." Have learners take out the paper sketch of the four tables from their homework: it comes into play after the break.

Live demo (you type, they follow): from connection to DataFrame

One notebook, session14_sql.ipynb, in the folder that holds data/. Thirteen cells; the marked minutes add up to 30. Type SQL one clause per line and run after each new clause, so every error is one clause old. The SQLite version printed in step 1 will differ from machine to machine.

  1. A working copy, then connect (2m). Say: "First habit of this module: work on a COPY. Some lessons create tables and indexes, and the original must stay exactly as documented." 
    import shutil
import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

shutil.copy("data/pinecrest.db", "pinecrest_work.db")    # a private working copy
conn = sqlite3.connect("pinecrest_work.db")
print("SQLite library version:", sqlite3.sqlite_version)
    SQLite library version: 3.53.1

    Your version will differ. "A connection is an open line to the file. Everything goes through it." Mention once: connect never complains about a wrong file name; it creates an empty database.

  2. What is in there? (2m). Say: "Every SQLite database keeps a catalog of itself. This is your first SQL query: read it left to right." 
    tables = conn.execute(
    "SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table' ORDER BY name")
print([name for (name,) in tables])
for row in conn.execute("PRAGMA table_info(orders)"):
    print(row)
    ['customers', 'employees', 'inventory', 'order_items', 'orders', 'products']
(0, 'order_id', 'INTEGER', 0, None, 1)
(1, 'customer_id', 'INTEGER', 1, None, 0)
(2, 'order_date', 'TEXT', 1, None, 0)
(3, 'channel', 'TEXT', 1, None, 0)
(4, 'store', 'TEXT', 1, None, 0)
(5, 'status', 'TEXT', 1, None, 0)
(6, 'payment_method', 'TEXT', 1, None, 0)
(7, 'promo_code', 'TEXT', 0, None, 0)
(8, 'discount_pct', 'INTEGER', 1, None, 0)
(9, 'shipping_cost', 'REAL', 1, None, 0)
(10, 'order_total', 'REAL', 1, None, 0)

    Four old friends and two tables that exist only here: employees and inventory (today's labs live in those). Point at order_date TEXT: "SQLite has no date type. 2024-03-05 sorts correctly as text, so date filters still work."

  3. A cursor walks the rows (1m). Say: "Running a statement gives a cursor: a pointer that moves forward through the result. Rows are tuples." 
    cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("SELECT order_id, store, order_total FROM orders")
print(cur.fetchone())        # the next row
print(cur.fetchmany(2))      # the next two, as a list
print(len(cur.fetchall()))   # everything that is left
    (100001, 'Flagstaff', 434.9)
[(100002, 'Asheville', 278.9), (100003, 'Online', 75.9)]
20299

    1 + 2 + 20,299 = 20,302. "Once a row is fetched it is gone from the cursor."

  4. A helper so we can read results (2m). Say: "Reading tuples by hand gets old. pandas can run a query and hand back a DataFrame. This helper is all we need for an hour." 
    def show(sql, params=()):
    """Run a query and print the result as a table."""
    print(pd.read_sql(sql, conn, params=params).to_string(index=False))

show("SELECT order_id, order_date, store, status, order_total FROM orders LIMIT 3")
     order_id order_date     store    status  order_total
   100001 2024-01-01 Flagstaff completed        434.9
   100002 2024-01-01 Asheville completed        278.9
   100003 2024-01-01    Online completed         75.9
  5. Rows: WHERE (3m). Say: "WHERE is the boolean mask of SQL. Text in SINGLE quotes, equality is a single =, conditions join with AND, OR, NOT." Type it clause by clause; run after each new line. 
    show("""
    SELECT name, price, rating
    FROM products
    WHERE category = 'Tents'
      AND price < 250
      AND rating >= 4.5
""")
                                  name  price  rating
          Quillback Wayfinder Tarp 132.95     4.9
Quillback Alpenglow Tent Footprint  67.95     5.0

    Ask for the pandas version aloud: products[(products.category == 'Tents') & (products.price < 250) & (products.rating >= 4.5)]. "Same idea, new spelling." IN, BETWEEN and LIKE are homework reading.

  6. Order and top N (1m). Say: "Without ORDER BY the order of rows is not guaranteed, even if it looks stable today. ORDER BY with LIMIT is how SQL says top N." 
    show("""
    SELECT order_id, order_date, store, order_total
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    ORDER BY order_total DESC, order_id
    LIMIT 3
""")
     order_id order_date  store  order_total
   106479 2024-09-15 Online       4893.0
   114268 2025-06-24 Online       4184.9
   113836 2025-06-11 Online       4150.4

    "There is the $4,893 bulk order from Lesson 0.1, found without loading 20,301 other rows."

  7. Aggregates, and three kinds of COUNT (3m). Say: "An aggregate turns many rows into one value. The five you will use daily: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX." 
    show("""
    SELECT COUNT(*)                   AS orders,
           ROUND(SUM(order_total), 2) AS revenue,
           ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2) AS avg_order
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
""")
show("""
    SELECT COUNT(*)             AS all_rows,
           COUNT(phone)         AS with_phone,
           COUNT(DISTINCT city) AS cities
    FROM customers
""")
     orders    revenue  avg_order
  18762 3624306.27     193.17
 all_rows  with_phone  cities
     4850        4570      35

    "$3,624,306.27: the number you have computed with pandas since Module 2, answered by the engine in one row." Then the three COUNTs: rows, non-NULL values, different values (.nunique()). "Aggregates skip NULL the way pandas skips NaN."

  8. GROUP BY: one row per group (3m). Say: "Split, apply, combine: Lesson 2.4. The rule for SQL: every column in SELECT is either in the GROUP BY or inside an aggregate." 
    show("""
    SELECT store,
           COUNT(*)                   AS orders,
           ROUND(SUM(order_total), 2) AS revenue,
           ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2) AS avg_order
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY store
    ORDER BY revenue DESC
""")
        store  orders    revenue  avg_order
   Online   11604 2357984.45     203.20
    Boise    2502  443386.85     177.21
Flagstaff    1648  300580.35     182.39
     Bend    1650  284575.25     172.47
Asheville    1358  237779.37     175.10
  9. HAVING filters the groups (2m). Say: "Which stores have an average order above $180? HAVING is the answer; then watch me put the condition in WHERE instead." The last line is the wrong version; read the error aloud. 
    show("""
    SELECT store, ROUND(AVG(order_total), 2) AS avg_order
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY store
    HAVING AVG(order_total) > 180
    ORDER BY avg_order DESC
""")
conn.execute("SELECT store FROM orders WHERE AVG(order_total) > 180 GROUP BY store")
        store  avg_order
   Online     203.20
Flagstaff     182.39
OperationalError: misuse of aggregate: AVG()

    misuse of aggregate: "WHERE runs before the groups exist, so there is nothing to average yet." Draw the running order on the board: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.

  10. Parameters, and the wrong way demonstrated safely (4m). Say: "Real queries are rarely fixed text. The store comes from a dropdown, the name from a form. How the value gets into the query is the most important safety habit in this module." 
    def count_customers_unsafe(last_name):
    sql = f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE last_name = '{last_name}'"  # NO
    return conn.execute(sql).fetchone()[0]

def count_customers_safe(last_name):
    sql = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM customers WHERE last_name = ?"
    return conn.execute(sql, (last_name,)).fetchone()[0]

print(count_customers_unsafe("Soto"), count_customers_safe("Soto"))
sneaky = "nobody' OR '1'='1"
print(count_customers_unsafe(sneaky), count_customers_safe(sneaky))
    45 45
4850 0

    Write the SQL the unsafe function built on the board: WHERE last_name = 'nobody' OR '1'='1'. "The quote in the input closed the string early and the rest became SQL. That is SQL injection. Had this returned names and emails, the visitor would have the customer list." Leave the rule on the board: never f-string, .format, % or + a value into SQL.

  11. Writing: create, insert, commit (2m). Say: "Analysts mostly read. When you do write: placeholders again, executemany for a list, and commit to make it permanent." 
    conn.execute("""
    CREATE TABLE store_targets (
        store          TEXT NOT NULL,
        quarter        TEXT NOT NULL,
        target_revenue REAL NOT NULL,
        PRIMARY KEY (store, quarter)
    )
""")
targets = [("Boise", "2025-Q1", 720000.0), ("Bend", "2025-Q1", 505000.0)]
conn.executemany("INSERT INTO store_targets VALUES (?, ?, ?)", targets)
conn.commit()
show("SELECT * FROM store_targets")
    store quarter  target_revenue
Boise 2025-Q1        720000.0
 Bend 2025-Q1        505000.0
  12. A transaction is all or nothing (2m). Say: "Two inserts in one with conn: block. The second breaks the primary key. Predict: how many rows afterward, two or three?" 
    insert = "INSERT INTO store_targets VALUES (?, ?, ?)"
try:
    with conn:
        conn.execute(insert, ("Asheville", "2025-Q1", 390000.0))
        conn.execute(insert, ("Boise", "2025-Q1", 999999.0))    # duplicate key
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("IntegrityError:", e)
show("SELECT store, quarter FROM store_targets")
    IntegrityError: UNIQUE constraint failed: store_targets.store, store_targets.quarter
store quarter
 Bend 2025-Q1
Boise 2025-Q1

    Two. "The Asheville row was fine, and it was rolled back anyway." One warning: for sqlite3, with conn: ends the transaction; it does not close the connection.

  13. SQLAlchemy and pandas: the pattern you will keep (3m). Say: "sqlite3 speaks only to SQLite. SQLAlchemy gives one way to connect to any database, and it is what pandas prefers. Three pieces: an engine, text(), and :name parameters in a dictionary." 
    from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text

engine = create_engine("sqlite:///pinecrest_work.db")
query = text("""
    SELECT store, COUNT(*) AS returned
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = :status AND order_date >= :since
    GROUP BY store
    ORDER BY returned DESC
""")
with engine.connect() as sa_conn:
    returned = pd.read_sql(query, sa_conn,
                           params={"status": "returned", "since": "2025-01-01"})
print(returned)
rows = returned.to_sql("returns_2025", engine, if_exists="replace", index=False)
print("rows written:", rows)
           store  returned
0     Online       467
1      Boise        36
2       Bend        34
3  Flagstaff        30
4  Asheville        30
rows written: 5

    "Database to DataFrame with read_sql, DataFrame to table with to_sql. Change the engine URL and the same code talks to PostgreSQL." Warn: if_exists="replace" drops the table first. The PostgreSQL comparison table is homework reading.

Three mistakes to expect
  • A string where a tuple of parameters belongs. conn.execute("... WHERE store = ?", "Boise") raises ProgrammingError: Incorrect number of bindings supplied. The current statement uses 1, and there are 5 supplied. Coach: "How many characters in Boise?" Fix: ("Boise",) with the trailing comma. It appears in the lab's Step 3 on purpose.
  • An aggregate in WHERE (or a selected column that is neither grouped nor aggregated). The message is misuse of aggregate. Coach with the running order on the board: "Point to where WHERE runs. Do the groups exist yet?" SQLite silently allows the ungrouped-column version; PostgreSQL refuses. Hold them to the rule either way.
  • The f-string out of habit. They have built strings with f-strings for two courses, and one will do it in the lab "because the value comes from my own code". Coach: "What happens to that query when the store is called O'Malley's?" The rule has no exceptions for values. (For a column NAME, which a placeholder cannot carry, the lab shows the allowed-list check.)
Guided lab (25 min)

Two short labs on tables the lesson does not touch. Learners open labs/module-14/l5_1-database-connections/staff_report_starter.py first; your references are the matching _solution.py files. Both labs open the database read-only, so nothing a learner types can change it.

Start the lesson project (10 min)

Open the lesson page at "Project: The Store Scorecard". The brief: one parameterized report function for any store and any year, saved back as a table and checked against pandas. In the room, everyone does Step 1 (a fresh copy called scorecard.db and a SQLAlchemy engine; the six table names print) and Step 2 (the headline query with :store, :start, :end for Boise in 2025). On track: one row with 1320 orders, 672 customers and revenue 240660.6. Ask why the year is written as >= :start AND < :end. Steps 3 to 6 are homework.

Checks for understanding

Workbook self-check, Q1 to Q6. Good cold calls: Q3 (the bindings error) and Q6 (predict the rollback).

Answers: Q1 C) FROM, because the engine has to pick the table before it can filter, group or select; Q2 (3, 2, 6); Q3 A) Pass a one-item tuple: ("Boise",); Q4 B) AVG(order_total) > 190; Q5 D) conn.execute("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE store = ?", (store,)); Q6 0. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners new to SQL type less and read more: let them run the demo cells from the lesson page and spend the lab on the staff report only, with the SQL-to-pandas table open. Give them the first line of each query (SELECT ... FROM employees). Stretch: safe_lookup TODO 4, then save_summary in the room. Learners who know SQL from work: have them explain to a neighbor why with conn: did not keep the Asheville row, then try the lesson's bonus (describe_database(engine) with inspect).

Break (1:25 to 1:35)

Leave the SQL-to-pandas table on the projector. Over the break: uncover the four numbers on the board, and have the short Checkpoint 1 conversations with anyone who had a row at Beginning.

5.2

Complex Queries

75 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Choose between inner, left, right, full outer, cross and self joins, and predict how many rows each returns when keys do not all match
  • Use subqueries and common table expressions (CTEs) to break a hard question into named steps
  • Walk a hierarchy of any depth with a recursive CTE
  • Build categories and side-by-side counts with CASE, and combine results with UNION, INTERSECT and EXCEPT
  • Explain how NULL behaves in comparisons, and avoid the three bugs it causes most often
Timing inside the block (75 minutes)
10mFrame and mental model
30mLive demo, steps 1 to 12
25mGuided lab: revenue by brand, then stock against sales
10mStart the Returns Investigation: Step 1
Mental model to say

"Picture a stack of order cards and a stack of customer cards. A join goes through the order cards one at a time, finds the customer card with the same customer_id, and staples the two together into one wider card. Every kind of join is the same stapling. They differ only in what happens to a card that finds no partner: throw it away, or keep it with a blank where the partner would be."

Then uncover the four numbers on the board: 739 orders belong to 150 closed accounts that are not in customers · 1,058 customers have never ordered · 609 order lines use 6 discontinued SKUs that are not in products · 8 products have never sold. Ask learners to look at their paper sketch: which side of each link is "one" and which is "many"?

Say what is coming: "Three results today will be wrong with no error message. I will make each mistake on purpose so that you recognize it when it is yours." (An inner join that drops rows, a sum after a fan-out, a comparison with NULL.)

Live demo (you type, they follow): joins without losing or inventing rows

Continue in the same notebook under a new heading, with a NEW connection (step 1 replaces conn and show). Twelve cells; the marked minutes add up to 30. Before every join, ask the room for the row count they expect.

  1. A read-only connection (2m). Say: "This lesson only reads. A second way to protect the file, besides a copy: open it read-only and let the engine refuse." 
    import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

conn = sqlite3.connect("file:data/pinecrest.db?mode=ro", uri=True)

def show(sql, params=()):
    """Run a query and print the result as a table."""
    print(pd.read_sql(sql, conn, params=params).to_string(index=False))

conn.execute("DELETE FROM orders")
    OperationalError: attempt to write a readonly database

    "Exactly what you want from a connection you only mean to read with." A bonus: a typo in the file name is now an error instead of a new empty database.

  2. INNER JOIN: only the matches (3m). Say: "A join goes in FROM: the first table, then JOIN the second ON the condition that pairs the rows. Short aliases, and every column wears its alias." Before the second query: "20,302 orders. How many rows come through?" 
    show("""
    SELECT o.order_id, o.order_total, c.first_name, c.last_name, c.city
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    ORDER BY o.order_id
    LIMIT 3
""")
show("""
    SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders) AS orders_in_table,
           COUNT(*)                      AS rows_after_inner_join
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
""")
     order_id  order_total first_name last_name     city
   100001        434.9     Xavier  Madrigal  Phoenix
   100002        278.9       Aiko    Larkin     Bend
   100003         75.9     Kareem      Pike Missoula
 orders_in_table  rows_after_inner_join
           20302                  19563

    "739 orders vanished: the closed accounts. No error, no warning." The habit: count after every join, the way you checked `.shape` after a merge.

  3. LEFT JOIN keeps the unmatched (3m). Say: "LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the table named first. Where there is no partner, the other side is NULL." 
    show("""
    SELECT COUNT(*)                   AS all_rows,
           COUNT(c.customer_id)       AS with_customer,
           SUM(c.customer_id IS NULL) AS without_customer
    FROM orders AS o
    LEFT JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
""")
     all_rows  with_customer  without_customer
    20302          19563               739
  4. The anti-join: which ones are missing? (2m). Say: "Start FROM the table you care about, LEFT JOIN the other, keep the rows with nothing on the other side." 
    show("""
    SELECT c.loyalty_tier, COUNT(*) AS never_ordered
    FROM customers AS c
    LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id
    WHERE o.order_id IS NULL
    GROUP BY c.loyalty_tier
""")
    loyalty_tier  never_ordered
       Basic           1058

    1,058, all Basic (higher tiers are earned by spending). Tick the second board number.

  5. Three tables: choose the join one link at a time (3m). Say: "Revenue by category: orders to order_items to products. For each link ask: if a row has no partner here, do I still want it?" 
    show("""
    SELECT p.category,
           COUNT(*)                                 AS lines,
           ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS item_revenue
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    LEFT JOIN products AS p ON p.sku = i.sku
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
    GROUP BY p.category
    ORDER BY item_revenue DESC
""")
        category  lines  item_revenue
 Accessories  11080     567699.20
    Sleeping   3386     516302.45
       Tents   2110     447114.75
     Apparel   4554     435424.65
    Footwear   4142     391188.90
       Packs   3103     387082.35
Camp Kitchen   7298     367311.60
    Climbing   3157     272994.05
        Snow   2391     216940.15
         NaN    567      34228.25

    The last row has no category: 567 lines, $34,228.25 on discontinued SKUs. "Real revenue that an inner join would have silently dropped." The lab names it with COALESCE.

  6. The fan-out trap (3m). Say: "Total completed revenue, but I have joined the lines first." 
    show("""
    SELECT ROUND(SUM(o.order_total), 2) AS after_join,
           COUNT(*)                     AS rows_summed,
           COUNT(DISTINCT o.order_id)   AS orders
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.status = 'completed'
""")
show("""
    SELECT ROUND(SUM(order_total), 2) AS true_revenue
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
""")
     after_join  rows_summed  orders
10073626.41        41788   18762
 true_revenue
   3624306.27

    "$10.3 million instead of $3.7 million, and it looks plausible. Each order's total was added once per line." The rule for the board: sum a column at the level where it lives. Connect to Session 13: the survey merged with orders went from 1,800 rows to 9,230. Same trap.

  7. A table joined to itself (2m). Say: "manager_id holds the employee_id of another row in the same table. Two aliases, two roles." 
    show("""
    SELECT e.first_name || ' ' || e.last_name AS employee,
           e.title,
           m.first_name || ' ' || m.last_name AS manager
    FROM employees AS e
    LEFT JOIN employees AS m ON m.employee_id = e.manager_id
    ORDER BY e.employee_id
    LIMIT 5
""")
         employee                   title      manager
   Clara Soto Chief Executive Officer          NaN
 Tamar Kimura            VP of Retail   Clara Soto
  Arjun Silva        VP of E-commerce   Clara Soto
Elise Delgado        VP of Operations   Clara Soto
 Elena Mistry  Regional Manager, West Tamar Kimura

    "LEFT JOIN, so the CEO is not dropped. A self join reaches exactly one level up. Hold that thought."

  8. A query used as a table (2m). Say: "How many orders does a typical buyer place? Count per customer first, then summarize the counts." 
    show("""
    SELECT COUNT(*)                AS buyers,
           ROUND(AVG(n_orders), 2) AS avg_orders,
           MAX(n_orders)           AS most_orders
    FROM (
        SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS n_orders
        FROM orders
        GROUP BY customer_id
    ) AS per_customer
""")
     buyers  avg_orders  most_orders
   3942        5.15           41
  9. CTEs: name the steps (3m). Say: "Nested queries read inside out. WITH name AS (...) gives a step a name. Does the loyalty rule hold: Silver from $600, Gold from $1,500?" 
    show("""
    WITH spend AS (
        SELECT customer_id, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(order_total) AS total_spent
        FROM orders
        WHERE status = 'completed'
        GROUP BY customer_id
    )
    SELECT c.loyalty_tier,
           COUNT(*)                     AS customers,
           ROUND(MIN(s.total_spent), 2) AS lowest_spend,
           ROUND(MAX(s.total_spent), 2) AS highest_spend
    FROM spend AS s
    JOIN customers AS c ON c.customer_id = s.customer_id
    GROUP BY c.loyalty_tier
    ORDER BY lowest_spend
""")
    loyalty_tier  customers  lowest_spend  highest_spend
       Basic       1710          7.50         599.91
      Silver       1294        600.43        1499.56
        Gold        734       1502.00        7945.54

    "The rule holds exactly. And spend has ONE row per customer before it is joined to anything: that is the cure for fan-out."

  10. A recursive CTE walks the whole tree (3m). Say: "How many levels does the company have? A recursive CTE is SQL's loop: an anchor, UNION ALL, and a part that joins the table to the rows found last round." 
    ORG_CTE = """
    WITH RECURSIVE org (employee_id, name, level) AS (
        SELECT employee_id, first_name || ' ' || last_name, 1
        FROM employees
        WHERE manager_id IS NULL                  -- anchor: top of the tree
        UNION ALL
        SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name || ' ' || e.last_name, org.level + 1
        FROM employees AS e
        JOIN org ON e.manager_id = org.employee_id   -- reports of the last round
    )
"""
show(ORG_CTE + "SELECT level, COUNT(*) AS people FROM org GROUP BY level")
     level  people
     1       1
     2       4
     3       7
     4      14
     5       8
     6      21

    Trace two rounds aloud: the anchor returns Clara Soto at level 1; the recursive part finds the four people who report to her; it runs again on those four. "It stops when a round finds nobody." The lesson's path column (an org chart) is homework reading.

  11. CASE inside an aggregate (2m). Say: "CASE is SQL's if / elif / else. Put it inside SUM and you count only the rows that meet a condition." 
    show("""
    SELECT channel,
           COUNT(*)                                             AS orders,
           SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'returned' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS returned,
           ROUND(100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'returned' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)
                 / COUNT(*), 1)                                 AS return_pct
    FROM orders
    GROUP BY channel
""")
show("SELECT 890 / 12854 AS int_division, 100.0 * 890 / 12854 AS correct")
    channel  orders  returned  return_pct
 online   12854       890         6.9
  store    7448       253         3.4
 int_division  correct
            0 6.923915

    "Why 100.0 and not 100? An integer divided by an integer is an integer." This table is Step 1 of the project.

  12. NULL means unknown (2m). Say: "NULL is not zero and not an empty string. It is 'unknown', and any comparison with unknown is unknown. WHERE keeps a row only when the condition is TRUE." 
    show("""
    SELECT COUNT(*)                     AS all_orders,
           SUM(promo_code = 'TRAIL15')  AS trail15,
           SUM(promo_code <> 'TRAIL15') AS not_trail15,
           SUM(promo_code IS NULL)      AS no_code
    FROM orders
""")
show("""
    SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees
            WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees)) AS not_in,
           (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees AS e
            WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees AS x
                WHERE x.manager_id = e.employee_id))             AS not_exists
""")
     all_orders  trail15  not_trail15  no_code
      20302      359         1789    18154
 not_in  not_exists
      0          32

    "A condition and its opposite do not add up: 359 + 1,789 is not 20,302." And NOT IN with one NULL in the list returns nothing: zero instead of 32. "Ask of every filter on a column that can be empty: what should happen to the rows with no value?"

Three mistakes to expect
  • Not counting after a join. The query runs, a table appears, and nobody asks how many rows it should have. Coach before they run it: "Write the number you expect in a comment. Now run it." The lab's first step forces it (45,490 lines: 44,881 after the inner join, 45,490 after the left join).
  • Summing after a fan-out. In stock_vs_sales both sides are "many" and both sums inflate (154,470 units sold instead of 30,894; 3,693,132 on hand instead of 22,815). Coach: "What is one row after this join? At what level does quantity live?" The cure: aggregate each side to the grain you need first (a CTE), then join.
  • A filter on the right-hand table in WHERE, which undoes the LEFT JOIN, and its cousin = NULL. Listing every customer with their December 2025 orders, WHERE o.order_date >= '2025-12-01' after the left join keeps only 898 customers instead of 4,850, because the NULL order rows fail the comparison. Coach: "Which table is that condition about? Conditions on the right table of a left join go in the ON clause." And = NULL never matches: IS NULL.
Guided lab (25 min)

Learners open labs/module-14/l5_2-complex-queries/join_row_counts_starter.py. The buying team wants item revenue by brand for completed orders: three tables. The starter has a line for three row-count predictions; do not let anyone skip it.

  • Minutes 0 to 5, predictions and TODO 1. 45,490 lines; inner join to products 44,881; left join 45,490. Anyone who predicted correctly used the board number 609.
  • Minutes 5 to 12, TODO 2 and 3. The tempting inner join reports 3,602,058.10; the left join with COALESCE(p.brand, 'Discontinued') shows nine rows that add up to 3,636,286.35. "How much did the inner join lose?" 34,228.25, on 567 lines. Top brand: Wrenfield, 515,811.85.
  • Minutes 12 to 15, TODO 4 (the anti-join): six SKUs, led by APL-1033 at 11,432.85; all last sold in September 2024. TODO 5 (NOT EXISTS) is for fast finishers: Granite Fork has 3 unsold products.
  • Minutes 15 to 25, labs/module-14/l5_2-complex-queries/stock_vs_sales_starter.py, Steps 1 and 2 only. Everyone computes the two true totals (30,894 units sold in 2025; 22,815 on hand), then writes the tempting three-table join and sees 154,470 and 3,693,132. Stop the room: "By what factor is units sold off, and why exactly that factor?" (Five: each SKU has five inventory rows.) The CTE fix, Steps 3 to 5, is homework; show the shape of the answer from the solution file for thirty seconds.
  • Goes home: the rest of stock_vs_sales, and labs/module-14/l5_2-complex-queries/org_payroll_starter.py (a recursive CTE that carries each branch's head down the tree, plus three NULL checks) as the stretch.
Start the lesson project (10 min)

Open the lesson page at "Project: The Returns Investigation". Learners who finished the Lesson 4.7 project already know the ending (online footwear): say so, and say what is new. "Last week you found it with merges. This week you pin it down in SQL across four tables, and prove both routes agree." In the room: Step 1 (read-only connection, return rate by channel with conditional aggregation: online 6.9%, store 3.4%) and a read-through of Step 2's plan: why the CTE uses DISTINCT and why the link to products is a LEFT JOIN with COALESCE. Steps 2 to 6 are homework.

Checks for understanding

Workbook self-check, Q7 to Q12. Good cold calls: Q7 (count the rows) and Q10 (where did 18,154 orders go?).

Answers: Q7 B) 19,563; Q8 350.0; Q9 A) SELECT c.* FROM customers AS c LEFT JOIN orders AS o ON o.customer_id = c.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL; Q10 D) For the 18,154 orders with no code the comparison with NULL is unknown, and WHERE keeps only rows where the condition is true; Q11 (3, 3.5, 25); Q12 C) A round of the recursive part finds no new rows. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: pair anyone new to SQL with someone who is not, and let them stop after TODO 3 of join_row_counts; that lab alone covers the core skill. In the demo they may copy the recursive CTE from the lesson page. Stretch: finish stock_vs_sales in the room, then org_payroll. Ask: "Your CTE joins products to on_hand with an inner join and to sold with a left join. Why the difference?" (Every product has inventory rows; a product that never sold has no sold row and must still appear, with 0.)

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions; answers)
  1. In one sentence each: what does WHERE filter, and what does HAVING filter? Answer: WHERE filters rows before they are grouped (so it cannot mention an aggregate). HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY (so it can).
  2. Why do values go into SQL through placeholders and never through an f-string? Answer: With a placeholder the SQL text and the value travel separately, so a value can never be read as part of the command. An f-string pastes the value into the command: a quote in the input can change the query (SQL injection), and an honest name like O'Brien breaks it.
  3. orders has 20,302 rows and 739 have no matching customer. How many rows from orders JOIN customers, and how many from orders LEFT JOIN customers? Answer: 19,563 and 20,302. The inner join drops the unmatched rows silently; the left join keeps them with NULL on the customer side.

  • Lesson 5.2: the Returns Investigation, Steps 2 to 6 (about 40 minutes), Exercises 1 to 4 (5 is a stretch), the quiz and the journal. Read the sections on set operations and on RIGHT / FULL OUTER JOIN.
  • Kit labs: labs/module-14/l5_1-database-connections/save_summary_starter.py and Steps 3 to 5 of labs/module-14/l5_2-complex-queries/stock_vs_sales_starter.py. Stretch: labs/module-14/l5_2-complex-queries/org_payroll_starter.py.
  • Keep: your show() helper and the ORG_CTE string. Session 15 uses both.
  • Workbook: self-check Q1 to Q12.

If You Run Long or Short

Long. Cut in this order: (1) 5.1 demo step 3 (the cursor walk): say it, the lab practices it. (2) 5.1 step 6 (top N). (3) 5.1 step 11 becomes "here is a table I made earlier": keep the rollback in step 12. (4) 5.2 steps 7 and 8 (self join, query used as a table): say them. (5) The second lab of each block (safe_lookup TODO 3 and 4; stock_vs_sales) becomes homework. (6) "Start the project" shrinks to five minutes. Never cut: the injection demonstration, the 739 missing rows, the fan-out trap.

Short (a group that has used SQL before). Run save_summary in the room after the first lab block, and all of stock_vs_sales after the second. Add the lesson's set-operations cell (2024 and 2025 buyers: 3,942 either year, 2,488 both, 431 lost) to the 5.2 demo, and give org_payroll to pairs. Experienced learners can rewrite one demo query for PostgreSQL using the lesson's comparison table.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 15: SQL Windows and Query Speed

How to teach window functions (a row that can see its neighbors without giving up its place) and query optimization (reading the engine's plan and changing it with evidence), with every result checked by a second route.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 5.3–5.4 Session 15 of 21

How to Use This Guide

  • Two SQL lessons that look advanced and are not: window functions are the pandas transform, rank, shift, cumsum and rolling that learners already know, and query optimization is careful measuring. Say both of those things early.
  • Same rhythm as every session: Frame → Live demo (you type, they follow) → Guided lab (new practice from the kit) → Start the project. The lesson projects are finished at home.
  • Every code block below was run on the course data. Times in the 5.4 demo come from the author's machine: they are printed so you know the size of the effect, and yours will differ. Plans and row counts will not.
  • Labs live in labs/module-15/: starters for learners, solutions for you. Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs.
  • Keep sql_window_functions.html and sql_query_optimization.html open for the train picture, the frame table, the B-tree diagram and the seven-day moving-average chart (shown, not typed).
The #1 risk of Session 15: answers that are wrong in one row, and speed claims from one stopwatch reading

A missing PARTITION BY or the default frame with ties produces a table that is right in almost every row. Teach the three questions (partition, order, frame) until the room says them with you. In 5.4 the risk is the opposite kind: learners will believe a single timing. The kit never asserts a time; it asserts plans and identical results. Hold the room to the same standard.

Before the Session

  • ☐ From the instructor-kit/ folder run python3 labs/check_labs.py module-15. Expect 10 passed, 0 failed. (The 5.4 labs copy the database to a temporary folder; the checker fails any lab that touches data/.)
  • ☐ Copy the starter files only to the shared folder: labs/module-15/l5_3-sql-window-functions/*_starter.py and labs/module-15/l5_4-query-optimization/*_starter.py. Keep every *_solution.py on your machine.
  • ☐ Files: data/pinecrest.db only, untouched (check that it has no idx_ indexes: SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'index' should list only sqlite_autoindex_... entries). About 10 MB of free disk space per learner for working copies. No server, no internet, no accounts.
  • ☐ SQLite 3.25 or later on every machine for window functions: python -c "import sqlite3; print(sqlite3.sqlite_version)". The course Python bundles 3.53. Learners flagged in Session 14 with an old version need a newer Python before today.
  • ☐ Projector: two empty notebooks, session15_sql.ipynb and session15_tuning.ipynb, in the folder that holds data/. Delete any old pinecrest_tuning.db there. Close other heavy programs: timing demos are noisier on a busy laptop.
  • ☐ Board: a train car labeled PARTITION BY / ORDER BY / ROWS BETWEEN on the left; on the right, "Read the plan, form a guess, change one thing, measure."
  • ☐ Skim the Session 14 homework: the Store Scorecard and the Returns Investigation (both should report matching SQL and pandas numbers), and who finished stock_vs_sales.
Known environment traps

Plan wording. SQLite 3.36 and later say SCAN orders; older versions say SCAN TABLE orders. Same meaning. A stale plan after DROP INDEX: Python's sqlite3 caches prepared statements by their text; connect with cached_statements=0 (as the lesson, the demo and the labs do) or open a new connection. index ... already exists when a cell runs twice: use CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS. Windows and OneDrive folders: a working copy inside a synced folder can be locked by the sync client (database is locked, or PermissionError on the copy). Work in a local folder. Timings on laptops in power-saving mode or on shared machines jump around; best-of-N absorbs most of it. Never let a learner conclude from a single number. The shipped database changed: if a learner ran CREATE INDEX on data/pinecrest.db itself, later lessons' plans will differ. Fix: unzip pinecrest-data.zip again (or python data/make_data.py).

Five retrieval questions (Lessons 5.1 and 5.2)
  1. In one sentence each: what does WHERE filter, and what does HAVING filter? Answer: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY. (Today adds a third stage: window functions run after both, in the SELECT step.)
  2. orders has 20,302 rows and 739 have no customer row. How many rows from JOIN customers, and from LEFT JOIN customers? Answer: 19,563 and 20,302.
  3. Total revenue came out as $10.3 million instead of $3.7 million after joining order_items. What happened, and what is the rule? Answer: Fan-out: each order's total was repeated once per line, then summed. Sum a column at the level where it lives; aggregate first (a CTE), then join.
  4. Why does WHERE employee_id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees) return 0 rows? Answer: The list contains a NULL (the CEO's manager_id), and a comparison with NULL is unknown, so NOT IN is never true. Use NOT EXISTS or filter the NULLs out of the list.
  5. A value travels into SQL through a placeholder. What can a placeholder NOT stand for, and what do you do then? Answer: A table name, a column name or a keyword. Check the name against a fixed list of allowed names in Python, and only then put it in the query text.
Homework check and roadmap

Ask two learners what their project checks printed: the Store Scorecard's revenue match (True for five stores) and the Returns Investigation's four rows adding up to 20,302. "Two routes, one answer: today every lab ends that way." Ask who finished stock_vs_sales and what the factor was (five: each SKU has five inventory rows).

Roadmap: "Before the break, a row learns to see its neighbors: rankings, running totals, month over month, without losing the rows. After the break, the same queries, fast: how to ask the engine what it is doing and change it with evidence."

Watch-outs
  • Question 1 sets up the first half: if the room cannot say where WHERE and HAVING run, redraw the running order now; window functions go in at the SELECT step.

5.3

SQL Window Functions

75 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Explain what OVER, PARTITION BY and the window's ORDER BY each control, and how a window function differs from GROUP BY
  • Number and rank rows with ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK, and select the top N rows of every group
  • Compare a row with earlier or later rows using LAG and LEAD
  • Compute running totals and moving averages with an explicit window frame, and say what the default frame does
  • Translate each of these between SQL and pandas (transform, rank, shift, cumsum and expanding, rolling with min_periods)
Timing inside the block (75 minutes)
10mFrame and mental model
30mLive demo, steps 1 to 11
25mGuided lab: pay within each location, then the Silver milestone
10mStart the Store Performance Table: Step 1
Mental model to say

"GROUP BY is the conductor's report: 'car 3 has 48 passengers'. The passengers have become a number. A window function leaves you in your seat and lets you look around. Through the window you can see the rest of your car, your partition; you know who sits in front of you and behind you, the order; and you can choose to look only at the two seats ahead, the frame. You get your answer, and you are still a passenger with a seat."

Draw a train car on the board with three labels: PARTITION BY (which car), ORDER BY (seat order), ROWS BETWEEN (how far you look). Leave it up through the break.

Bridge to what they own: "You have done all of this in pandas. transform from Lesson 2.4; rank, shift, cumsum, rolling from Lesson 2.8. Today is the SQL spelling." The workbook has the two-column phrase book; put it on the projector after the demo.

Live demo (you type, they follow): eleven windows on Pinecrest's orders

A notebook session15_sql.ipynb in the folder that holds data/. Read-only connection. The marked minutes add up to 30. For each window, say the three questions aloud before you type it: partition, order, frame.

  1. Setup and a version check (1m). Say: "Read-only again, the same show() helper. Window functions need SQLite 3.25 or later; this line checks." 
    import sqlite3
import pandas as pd

conn = sqlite3.connect("file:data/pinecrest.db?mode=ro", uri=True)

def show(sql, params=()):
    """Run a query and print the result as a table."""
    print(pd.read_sql(sql, conn, params=params).to_string(index=False))

print(sqlite3.sqlite_version_info >= (3, 25, 0))
    True
  2. OVER (PARTITION BY): a group value on every row (3m). Say: "Each order next to its own store's average. Five orders in, five rows out, each carrying a number computed from thousands of other rows." 
    show("""
    SELECT order_id, store, order_total,
           ROUND(AVG(order_total) OVER (PARTITION BY store), 1) AS store_avg,
           ROUND(order_total - AVG(order_total) OVER (PARTITION BY store), 2)
               AS vs_avg
    FROM orders
    WHERE status = 'completed'
    ORDER BY order_id
    LIMIT 4
""")
     order_id     store  order_total  store_avg  vs_avg
   100001 Flagstaff        434.9      182.4  252.51
   100002 Asheville        278.9      175.1  103.80
   100003    Online         75.9      203.2 -127.30
   100004    Online        399.8      203.2  196.60

    Write the comparison on the board: GROUP BY store gives 5 rows; OVER (PARTITION BY store) gives 18,762. pandas twin: groupby("store")["order_total"].transform("mean").

  3. An empty OVER (): a share of the whole (2m). Say: "Windows run after GROUP BY, so they can work on grouped rows. An empty OVER() is one window holding every row." 
    show("""
    WITH by_store AS (
        SELECT store, ROUND(SUM(order_total), 2) AS revenue
        FROM orders
        WHERE status = 'completed'
        GROUP BY store
    )
    SELECT store, revenue,
           ROUND(100.0 * revenue / SUM(revenue) OVER (), 1) AS pct_of_total
    FROM by_store
    ORDER BY revenue DESC
""")
        store    revenue  pct_of_total
   Online 2357984.45          65.1
    Boise  443386.85          12.2
Flagstaff  300580.35           8.3
     Bend  284575.25           7.9
Asheville  237779.37           6.6
  4. Three ways to rank, and what they do with ties (3m). Say: "The two cheapest items in Tents share a price. Predict the three columns for those two rows." 
    show("""
    SELECT name, price,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY price) AS row_number,
           RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY price) AS rank,
           DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY price) AS dense_rank
    FROM products
    WHERE category = 'Tents'
    ORDER BY price, name
    LIMIT 4
""")
                                  name  price  row_number  rank  dense_rank
  Cedar Notch Cairn Tent Footprint  41.95           2     1           1
 Quillback Foothill Tent Footprint  41.95           1     1           1
Quillback Alpenglow Tent Footprint  67.95           3     3           2
              Pinecrest Drift Tarp  94.95           4     4           3

    "RANK is a race: two golds, no silver. DENSE_RANK does not skip. ROW_NUMBER picks arbitrarily among ties unless the ORDER BY breaks them": point at the two footprints, numbered in an order nothing in the query decided. pandas: rank(method="min" / "dense" / "first").

  5. Top N per group: number, wrap, filter (4m). Say: "The two best-selling products in every category. ORDER BY ... LIMIT 2 gives two rows in total, not two per category. The recipe has three steps, and step 2 is not optional." 
    show("""
    WITH product_revenue AS (
        SELECT p.category, p.name,
               ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS revenue
        FROM order_items AS i
        JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
        JOIN products AS p ON p.sku = i.sku
        WHERE o.status = 'completed'
        GROUP BY p.sku
    ),
    ranked AS (
        SELECT *,
               ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rn
        FROM product_revenue
    )
    SELECT category, rn, name, revenue
    FROM ranked
    WHERE rn <= 2
    ORDER BY category, rn
    LIMIT 6
""")
        category  rn                               name   revenue
 Accessories   1 Cedar Notch Sawtooth First-Aid Kit 148120.20
 Accessories   2      Larkspur Ridge Mesa Multitool  47968.95
     Apparel   1   Granite Fork Cascade Rain Jacket 104981.25
     Apparel   2        Tallgrass Drift Rain Jacket  51019.70
Camp Kitchen   1 Quillback Timberline Insulated Mug  46581.65
Camp Kitchen   2   Granite Fork Meadow Water Bottle  28923.80

    Then break it on purpose: move rn <= 2 into the first SELECT with the window. The engine answers misuse of window function ROW_NUMBER(). "WHERE runs before windows exist. The CTE turns the number into an ordinary column."

  6. LAG and LEAD: the neighbors (3m). Say: "Monthly revenue is the series for the next three steps. Store the CTE in a Python string so we never retype it." 
    MONTHLY = """
    WITH monthly AS (
        SELECT strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) AS month,
               ROUND(SUM(order_total), 2)    AS revenue
        FROM orders
        WHERE status = 'completed'
        GROUP BY month
    )
"""
show(MONTHLY + """
    SELECT month, revenue,
           LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_month,
           ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month))
                 / LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month), 1) AS pct_change
    FROM monthly
    ORDER BY month
    LIMIT 4
""")
      month   revenue  prev_month  pct_change
2024-01 106287.63         NaN         NaN
2024-02 104687.91   106287.63        -1.5
2024-03 128400.63   104687.91        22.7
2024-04 129716.87   128400.63         1.0

    "January 2024 has nothing before it: NULL, the honest answer." pandas: shift(1) and pct_change(). One difference to say aloud: pandas shifts by position, so you must sort first; SQL takes the order from the OVER.

  7. LAG within a group: days between a customer's orders (2m). Say: "With PARTITION BY, 'previous' means previous within the group. julianday() turns a date into a day count." 
    show("""
    WITH gaps AS (
        SELECT order_date,
               LAG(order_date) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id
                                     ORDER BY order_date, order_id) AS prev_date
        FROM orders
    )
    SELECT COUNT(*)         AS orders,
           COUNT(prev_date) AS with_earlier,
           ROUND(AVG(julianday(order_date) - julianday(prev_date)), 1) AS avg_days
    FROM gaps
""")
     orders  with_earlier  avg_days
  20302         16360      83.1

    20,302 orders minus 3,942 first orders = 16,360 gaps, averaging about 83 days. "order_id breaks ties when a customer orders twice in one day, so the result is the same every run."

  8. Running total and year to date (3m). Say: "Give an aggregate window an ORDER BY and it covers the partition from the start to the current row: a running total. Partition by year and it restarts each January." 
    show(MONTHLY + """
    SELECT month, revenue,
           ROUND(SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
             ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS running_total,
           ROUND(SUM(revenue) OVER (PARTITION BY substr(month, 1, 4) ORDER BY month
             ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS year_to_date
    FROM monthly
    ORDER BY month
    LIMIT 4 OFFSET 10
""")
      month   revenue  running_total  year_to_date
2024-11 143304.56     1498118.16    1498118.16
2024-12 185181.35     1683299.51    1683299.51
2025-01 132423.89     1815723.40     132423.89
2025-02 126414.41     1942137.81     258838.30

    "I wrote the frame out on purpose. In ten minutes you will see why." pandas: cumsum(), and groupby(year).cumsum() for year to date.

  9. Frames: a moving average, and what the first rows do (3m). Say: "The frame is the part of the partition the function looks at: from here to here. Three months, and a column that counts how many rows the frame really held." 
    show(MONTHLY + """
    SELECT month, revenue,
           ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                 ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS moving_avg_3,
           COUNT(*) OVER (ORDER BY month
                 ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)     AS rows_in_frame,
           ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month
                 ROWS BETWEEN 3 PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING), 2) AS prior_3_avg
    FROM monthly
    ORDER BY month
    LIMIT 4
""")
      month   revenue  moving_avg_3  rows_in_frame  prior_3_avg
2024-01 106287.63     106287.63              1          NaN
2024-02 104687.91     105487.77              2    106287.63
2024-03 128400.63     113125.39              3    105487.77
2024-04 129716.87     120935.14              3    113125.39

    Two points. (1) SQL averages whatever part of the frame exists: January's "three-month average" is one month. pandas rolling(3) gives NaN there unless min_periods=1. (2) A frame that ends at 1 PRECEDING never sees the current row: the leak-free feature from Lesson 2.8, shift(1).rolling(3, min_periods=1).

  10. The tie trap in the default frame (3m). Say: "Bend's completed orders as a running total by date, written with the default frame and with an explicit one. Three orders share January 1."

           ROUND(SUM(order_total) OVER (ORDER BY order_date), 2) AS default_frame,

             ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 2) AS explicit_rows
    FROM orders

""")

  11. Forgetting PARTITION BY with LAG (3m). Say: "One more silent mistake. Two stores, one row per month, and a 'previous month' column with and without a partition. Look at the middle row."

Asheville 2025-12  8253.61     8067.69     8067.69

Three mistakes to expect
  • Filtering on a window function in the same query. WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) <= 3 raises OperationalError: misuse of window function ROW_NUMBER(), and giving it an alias does not help. Coach with Session 14's running order: "Where do window functions run? After WHERE. So the filter needs another SELECT around it: a CTE."
  • A missing PARTITION BY. LAG over several series without a partition compares one series with the last row of another (demo step 11). No error, one wrong row in the middle of a correct table. Coach: "How many series are in this table? Then what is the partition?"
  • The default frame with ties, and an order that does not decide. A running total ordered by date gives tied rows the same total; ROW_NUMBER over a date with two orders on one day numbers them arbitrarily. Coach: "Is your ORDER BY unique? Add the key as a tiebreaker. Aggregating over an ordered window? Write the ROWS frame." The Silver lab depends on both.
