5.4

Query Optimization

75 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Describe how SQLite turns a query into a plan, and read EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN output line by line
  • Create single-column, composite and covering indexes, and show their effect on both the plan and the measured time
  • Recognize the situations where an index does not help, and rewrite a filter so that an index can be used
  • Measure what indexes cost in file size and write speed, and use ANALYZE to give the planner statistics
  • Decide what work belongs in SQL and what belongs in pandas, and fetch only what you need
Timing inside the block (75 minutes)
10mFrame and mental model
30mLive demo, steps 1 to 9
25mGuided lab: plans for a lookup screen, then one query instead of 300
10mStart the Tuning Report: Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

"A table is a thick reference book whose pages are in the order they were written. To find every mention of 'crampons' you have one strategy: start at page 1 and read to the end. That is a scan. An index is the alphabetical list at the back: each term, then the pages where it appears. Jump to 'crampons', turn straight to those pages. That is a search. The index is extra paper, and somebody has to update it every time a page changes."

Then the method, which matters more than any single index: "SQL says WHAT you want; the planner decides HOW. We will ask it how, change one thing, and measure again. Read the plan, form a guess, change one thing, measure." Write that sentence on the board.

Set expectations about numbers: "On a 3.5 MB database everything is fast. We look at the plan first and the stopwatch second, and every time I print a time I will say: your numbers will differ."

Live demo (you type, they follow): plans, indexes and the stopwatch

A second notebook, session15_tuning.ipynb. The demo creates indexes, so step 1 copies the database to pinecrest_tuning.db first. Nine cells; the marked minutes add up to 30. The times below are from the author's machine; yours will differ and that is the point of best-of-N.

  1. A copy, a plan printer, a stopwatch (3m). Say: "This lesson creates indexes, so it works on a copy. Two helpers: plan() prints the engine's strategy, timed() runs a query many times and keeps the best. And one detail in the connect line, which I will explain in step 7." 
    import os
import shutil
import sqlite3
import time
import pandas as pd

shutil.copy("data/pinecrest.db", "pinecrest_tuning.db")
conn = sqlite3.connect("pinecrest_tuning.db", cached_statements=0)

def plan(sql, params=()):
    """Print the query plan, one step per line."""
    for row in conn.execute("EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN " + sql, params):
        print("   ", row[3])

def timed(sql, param_list, repeat=5):
    """Best time in milliseconds to run the query once per item of param_list."""
    best = float("inf")
    for _ in range(repeat):
        start = time.perf_counter()
        for params in param_list:
            conn.execute(sql, params).fetchall()
        best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - start)
    return best * 1000

    plan() here prints the steps without indentation; the lesson's version indents nested steps.

  2. Reading a plan: SCAN and SEARCH (3m). Say: "EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN returns the strategy instead of running the query. Nothing is read or changed, so it is always safe. Two verbs do nearly all the work." 
    print("by primary key")
plan("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_id = ?", (100500,))
print("by another column")
plan("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = ?", (12673,))
print("filter, then sort")
plan("SELECT * FROM orders WHERE store = ? ORDER BY order_date", ("Bend",))
    by primary key
    SEARCH orders USING INTEGER PRIMARY KEY (rowid=?)
by another column
    SCAN orders
filter, then sort
    SCAN orders
    USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY

    SCAN: read every row and test each. SEARCH: jump. TEMP B-TREE: a separate sort. "SCAN is not a dirty word: for a yearly total it is the best plan. It is a problem when you wanted a few rows and paid for all of them."

  3. One index, the plan and the stopwatch (4m). Say: "The classic slow query here: the lines of one order. order_items has 45,490 rows and no index on order_id. Two hundred lookups, before and after." 
    ITEMS_SQL = "SELECT * FROM order_items WHERE order_id = ?"
order_ids = [(100000 + 100 * k,) for k in range(1, 201)]      # 200 different orders
plan(ITEMS_SQL, (100500,))
before = timed(ITEMS_SQL, order_ids)
conn.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_order_items_order_id ON order_items (order_id)")
conn.commit()
plan(ITEMS_SQL, (100500,))
after = timed(ITEMS_SQL, order_ids)
print(f"200 lookups: {before:.1f} ms before, {after:.1f} ms after")
        SCAN order_items
    SEARCH order_items USING INDEX idx_order_items_order_id (order_id=?)
200 lookups: 151.8 ms before, 1.3 ms after

    Your timings will differ: say so every time, and read the plan line before the number. "SCAN became SEARCH ... USING INDEX. The query did not change; the planner found the index by itself."

  4. Joins: the inner loop should be a SEARCH (3m). Say: "A join runs as a nested loop: for each row of the outer table, find the matches in the inner one. The plan lists the outer table first. One customer's history, with one index, then two." 
    HISTORY_SQL = """
    SELECT o.order_id, o.order_date, i.sku, i.quantity
    FROM orders AS o
    JOIN order_items AS i ON i.order_id = o.order_id
    WHERE o.customer_id = ?
"""
print("index on order_items(order_id) only:")
plan(HISTORY_SQL, (12673,))
conn.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_id ON orders (customer_id)")
conn.commit()
print("plus an index on orders(customer_id):")
plan(HISTORY_SQL, (12673,))
    index on order_items(order_id) only:
    SCAN o
    SEARCH i USING INDEX idx_order_items_order_id (order_id=?)
plus an index on orders(customer_id):
    SEARCH o USING INDEX idx_orders_customer_id (customer_id=?)
    SEARCH i USING INDEX idx_order_items_order_id (order_id=?)

    "No scans at all: search for the customer's few orders, then search for each order's lines. This is the plan you want behind a 'show me one customer' page. And notice: the planner chose the outer table, not the order in your FROM clause."

  5. Composite index and the leftmost prefix (4m). Say: "A store manager's report filters on a store and a date range. One index on two columns, in the order a phone book uses: last name, then first name." 
    REPORT_SQL = ("SELECT order_id, order_total FROM orders "
              "WHERE store = ? AND order_date BETWEEN ? AND ?")
plan(REPORT_SQL, ("Bend", "2025-07-01", "2025-07-07"))
conn.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_orders_store_date ON orders (store, order_date)")
conn.commit()
plan(REPORT_SQL, ("Bend", "2025-07-01", "2025-07-07"))
print("date only:")
plan("SELECT order_id FROM orders WHERE order_date = ?", ("2025-07-04",))
        SCAN orders
    SEARCH orders USING INDEX idx_orders_store_date (store=? AND order_date>? AND order_date<?)
date only:
    SCAN orders USING COVERING INDEX idx_orders_store_date

    "Equality columns first, the range or the sort last. And the index is no help for the date alone: dates are sorted only within each store, like finding everyone named Maria in a phone book."

  6. A function around the column hides it (3m). Say: "Both of these count Bend's orders in July 2025. Same answer. Look at how much of the index each can use." 
    FUNC = ("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders "
        "WHERE store = ? AND strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) = ?")
RANGE = ("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders "
         "WHERE store = ? AND order_date >= ? AND order_date < ?")
plan(FUNC, ("Bend", "2025-07"))
plan(RANGE, ("Bend", "2025-07-01", "2025-08-01"))
print(conn.execute(FUNC, ("Bend", "2025-07")).fetchone()[0],
      conn.execute(RANGE, ("Bend", "2025-07-01", "2025-08-01")).fetchone()[0])
        SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX idx_orders_store_date (store=?)
    SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX idx_orders_store_date (store=? AND order_date>? AND order_date<?)
83 83

    "The index is sorted by order_date, not by strftime('%Y-%m', order_date). Keep the bare column on one side of the comparison." A pattern that starts with % and a column where most rows match (status: 92% completed) are the other two cases; they are in the lesson, as reading.

  7. DROP INDEX and plan again: why cached_statements=0 (2m). Say: "Experiments need undoing. Drop the composite index and ask for the same plan text again." 
    conn.execute("DROP INDEX idx_orders_store_date")
conn.commit()
plan(REPORT_SQL, ("Bend", "2025-07-01", "2025-08-01"))
        SCAN orders

    "Back to SCAN, as it should be. Python's sqlite3 normally caches prepared statements by their text, and a cached one can still carry the plan it was made with while the index existed. That is why this connection was opened with cached_statements=0. Harmless in normal work; confusing in a lesson about plans. A new connection does the same job."

  8. ANALYZE: statistics for the planner (3m). Say: "So far the planner has chosen with no knowledge of the data. ANALYZE measures it. Watch a date-only query on a three-column index." 
    conn.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_orders_store_date_total "
             "ON orders (store, order_date, order_total)")
conn.commit()
DATE_SQL = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE order_date = ?"
plan(DATE_SQL, ("2025-07-04",))
conn.execute("ANALYZE")
conn.commit()
plan(DATE_SQL, ("2025-07-04",))
        SCAN orders USING COVERING INDEX idx_orders_store_date_total
    SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX idx_orders_store_date_total (ANY(store) AND order_date=?)

    "The statistics told the planner that store has only five values, so five small searches, one per store, beat a scan: a skip-scan, ANY(store)." The sqlite_stat1 table and what indexes cost in file size and insert time are reading; the project measures the size.

  9. Ask for less: aggregate where the data lives (5m). Say: "The cheapest row is the one you never fetch. Item revenue by store, two ways." 
    def pandas_way():
    df = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM order_items AS i "
                     "JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id", conn)
    df = df[df["status"] == "completed"]
    return (df["quantity"] * df["unit_price"]).groupby(df["store"]).sum().round(2)

def sql_way():
    return pd.read_sql("""
        SELECT o.store, ROUND(SUM(i.quantity * i.unit_price), 2) AS revenue
        FROM order_items AS i JOIN orders AS o ON o.order_id = i.order_id
        WHERE o.status = 'completed'
        GROUP BY o.store""", conn).set_index("store")["revenue"]

for func in (pandas_way, sql_way):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    result = func()
    print(f"{func.__name__}: {(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.1f} ms")
print("same numbers:", (pandas_way() - sql_way()).abs().max() < 0.01)
    pandas_way: 143.0 ms
sql_way: 14.0 ms
same numbers: True

    "Same answer; one moved 45,490 rows into Python, the other five." Three habits for the board: name your columns, LIMIT while exploring, one query not a loop of queries. The second lab is about the third.

Three mistakes to expect
  • Assuming the index is used. Creating an index proves nothing; the planner may ignore it (a function on the column, a wildcard at the start, a filter that matches most rows). Coach: "Show me the plan line for the query it was meant for. Which index does it name?" In the lab, the city-only query still scans after the composite index.
  • Trusting one timing. A single before and after can show only the cache warming up. Coach: "How many times did you run it? Which number did you keep?" Both labs time with best-of-several and print "your numbers will differ"; nothing in the kit asserts a time.
  • A stale plan after DROP INDEX, or editing the shipped database. Re-asking the same plan text on a connection that caches statements can show the old plan; the demo and labs connect with cached_statements=0. And an index created on data/pinecrest.db itself changes the file every later lesson expects. Coach: "Which file is your connection open on?" Always a copy.
Guided lab (25 min)

Learners open labs/module-15/l5_4-query-optimization/customer_lookup_plans_starter.py. Both labs copy the database into their output folder first and open the copy with cached_statements=0.

  • Minutes 0 to 12, plans for a lookup screen (customers). TODO 1: predictions first (in a comment), then three plans, all SCAN, one with a TEMP B-TREE. TODO 2: one index on (state, city): state-and-city becomes a SEARCH; city alone is still a SCAN (of the index: the leftmost-prefix rule); the newest-first query still sorts. The speedup is modest (488 of 4,850 customers live in Boise, ID: an index pays most when it skips most of the table). TODO 3: a third column, signup_date, removes the sort step. TODO 4: DROP and plan again: SCAN.
  • Minutes 12 to 25, one query instead of 300 (labs/module-15/l5_4-query-optimization/n_plus_one_starter.py). A colleague's script runs one query per Gold customer. TODO 1 plans it (SCAN orders) and times the loop. TODO 2 writes ONE IN (...) GROUP BY query (one placeholder per id, so values still travel as parameters) and checks "same answers: True". TODO 3 adds idx_orders_customer_id and times both again. Debrief: "Either fix works here. Which one survives a server database, where each loop query also pays a network round trip?" (The single query.)
  • If the room is slow, stop after TODO 2 of the first lab; the second goes home whole. Its point (the N+1 problem) is one sentence in the lesson, so it is worth doing.
Start the lesson project (10 min)

Open the lesson page at "Project: The Tuning Report". The brief: three dashboard queries, the fewest indexes that fix them, before-and-after plans and times, proof that results are unchanged, and the cost in file size. In the room: Step 1 (a fresh tuning_project.db and the workload: {'customer history': 100, 'product sales by month': 50, 'store daily report': 100}) and Step 2 (the baseline: every plan contains a SCAN of a large table). Ask the room to propose the indexes from the WHERE and ON clauses before anyone opens Step 3. Steps 3 to 6 are homework.

Checks for understanding

Workbook self-check, Q7 to Q12. Good cold calls: Q8 (which filter cannot seek) and Q12 (one timing each).

Answers: Q7 C) SEARCH orders USING COVERING INDEX idx_orders_store_date_total (store=? AND order_date>? AND order_date<?); Q8 A) WHERE order_date = '2025-07-04'; Q9 C) Python's sqlite3 reused its cached prepared statement, planned while the index existed; connect with cached_statements=0 or open a new connection; Q10 SCAN t; Q11 D) Slower inserts and a larger file, because every index is a sorted copy that must be kept up to date; Q12 C) Repeat each measurement several times, take the best, and check the plan changed from SCAN to SEARCH. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: the plan-words table in the workbook is the whole vocabulary; learners who are lost read plans aloud with it ("SCAN customers: read every customer"). Let them do the first lab only, TODO 1 and 2. Stretch: the lesson's Exercise 4 (is a covering index worth it?) after n_plus_one, or measure the file-size cost of the lab's two indexes with os.path.getsize. Ask: "Why does the composite index put state before city, and could city first ever be better?"

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions; answers)
  1. orders has 20,302 rows and 5 stores. How many rows from SELECT store, AVG(order_total) FROM orders GROUP BY store, and from SELECT store, AVG(order_total) OVER (PARTITION BY store) FROM orders? Answer: 5 and 20,302. GROUP BY collapses the rows; a window function keeps every row and attaches the group value to it.
  2. Give the three steps of "top N per group". Answer: Number the rows with ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group ORDER BY measure DESC, tiebreaker); put that in a CTE; filter the CTE with WHERE rn <= N. (WHERE cannot see a window function in the same SELECT.)
  3. You have just created an index. Name two things you check before saying it helped. Answer: Any two of: the plan for the query it was meant for now says SEARCH ... USING INDEX (or COVERING INDEX) instead of SCAN; best-of-several timings before and after; the query returns exactly the same rows; what it costs in file size and write speed.

  • Lesson 5.4: the Tuning Report, Steps 3 to 6, including the written recommendation; Exercises 1 to 3 (4 is a stretch); the quiz and the journal. Read "What Indexes Cost".
  • Kit labs: labs/module-15/l5_3-sql-window-functions/weekly_trend_starter.py; TODO 4 of the Silver lab; labs/module-15/l5_4-query-optimization/n_plus_one_starter.py if it was not finished.
  • Tidy up: delete the working copies (pinecrest_tuning.db, tuning_project.db, the labs' output/ folders), or keep them out of any shared folder.
  • Workbook: self-check Q1 to Q12.

If You Run Long or Short

Long. Cut in this order: (1) 5.3 step 3 (share of the total) and step 7 (days between orders): say them. (2) 5.3 step 11 (missing PARTITION BY) becomes a slide; the lab and Q-cards cover it. (3) 5.4 step 4 (join plans): show the output from the lesson page. (4) 5.4 step 8 (ANALYZE) becomes one sentence. (5) The second lab of each block (silver_milestone after TODO 3; n_plus_one) goes home. (6) "Start the project" shrinks to the first cell. Never cut: top N per group, the frame and tie cells, reading a plan, one index measured properly.

Short. Run weekly_trend after the first lab block and the lesson's Exercise 4 (Pareto: 41 products make half of revenue) as a class discussion. In 5.4 add the lesson's "What Indexes Cost" cell (file size and insert time with 0, 1, 2 and 4 indexes) and have pairs propose the Tuning Report indexes before reading Step 3.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 16: Documents and HTTP

How to teach the session where the data stops being a file someone prepared. The first half finishes Module 5 with a document database: nested website sessions, queried with dictionaries and aggregation pipelines, and flattened back into pandas. The second half opens Module 6 with the conversation every web page and API is built on: one request, one response, and the habits (rules first, identify yourself, timeout, check the status) that make a program a good guest.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 5.5–6.1 Session 16 of 21

How to Use This Guide

  • Session 16 closes Module 5 and opens Module 6. Before the break learners query a document database (Lesson 5.5); after it they make their first HTTP requests (Lesson 6.1). The link between the halves is JSON: the nested documents of the first hour are what web APIs send in the second.
  • Same rhythm as every session: frame (the mental model, said aloud) → live demo (you type, they follow) → guided lab (the kit lab) → start the lesson project. Finishing the projects, the lessons' exercises, quizzes and journals is homework.
  • Every code block below was run for this guide: mongomock 4.3 and pandas 3.0.6 on data/web_sessions.json; requests 2.34.2 against the practice shop and data/mock_api.py. The output shown is real. Where your room will see something different (dates, the local copy of the shop), the guide says so.
  • Type, do not paste. Ask for a prediction before every line whose output is a number. Two of today's most valuable moments are lines that raise no error and print a wrong answer (a misspelled field in 5.5, a 404 page parsed as data in 6.1).
  • Labs live in labs/module-16/: starters for learners, solutions for you. Teal blocks are hands-on; amber blocks are watch-outs.
The risk in Session 16: quiet wrong answers

Both lessons teach tools that are forgiving in the same dangerous way. A collection accepts a query on a field nobody has and answers 0. requests accepts a 404 and hands you an error page to parse. Learners who have spent five lessons being corrected by SQL's error messages will trust the zero. Say the rule early and repeat it in both halves: "Be suspicious of zero. Look at one real document, or one real response, before you believe a count."

Before the Session

  • ☐ Run python3 labs/check_labs.py module-16 from the kit folder. Expect 8 passed, 0 failed (four starters, four solutions; the two network labs run from saved responses).
  • ☐ Copy the starter files only (*_starter.py) plus the whole _fixtures/ folder and labs_paths.py to the shared folder, keeping the folder layout. Keep every *_solution.py on your machine.
  • ☐ MongoDB: nothing to install and no server to start. Lesson 5.5 runs on mongomock, which was installed with the course environment in Lesson 0.1. Check it on the projector machine: python -c "import mongomock, pymongo; print(mongomock.__version__, pymongo.version)" (this kit was run with 4.3.0 and 4.18.3). If a learner's import fails: pip install mongomock pymongo inside the course environment.
  • ☐ The practice shop, online. Open https://rays-python-datascience.netlify.app/practice/shop/ in a browser on the venue network, not at home. You should see the Pinecrest Outfitters catalog with a banner that says it is a practice site. Then open https://rays-python-datascience.netlify.app/practice/robots.txt. If either fails, use the offline copy below for the whole room.
  • ☐ The practice shop, offline fallback. In the project folder (the one that holds data/), in a second terminal: python -m zipfile -e data/pinecrest-practice-site.zip . and then python -m http.server 8001. Leave it running. Everyone sets BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8001/practice/shop/". (The lesson writes the first command for a zip downloaded into the project folder; from the course data folder the path is data/pinecrest-practice-site.zip.) Lesson 6.1 needs no flags. Check it: http://127.0.0.1:8000/health in a browser shows {"status": "ok"}. Start it during the break, not before: a terminal left open for 80 minutes gets closed by accident.

What differs on the offline copy (checked for this kit)

The kit's author unzipped pinecrest-practice-site.zip in an empty folder and served it with python -m http.server, exactly as Lesson 6.1 describes. The lesson's code runs unchanged. These printed details differ from the lesson and from this guide:

  • Content-Type is text/html with no charset, and the Server header is SimpleHTTP/0.6 Python/3.12.x instead of Netlify.
  • Because no charset is sent, r.encoding is ISO-8859-1, and r.text shows â˜… where the stars should be: on the front page r.text.count("★") is 0 until you set r.encoding = "utf-8" (then 20). The byte count is the same (11,783); the character count is 11,783 before the fix and 11,725 after. This is the lesson's encoding section happening for real: use it.
  • A missing page returns Python's own short 404 page (335 bytes, text/html;charset=utf-8), not the course site's 404 page (2,514 bytes).
  • robots.txt is at http://127.0.0.1:8001/practice/robots.txt and is served as text/plain with no charset. RobotFileParser gives the same answers (True, False, crawl delay 1).
  • A HEAD request (lesson Exercise 3) returns text/html instead of text/html; charset=UTF-8.
  • Both kit labs print the right answers on the offline copy (the labs set the encoding themselves); only the type column and the size of the 404 body differ.

Warm-up

0:00

Warm-up: Retrieval from Session 15

10 min

Five questions on the projector, answered on paper with notes closed (4 minutes), then answers aloud (3 minutes). Retrieval practice works because it is effortful: do not let it turn into a re-teach. Anything more than half the room misses goes on the board as a note for the break.

  1. How does a window function differ from GROUP BY? Answer: A window function computes over a set of related rows and keeps every row; GROUP BY collapses each group to one row.
  2. Three orders tie for first place. What do ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK give the fourth row? Answer: ROW_NUMBER 4, RANK 4, DENSE_RANK 2. They differ only in how they treat ties.
  3. You want the top 3 products per category. Why does WHERE rn <= 3 fail in the same query, and what is the fix? Answer: WHERE runs before window functions are computed. Number the rows in a CTE, then filter in the outer query.
  4. In EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN, what is the difference between SCAN and SEARCH? Answer: SCAN reads the whole table; SEARCH jumps to the rows it needs through a primary key or an index.
  5. Name one situation in which an index does not help. Answer: Any one of: the column is wrapped in a function, the LIKE pattern starts with a wildcard, most rows match, the table is small.

Homework check (3 minutes). Lesson 5.4 asked everyone to open data/web_sessions.json in a text editor and decide which parts would be awkward to store in one flat table. Take two answers (the list of pages; the cart's items; the utm block that is sometimes missing). That is the bridge: "Today that file stops being awkward." Ask who finished the 5.4 tuning report; note names of anyone who did not start it and check in at the break.

Lesson Plans

5.5

NoSQL with MongoDB

70 min
Objectives (from the lesson)
  • Explain how a document differs from a row, and judge when a document store fits a dataset better than relational tables
  • Insert, find, update and delete documents with pymongo
  • Write queries with operators, dot notation and array conditions, and choose the fields returned with a projection
  • Build an aggregation pipeline with $match, $group, $sort, $unwind and $addFields, and relate each stage to SQL and pandas
  • Create indexes on a collection and flatten nested results into a tidy DataFrame
Timing (70 minutes)
10mFrame: the ledger and the folder; the SQL-to-MongoDB word table
25mLive demo, steps 1 to 13
25mGuided lab: the sale page audit (then landing pages)
10mStart the Funnel Report: Step 1 runs for everyone
Mental model to say

"A relational database is a set of ledgers. Each ledger has fixed columns, every entry fills the same columns, and the facts about one website visit are spread over several ledgers that point at each other by number. A document database is a filing cabinet of folders. Each folder holds everything about one thing, in whatever shape that thing has: one visit's pages, cart and all. Pull one folder and you have the whole story, with no assembly. And two folders need not contain the same sheets."

Put the lesson's comparison table on the projector and read it as a translation exercise: table → collection, row → document, column → field, primary key → _id, a join to a child table → an embedded list. Then the honest caveat, in one sentence: "Neither is better. Orders, customers and products point at each other constantly, so they live in pinecrest.db. Web sessions are self-contained, nested and irregular, so they suit documents."

One sentence on tooling, so nobody goes looking for a server: "We use mongomock, which imitates MongoDB inside Python. Every line you write is real pymongo code; only the line that connects would change."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

One notebook, session16_mongo, started in the project folder so that data/web_sessions.json resolves. Thirteen short steps; the minutes are in the timing table above.

  1. One session is not a row. Say: "This is one visit to the website, exactly as it is stored. Count the levels with me: a device object, a list of pages, a cart with a list inside it. Which three tables would this be in SQL?" 
    import json
from pprint import pprint

with open("data/web_sessions.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    sessions = json.load(f)["sessions"]

print(len(sessions), "sessions")
pprint(sessions[2], sort_dicts=False, width=100, depth=2)
    2400 sessions
{'session_id': 'S00003',
 'customer_id': 11550,
 'started_at': '2025-11-01T07:07:11',
 'device': {'type': 'desktop', 'os': 'Windows', 'browser': 'Edge'},
 'pages': [{...}, {...}, {...}, {...}, {...}, {...}, {...}],
 'cart': {'items': [...], 'value': 122.9},
 'converted': True,
 'order_id': 118263}
  2. Two folders, different sheets. Say: "Same collection, different keys. The second one has no utm at all: the visitor typed the address. In a table that is NULL in three columns. Here the field is simply not there. Remember this; it comes back in five minutes." 
    print(sorted(set(sessions[1]) - set(sessions[0])))
print(sum("utm" not in s for s in sessions), "sessions have no utm key")
    ['utm']
916 sessions have no utm key
  3. A database in one line. Say: "mongomock imitates a MongoDB server inside Python: no install, no server, same methods as pymongo. Nothing is created until we insert. On a real server only the first line changes." Point at the count going from 0 to 2400. 
    import mongomock
import pandas as pd

client = mongomock.MongoClient()      # real server: pymongo.MongoClient(uri)
coll = client["pinecrest"]["sessions"]
print(coll.count_documents({}))

result = coll.insert_many(sessions)
print(len(result.inserted_ids), "inserted;",
      coll.count_documents({}), "in the collection")
    0
2400 inserted; 2400 in the collection
  4. A query is a dictionary. Say: "This replaces WHERE. Field, value. Two pairs in one dictionary mean AND. To reach inside the device object, join the names with a dot, in quotes." Ask before running the third line: "More or fewer than 1,326?" 
    print(coll.count_documents({"converted": True}))
print(coll.count_documents({"device.type": "mobile"}))
print(coll.count_documents({"device.type": "mobile", "converted": True}))
    230
1326
130
  5. Operators start with a dollar sign. Say: "Anything that is not 'equals' becomes a small dictionary with an operator. Read $gte as 'greater than or equal'. $in is SQL's IN." Have learners type the second line themselves and call out the number. 
    print(coll.count_documents({"cart.value": {"$gte": 500}}))
print(coll.count_documents({"device.os": {"$in": ["iOS", "iPadOS"]},
                            "cart.value": {"$gte": 500}}))
print(sorted(coll.distinct("device.os")))
    73

Three mistakes to expect
  • A misspelled field or a value in the wrong case returns 0, and they report the 0. {"device.typ": "mobile"} and {"device.type": "Mobile"} both count nothing. Coach: "What does one real document look like? Run coll.find_one({}, {"_id": 0, "device": 1}). Now which values exist? coll.distinct("device.type")." Do not point at the typo; let the document show it.
  • The dollar sign in the wrong place. In a query or $match the field name is the key, with no dollar: {"device.type": "mobile"}. Inside $group, $addFields or $project a field's value is written "$device.type". Learners write "_id": "device.type" and get one group of 2,400. Coach: "How many groups did you expect? How many did you get? What is the _id of the one you got?"
  • Two list conditions without $elemMatch. In the lab the loose query counts 218 and the strict one 81. Learners who skip the strict version report 218 for "a minute or more on the sale page". Coach: "Read your query aloud as a sentence. Does it say the minute was spent on /sale, or on some page?"

Also common: list(cursor) twice (the second is empty: a cursor reads once), and update_one(query, {"reviewed": True}) without $set (ValueError: update only works with $ operators, which is a kindness).

  • Minutes 0 to 5: everyone runs the starter as shipped. It prints the field list and a row of Nones. Have them read the field list: that habit is the cure for mistake 1.
  • Minutes 5 to 18: TODOs 1 to 5 in pairs. Walk the room during TODO 3; that is where the thinking is.
  • Minutes 18 to 22: results on the projector. Reference answers: 290 sessions saw /sale; 37 of them ordered; 20 were on mobile with a cart of $200 or more; loose 218 versus strict 81; 92 arrived with no utm; biggest carts S00039 ($1,265.85), S01848 ($1,202.85), S00806 ($1,023.90); order rate 12.8% of /sale visitors versus 9.6% of all sessions.
  • Minutes 22 to 25: the discussion that matters. "12.8% against 9.6%. Should marketing conclude that the sale page causes orders?" (No: people who browse more pages are more likely to see /sale and more likely to buy. Module 4's lesson, in a new costume.)

6.1

HTTP with Requests

80 min
Objectives (from the lesson)
  • Describe an HTTP request and response (method, URL, headers, status code, body) and read each part from Python
  • Check a site's robots.txt and decide whether, and how fast, your program may fetch a page
  • Fetch HTML and JSON with requests.get(), sending a User-Agent that identifies you, query parameters and a timeout
  • Tell success from failure with status codes and raise_for_status(), and handle timeouts and HTTP errors without crashing
  • Reuse settings with a Session, fix a wrong text encoding, and save raw responses to disk
Timing (80 minutes)
2mGround rules for Module 6, read aloud
13mFrame: the order counter; the three-part shape; status code ranges
25mLive demo, steps 1 to 14
25mGuided lab: three category pages (then the API price check)
15mStart the Polite Snapshot: Steps 1 and 2
Ground rules: the 2-minute opener for every Module 6 session

Before any fetching code, put these six on the projector and read them aloud, one learner per rule. Say why first: "A program can do in a minute what would take a person a week. A website is somebody's property, runs on somebody's bill, and often holds information about real people."

  1. Read robots.txt and obey it. It is the owner's published request to programs: where they may go and how fast.
  2. Read the terms of use. If they forbid automated collection, the answer is no, however easy the code would be.
  3. Prefer an API or a download when one exists. It is the front door.
  4. Go slowly and say who you are. Pause between requests; send a User-Agent with a way to contact you.
  5. Never go around a login, a paywall or a block. If you are asked to stop, stop.
  6. Do not collect personal data. Names, emails, profiles and photos of real people are protected by law in many places.

Then the reassurance: "Every request in this module goes to the practice shop or to the practice API on your own computer. You have the owner's permission, nothing on them is real, and you cannot break anything. We practice the polite habits here so they are automatic everywhere else." This is not legal advice, and the lesson says so; if someone asks "is scraping legal?", the lesson's FAQ has the careful answer.

Mental model to say

"Think of the counter at a deli. You hand over a slip: what you want, plus a few notes about yourself. A moment later a tray comes back. On top is a ticket with a number that says how it went: order filled, we are out of that, you may not order that, the kitchen is on fire. Under the ticket is the food, if there is any. That is the whole of HTTP. The slip is a request, the tray is a response. The server never calls you; it only answers. And it does not remember your last order unless you remind it."

Draw the three-part shape twice on the board, side by side: first line (method and URL | status code), headers (who is asking | what the answer is), body (usually empty for GET | the page or the JSON). Then the status ranges as "whose move is it": 2xx use it, 3xx nothing to do, 4xx fix your request, 5xx wait and try later.

Live demo (you type, they follow)

A new notebook, session16_http. The practice API must be running in a second terminal from step 9 on. The outputs below were produced against a local copy of the practice shop that sends the same headers as the course website; on the public site only the Date header differs. If your room uses the offline copy, read "What differs on the offline copy" above before step 4.

  12. Timeouts, always. Say: "A fact that surprises people: with no timeout, requests waits forever. /slow answers late on purpose. I ask it to take three seconds and I am willing to wait one." After the error: "That is the behavior you want: a clear error, at a moment you chose." 
    requests.get(f"{API}/slow", params={"seconds": 3}, headers=HEADERS, timeout=1)
    ReadTimeout: HTTPConnectionPool(host='127.0.0.1', port=8000): Read timed out. (read timeout=1)
  13. One function that does it right. Say: "Four habits: say who you are, set a timeout, check the status, expect failure. Typing all four on every call is how they get skipped, so they go in one function. Specific exceptions first, the general one last." Type it together; this is the function Session 17 builds on. 
    def fetch(url, **kwargs):
    """GET a URL politely. Return the response, or None after saying why."""
    kwargs.setdefault("headers", HEADERS)
    kwargs.setdefault("timeout", 10)
    try:
        resp = requests.get(url, **kwargs)
        resp.raise_for_status()
    except requests.exceptions.Timeout:
        print(f"TIMEOUT   {url}")
    except requests.exceptions.HTTPError as err:
        print(f"HTTP {err.response.status_code}  {url}")
    except requests.exceptions.RequestException as err:
        print(f"FAILED    {url} ({type(err).__name__})")
    else:
        return resp
    return None

print(fetch(urljoin(BASE_URL, "category-tents.html")))
print(fetch(urljoin(BASE_URL, "category-golf.html")))
print(fetch(f"{API}/slow", params={"seconds": 3}, timeout=1))
    <Response [200]>
HTTP 404  https://rays-python-datascience.netlify.app/practice/shop/category-golf.html
None
TIMEOUT   http://127.0.0.1:8000/slow
None
  14. A session, a pause, and the raw bytes on disk. Say: "A Session keeps the connection open and remembers the headers. It does NOT remember a timeout. time.sleep(1) is the crawl delay we read at the start. And we save resp.content, the bytes, so every parsing experiment next session runs without a new request." 
    import time
from pathlib import Path

raw = Path("raw")
raw.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

with requests.Session() as session:
    session.headers.update(HEADERS)
    for name in ["category-tents.html", "category-packs.html"]:
        resp = session.get(urljoin(BASE_URL, name), timeout=10)
        resp.raise_for_status()
        (raw / name).write_bytes(resp.content)
        print(name, resp.status_code, len(resp.content), "bytes saved")
        time.sleep(1)

print(sorted(p.name for p in raw.iterdir()))
    category-tents.html 200 12997 bytes saved
category-packs.html 200 12863 bytes saved
['category-packs.html', 'category-tents.html']
Three mistakes to expect
  • Parsing an error page as if it were data. A loop over page-12.html to page-15.html reports 20, 2, 0, 0 products and nobody notices that the zeros are 404s. Coach: "What was the status of that response? Where in your loop would you find out?" The fix is one line after every get.
  • No timeout, or ConnectionError because the API is not running. A cell that says "running" for a minute has a call with no timeout=. A long red message ending in Connection refused means the second terminal was closed. Coach: "Is the API's terminal still open? What does http://127.0.0.1:8000/health show in your browser?"
  • Building the query string by hand, or calling .json() on HTML. f"{API}/products?category=Camp Kitchen" breaks on the space; r.json() on a page gives JSONDecodeError: Expecting value: line 1 column 1 (char 0). Coach: "Print r.url. Print r.headers["Content-Type"]. Print r.text[:200]. What did you really receive?"

Also common: leaving off https:// (MissingSchema), and on the offline copy, stars that print as â˜… (set r.encoding = "utf-8").

Lab 6.1-A, everyone: labs/module-16/l6_1-http-requests/category_check_starter.py (reference: category_check_solution.py). Question: how many products do the Footwear, Snow and Skis category pages list, and how many show a rating star? One of the three pages does not exist.

  • How the lab reaches the network. One function, get(), hides the choice. Normally it sends a real request to BASE_URL and pauses one second. With LABS_OFFLINE=1 in the environment it rebuilds real Response objects from labs/module-16/_fixtures/ and touches nothing. Teaching with no network at all: LABS_OFFLINE=1 python category_check_starter.py (PowerShell: $env:LABS_OFFLINE = "1"; python category_check_starter.py). Teaching from the unzipped copy: change the BASE_URL line, or set PINECREST_BASE_URL.
  • Minutes 0 to 4: run the starter as shipped. It already fetches; the report shows status 200, 200, 404 and TODO 2: status not checked yet.
  • Minutes 4 to 18: TODO 1 (ask robots.txt), TODO 2 (check the status before counting), TODO 4 (decode with the wrong table, then the right one).
  • Minutes 18 to 25: results. Reference answers: robots.txt allows the three category pages and refuses staff/, crawl delay 1; Footwear 28 products, 25 with a star, 3 not rated yet; Snow 22 and 22; Skis is a 404 whose body (2,514 bytes of HTML) contains 0 product cards. Under cp1252 the Snow page has 0 stars and 22 pieces of â˜…; under utf-8, 22 stars. 11,987 bytes became 11,939 characters.
  • Ask: "Step 3 counted zero product cards on the Skis page. Is 'Skis: 0 products' a true statement?" (No. There is no such page. Zero and 'no answer' are different results, and only the status code tells them apart.)

Lab 6.1-B, for pairs who finish (or homework): labs/module-16/l6_1-http-requests/api_price_check_starter.py, which needs the practice API running (or LABS_OFFLINE=1). Reference answers: the URL is http://127.0.0.1:8000/products?category=Camp+Kitchen&per_page=100; 75 products in three categories; median price Tents $298.45 (24 products), Snow $78.45 (22), Camp Kitchen $39.95 (29); category Skis answers 200 with total 0; product TNT-9999 answers 404 with the message No product with SKU 'TNT-9999'. The point of steps 3 and 4: an empty result is not an error, and a real error explains itself in the body.

Start the lesson project (15 minutes)

Open the lesson at "Project: The Polite Snapshot". Learners type Step 1 (session, robots.txt, crawl delay) and Step 2 (polite_get()), and run the last two lines of Step 2: the staff URL comes back as skipped: robots.txt without a request being sent. Stop there and ask: "Where in the function does the robots check sit, and why there?" (Before the network is touched: the only place it does any good.) Steps 3 to 5 are homework. Step 5 needs the practice API; remind them how to start it at home.

Checks for understanding

Workbook self-check, Q7 to Q12. Q7 is the hinge question for this lesson: ask it by show of hands right after demo step 6, before you run step 7.

Answers: Q7 D) A normal response comes back; r.ok is False and nothing is raised; Q8 1 3 False; Q9 A) r.encoding and the Content-Type header; Q10 http://127.0.0.1:8000/orders?status=returned&since=2025-12-01; Q11 C) Skip the staff page, and wait at least one second between its other requests; Q12 B) False then caught. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: give the three-line pattern on a card: r = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=10) / r.raise_for_status() / use r.text or r.json(). In Lab A, TODO 2 is already written in comments: uncommenting and indenting it is a legitimate way through.

Stretch: lesson Exercise 4 (get_json() that returns (data, problem)), or the bonus challenge: turn polite_get() into a cache that reads raw/ before it touches the network.

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, on a sticky note; answers)
  1. In a pymongo query, what does {"utm": None} match, and which operator asks the precise question? Answer: Documents where utm is null and documents where it is missing. $exists tells the two apart.
  2. requests.get() comes back with status 404. What has happened in your program, and which one line makes the failure loud? Answer: Nothing was raised; you hold a normal response whose body is an error page. r.raise_for_status().
  3. Name any two of the six ground rules. Answer: Any two of: obey robots.txt; read the terms; prefer an API; go slowly and identify yourself; never go around a login or block; no personal data.

Read the notes before Session 17. If more than a third miss question 2, open Session 17 by parsing a 404 page on purpose.

If You Run Long or Short

Running long. At 1:10 you should be starting the Funnel Report; if you are still in the lab, skip the project start (assign Step 1 as homework: it is five lines) and take the break on time. In the second half the fixed points are the ground rules, demo steps 6 and 7, and Lab A. Demo steps 10, 11 and 14 can be shown from the lesson page instead of typed. If the practice API will not start in the room, do steps 9 to 12 from the guide's printed output and move Lab B to homework; Lab A does not need the API.

Running short. Run Lab 5.5-B in the room and compare the pipeline with the pandas check. In 6.1, do lesson Exercise 2 together (count products per category by asking for per_page=1 and reading total: Tents 24, Snow 22, Footwear 28), then Exercise 3 (a HEAD request: status 200 and 0 bytes of body). Or take the lesson's "Common Questions" as a five-minute discussion: "pandas can read a URL directly; why not just use pd.read_csv(url)?"

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 17: Scraping Static and Dynamic Pages

How to teach the scraping session. The first half turns static HTML into a tidy, checked DataFrame with Beautiful Soup: labels over positions, one block one dictionary, missing values on purpose, pagination without counting. The second half meets pages that JavaScript fills in, teaches learners to look for the data file first, and drives headless Chrome with explicit waits when nothing else will do.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 6.2–6.3 Session 17 of 21

How to Use This Guide

  • Session 17 is the scraping session. Before the break learners turn static HTML into a checked DataFrame with Beautiful Soup (Lesson 6.2); after it they meet pages that JavaScript fills in, learn to look for the data file first, and drive headless Chrome with Selenium when they must (Lesson 6.3).
  • Same rhythm as every session: frame → live demo (you type, they follow) → guided lab → start the lesson project. Finishing the projects, the exercises, quizzes and journals is homework.
  • Every code block below was run for this guide: Beautiful Soup 4.15, pandas 3.0.6, requests 2.34.2 and Selenium 4.51 with headless Chromium, against a local copy of the practice shop that sends the course website's headers. The output is real; on the public site only the addresses you see are different, and they are shown as the public ones.
  • The single most useful moment in the first half is a crash: parse_card() works on the first cards and raises KeyError: 'data-rating' on the Packs page. Let it happen live. The most useful idea in the second half is the order of the routes: data file first, browser last.
  • Labs live in labs/module-17/. The Selenium labs fall back to saved finished pages when Chrome cannot start, so nobody is left without a lab.
The risk in Session 17: the browser as a hammer

Selenium is exciting, and learners who have just watched it click buttons will want to use it for everything, with time.sleep() sprinkled in until it works. Both habits are expensive. Keep two sentences on the board all afternoon: "Is the data in the HTML? Is it in a file the page loads? Only then a browser." and "Never sleep: wait for something by name."

Before the Session

  • ☐ Run python3 labs/check_labs.py module-17 from the kit folder. Expect 8 passed, 0 failed (offline: the Selenium labs read saved finished pages and start no browser).
  • ☐ Copy the starters, _fixtures/ and labs_paths.py to the shared folder, keeping the layout. Keep the *_solution.py files on your machine.
  • ☐ The practice shop, online. Open https://rays-python-datascience.netlify.app/practice/shop/ and its Deals page on the venue network. The Deals page should show 8 deals after a second or two. If the shop does not load, use the offline copy for the whole room.
  • ☐ The practice shop, offline fallback. In the project folder: python -m zipfile -e data/pinecrest-practice-site.zip . then python -m http.server 8001 (leave it running). Everyone sets BASE_URL = "http://127.0.0.1:8001/practice/shop/"; for the kit labs, set PINECREST_BASE_URL to the same address or edit the BASE_URL line. Selenium loads local pages the same way, and the deals and search pages work offline because their data files are in the zip.
  • ☐ The practice API is not needed today. Neither 6.2 nor 6.3 uses it. (Session 18 starts it with flags: python data/mock_api.py --token-ttl 5 for Lesson 6.4 and python data/mock_api.py --rate 10 --per 5 for Lesson 6.5.)
  • ☐ Chrome and Selenium on the projector machine. Run the one-minute check from the Session 16 bring list (below). The first run downloads a driver, so do it on the venue network before learners arrive. Keep the printed page title on screen as proof.
  • ☐ MongoDB: nothing needed (Session 16 ran on mongomock, no server).
  • ☐ Browser tabs: webscraping_beautifulsoup.html, webscraping_selenium.html, the shop's Packs category page and Deals page, and the Deals page with developer tools open on the Network tab (Fetch/XHR filter).
  • ☐ Whiteboard: "Is the data in the HTML? In a file the page loads? Only then a browser." and "Never sleep: wait for something by name."
The Chrome check (from the Session 16 bring list)
from selenium import webdriver

options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
options.add_argument("--headless=new")
driver = webdriver.Chrome(options=options)
driver.get("https://rays-python-datascience.netlify.app/practice/shop/")
print(driver.title)
driver.quit()

It prints All products, page 1 | Pinecrest Outfitters (practice site) within about ten seconds. What the failures mean:

  • NoSuchDriverException or "unable to obtain driver": Selenium Manager could not download the driver (blocked network or proxy) or could not find Chrome. Run it once on an open network, or install Chrome.
  • "cannot find Chrome binary": Chrome is not installed, or is installed somewhere unusual. The kit labs accept PINECREST_CHROME = the path of a Chrome or Chromium program.
  • It hangs for a minute, then fails: a corporate machine blocking automation. Treat it as locked down.
A locked-down venue machine: the plan
  • Pair up. Seat learners whose Chrome failed with a neighbor whose check worked; the driver types, the navigator reads the lab aloud, and they swap at TODO 3.
  • Use the JSON route. Lesson 6.3 teaches it first for a reason: deals.json and products.json hold the same data the browser shows, and need nothing but requests. Learners without a browser do the lesson's first section, Exercise 4 and lab step 6 of budget_search in full.
  • The kit labs never strand anyone. If Chrome cannot start, they print [no browser] Chrome could not be started (...) and continue with the saved finished page. Everything after the browser step still runs.
  • Nothing to install on the spot. If a learner can install Chrome, do it at the break, not during the demo.
What differs on the offline copy (checked for this kit)
  • Python's server sends text/html with no charset, so resp.text shows â˜… for stars. Lesson 6.2 passes resp.content to Beautiful Soup, which reads the page's <meta charset>, so every parsed value is identical. Only learners who use resp.text see junk: a live reminder of why the lesson does it this way.
  • pd.read_html(io.BytesIO(resp.content), encoding="utf-8") gives the same two tables.
  • A missing page is Python's own 335-byte 404 page, not the site's. raise_for_status() behaves the same.
  • Selenium: the deals appear after the same 1.5 seconds and the search form produces the same URLs with 127.0.0.1:8001 in front. Links read with get_attribute("href") start with the local address.
  • All four kit labs give the same answers on the offline copy (checked against both servers).

Warm-up

0:00

Warm-up: Retrieval from Session 16

10 min

Five questions on the projector, answered on paper, notes closed (4 minutes), then aloud (3 minutes).

  1. In a pymongo query, what does {"utm": None} match? Answer: Documents where utm is null and documents where it is missing. $exists tells the two apart.
  2. Which aggregation stage does what pandas explode does? Answer: $unwind: one document per element of a list.
  3. requests.get() comes back with status 404. Has an exception been raised? Answer: No. You hold a normal response with .ok False; r.raise_for_status() makes it loud.
  4. Why does every request in this course carry timeout=? Answer: Without it requests waits forever for a server that has gone quiet.
  5. You see â˜… where a star should be. What happened, and what is one fix? Answer: UTF-8 bytes were decoded with the wrong table (no charset sent). Set r.encoding = "utf-8", or hand r.content to a parser that reads the page's <meta charset>.

Homework check (3 minutes). Funnel Report: hands up if your funnel read 2,400 → 1,610 → 543 → 230 → 230. Polite Snapshot: four files in raw/ and a six-row manifest. Chrome check: "Who saw the page title print? Who got an error?" Write the names of anyone with an error on a sticky note: they are your pairing list for the second half.

Ground Rules Opener (2 minutes)

0:10

The Six Ground Rules for Module 6

2 min

Every Module 6 session opens here. Six learners read one rule each, aloud. Add one sentence for today: "A browser is a heavier guest than requests: it downloads every script, style and image. That is one more reason to reach for it last."

  1. Read robots.txt and obey it. It is the owner's published request to programs: where they may go and how fast.
  2. Read the terms of use. If they forbid automated collection, the answer is no, however easy the code would be.
  3. Prefer an API or a download when one exists. It is the front door.
  4. Go slowly and say who you are. Pause between requests; send a User-Agent with a way to contact you.
  5. Never go around a login, a paywall or a block. If you are asked to stop, stop.
  6. Do not collect personal data. Names, emails, profiles and photos of real people are protected by law in many places.

Lesson Plans

6.2

Parsing HTML with Beautiful Soup

73 min
Objectives (from the lesson)
  • Read a page's HTML as a tree and locate the elements that hold the data you want
  • Select elements with find(), find_all() and CSS selectors, and choose selectors that survive small changes to a page
  • Write a function that turns one repeated block of HTML into a dictionary, including when optional pieces are missing
  • Follow "next" links to the last page of a paginated listing, politely, and visit detail pages for extra fields
  • Read HTML tables with pandas.read_html(), validate what you scraped, and save a tidy DataFrame
Timing (73 minutes)
13mFrame: the filing cabinet; Inspect one card in the browser
25mLive demo, steps 1 to 13
25mGuided lab: the sleeping bag shortlist (then the price list tables)
10mStart the Category Price Report: Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

"A page is a filing cabinet. Drawers hold folders, folders hold sheets, and nearly everything has a label on it: a class such as price, a data-sku such as TNT-1001. You do not find a document by counting 'third drawer, second folder, fifth sheet'. You read the labels: 'the sheet labeled price inside the folder labeled product-card'. Scraping well is mostly the skill of choosing good labels."

Then the whole job in one line on the board: fetch → parse → select the repeated block → one dictionary per block → DataFrame → check it. Open the Packs category page, right-click a product name, Inspect, and walk up to the li.product-card. Read its labels aloud.

Live demo (you type, they follow)

Notebook session17_soup. Thirteen steps; each runs in seconds except step 10, which pauses one second between three requests.

  1. Same polite setup, one new helper. Say: "Everything from Session 16 stays: one address, an honest User-Agent, a timeout, raise_for_status. The new line is the last one in the function: we hand the BYTES to Beautiful Soup, which reads the page's own charset tag." Run it and point at the title. 
    import re
import time
from urllib.parse import urljoin

import pandas as pd
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

BASE_URL = "https://rays-python-datascience.netlify.app/practice/shop/"
HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "pinecrest-course-bot/1.0 (learning project; contact: you@example.com)"}
DELAY = 1        # the Crawl-delay in robots.txt


def get_soup(url):
    """Fetch one page politely and return it as a parsed tree."""
    resp = requests.get(url, headers=HEADERS, timeout=10)
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return BeautifulSoup(resp.content, "html.parser")


packs = get_soup(urljoin(BASE_URL, "category-packs.html"))
print(packs.title.string)
    Packs | Pinecrest Outfitters (practice site)
  2. An element: a name, attributes, text. Say: "Predict: is the first li on the page a product?" It is not: it is the breadcrumb. "That is why we search by LABEL, not by tag name alone. Attributes behave like a dictionary; class is a LIST, because an element can have several." 
    print(repr(packs.find("li").get_text(strip=True)))
card = packs.find("li", class_="product-card")
print(card.attrs)
print(card["data-sku"])
print(card.get_text(" | ", strip=True))
    'Shop'
{'class': ['product-card'], 'data-sku': 'PCK-1001'}
PCK-1001
Wrenfield Canyon 22L Daypack | Packs | $136.95 | ★ 4.7 | (200 reviews) | In stock
  3. find, find_all, and the underscore. Say: "find gives the first match or None. find_all gives a list, maybe empty. class_ has an underscore because class is a Python keyword. And notice the key move: once we hold one card, we search INSIDE it." 
    cards = packs.find_all("li", class_="product-card")
print(len(cards))
link = cards[0].find("a")
print(link.get_text(), "->", link["href"])
print(cards[0].find("p", class_="price").get_text())
    24
Wrenfield Canyon 22L Daypack -> products/PCK-1001.html
$136.95
  4. CSS selectors: the labels on the drawers. Say: "select returns a list, select_one the first match or None. Read each selector aloud as a sentence: 'the price paragraph inside the card whose data-sku is PCK-1003'." 
    print(len(packs.select("li.product-card")))
print(packs.select_one("p.result-count").get_text())
print(len(packs.select("p.stock.out-of-stock")), "out of stock on this page")
print(packs.select_one('li[data-sku="PCK-1003"] p.price').get_text())
    24
24 products
3 out of stock on this page
$182.95
  5. Fragile and sturdy. Say: "Both lines find the same price today. The first is directions by position: it breaks silently the day the shop adds a badge or reorders the list. The second reads the labels. Choose meaning over position, and keep it short." 
    fragile = packs.select_one("main > ul > li:nth-of-type(3) > p:nth-of-type(2)")
sturdy = packs.select_one('li[data-sku="PCK-1003"] p.price')
print(fragile.get_text(), sturdy.get_text())
    $182.95 $182.95
  6. Take the machine-readable value. Say: "The text is for people; the data- attribute is for the site's own scripts. Either way, HTML gives you strings: converting is your job." 
    price = cards[0].select_one("p.price")
print(repr(price.get_text()), repr(price["data-price"]))
print(float(price["data-price"]) * 2)
    '$136.95' '136.95'
273.9
  7. One card, one dictionary (first version). Say: "This is the function that makes scraping manageable: it knows the HTML so the rest of the code does not have to. Predict: will it work on all 24 packs?" Let them vote, then run. 
    def parse_card(card):
    """Turn one product card into a flat dictionary. First version."""
    link = card.select_one("h2.product-name a")
    return {
        "sku": card["data-sku"],
        "name": link.get_text(strip=True),
        "price": float(card.select_one("p.price")["data-price"]),
        "rating": float(card.select_one("p.rating")["data-rating"]),
    }


rows = [parse_card(c) for c in packs.select("li.product-card")]
    KeyError: 'data-rating'
  8. Ask the page, do not guess. Say: "A KeyError on an attribute. Which card? Don't guess: ask." After the output: "Two packs have no reviews yet, so the shop writes different HTML for them. Real sites are full of this. The crash was the process working." 
    for c in packs.select("li.product-card"):
    tag = c.select_one("p.rating")
    if "data-rating" not in tag.attrs:
        print(c["data-sku"], tag)
    PCK-1002 <p class="rating no-rating">No reviews yet</p>
PCK-1009 <p class="rating no-rating">No reviews yet</p>
  9. Decide what missing means, field by field. Say: ".get() returns None for a missing attribute instead of raising. A product without a rating is normal: record missing. A product without a price is NOT normal: keep the square brackets so that one crashes loudly." 
    def parse_card(card):
    """Turn one product card into a flat dictionary."""
    link = card.select_one("h2.product-name a")
    rating = card.select_one("p.rating").get("data-rating")     # None if unrated
    return {
        "sku": card["data-sku"],
        "name": link.get_text(strip=True),
        "price": float(card.select_one("p.price")["data-price"]),
        "rating": float(rating) if rating else None,
        "stock": card.select_one("p.stock")["class"][1],
    }


packs_df = pd.DataFrame([parse_card(c) for c in packs.select("li.product-card")])
print(packs_df.shape)
print(packs_df.loc[packs_df["rating"].isna(), ["sku", "name", "rating"]])
print(packs_df["stock"].value_counts().to_dict())
    (24, 5)
        sku                               name  rating
1  PCK-1002    Pinecrest Headwater 30L Daypack     NaN
8  PCK-1009  Juniper Vane Sawtooth 30L Daypack     NaN
{'in-stock': 20, 'out-of-stock': 3, 'low-stock': 1}
  10. Follow "next" until there is none. Say: "The catalog is paginated. We never count pages by hand: we follow the next link until a page has none. max_pages is a seat belt. I start at page 11 so the demo sends three requests, not thirteen." 
    def scrape(start_url, max_pages=50):
    """Follow 'next' links from start_url. Returns (rows, pages_fetched)."""
    rows, url, pages = [], start_url, 0
    while url and pages < max_pages:
        soup = get_soup(url)
        rows.extend(parse_card(c) for c in soup.select("li.product-card"))
        pages += 1
        nxt = soup.select_one("nav.pagination a.next")
        url = urljoin(url, nxt["href"]) if nxt else None
        time.sleep(DELAY)
    return rows, pages


rows, pages = scrape(urljoin(BASE_URL, "page-11.html"))
print(pages, "pages,", len(rows), "products")
print(rows[-1]["sku"], rows[-1]["name"])
    3 pages, 42 products
ACC-1032 Larkspur Ridge Mesa Multitool
  11. Check before you trust. Say: "Scraped data deserves more suspicion than a file someone handed you. Three questions: does the count match what the page claims, is the key unique, do the values look plausible?" 
    claimed = int(re.search(r"\d+", packs.select_one("p.result-count").get_text()).group())
print("claimed", claimed, "| scraped", len(packs_df), "| match", claimed == len(packs_df))
print("unique SKUs:", packs_df["sku"].is_unique)
print(packs_df["price"].describe().round(2)[["min", "50%", "max"]].to_dict())
    claimed 24 | scraped 24 | match True
unique SKUs: True
{'min': 20.95, '50%': 118.95, 'max': 335.95}
  12. A real table? read_html. Say: "When the data is already a <table>, skip the selectors. Fetch it yourself so your User-Agent and timeout apply, wrap the bytes, and pick the table by its id, not its position." 
    import io

resp = requests.get(urljoin(BASE_URL, "price-list.html"), headers=HEADERS, timeout=10)
resp.raise_for_status()
hours = pd.read_html(io.BytesIO(resp.content), encoding="utf-8",
                     attrs={"id": "store-hours"})[0]
print(hours)

2  Flagstaff    AZ  10 am to 7 pm  (928) 555-0167
3  Asheville    NC  10 am to 8 pm  (828) 555-0193
  13. Two errors you will see today. Say: "Read the type in the message. NoneType means your search found nothing. ResultSet means you have a LIST and treated it as one element: Beautiful Soup even tells you which method you probably meant." 
    for code in ['packs.select_one("p.sale-price").get_text()',
             'packs.select("p.price").get_text()']:
    try:
        eval(code)
    except AttributeError as err:
        print(str(err).split(". ")[0])
    'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get_text'
ResultSet object has no attribute "get_text"
Three mistakes to expect
  • AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'get_text'. The selector found nothing (usually a typo in a class name, or a class that the card does not have). Coach: "How many does len(soup.select(your_selector)) find? Now Inspect the page: what is the class really called?"
  • A list treated as one element, soup.select("p.price").get_text(). Beautiful Soup's own message says "You're probably treating a list of elements like a single element". Coach: "Do you want one, or all of them? One: select_one. All: a loop."
  • KeyError on an optional attribute, "fixed" with try/except: pass. That hides the product. Coach: "What should a missing rating MEAN in your table?" Then .get() and None. Keep square brackets for fields that must exist (SKU, price) so those crash loudly.

Also common: class= instead of class_= (a SyntaxError), and requesting a relative href (MissingSchema: use urljoin).

Guided lab (25 minutes)

Lab 6.2-A, everyone: labs/module-17/l6_2-beautifulsoup/sleeping_bag_shortlist_starter.py (reference: sleeping_bag_shortlist_solution.py). Question: a customer wants a sleeping bag for $260 or less that can be bought today, as light as possible. Which bag, and what do we not know?

  • Minutes 0 to 3: run it as shipped. The listing prints with None for price, rating and stock: that is TODO 2.
  • Minutes 3 to 15: TODO 2 (finish parse_card(): data-price, .get("data-rating"), the second stock class) and TODO 3 (the shortlist).
  • Minutes 15 to 22: TODO 4 (the specs table as a dictionary) and TODO 5 (clean weight and temperature). The lab fetches only the shortlisted detail pages: 6, not 24. Ask why that matters.
  • Minutes 22 to 25: results. 24 cards (the page claims 24); 12 sleeping bags, 6 at $260 or less and available; lightest SLP-1002 Juniper Vane Foothill 30F, 0.81 kg, $132.95; SLP-1019 shows Not listed for weight.
  • Ask: "Is SLP-1019 the heaviest bag?" (We do not know. Missing is 'unknown', not 'zero' and not 'heaviest'. sort_values puts NaN last, which is not the same as saying it is heavy.)

6.3

Dynamic Pages with Selenium

75 min
Objectives (from the lesson)
  • Tell a static page from one that JavaScript fills in, and explain why requests sees no data on the second kind
  • Find the JSON a dynamic page loads and use it directly when you can
  • Start headless Chrome with Selenium 4, open a page, and locate elements with By locators
  • Wait for content with WebDriverWait and expected conditions instead of time.sleep()
  • Click buttons, fill in a form, take a screenshot, and always quit the browser, even after an error
Timing (75 minutes)
12mFrame: flat-pack furniture; the order of the routes
25mLive demo, steps 1 to 12
25mGuided lab: the budget shelf (then page triage)
13mStart Deals Watch: Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

"A static page arrives like a finished bookcase: what comes off the truck is what you see. A dynamic page arrives flat-packed: a nearly empty frame (the HTML), a bag of parts to be fetched (data files), and an instruction sheet (JavaScript). Your browser does the assembly after delivery. requests is a delivery driver, not a carpenter: it hands you the box exactly as shipped and never opens the instructions."

Then draw the decision on the board: visible in the browser → in the raw HTML? Beautiful Soup. → No: does the page load a data file? Request it. → No: drive a browser. "We will collect the deals both ways today, because you will check the browser's answer against the file."

Live demo (you type, they follow)

Notebook session17_selenium. One browser stays open from step 3 to step 12; if the demo is interrupted, run driver.quit() before anything else. On your projector machine Chrome is found automatically; this kit's run used a Chromium program set with two extra options that learners do not need.

  1. The page that comes back empty. Say: "In the browser the Deals page shows eight offers. Watch what requests receives." After the output: "The request worked. The list is there. It is empty, next to a message saying the deals are loading. They never will, in this program."

  5. Wait for the thing you need, by name. Say: "Never sleep. Say what you are waiting for and how long you will give it. Selenium checks twice a second and continues the moment it is true." Write the double parentheses on the board: the locator is ONE tuple. 
    from selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as EC
from selenium.webdriver.support.ui import WebDriverWait

wait = WebDriverWait(driver, 10)

print(len(driver.find_elements(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "li.deal")), "deals now")
print(driver.find_element(By.ID, "deal-status").text)

  7. Let the browser render, let Beautiful Soup parse. Say: "Each find_element is a round trip to the browser. Division of labor: Selenium does what only a browser can, then we take the finished HTML and use the tool we already know." 
    def parse_deals(html):
    """Parse the deal cards in a rendered deals page into a DataFrame."""
    soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")
    return pd.DataFrame([{
        "sku": li["data-sku"],
        "price": float(li.select_one("s.was").get_text().lstrip("$")),
        "deal_price": float(li.select_one("span.deal-price").get_text().lstrip("$")),
    } for li in soup.select("#deal-list li.deal")])

  11. Two errors to read on purpose. Say: "Selenium's tracebacks are long; read the first line. NoSuchElement right after get(): not YET. A TimeoutException: the thing never came, often a typo. Give every wait a message so the error says what you were waiting for." 
    from selenium.common.exceptions import NoSuchElementException, TimeoutException

driver.get(DEALS_URL)
try:
    driver.find_element(By.CSS_SELECTOR, "li.deal")
except NoSuchElementException as err:
    print(type(err).__name__, "|", err.msg.split(":")[0])
try:
    WebDriverWait(driver, 3).until(
        EC.presence_of_element_located((By.CSS_SELECTOR, "li.deals")),
        message="no li.deals after 3 seconds")
except TimeoutException as err:
    print(type(err).__name__, "|", err.msg)
    NoSuchElementException | no such element
TimeoutException | no li.deals after 3 seconds
  12. You own a running program: quit it. Say: "driver is a real Chrome process. It runs until you quit it, even after your script crashes. So: one function that starts it, and try/finally around the work, every time." 
    driver.quit()


def make_driver():
    """Start Chrome with this course's settings. Whoever calls this must quit it."""
    options = Options()
    options.add_argument("--headless=new")
    options.add_argument("--window-size=1000,800")
    options.add_argument(f"--user-agent={USER_AGENT}")
    return webdriver.Chrome(options=options)


driver = make_driver()
try:
    driver.get(DEALS_URL)
    WebDriverWait(driver, 10).until(
        EC.presence_of_element_located((By.CSS_SELECTOR, "li.deal")))
    print(driver.find_element(By.ID, "deal-status").text)
finally:
    driver.quit()
    print("browser closed")
    Showing 8 of 24 deals
browser closed
Three mistakes to expect
  • time.sleep() to make it work. It passes in class and fails at home on a slow connection. Coach: "What exactly are you waiting for? Name it, and wait for that."
  • Missing the inner parentheses in EC.presence_of_element_located((By.ID, "x")). The error is a TypeError about arguments. Coach: point at the board: the locator is ONE tuple.
  • Orphaned browsers. A crash before quit() leaves Chrome running; after a few runs the laptop is slow. Coach: "Where is your finally?" On Windows, Task Manager shows them; on macOS and Linux, Activity Monitor or ps.

Also common: NoSuchElementException right after get() (not yet: wait), a TimeoutException caused by a selector typo (give every wait a message=), StaleElementReferenceException after a reload, and old tutorials' find_element_by_id (removed in Selenium 4).

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, on a sticky note; answers)
  1. Which Beautiful Soup method returns None when nothing matches, and which returns an empty list? Answer: select_one() (and find()) return None; select() (and find_all()) return a list, empty if nothing matches.
  2. Why is WebDriverWait(...).until(...) better than time.sleep(5)? Answer: It continues the moment the condition is true and raises a clear TimeoutException if it never is. A sleep is always too short or too long.
  3. Before you start a browser for a page that JavaScript fills in, what do you look for first? Answer: The data file or API the page loads (Network tab, or the page's script). If you may request it, do that instead.

If more than a third miss question 3, open Session 18 with the decision drawn on the board again: it is the same question APIs answer.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 18: APIs: Keys, Tokens and Polite Clients

How to teach the session that closes Module 6. Before the break, API keys and bearer tokens: secrets from the environment, 401 versus 403, logging in, expiry and renewing once, pagination into a DataFrame. After the break, the habits of a welcome client: reading the limit, pacing, honoring 429, backoff with jitter, retry policies, caching and resumable jobs. Then Checkpoint 2, a 15-minute data-access task on Modules 5 and 6.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 6.4–6.5 Checkpoint 2 Session 18 of 21

How to Use This Guide

  • Session 18 closes Module 6 with the front door: APIs. Before the break, keys and tokens (Lesson 6.4); after it, the habits that make a client welcome and dependable (Lesson 6.5). Then Checkpoint 2, 15 minutes, on data access across Modules 5 and 6.
  • Same rhythm as every session: frame → live demo → guided lab → start the project. The checkpoint takes 15 minutes and its debrief 10, so the lesson blocks are a little shorter than usual and both projects are mostly homework.
  • Every code block below was run for this guide against data/mock_api.py: with --token-ttl 5 for 6.4 and --rate 10 --per 5 for 6.5, with the three demo environment variables set. Tokens, and some timings, will differ on your screen; the guide says where.
  • The practice shop is not used today. Everything happens on http://127.0.0.1:8000, a server on each learner's own computer.
  • Labs and the checkpoint live in labs/module-18/. With LABS_OFFLINE=1 they replay real saved responses and run their waits on a pretend clock.
The risk in Session 18: secrets on screens, loops that hammer

Two habits to make automatic today. Secrets never appear in code, output or logs: the projector itself is a test (never print a key; print a hint). Every retry has a reason, a wait and a limit: retry 429, 5xx and timeouts; never 400, 403 or 404; renew an expired token once. A loop that retries a 401 forever looks like an attack.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Run python3 labs/check_labs.py module-18 from the kit folder. Expect 10 passed, 0 failed (offline; the checker sets the three variables to the demo values).
  • ☐ Copy the starters (including checkpoint-2/checkpoint2_starter.py), _fixtures/ and labs_paths.py to the shared folder. Keep every *_solution.py on your machine; the checkpoint solution is the model answer.
  • ☐ The practice API, with the flags of each lesson. Lesson 6.4: python data/mock_api.py --token-ttl 5 (tokens last five seconds so learners can watch one expire). Lesson 6.5: stop it with Ctrl+C at the break and start python data/mock_api.py --rate 10 --per 5 (ten requests every five seconds, so the limit is easy to hit). The checkpoint works with either. Check: http://127.0.0.1:8000/health shows {"status": "ok"}, and the start line names the limit, for example (limit: 10 requests per 5 s; Ctrl+C to stop).
  • ☐ Why restart at the break: the 6.5 demos need the small limit to show a 429 within seconds, and the 6.4 token demos need short tokens. With default flags (30 per 10 s, 60-second tokens) nothing goes wrong, it just takes too long to see.
  • ☐ The three environment variables on the projector machine, set before starting Jupyter or VS Code from the same terminal (commands below). Test with the first demo cell: it prints key loaded: pine... (18 characters).
  • ☐ The practice shop: not used today. If a learner asks, it is at https://rays-python-datascience.netlify.app/practice/shop/, with the offline copy served from data/pinecrest-practice-site.zip on port 8001 (Session 16).
  • ☐ Chrome and Selenium: not used today (Session 17). MongoDB: nothing needed (Session 16 ran on mongomock).
  • ☐ Print the Checkpoint 2 task sheet from the workbook, or keep it on the projector during the checkpoint.
  • ☐ Whiteboard: "401: who are you? 403: no." and "Retry: a reason, a wait, a limit."
The three environment variables (public demo values for the practice API)
# Windows PowerShell (this terminal only)
$env:PINECREST_API_KEY = "pinecrest-demo-key"
$env:PINECREST_USER = "analyst"
$env:PINECREST_PASSWORD = "trailmix"

# macOS and Linux (this terminal only)
export PINECREST_API_KEY="pinecrest-demo-key"
export PINECREST_USER="analyst"
export PINECREST_PASSWORD="trailmix"
  • The trap: variables set this way exist only in that terminal and in programs started from it afterward. A notebook started earlier, or from the Start menu, does not see them: close it, set the variables, start it again from that terminal. The demo's require_env() turns this into a clear message instead of a mystery.
  • Other routes (Lesson 6.4): getpass.getpass("API key: ") to type a secret into a hidden box, or a .env file read by python-dotenv, which is safe only if .env is listed in .gitignore before the first commit.
  • These are teaching values for a server on your own computer. Real keys are personal: never share one on a slide or in a chat.
