Warm-up

0:00

Warm-up: Retrieval from Session 17

10 min

Five questions, notes closed, then answers aloud.

  1. Which Beautiful Soup method returns None when nothing matches? Answer: select_one() (and find()). select() and find_all() return a list, empty when nothing matches.
  2. Why does get_soup() pass resp.content, not resp.text? Answer: From bytes, Beautiful Soup reads the page's own <meta charset>, so the text decodes correctly whatever the server said.
  3. How does a pagination loop know it has reached the last page of the catalog? Answer: There is no a.next link on the last page, so select_one("nav.pagination a.next") returns None.
  4. requests sees an empty list where the browser shows deals. What do you try before Selenium? Answer: Find the data file the page loads (Network tab or the script) and request it directly, if allowed.
  5. Why WebDriverWait(...).until(...) instead of time.sleep(), and where does driver.quit() go? Answer: The wait continues as soon as the condition is true and raises clearly if it never is. quit() goes in a finally block.

Homework check (3 minutes). Category Price Report: nine rows, Tents first. Deals Watch: 24 rows equal to deals.json. Then: "Who has the three variables set and the API started with --token-ttl 5?" Fix the rest now, while the room does question 5.

Ground Rules Opener (2 minutes)

0:10

The Six Ground Rules for Module 6

2 min

Six learners, one rule each, aloud. Today's sentence: "An API is the front door rule 3 asked for. It comes with its own rules: a key that is yours alone, and a limit the owner sets. Keep both."

  1. Read robots.txt and obey it. It is the owner's published request to programs: where they may go and how fast.
  2. Read the terms of use. If they forbid automated collection, the answer is no, however easy the code would be.
  3. Prefer an API or a download when one exists. It is the front door.
  4. Go slowly and say who you are. Pause between requests; send a User-Agent with a way to contact you.
  5. Never go around a login, a paywall or a block. If you are asked to stop, stop.
  6. Do not collect personal data. Names, emails, profiles and photos of real people are protected by law in many places.

6.4

API Authentication

63 min
Objectives (from the lesson)
  • Send an API key in a request header and tell a 401 from a 403
  • Keep keys and passwords out of your code with environment variables
  • Log in for a bearer token, use it, and recover when it expires
  • Turn an API's error responses into clear Python exceptions, and decide by status code what to do next
  • Follow pagination to the last page and build a DataFrame, using a small reusable client class
Timing (63 minutes)
10mFrame: the wristband; 401 versus 403; where secrets live
23mLive demo, steps 1 to 13
22mGuided lab: cancelled orders (then the token lifecycle)
8mStart the December Returns Brief: Steps 1 and 2
Mental model to say

"Think of a festival. At the gate you show your ticket once (your username and password). They give you a wristband (the token) and you wear it everywhere inside: no one asks for the ticket again. The wristband is dated: tomorrow it does not work, and you go back to the gate. Some stalls only want to see your membership card (the API key) every time. And two different refusals: 'I cannot see a wristband' is 401; 'I see it, and you are not allowed in here' is 403."

Draw the decision table from the lesson on the board: 400 fix the code, 401 renew once or stop, 403 stop, 404 stop or record, 429 wait and retry, 5xx wait and retry a few times.

Live demo (you type, they follow)

Notebook session18_auth, with the practice API started as python data/mock_api.py --token-ttl 5. Step 8 and step 9 each wait six seconds on purpose: talk while they run.

  1. Secrets come from the environment. Say: "Before any request: where does the key live? Not in this notebook. You set three variables in the terminal before starting Jupyter. When you need to confirm a secret loaded, print a HINT of it, never the value: output cells are saved with the notebook." 
    import os
import time

import pandas as pd
import requests

API = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"
HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "pinecrest-course-bot/1.0 (learning project; contact: you@example.com)"}


def require_env(name):
    """Read a required setting from the environment, or stop with a clear message."""
    value = os.environ.get(name)
    if not value:
        raise RuntimeError(f"Set the environment variable {name} before running this code.")
    return value


API_KEY = require_env("PINECREST_API_KEY")
USERNAME = require_env("PINECREST_USER")
PASSWORD = require_env("PINECREST_PASSWORD")
print("key loaded:", API_KEY[:4] + "...", f"({len(API_KEY)} characters)")
    key loaded: pine... (18 characters)
  2. A variable that is not set. Say: "This is the message a learner sees when Jupyter was started from a different terminal. It says exactly what to do." 
    require_env("PINECREST_REPORTS_KEY")
    RuntimeError: Set the environment variable PINECREST_REPORTS_KEY before running this code.
  3. 401 and 403 are different answers. Say: "No key: 401, 'I cannot tell who you are'. A wrong key: 403, 'I understood, and the answer is no'. Sending a 403 again never helps." Ask before running the second request: "Which status?" 
    r = requests.get(f"{API}/orders", headers=HEADERS, timeout=10)
print(r.status_code, r.json()["error"]["code"])
r = requests.get(f"{API}/orders", headers={**HEADERS, "X-API-Key": "pinecrest-demo"},
                 timeout=10)
print(r.status_code, r.json()["error"]["code"])
    401 missing_api_key
403 invalid_api_key
  4. The key in a header, never in the URL. Say: "The documentation says where the key goes: a header named X-API-Key. URLs end up in logs, browser history and bug reports; headers mostly do not." 
    KEY_HEADERS = {**HEADERS, "X-API-Key": API_KEY}
r = requests.get(f"{API}/orders", headers=KEY_HEADERS,
                 params={"status": "cancelled", "since": "2025-12-15", "per_page": 3},
                 timeout=10)
data = r.json()
print(r.status_code, {k: v for k, v in data.items() if k != "items"})
print([(o["order_id"], o["store"], o["order_total"]) for o in data["items"]])
    200 {'page': 1, 'per_page': 3, 'total': 15, 'total_pages': 5, 'next': '/orders?page=2&per_page=3&since=2025-12-15&status=cancelled'}
[(119812, 'Online', 81.9), (119840, 'Online', 53.9), (119860, 'Online', 62.9)]
  5. Errors you can act on. Say: "raise_for_status throws the API's explanation away. A tiny exception class keeps the status, the code and the message, so code can branch on err.code." 
    class ApiError(Exception):
    """An error response from the API, with its status, code and message."""
    def __init__(self, status, code, message):
        super().__init__(f"{status} {code}: {message}")
        self.status, self.code, self.message = status, code, message


def check(resp):
    """Return the response if it succeeded. Otherwise raise ApiError."""
    if resp.ok:
        return resp
    try:
        error = resp.json()["error"]
        code, message = error["code"], error["message"]
    except (requests.exceptions.JSONDecodeError, KeyError, TypeError):
        code, message = "http_error", resp.reason
    raise ApiError(resp.status_code, code, message)


check(requests.get(f"{API}/orders", headers=KEY_HEADERS,
                   params={"since": "Dec 1 2025"}, timeout=10))
    ApiError: 400 bad_request: 'since' must look like 2025-01-31, got 'Dec 1 2025'.
  6. Your first POST: log in for a token. Say: "GET reads; POST sends. json= encodes the dictionary as a JSON body. The password crosses the network once; what you carry afterward stops working on its own. We started the API with --token-ttl 5, so this one lasts five seconds." 
    resp = check(requests.post(f"{API}/login",
                           json={"username": USERNAME, "password": PASSWORD},
                           headers=HEADERS, timeout=10))
body = resp.json()
print(list(body))
print(body["token_type"], "token, valid for", body["expires_in"], "seconds")
token = body["access_token"]
print(token[:6] + "...  (your token will differ)")
    ['access_token', 'token_type', 'expires_in']
Bearer token, valid for 5 seconds
clP_eI...  (your token will differ)
  7. Bearer means bearer. Say: "The header is the word Bearer, a space, the token. Whoever bears it gets in, no other questions: treat it like a key." 
    auth = {**HEADERS, "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}
me = check(requests.get(f"{API}/me", headers=auth, timeout=10)).json()
print(me["username"], "|", me["name"], "|", me["role"])
    analyst | Demo Analyst | analyst
  8. The wristband runs out. Say: "Wait six seconds and use the same token. Nothing is wrong with your account. This is the normal life of a token, and your code must expect it in the middle of a job." 
    time.sleep(6)
try:
    check(requests.get(f"{API}/me", headers=auth, timeout=10))
except ApiError as err:
    print(err.status, err.code)
    print(err.message)
    401 token_expired
The token has expired. Log in again with POST /login.
  9. Renew and retry ONCE. Say: "Recover from token_expired by logging in again and repeating the request one time. Anything else, and a second failure, goes up to the caller. A loop that retries a 401 forever looks like an attack and gets accounts locked." 
    def login():
    resp = check(requests.post(f"{API}/login", timeout=10, headers=HEADERS,
                               json={"username": USERNAME, "password": PASSWORD}))
    return resp.json()["access_token"]


def get_me(token):
    try:
        return check(requests.get(f"{API}/me", timeout=10,
                                  headers={**HEADERS, "Authorization": f"Bearer {token}"}))
    except ApiError as err:
        if err.code != "token_expired":
            raise
    print("  (token expired: logging in again)")
    return check(requests.get(f"{API}/me", timeout=10,
                              headers={**HEADERS, "Authorization": f"Bearer {login()}"}))


old = login()
time.sleep(6)
print(get_me(old).json()["username"])
      (token expired: logging in again)
analyst
  10. One small request first: how big is the job?. Say: "Before downloading, ask for one record with the same filter and read the total. The size of the job for the price of one request." 
    params = {"status": "returned", "since": "2025-12-15", "per_page": 1}
probe = check(requests.get(f"{API}/orders", headers=KEY_HEADERS, params=params,
                           timeout=10)).json()
print(probe["total"], "orders;", probe["next"])
    34 orders; /orders?page=2&per_page=1&since=2025-12-15&status=returned
  11. Follow next to the end. Say: "The same loop as the catalog in Session 17, with JSON. The filters go in params for the FIRST request only: next already carries them, so we set params to None." 
    def get_all(path, params=None):
    """Collect every item from a paginated endpoint by following 'next'."""
    items, url = [], f"{API}{path}"
    while url:
        data = check(requests.get(url, headers=KEY_HEADERS, params=params,
                                  timeout=10)).json()
        items.extend(data["items"])
        url = f"{API}{data['next']}" if data["next"] else None
        params = None              # 'next' already carries the filters
    return items


late = pd.DataFrame(get_all("/orders", {"status": "returned", "since": "2025-12-15",
                                        "per_page": 10}))
print(late.shape, "| unique ids:", late["order_id"].is_unique)
print(late.groupby("channel")["order_total"].agg(["count", "sum"]).round(2))
    (34, 11) | unique ids: True

channel                
online      28  6618.27
store        6   567.10

    csv = pd.read_csv("data/orders.csv")
expected = csv[(csv["status"] == "returned") & (csv["order_date"] >= "2025-12-15")]
print(len(expected), "expected | same ids:",

    34 expected | same ids: True
  13. Two mistakes with no traceback to warn you. Say: "Leave out the word Bearer and the server does not recognize a token at all. Send data= instead of json= and you sent a form, not JSON." 
    t = login()
r = requests.get(f"{API}/me", headers={**HEADERS, "Authorization": t}, timeout=10)
print(r.status_code, r.json()["error"]["code"])
r = requests.post(f"{API}/login", data={"username": USERNAME, "password": PASSWORD},
                  headers=HEADERS, timeout=10)
print(r.status_code, r.json()["error"]["message"])

400 The request body must be JSON.
Three mistakes to expect
  • RuntimeError: Set the environment variable ... because Jupyter was started before the variables were set, or from another terminal. Coach: close it, set them, start it from that terminal. Do not let anyone "fix" it by typing the key into the notebook.
  • Leaving out the word Bearer, or using data= instead of json= for the login (401 missing_token; 400 The request body must be JSON.). Coach: "Print the headers you are sending. What does the documentation say the value looks like?"
  • KeyError: 'access_token' after a failed login. The KeyError is a symptom: the login answered 401 and the body is an error object. Coach: "What was the status of the line BEFORE?" Then check().

Also common: sending params again on every page (filters doubled), and a retry loop around a 401 with no limit.

6.5

Rate Limiting and Retries

60 min
Objectives (from the lesson)
  • Read an API's rate-limit headers and pace your requests to stay inside the limit
  • Respond correctly to 429 Too Many Requests by honoring Retry-After
  • Retry temporary failures with exponential backoff and jitter, and recognize errors that must not be retried
  • Configure automatic retries on a Session with urllib3's Retry and HTTPAdapter
  • Cache responses on disk, make a long download resumable, and log what your job did
Timing (60 minutes)
10mFrame: the on-ramp light; politeness and resilience
23mLive demo, steps 1 to 11
20mGuided lab: the stock check (then retry and cache)
7mStart the Resumable Order Pull: Step 1
Mental model to say

"Many freeway on-ramps have a light that lets one car go every few seconds. Nobody enjoys it, but without it everyone merges at once and the whole freeway crawls, including the cars from that ramp. A rate limit is that light. A good driver arrives at the pace the light allows, waits when it is red for exactly as long as it says, and does not honk."

Two halves on the board: politeness (pace yourself, obey Retry-After, never fetch the same thing twice) and resilience (retry what is temporary with backoff, give up clearly, save work so an interruption loses nothing).

Live demo (you type, they follow)

Notebook session18_limits, with the API restarted as python data/mock_api.py --rate 10 --per 5. fresh_window() waits five seconds so each demonstration starts from zero: use the pause to ask the next prediction. The 429 wait in step 4 can print 4 or 5 seconds depending on where in the window the burst landed.

  1. The limit, in the headers. Say: "The API was restarted with --rate 10 --per 5: ten requests every five seconds. Every response tells you where you stand. Read them like a fuel gauge." 
    import hashlib
import json
import logging
import random
import sys
import time
from pathlib import Path

import requests

API = "http://127.0.0.1:8000"
HEADERS = {"User-Agent": "pinecrest-course-bot/1.0 (learning project; contact: you@example.com)"}
LIMIT, PER = 10, 5


def fresh_window():
    """Wait out the current window so a demonstration starts from zero."""
    time.sleep(PER)


r = requests.get(f"{API}/products", params={"per_page": 1}, headers=HEADERS, timeout=10)
print(r.status_code, {k: v for k, v in r.headers.items() if k.startswith("X-RateLimit")})
    200 {'X-RateLimit-Limit': '10', 'X-RateLimit-Remaining': '9', 'X-RateLimit-Reset': '5'}
  2. Ignore it, and hit the wall. Say: "Thirteen requests as fast as Python can. Predict how many succeed." After: "429 is the server holding up a hand, with an instruction: Retry-After says how long to wait. The refused requests were pure waste." 
    fresh_window()
statuses = []
for i in range(13):
    r = requests.get(f"{API}/products", params={"per_page": 1}, headers=HEADERS,
                     timeout=10)
    statuses.append(r.status_code)
print(statuses)
print("Retry-After:", r.headers["Retry-After"], "|", r.json()["error"]["message"])
    [200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 200, 429, 429, 429]
Retry-After: 5 | Too many requests. Try again in 5 second(s).
  3. Plan A: pace yourself. Say: "The freeway on-ramp light. Ten per five seconds is one every half second; add ten percent for clock drift. The Throttle sleeps only for whatever is left of the interval." 
    class Throttle:
    """Keep calls at least `interval` seconds apart."""
    def __init__(self, interval):
        self.interval, self.last = interval, None

    def wait(self):
        if self.last is not None:
            remaining = self.interval - (time.monotonic() - self.last)
            if remaining > 0:
                time.sleep(remaining)
        self.last = time.monotonic()


interval = PER / LIMIT * 1.1
fresh_window()
throttle, statuses, started = Throttle(interval), [], time.monotonic()
for i in range(13):
    throttle.wait()
    statuses.append(requests.get(f"{API}/products", params={"per_page": 1},
                                 headers=HEADERS, timeout=10).status_code)
print(f"every {interval:.2f} s:", statuses.count(200), "of 13 succeeded,",
      f"about {time.monotonic() - started:.0f} s")
    every 0.55 s: 13 of 13 succeeded, about 7 s
  4. Plan B: when told to wait, wait. Say: "Pacing is plan A; limits change and keys get shared, so you still need plan B. Three details make it trustworthy: a default for Retry-After, a maximum number of tries, and retrying ONLY 429." 
    def get_polite(url, max_tries=5, **kwargs):
    """GET that waits and retries when the server answers 429."""
    kwargs.setdefault("headers", HEADERS)
    kwargs.setdefault("timeout", 10)
    for attempt in range(1, max_tries + 1):
        resp = requests.get(url, **kwargs)
        if resp.status_code != 429:
            return resp
        wait = float(resp.headers.get("Retry-After", 1))
        print(f"  429 (try {attempt}): waiting {wait:.0f} s, as asked")
        time.sleep(wait)
    return resp


fresh_window()
codes = [get_polite(f"{API}/products", params={"per_page": 1}).status_code
         for i in range(15)]
print(codes.count(200), "of", len(codes), "succeeded")
      429 (try 1): waiting 5 s, as asked
15 of 15 succeeded
  5. Backoff, and why it needs jitter. Say: "No instruction from the server? Wait a little, then twice as long, then twice again, up to a cap. And add randomness, or a hundred clients that failed together retry together, in waves." The seed is only so this page matches the screen. 
    def backoff_delay(attempt, base=0.5, cap=8.0):
    """Seconds to wait after failed attempt number `attempt` (from 0)."""
    return min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt)


print([backoff_delay(n) for n in range(6)])
rng = random.Random(7)
print([round(rng.uniform(0, backoff_delay(n)), 2) for n in range(6)])
    [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0, 8.0]
[0.16, 0.15, 1.3, 0.29, 4.29, 2.93]
  6. A flaky endpoint. Say: "/flaky fails twice with 503 and then succeeds, over and over. Notice its 503 also carries Retry-After: an instruction always beats your guess." 
    fresh_window()
for i in range(3):
    r = requests.get(f"{API}/flaky", headers=HEADERS, timeout=10)
    print(r.status_code, "| Retry-After:", r.headers.get("Retry-After"))
    503 | Retry-After: 1
503 | Retry-After: 1
200 | Retry-After: None
  7. Retry what is temporary, return what is not. Say: "Temporary: 429, 5xx, a timeout, a dropped connection. Not temporary: 400, 401, 403, 404. A missing product will still be missing in two seconds, so it comes back at once." 
    RETRY_STATUSES = {429, 500, 502, 503, 504}


def get_with_backoff(url, max_tries=5, base=0.5, **kwargs):
    """GET with retries: obeys Retry-After, otherwise backs off with jitter."""
    kwargs.setdefault("headers", HEADERS)
    kwargs.setdefault("timeout", 10)
    for attempt in range(max_tries):
        try:
            resp = requests.get(url, **kwargs)
            if resp.status_code not in RETRY_STATUSES:
                return resp
            problem, asked = f"HTTP {resp.status_code}", resp.headers.get("Retry-After")
        except (requests.exceptions.Timeout, requests.exceptions.ConnectionError) as err:
            problem, asked = type(err).__name__, None
        if attempt == max_tries - 1:
            break
        delay = float(asked) if asked else random.uniform(0, backoff_delay(attempt, base))
        print(f"  try {attempt + 1}: {problem}; next try in {delay:.1f} s")
        time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError(f"gave up after {max_tries} tries (last problem: {problem})")


resp = get_with_backoff(f"{API}/flaky")
print(resp.status_code, resp.json())
print(get_with_backoff(f"{API}/products/SNW-9999").status_code)
      try 1: HTTP 503; next try in 1.0 s
  try 2: HTTP 503; next try in 1.0 s
200 {'status': 'ok', 'attempts_needed': 3}
404
  8. The same policy, built in. Say: "For everyday work, urllib3's Retry does all of this, mounted on a Session. allowed_methods keeps retries to requests that only read: repeating a POST that places an order could place it twice." 
    from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter
from urllib3.util.retry import Retry


def make_session(total=5, backoff_factor=0.5):
    """A Session that identifies itself and retries temporary failures."""
    retry = Retry(total=total, backoff_factor=backoff_factor,
                  status_forcelist=[429, 500, 502, 503, 504],
                  allowed_methods=["GET", "HEAD"], respect_retry_after_header=True)
    adapter = HTTPAdapter(max_retries=retry)
    session = requests.Session()
    session.mount("https://", adapter)
    session.mount("http://", adapter)
    session.headers.update(HEADERS)
    return session


fresh_window()
session = make_session()
resp = session.get(f"{API}/flaky", timeout=10)
print(resp.status_code, "| retried after:", [a.status for a in resp.raw.retries.history])
    200 | retried after: [503, 503]
  9. The politest request is the one you never send. Say: "Same request, same file name: built from the URL and the parameters, hashed. check() runs BEFORE anything is written, so an error is never cached." 
    class ApiError(Exception):
    def __init__(self, status, code, message):
        super().__init__(f"{status} {code}: {message}")
        self.status, self.code, self.message = status, code, message


def check(resp):
    if resp.ok:
        return resp
    error = resp.json()["error"]
    raise ApiError(resp.status_code, error["code"], error["message"])


CACHE_DIR = Path("cache")


def cache_path(url, params=None):
    key = url + "?" + json.dumps(params or {}, sort_keys=True)
    return CACHE_DIR / (hashlib.sha256(key.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16] + ".json")


def cached_get_json(session, url, params=None):
    """Return (data, source): the cache when it can, the network when it must."""
    path = cache_path(url, params)
    if path.exists():
        return json.loads(path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")), "cache"
    resp = check(session.get(url, params=params, timeout=10))
    CACHE_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    path.write_text(resp.text, encoding="utf-8")
    return resp.json(), "network"


for category in ["Packs", "Climbing", "Packs", "Climbing", "Packs"]:
    data, source = cached_get_json(session, f"{API}/products",
                                   {"category": category, "per_page": 5})
    print(category, data["total"], "from", source)

  10. A log you can read afterward. Say: "A job that runs overnight needs a record: what was asked, what failed, what was retried. The level is a filter. And never log a key, a token or an Authorization header." 
    log = logging.getLogger("pinecrest")
log.setLevel(logging.INFO)
handler = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout)
handler.setFormatter(logging.Formatter("%(levelname)-7s %(message)s"))
log.handlers = [handler]

    INFO    starting download: 7 pages
WARNING rate limited; waiting 5 s
  11. Resumable: one file per page, skip what is done. Say: "A long download WILL be interrupted. Save each page as it arrives; on the next run, skip pages already on disk. The .part rename means a half-written file is never mistaken for a finished one." 
    def download_pages(session, path, params, out_dir, throttle, max_new=None):
    """Save every page as JSON, skipping pages already saved."""
    out_dir = Path(out_dir)
    out_dir.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    page, fetched, skipped = 1, 0, 0
    while True:
        file = out_dir / f"page_{page:04d}.json"
        if file.exists():
            data = json.loads(file.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
            skipped += 1
        else:
            if max_new is not None and fetched >= max_new:
                return {"complete": False, "fetched": fetched, "skipped": skipped}
            throttle.wait()
            resp = check(session.get(f"{API}{path}", params={**params, "page": page},
                                     timeout=10))
            partial = file.with_suffix(".part")
            partial.write_text(resp.text, encoding="utf-8")
            partial.replace(file)
            data, fetched = resp.json(), fetched + 1
        if page >= data["total_pages"]:
            return {"complete": True, "fetched": fetched, "skipped": skipped}
        page += 1


throttle = Throttle(interval)
job = {"per_page": 50}
print(download_pages(session, "/products", job, "product_pages", throttle, max_new=2))
print(download_pages(session, "/products", job, "product_pages", throttle))
print(download_pages(session, "/products", job, "product_pages", throttle))

{'complete': True, 'fetched': 3, 'skipped': 2}

Three mistakes to expect
  • int(resp.headers.get("Retry-After")) with no default: TypeError exactly when things are already going wrong. Coach: "What if the header is not there?" .get("Retry-After", 1).
  • Retrying everything, 404s and 403s included, or retrying with no wait and no limit. Coach: "Could this exact request succeed in two seconds? If not, why ask again?"
  • Caching before checking: one 429 saved and served forever. Coach: "Which line writes the file, and which line checks the status? Swap them."

Also common: thinking a retry policy replaces pacing (it catches the rare miss; the Throttle is plan A), and running several copies of a script to go faster (the limit is per client).

Lab 6.5-A, everyone: labs/module-18/l6_5-rate-limiting/stock_check_starter.py (reference: stock_check_solution.py). Question: which categories have the most products out of stock or low, and what happens to thirteen requests sent at once?

  • Minutes 0 to 6: TODO 1 (the headers and a polite pace: one request every 0.55 s) and TODO 2 (Retry-After with a default).
  • Minutes 6 to 16: TODO 3 (plan B: on 429, wait as asked, a few tries) and TODO 4 (plan A: the Throttle, one line).
  • Reference answers: the burst gets 10 answers and 3 refusals, Retry-After: 5; plan B ends with 0 refused after one wait (about 5 s); plan A ends with 0 refused in about 7 s; Packs has the most out of stock (3); two of the four SKUs are 404 and are asked once.
  • Minutes 16 to 20: TODO 5, the sentence: only the 429s earned a second try; a product that does not exist will not exist in five seconds either.

Lab 6.5-B (finish-if-fast, or homework): labs/module-18/l6_5-rate-limiting/retry_and_cache_starter.py. Backoff with jitter, /flaky (success on try 3), what not to retry, a urllib3 Retry policy (offline it says why that step is skipped), and a cache that answers six questions with three requests and never stores a 404.

For 50,000 requests it tells you to run overnight." Steps 2 to 6 (log file, interruption, resume, prove it, read the log) are homework.

Closing

Exit ticket (3 questions, on a sticky note; answers)
  1. What is the difference between a 401 and a 403, and what does your program do with each? Answer: 401: no valid credential (missing, malformed, expired): fix how you send it, or renew an expired token and retry once. 403: understood and refused: stop; a person must fix the key or permission.
  2. The server answers 429 with Retry-After: 5. What does your client do? Answer: Wait at least 5 seconds, then send the request again (with a maximum number of tries). Better still: pace requests so this rarely happens.
  3. Name one failure that must NOT be retried, and say why. Answer: Any of 400, 401 (except an expired token, once), 403, 404: they describe the request, so the same request gets the same answer.

Session 19: Seaborn and Plotly

How to teach the session where charts start doing statistics and then start answering back. Before the break, seaborn: describe a chart by naming columns, and learn to say exactly what an error bar shows. After it, Plotly: a chart the reader can hover, zoom and filter, in one HTML file that carries its data with it.

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm as every session: warm-up, then for each lesson a frame (the goal and a mental model), a live demo (you type, they type along), a guided lab from the kit, and the first step of the lesson's own project. The rest of each project, the lesson exercises, quiz and journal are homework.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep visualization_seaborn.html and visualization_plotly.html open in browser tabs for the diagrams (the function-family tree, the figure-to-browser flow, the "who will read it?" chooser). The kit's labs for today live in labs/module-19/: starters for learners, solutions for you.
  • Type, do not paste. Every code block in the two demos is what to type live; every output was produced by running it on the course data with the course environment (seaborn 0.13.2, Plotly 7.1.0, pandas 3.0). Break something on purpose once per lesson and read the message aloud.
  • Teal blocks are hands-on, amber blocks are watch-outs.
The one risk of Session 19: charts that look right and say something else

Both libraries will happily compute or skip a statistic without telling you. Seaborn aggregates silently (lineplot, barplot and pointplot draw a mean and an interval you did not ask for). Plotly Express does not aggregate at all (px.bar stacks every row). Neither raises an error. Say the two rules early and keep pointing at them: "In seaborn, ask what the bar shows. In Plotly, aggregate first." The second risk comes at the end: an HTML chart carries its data. Learners are two sessions from a capstone they may publish, so the habit of passing a figure only the columns it needs starts today.

If the cell shows a blank box, restart the kernel; if it still does, import plotly.io as pio; pio.renderers.default = "browser" sends every chart to a browser tab. fig.write_html("chart.html") is the fallback that cannot fail. Warm-up

0:00

Warm-up: Retrieval from Session 18

10 min
How to run it

Six minutes, no notes, answers on paper, then two minutes of answers called out and two for the homework check. These reach back to Lessons 6.4 and 6.5: the point is retrieval, not a grade.

Five questions (with answers)
  1. A request comes back 401. Another comes back 403. What does each one tell you, and what should your client do next? Answer: 401: the server does not know who you are (no token, or token_expired): log in again and repeat the request once. 403: it knows who you are and refuses: stop and fix the credential or the permission. Neither is retried in a loop.
  2. Where does an API key live while you work on a notebook you will share, and where in the request does it travel? Answer: In an environment variable (or typed at a prompt), read at run time; never in the code. It travels in a header (X-API-Key), not in the URL, because URLs end up in logs and browser history.
  3. The server answers 429 with the header Retry-After: 4. What does a polite client do? What if the header is missing? Answer: Wait at least 4 seconds, then send the same request again. With no header, fall back to a default wait (exponential backoff with jitter), with a maximum number of tries.
  4. What does this print? 
    print([min(4.0, 1.0 * 2 ** n) for n in range(4)])
    Answer: [1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 4.0]: the delay doubles (1, 2, 4) and then the cap of 4.0 holds it. That is exponential backoff with a ceiling; real clients add random jitter on top.
  5. Name two failures a retry policy should retry and two it never should. Then: what made the Lesson 6.5 download resumable? Answer: Retry: 429, 5xx, timeouts (temporary). Never: 400, 401, 403, 404 (the same request will fail the same way). Resumable: each page is saved to its own file as soon as it arrives, written completely or not at all, and pages whose files exist are skipped.
Homework check (2 min)

Hands up: whose orders_since_november.csv has 2,056 rows? Ask one volunteer: "You interrupted the job. How did it know what was left?" (One file per page; pages whose files exist are skipped.) Then the bridge: "Five lessons getting data. From today, showing it. Open the notebook from Module 3 in your head: fig, ax = plt.subplots(). Seaborn draws on that ax."

Mental model to say (12 min frame)

"Matplotlib is a drawing table with excellent pens: put a dot here, a line there. Seaborn is an assistant at the same table who takes orders at a higher level: revenue against visitors, one color per store. The assistant splits the table into groups, picks colors, computes any averages and intervals, draws with the same pens and writes the legend. When the assistant is done, you can still pick up a pen."

Draw two boxes on the board, axes-level (takes ax=, returns an Axes) and figure-level (relplot, displot, catplot: makes its own figure, col= / row=, returns a FacetGrid), and leave them up all session. Then write the second idea under them: "What does this bar show: spread, or uncertainty?" Show the lesson page's function-family diagram for thirty seconds; do not read the theme table aloud.

sns.ecdfplot(data=completed, x="order_total", hue="channel", log_scale=True,
             ax=axes[1])
axes[1].axhline(0.5, color="gray", linewidth=1, linestyle="--")
plt.show()
print(completed.groupby("channel")["order_total"].median().round(2).to_dict())
    {'online': 153.95, 'store': 133.46}
  8. Same means, four error bars (5m). This is the heart of the lesson. Build the loop, run it, then stop talking for ten seconds. Ask: "Four panels, identical dots. Which panel says Asheville is different? Which says customers disagree with each other?" 
    survey = pd.read_csv("data/survey.csv")
stores = ["Boise", "Bend", "Flagstaff", "Asheville"]
in_store = survey[survey["store"].isin(stores)]
choices = [("ci", 95), "se", "sd", ("pi", 50)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(10, 3.4), sharey=True, layout="constrained")
for ax, choice in zip(axes, choices):
    sns.pointplot(data=in_store, x="store", y="sat_staff", order=stores,
                  errorbar=choice, seed=42, linestyle="none", capsize=0.2, ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(f"errorbar={choice!r}", fontsize=10)
    ax.tick_params(axis="x", rotation=45)
plt.show()
by_store = in_store.groupby("store")["sat_staff"]
summary = by_store.agg(n="count", mean="mean", sd="std", se="sem")
print(summary.loc[stores].round(2))
                 n  mean    sd    se
store                           
Boise      320  4.11  0.82  0.05
Bend       228  4.16  0.86  0.06
Flagstaff  206  4.02  0.86  0.06
Asheville  193  3.62  1.02  0.07
    Say: "Short bars: how well we know the mean. Long bars: how much people vary. Both are true. The bar you draw decides which one the reader hears, so the caption must say which it is." Note seed=42: the default interval is bootstrapped, so without a seed it wiggles between runs.
  9. Figure-level: seaborn builds the grid (3m). Say: "With four stores on one scatter the points pile up. col= gives one panel per store." Ask the room to predict the two printed values before you run. 
    g = sns.relplot(data=sales, x="visitors", y="revenue", col="store", col_wrap=2,
                hue="promo_day", s=12, alpha=0.6, height=2.8, aspect=1.5)
g.set_axis_labels("visitors per day", "revenue ($)")
g.set_titles("{col_name}")
plt.show()
print(type(g).__name__, g.axes.shape, type(g.figure).__name__)
    FacetGrid (4,) Figure
    Size is height and aspect per panel, not figsize. The grid has its own methods (set_titles, set_axis_labels); for anything else reach in through g.figure and g.axes.
  10. Break it on purpose, twice (3m). Say: "Two mistakes everyone makes this week. First: handing my own Axes to a figure-level function." Read the warning aloud. "Second: treating the grid like an Axes." 
    import warnings
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3))
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    sns.relplot(data=sales, x="visitors", y="revenue", ax=ax)
print(caught[0].category.__name__ + ":", caught[0].message)
g = sns.catplot(data=sales, x="store", y="revenue", kind="box", height=3)
try:
    g.set_title("Revenue by store")
except AttributeError as error:
    print("AttributeError:", error)
    UserWarning: relplot is a figure-level function and does not accept the `ax` parameter. You may wish to try scatterplot
AttributeError: 'FacetGrid' object has no attribute 'set_title'
    Say: "When a seaborn object lacks a method you expected, print type(obj). It tells you which of the two kinds you are holding."
  11. Finish with Matplotlib, and save (3m). Say: "Seaborn got us most of a chart in one line. The last part, a title that states the finding, dollars on the axis, the legend moved, is Module 3 work on the Axes that came back." 
    from matplotlib.ticker import StrMethodFormatter
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4), layout="constrained")
sns.barplot(data=sales, x="weekday", y="revenue", hue="year", order=days,
            errorbar=("ci", 95), seed=42, ax=ax)
ax.set_title("Saturday is the biggest day of the week, in both years", loc="left")
ax.set(xlabel="", ylabel="mean daily revenue per store (bars: 95% CI)")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(StrMethodFormatter("${x:,.0f}"))
sns.move_legend(ax, "upper left", title="Year")
fig.savefig("weekday_revenue.png", dpi=150)
by_day = sales.groupby("weekday")["revenue"].mean()
print(by_day.loc[["Tue", "Sat"]].round(0).to_dict())

Three mistakes to expect
  • Passing `ax=` to `relplot`, `displot` or `catplot` (or the reverse: expecting col= to work on scatterplot). Symptom: two figures, one empty, and a UserWarning that scrolls by unread. Coach: "Read the last sentence of the warning. Who owns the figure in your plan, you or seaborn?" Point at the two boxes on the board.
  • Reading a band or bar without knowing what it is. A learner draws lineplot on daily rows and describes the band as "the range". Coach: "How many rows share each x? Print groupby(...).size(). What did seaborn have to do to get one y?" Then: "Which errorbar= would give you the range you had in mind?" (("pi", 100).)
  • Categories in first-seen order. Weekdays come out Mon, Tue, ... only by luck of the file; age groups come out 65+, 18-24, 25-34. There is no error, so it reaches the saved figure. Coach: "Read your x axis aloud, left to right. Is that the order you would say them in?" Fix: order=, hue_order=, col_order=.

Median order total: Basic $110.66, Silver $146.98, Gold $162.28. Mean completed orders per customer: Basic 2.05, Silver 5.12, Gold 10.81. Gold against Basic: order size ×1.47, orders per customer ×5.26.

The gap is the same for online shoppers (65+ 3.06) and store shoppers (65+ 3.02). catplot returns a FacetGrid with axes shape (1, 2). No website rating: 3% of online shoppers, 46% of store shoppers.

7.2

Interactive Charts with Plotly

75 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Build line, scatter, bar, box and heatmap charts with one Plotly Express call each
  • Control what a reader sees on hover, and format axes, legends and facet titles
  • Decide when animation helps and when small multiples say the same thing better
  • Drop down to graph objects to combine trace types, add a second y axis and annotate
  • Save a chart as a standalone HTML file, export a static image, and explain what data travels inside the file
In the room / at home

Room (75 min): the frame, the eleven-step demo, lab 7.2-A (and 7.2-B for fast finishers), and Step 1 plus the first chart of the Sales Explorer. Home: the rest of the project (three charts assembled into sales_explorer.html), Exercises 1 to 4, the quiz and the journal. Not demonstrated in the room: facets and trendlines, animation, the dual-axis chart and write_image. Say so, and say where they are in the lesson; the animation section's table (when animation helps) is worth two sentences in the wrap-up.

Mental model to say (12 min frame)

"A static chart is a map printed on the wall: beautifully composed, the same for everyone, fixed. An interactive chart is a map app: the reader pinches to zoom, taps a pin, switches layers. You, the mapmaker, still decide what is on the map and what the default view is. The reader decides where to look next."

Then the mechanism, in one breath, with the lesson's flow diagram on screen: "Your Python does not draw anything. It builds a figure: traces (the data) plus a layout (titles, axes, legend). That description goes, as JSON text, to a JavaScript library, plotly.js, which draws it in a browser. A notebook is a web page. An HTML file is a web page. That is why the chart works in both, and why the data is in the file." Write on the board: figure = data + layout and aggregate first.

Live demo (you type, they follow) · 28 min

New notebook, session19_plotly.ipynb. In a notebook fig.show() draws under the cell. The outputs below were produced on a machine with no screen, where fig.show() does nothing; the printed lines are what learners should see under each cell as well as the chart. If charts do not appear in the room's notebooks, see Before the Session.

  1. Imports and a monthly table (2m). Say: "Two interfaces. Plotly Express, px, is the seaborn-style one: name the columns. We start there." 
    import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import plotly
import plotly.express as px

sales = pd.read_csv("data/daily_sales.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
sales["month_start"] = sales["date"].dt.to_period("M").dt.to_timestamp()
monthly = sales.groupby(["store", "month_start"], as_index=False)[
    ["revenue", "visitors", "transactions"]].sum()
print(plotly.__version__, monthly.shape)
    7.1.0 (96, 5)
  2. The first figure, and why nothing appears (3m). Run the first two lines only. Wait. Say: "Nothing. px.line returned a Figure object. Python has built a description; nothing has drawn it yet." Then run fig.show() and spend a full minute on the live chart: hover, click a legend entry, double-click one, drag a box, double-click to reset. 
    fig = px.line(monthly, x="month_start", y="revenue", color="store",
              title="Monthly revenue by store")
print(type(fig).__name__, "with", len(fig.data), "traces")
fig.show()
    Figure with 4 traces
  3. A figure is data (2m). Say: "Because a figure is a description, you can inspect it like any object. This habit is what makes Plotly debuggable." 
    trace = fig.data[0]
print(trace.type, "|", trace.name, "|", trace.mode, "|", len(trace.x), "points")
print(fig.layout.title.text, "|", fig.layout.xaxis.title.text)
print(list(fig.to_dict()))
    scatter | Asheville | lines | 24 points
Monthly revenue by store | month_start
['data', 'layout']
    A line chart is a scatter trace in lines mode. The whole figure is two things, data and layout, and everything else today changes one or the other.
  4. px.bar does not aggregate (3m). Ask first: "sns.barplot(data=sales, x=\"store\", y=\"revenue\") gave four bars at the mean. What will px.bar do with the same table?" Take guesses, then run. 
    wrong = px.bar(sales, x="store", y="revenue")
print(len(wrong.data[0].x), "bar segments")
by_store = sales.groupby("store", as_index=False)["revenue"].mean()
by_store = by_store.sort_values("revenue", ascending=False)
right = px.bar(by_store, x="store", y="revenue", text_auto=",.0f")
print(len(right.data[0].x), "bars:", by_store.round(0).to_dict("records")[0])
    2903 bar segments
4 bars: {'store': 'Boise', 'revenue': 10144.0}
    Say: "No error. The first chart looks like four bars and is 2,903 slivers stacked up. In Plotly you aggregate with pandas first, then plot."
  5. The default hover is rarely the one you want (3m). Say: "Here is what Express wrote for a scatter. It is a small template with placeholders. It does not say the one thing I want to know about an odd point: which day is it?" 
    fig = px.scatter(sales, x="visitors", y="revenue", color="store")
print(fig.data[0].type, "|", fig.data[0].hovertemplate)
    scattergl | store=Asheville<br>visitors=%{x}<br>revenue=%{y}<extra></extra>
    Note the trace type: above a thousand points Express switches to a WebGL trace (scattergl) by itself.
  6. Design the hover (4m). Say: "hover_name is the bold first line. hover_data is a dictionary: True adds a column, a string starting with a colon adds it with a number format." Show the chart and hover the top point: the Saturday of the 2024 Labor Day sale, in Boise. 
    stores = ["Boise", "Bend", "Flagstaff", "Asheville"]
sales["day"] = sales["date"].dt.strftime("%a %b %d, %Y")
fig = px.scatter(sales, x="visitors", y="revenue", color="store", opacity=0.5,
                 category_orders={"store": stores}, hover_name="day",
                 hover_data={"store": True, "revenue": ":$,.0f", "visitors": ":,"},
                 labels={"visitors": "Visitors", "revenue": "Revenue"})
print(fig.data[0].hovertemplate)
best = sales.loc[sales["revenue"].idxmax()]
print(best["day"], "|", best["store"], "|", f"${best['revenue']:,.0f}")
fig.show()
    <b>%{hovertext}</b><br><br>store=%{customdata[0]}<br>Visitors=%{x:,}<br>Revenue=%{y:$,.0f}<extra></extra>
Sat Aug 31, 2024 | Boise | $27,677
  7. Time series: one box per date (3m). Say: "For lines compared at the same dates, write the template yourself and unify the hover." 
    fig = px.line(monthly, x="month_start", y="revenue", color="store",
              category_orders={"store": stores}, template="plotly_white",
              labels={"month_start": "", "revenue": "", "store": ""})
fig.update_traces(hovertemplate="%{y:$,.0f}")
fig.update_layout(hovermode="x unified")
print(fig.layout.hovermode, "|", fig.data[0].hovertemplate)
fig.show()
    x unified | %{y:$,.0f}
  8. Finish the layout (3m). Say: "Three methods do the finishing. update_layout for the whole figure, update_xaxes / update_yaxes for axes, update_traces for the series. The title is still the message." 
    fig.update_layout(
    title_text="Flagstaff has overtaken Bend; Asheville is drifting down",
    height=450, legend=dict(orientation="h", yanchor="bottom", y=1.0, x=0))
fig.update_yaxes(tickprefix="$", tickformat=",.0f", rangemode="tozero")
fig.update_xaxes(dtick="M3", rangeslider_visible=True)
y_axis = fig.layout.yaxis
print(y_axis.tickprefix, fig.layout.xaxis.dtick, y_axis.rangemode)
fig.show()
    $ M3 tozero
  9. Break it on purpose: a misspelled property (2m). Say: "Plotly checks every property name. The real message is about five hundred lines. Read the first lines and the last three, nothing in between." 
    try:
    fig.update_layout(tittle="Monthly revenue")
except ValueError as error:
    lines = str(error).splitlines()
    print(lines[0])
    print([ln for ln in lines if "Did you mean" in ln][0])
    print(len(lines), "lines in the full message")
    Invalid property specified for object of type plotly.graph_objs.Layout: 'tittle'
Did you mean "title"?
511 lines in the full message
  10. Point at something: shapes and annotations (2m). Say: "Reference lines and shaded regions live in the layout, so they zoom and pan with the data." 
    boise = sales[(sales["store"] == "Boise") & (sales["date"] >= "2025-10-01")]
fig = px.line(boise, x="date", y="revenue", template="plotly_white",
              title="Boise, fourth quarter of 2025")
fig.add_hline(y=boise["revenue"].mean(), line_dash="dash", line_color="gray",
              annotation_text="quarter average")
fig.add_vrect(x0="2025-11-28", x1="2025-12-01", fillcolor="orange", opacity=0.25,
              line_width=0)
print(len(fig.layout.shapes), "shapes,", len(fig.layout.annotations), "annotation")
fig.show()
    2 shapes, 1 annotation
  11. Save it, and look inside the file (4m). Say: "One file, no Python needed to open it. Where the plotly.js library comes from decides the size." Then open the small file in a text editor and search for Asheville. 
    from pathlib import Path
fig = px.line(monthly, x="month_start", y="revenue", color="store",
              title="Monthly revenue by store")
fig.write_html("revenue_full.html")
fig.write_html("revenue_cdn.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn")
for name in ["revenue_full.html", "revenue_cdn.html"]:
    print(f"{name:<20} {Path(name).stat().st_size / 1024:8,.0f} KB")
text = Path("revenue_cdn.html").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
print("Asheville" in text, '"x":' in text)
    revenue_full.html       4,716 KB
revenue_cdn.html           13 KB
True True
    Say, slowly: "An HTML chart is not a picture of your data. It contains your data. Plot one point per customer and you have sent the reader your customer table."
Three mistakes to expect
  • Handing `px.bar` or `px.line` unaggregated rows. Fresh from seaborn, learners expect a mean. They get 2,903 stacked slivers, or a line that scribbles back and forth. No error. Coach: "Print len(fig.data[0].x). How many bars did you mean to draw?" Then: "Which pandas line makes that table?"
  • Seaborn words in a Plotly call: hue= for color=, col= for facet_col=, order= for category_orders={...}. The TypeError names the unexpected argument. Coach: point at the workbook's two-column translation table; do not supply the word.
  • Nothing appears, or the wrong thing is sent. A cell that ends with fig = px... shows nothing (no fig.show()); a script that calls fig.show() in the lab opens browser tabs for every run. And at the end, a learner writes the full sales table into an HTML file when the chart needed three columns. Coach: "Open your file in a text editor and search for a column you did not plot."

The lab files never call fig.show(): learners open output/product_map.html from the file manager.

Weekly table (210, 4); median weekly share 6.6% online, 7.9% in store. 2 traces, hover mode x unified. Six sale weekends shaded, each four days (Friday to Monday). Share of orders using a code: 51.0% on sale-weekend days, 8.0% on all other days. January 2024 is 25.3% with no sale on: the data starts there and WELCOME10 marks a customer's first order in the data.

Checks for understanding

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12.

Answers: Q7 A) The call only builds a Figure object; it is displayed when you call fig.show() (or write it to a file); Q8 8; Q9 C) "revenue": ":$,.0f"; Q10 B) One hover box appears for the x position under the mouse, listing all four stores; Q11 bar 4; Q12 D) Aggregate to what you mean to publish, pass only the columns the chart needs, then fig.write_html("chart.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn"). Differentiation

Stretch: the lesson's bonus challenge (a dropdown that switches the trend chart between revenue and visitors with updatemenus); or in lab 7.2-B add facet_row="channel" and clean the facet titles with for_each_annotation; or export the chart with write_image after running plotly_get_chrome.

Closing

Exit ticket · 5 min (answers)
  1. You call sns.barplot(data=sales, x="store", y="revenue") and black lines appear on the bars. What are they, by default, and which argument changes them? Answer: A bootstrapped 95% confidence interval for the mean of each bar (uncertainty of the estimate, not spread of the days). errorbar= changes it: "sd", "se", ("pi", 50) or None. Say which one in the caption.
  2. Give one job for an axes-level function and one for a figure-level function. Answer: Axes-level (scatterplot, histplot, barplot): one panel inside your own plt.subplots() layout, with ax=. Figure-level (relplot, displot, catplot): seaborn builds a grid of panels from a column with col= / row= and returns a FacetGrid.
  3. You plot one point per customer with email in hover_data and send the HTML file to a colleague. What have you sent? Answer: The customer table: every x, y and hover column is stored as readable text inside the file. Aggregate first and pass Plotly only the columns the chart needs.

Collect the cards. Anyone who misses the first question gets a one-line note back next session; anyone who misses the third hears it again before the capstone.

If You Run Long or Short

Long, in 7.1: cut demo step 7 (the skewed distribution: it is Lesson 4.2 again) and step 6 (aggregate yourself: say it in one sentence instead). Never cut step 8 (error bars) or the lab's merge check. Long, in 7.2: cut step 10 (shapes and annotations) and step 9 (the misspelled property); shorten step 8 to the title and the dollar axis. Never cut step 4 (px.bar) or step 11 (the data is in the file). If the whole session is ten minutes behind at the break, start each project by reading the brief only and move Step 1 to homework. Short: run lab 7.1-B and 7.2-B in the room; then the lesson's facet-and-trendline example (trendline="ols", the slopes are about $21 per visitor in every store) with the question "does one more visitor cause $21 of revenue?"; or have pairs trade product_map.html files and find one thing in the other pair's hover that a reader would not understand.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 20: Bokeh and Streamlit

How to teach the last tools session. Before the break, Bokeh: several charts looking at one table, so that selecting rows in one lights them up in the others. After it, Streamlit: an app whose controls run pandas, built on one idea, the script reruns. The session ends with the capstone kickoff: every learner chooses a question and leaves with a written plan.

2 lessons 3 hrs session Lessons 7.3–7.4 Session 20 of 21 Capstone question chosen

How to Use This Guide

  • Same rhythm, one addition. Warm-up; for each lesson a frame, a live demo, a guided kit lab and the first step of the lesson project; then, in place of the usual last stretch, a 20-minute capstone kickoff before the wrap-up.
  • The lessons are the reference. Keep visualization_bokeh.html, visualization_streamlit.html and the top of capstone_project.html open in browser tabs. Labs are in labs/module-20/.
  • Two tools, two working styles. Bokeh is demonstrated from a notebook or script that writes HTML files. Streamlit is demonstrated from an editor and a terminal: it cannot run in a notebook cell.
  • Every output in this guide is from a real run on the course data (Bokeh 3.10.0, Streamlit 1.65.0). Streamlit outputs come from its testing tool, AppTest, so you can reproduce them without a browser.
  • Checkpoint 2 is not in this session. The Modules 5 to 6 data-access checkpoint sits in Session 18. Tonight's assessment moment is the capstone plan.
The one risk of Session 20: running out of time before the kickoff

Both tools are new, both are fun, and each demo can swallow forty minutes. The capstone kickoff at 2:30 is not optional: learners who leave without a chosen question and a written plan arrive at the Session 21 studio with nothing to work on. Protect it by cutting demo steps (the lists under If You Run Long name them), never by shortening the kickoff. The second risk is conceptual and lives after the break: learners carry the notebook's mental model (variables persist) into Streamlit, where the whole script reruns. Say that sentence until they finish it for you.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Run the kit check: python3 labs/check_labs.py module-20. Expect 9 passed, 0 failed (four starters, four solutions, one pytest file). It starts no servers and opens no browser.
  • ☐ Hand out starters only (margin_brush_starter.py, category_picker_starter.py, gear_shortlist_starter.py, catalog_browser_starter.py) with labs/labs_paths.py. Keep the solutions and test_catalog_browser.py on your machine until the lab is done.
  • ☐ Versions: python -c "import bokeh, streamlit; print(bokeh.__version__, streamlit.__version__)" should print versions starting with 3 and 1. streamlit version in the terminal is the same check for learners.
  • ☐ Streamlit's first run may ask for an email address in the terminal: press Enter to skip. Do one streamlit run on the projector machine before class so the prompt does not appear live. To silence it on shared machines, create ~/.streamlit/config.toml with [browser] and gatherUsageStats = false.
  • ☐ Port 8501. streamlit run serves on http://localhost:8501. If a learner has an app still running, the next one takes 8502 and the old tab shows the old app: teach Ctrl+C early. Venue firewalls are not an issue: everything is on localhost. If the browser does not open by itself, copy the Local URL from the terminal.
  • ☐ No internet in the room? Bokeh's default mode="cdn" files open blank offline: have learners pass mode="inline" to output_file (about 1.4 to 1.8 MB per file). Streamlit works offline; its charts do too.
  • ☐ Projector: editor and terminal side by side for the second half, font 18 pt or larger; a notebook or second terminal for the AppTest checks.
  • ☐ Whiteboard: "share a range → same view", "share a source → same rows"; for after the break, "the whole script reruns".
  • ☐ Capstone: print the four questions (from Lesson 8.1, Choose Your Question) one set per table, bring sticky notes, and read the answer notes in ../../final-assessment.html beforehand so that you can ask good questions without giving anything away.
  • ☐ Skim the Session 19 homework in the warm-up: store_brief.png (four panels) and sales_explorer.html (three charts, about 174 KB).
