Warm-up

0:00

Warm-up: Retrieval from Session 19

10 min
How to run it

Six minutes on paper, no notes; two minutes of answers; two for the homework check.

Five questions (with answers)
  1. Which kind of seaborn function takes ax=, and what does the other kind return? Answer: Axes-level functions (scatterplot, barplot, histplot, ...) take ax= and return that Axes. Figure-level functions (relplot, displot, catplot) make their own figure and return a FacetGrid.
  2. sns.barplot draws a black line on each bar. With default settings, what is it? Name one setting that shows spread instead. Answer: A bootstrapped 95% confidence interval for the mean (uncertainty of the estimate). errorbar="sd" or errorbar=("pi", 50) shows spread of the data.
  3. You pass 2,903 daily rows to px.bar(sales, x="store", y="revenue"). What do you get, and what should you have done? Answer: 2,903 bar segments stacked into four piles, with no error: Plotly Express does not aggregate. Group with pandas first (groupby("store", as_index=False)["revenue"].mean()), then plot four rows.
  4. monthly has one row per store and month (4 stores, 24 months). What does this print? 
    fig = px.line(monthly, x="month_start", y="revenue", color="store")
print(len(fig.data), fig.data[0].type, len(fig.data[0].x))
    Answer: 4 scatter 24: one trace per store, each a scatter trace in lines mode holding 24 points. A figure is data: you can count it before you look at it.
  5. You wrote a chart with fig.write_html("chart.html", include_plotlyjs="cdn"). Name two things that are true of that file. Answer: It is small because the reader's browser fetches plotly.js from a public server, so the reader must be online; and it contains the data you passed to the figure (every x, y and hover column) as readable text.
Homework check (2 min)

Two volunteers put sales_explorer.html on the projector. Ask the room: "Find the best single day. Now find that same day in the trend chart." Let them struggle for ten seconds. "Three charts that ignore each other. Fixing that is the first half of today."

Lesson Plans

7.3

Interactive Charts with Bokeh

65 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Build a Bokeh figure by adding glyphs (lines, markers, bars) and save it with output_file
  • Put data in a ColumnDataSource and refer to its columns by name
  • Configure a hover tool with formatted fields, including dates
  • Link plots by shared ranges (panning) and by a shared data source (brushing), and arrange them with layouts
  • Add a widget that works in a standalone file using js_link or CustomJS, and choose between Bokeh and Plotly for a job
In the room / at home

Room (65 min): the frame, the ten-step demo, lab 7.3-A (7.3-B for fast finishers) and Step 1 of the Linked Store Explorer. Home: the rest of the project (three linked plots, the store picker, the live selection summary, store_explorer.html, about 154 KB), Exercises 1 to 4, quiz and journal. Not demonstrated: bars on a categorical axis beyond the last step, gridplot, js_link sliders (lab 7.3-B uses one), date formatters in tooltips and static export. Point at the lesson's Bokeh-or-Plotly table in one sentence: "Plotly for a chart, Bokeh for charts that talk to each other."

Mental model to say (10 min frame)

"Picture your data as one large table in the middle of a room, and each chart as a window in the wall looking at that table from a different side. One window shows revenue against visitors, another shows revenue against the date. Walk in and put red stickers on thirty rows of the table: every window shows those thirty rows in red, because there is only one table. In Bokeh the table is a ColumnDataSource, the windows are plots, and the stickers are a selection."

Start from the homework: "Your sales_explorer.html has three charts that ignore each other. You found the best day in the scatter; then you hunted for it in the trend by eye." Write on the board: share a range → same view and share a source → same rows. Show the lesson's two-branch diagram (what should stay in sync?) while you say it.

Live demo (you type, they follow) · 25 min

One notebook or one script, session20_bokeh, started from the course folder. show(...) writes the HTML file named by output_file and opens it in a browser tab; on the machine that produced the outputs below no browser opens, and the printed lines are identical. To draw inside a notebook instead, run from bokeh.io import output_notebook; output_notebook() once and skip the output_file lines.

  1. A figure, then a glyph (2m). Say: "Two moves. Make an empty plot, then add marks to it. If Plotly Express felt like ordering from a menu, this feels like Matplotlib." In a notebook or script, show writes the file and opens it in a browser tab. 
    import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import bokeh
from bokeh.plotting import figure, output_file, save, show

sales = pd.read_csv("data/daily_sales.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
boise = sales[sales["store"] == "Boise"]
p = figure(width=800, height=320, x_axis_type="datetime",
           title="Boise daily revenue")
p.line(boise["date"], boise["revenue"], line_width=1.5, color="#667eea")
p.yaxis.axis_label = "revenue ($)"
output_file("first.html", title="Boise daily revenue")
show(p)
print(bokeh.__version__, type(p).__name__, "with", len(p.renderers), "renderer")
    3.10.0 figure with 1 renderer
    Walk the toolbar on the right: pan, box zoom, wheel zoom (click it on first), save, reset. Everything on the plot is an object with properties: p.yaxis.axis_label, p.title.text.
  2. Layers: one line and one set of markers per store (3m). Say: "Bokeh does not pick colors for you. A palette is a list of color codes. legend_label builds the legend." Ask before the print: "Four stores. How many renderers? How many legend entries?" 
    from bokeh.models import NumeralTickFormatter
from bokeh.palettes import Colorblind

stores = ["Boise", "Bend", "Flagstaff", "Asheville"]
store_palette = [Colorblind[8][i] for i in (0, 1, 3, 6)]
colors = dict(zip(stores, store_palette))
sales["month_start"] = sales["date"].dt.to_period("M").dt.to_timestamp()
monthly = sales.groupby(["store", "month_start"], as_index=False)["revenue"].sum()
p = figure(width=800, height=360, x_axis_type="datetime",
           title="Monthly revenue by store")
for store in stores:
    one = monthly[monthly["store"] == store]
    p.line(one["month_start"], one["revenue"], line_width=2, color=colors[store],
           legend_label=store)
    p.scatter(one["month_start"], one["revenue"], size=6, color=colors[store],
              legend_label=store)
p.yaxis.formatter = NumeralTickFormatter(format="$0,0")
p.legend.location = "top_left"
p.legend.click_policy = "hide"
output_file("monthly.html", title="Monthly revenue by store")
show(p)
print(len(p.renderers), "renderers,", len(p.legend.items), "legend items")
    8 renderers, 4 legend items
  3. The table in the middle of the room: ColumnDataSource (3m). Say: "Until now I passed columns straight to each glyph. Making the source myself unlocks everything else today. And look at what I do first: I keep only the columns the page needs." 
    from bokeh.models import ColumnDataSource

sales["day"] = sales["date"].dt.strftime("%a %b %d, %Y")
sales["promo"] = sales["promo_day"].map({0: "no", 1: "yes"})
tidy = sales[["date", "day", "store", "visitors", "revenue", "promo"]].dropna()
source = ColumnDataSource(tidy)
print(source.column_names)
print(len(source.data["revenue"]), "rows;", type(source.data["revenue"]).__name__)
    ['index', 'date', 'day', 'store', 'visitors', 'revenue', 'promo']
2897 rows; ndarray
    A source is a dictionary of equal-length columns. The DataFrame's index came along as a column named index. Six store-days with no revenue were dropped: a marker with no y cannot be drawn.
  4. Glyph arguments become column names (3m). Say: "With a source, a string means: look this column up. A number still means: this value for every mark." Ask: "One call to scatter. How many renderers, how many markers?" 
    from bokeh.transform import factor_cmap

store_color = factor_cmap("store", palette=store_palette, factors=stores)
p = figure(width=800, height=400, title="Daily revenue against foot traffic",
           x_axis_label="visitors per day", y_axis_label="revenue ($)")
p.scatter("visitors", "revenue", source=source, size=5, alpha=0.5,
          color=store_color, legend_group="store")
p.legend.location = "top_left"
p.yaxis.formatter = NumeralTickFormatter(format="$0,0")
output_file("scatter.html", title="Revenue and foot traffic")
show(p)
print(len(p.renderers), "renderer draws", len(tidy), "markers")
    1 renderer draws 2897 markers
  5. A hover that names the day (3m). Say: "@name is this row's value in that column. A format goes in braces. Any column in the source can appear, plotted or not." Hover the top point live: the Saturday of the 2024 Labor Day sale, in Boise. Note the fresh source: a new page needs new objects. 
    from bokeh.models import HoverTool

tips = [("Day", "@day"), ("Store", "@store"),
        ("Visitors", "@visitors{0,0}"), ("Revenue", "@revenue{$0,0}")]
hover = HoverTool(tooltips=tips)
source = ColumnDataSource(tidy)
p = figure(width=800, height=400, title="Hover a point to identify the day",
           tools=["pan", "wheel_zoom", "box_zoom", "reset", hover])
p.scatter("visitors", "revenue", source=source, size=5, alpha=0.5,
          color=factor_cmap("store", palette=store_palette, factors=stores))
output_file("hover.html", title="Hover")
show(p)
print([type(t).__name__ for t in p.toolbar.tools])
    ['HoverTool', 'PanTool', 'WheelZoomTool', 'BoxZoomTool', 'ResetTool']
  6. Break it on purpose: a typo that raises nothing (2m). Say: "Watch. I misspell a column." Run it. "No exception. When I show this plot I get axes and no points, and one line in the terminal: E-1001, BAD_COLUMN_NAME. An empty Bokeh plot is nearly always this." 
    p = figure(width=400, height=250)
renderer = p.scatter("visitors", "revenu", source=ColumnDataSource(tidy))
print("no exception raised; y =", renderer.glyph.y,
      "| column exists:", "revenu" in tidy.columns)
    no exception raised; y = revenu | column exists: False
  7. Linked panning: share a range (3m). Say: "Two ways to connect plots, and they connect different things. First, the view. Give the second plot the first plot's range object." Zoom the top plot with the wheel; the bottom follows. 
    from bokeh.layouts import column

boise_source = ColumnDataSource(tidy[tidy["store"] == "Boise"])
top = figure(width=800, height=230, x_axis_type="datetime", title="Boise: revenue",
             tools="xpan,xwheel_zoom,reset", active_scroll="xwheel_zoom")
top.line("date", "revenue", source=boise_source, color="#667eea")
bottom = figure(width=800, height=230, x_axis_type="datetime",
                title="Boise: visitors", x_range=top.x_range,      # the link
                tools="xpan,xwheel_zoom,reset", active_scroll="xwheel_zoom")
bottom.line("date", "visitors", source=boise_source, color="#d97706")
output_file("linked_pan.html", title="Linked panning")
show(column(top, bottom))
print(bottom.x_range is top.x_range)
    True
  8. Linked brushing: share a source (5m). This is the reason to learn Bokeh. Say: "Second, the rows. Two plots, one source, a selection tool. I write no linking code at all." Drag a box around the busiest days on the left and wait. Ask: "What are the orange days on the right?" (Sale weekends, summer Saturdays, the weeks before Christmas.) Then let two learners drive: select December on the right. 
    from bokeh.layouts import row

boise_2025 = tidy[(tidy["store"] == "Boise") & (tidy["date"] >= "2025-01-01")]
brush_source = ColumnDataSource(boise_2025)
select_tools = "box_select,lasso_select,tap,reset"
style = dict(source=brush_source, size=6, color="#667eea",
             nonselection_alpha=0.15, selection_color="#d97706")
left = figure(width=400, height=360, title="Drag a box here...", tools=select_tools,
              active_drag="box_select", x_axis_label="visitors",
              y_axis_label="revenue ($)")
left_dots = left.scatter("visitors", "revenue", **style)
right = figure(width=500, height=360, title="...and see when those days were",
               tools=select_tools, active_drag="box_select", x_axis_type="datetime")
right_dots = right.scatter("date", "revenue", **style)
output_file("linked_brush.html", title="Linked brushing")
show(row(left, right))
print(len(brush_source.data["revenue"]), "rows shared by 2 plots |",
      "same source:", left_dots.data_source is right_dots.data_source)
    363 rows shared by 2 plots | same source: True
    Say: "One drag answered: when were the busiest days? No filter, no query, no new chart." Then the opposite slip: "If I had written ColumnDataSource(boise_2025) twice, I would have two tables. No error, and no brushing."
  9. A dropdown that works in a plain HTML file (4m). Say: "When the reader moves a widget in a saved file, what code runs? There is no Python on their machine. Only JavaScript can run. Read these two lines of JavaScript as you would read Python." The plot draws through a view that shows only rows passing a filter; the dropdown changes the filter. 
    from bokeh.models import CDSView, CustomJS, GroupFilter, Select

source = ColumnDataSource(tidy)
store_filter = GroupFilter(column_name="store", group="Boise")
view = CDSView(filter=store_filter)
p = figure(width=800, height=360, title="Boise: daily revenue against foot traffic",
           tools="pan,wheel_zoom,reset")
p.scatter("visitors", "revenue", source=source, view=view, size=5, alpha=0.5)
picker = Select(title="Store", value="Boise", options=stores, width=200)
picker.js_on_change("value", CustomJS(args=dict(flt=store_filter, plot=p), code="""
    flt.group = cb_obj.value;
    plot.title.text = cb_obj.value + ": daily revenue against foot traffic";
"""))
output_file("select.html", title="Store picker")
show(column(picker, p))
print(view.filter.column_name, "=", view.filter.group)
    store = Boise
    cb_obj is the widget that changed. flt and plot exist because they were passed in args. A Python callback (picker.on_change) is silently ignored in a saved file: it needs a running Bokeh server, or the next lesson's tool.
  10. Two ways to save, and what travels (2m). Say: "Same choice as Plotly. cdn is small and needs the internet; inline works offline. And the same warning: every column of every source is in the file." 
    from pathlib import Path

days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri", "Sat", "Sun"]
sales["weekday"] = sales["date"].dt.day_name().str[:3]
by_day = sales.groupby("weekday")["revenue"].mean().loc[days]
for mode in ["cdn", "inline"]:
    name = f"weekday_{mode}.html"
    p = figure(width=600, height=300, x_range=days, title="Mean revenue by weekday")
    p.vbar(x=days, top=by_day.values, width=0.8, color="#667eea")
    output_file(name, title="Weekday", mode=mode)
    save(p)
    print(f"{name:<20} {Path(name).stat().st_size / 1024:8,.0f} KB")
print(by_day.round(0).tolist())
    weekday_cdn.html            7 KB
weekday_inline.html     1,362 KB
[6138.0, 5716.0, 5985.0, 6321.0, 7713.0, 10933.0, 9211.0]
Three mistakes to expect
  • A blank plot from a misspelled column. No Python exception: axes, no points, and E-1001 (BAD_COLUMN_NAME) in the terminal that nobody reads. Coach: "Print source.column_names. Read your glyph call aloud, string by string."
  • `RuntimeError: Models must be owned by only a single document` when a cell is rerun or a source is reused on a second saved page. Coach: "Which objects were made in an earlier cell? A new page needs new objects." The habit: create figures and sources in the same cell (or function) that saves them.
  • Two sources where one was meant (no brushing, no error), and its cousin, old-tutorial arguments (plot_width, p.circle(size=...)). Coach the first with: "How many times does ColumnDataSource( appear on this page?" For the second, read the message: it names the replacement (width, scatter).
Guided lab · 22 min

Lab 7.3-A labs/module-20/l7_3-bokeh/margin_brush_starter.py (everyone; reference: margin_brush_solution.py). Question: are Pinecrest's high-margin products also the well-reviewed ones? Two scatter plots on one source: price against margin, and reviews against rating. Labs use save, never show: learners open output/margin_brush.html from the file manager.

  • Minutes 0 to 4: run the starter as shipped. Ask: "The starter computes margin from cost and then leaves cost out of table. Why?" (Every column of the source is in the file. Margin is what the page needs; cost per product is not for publishing.)
  • Minutes 4 to 16: TODO 1 to 5. Stall to expect: source=source left out of the second scatter, or a second ColumnDataSource(table) created for it. Ask them to print left_dots.data_source is right_dots.data_source.
  • Minutes 16 to 22: everyone opens the file and drags a box around the top band of margins. Then TODO 6 and the debrief: "What did the brush show? What does pandas say?" The honest answer is nothing much: high-margin products are rated about the same as the rest.
  • Expected numbers: 234 products with a rating; margin runs from 34% to 58%. Source columns: index, name, category, price, margin, rating, review_count (no cost). renderers: 1 + 1 | same source: True. The left plot has seven tools (BoxSelect, LassoSelect, Tap, WheelZoom, Pan, Reset, Hover). margin_brush.html is about 29 KB. Margin of 50% or more: 67 products, mean rating 4.17; under 50%: 167 products, mean rating 4.12; Spearman correlation of margin and rating +0.01.
  • Lab 7.3-B labs/module-20/l7_3-bokeh/category_picker_starter.py (fast finishers now, everyone at home; reference: category_picker_solution.py). 234 rated products in 9 categories. view shows: category = Tents | 24 products to start with. category_picker.html (cdn) is about 21 KB; category_picker_offline.html (inline) about 1,750 KB. Counts the page should show: Accessories 30, Apparel 35, Camp Kitchen 28, Climbing 24, Footwear 25, Packs 22, Sleeping 24, Snow 22, Tents 24.
  • If a callback does nothing in the browser, open the developer tools (F12) and read the Console tab: JavaScript errors appear there, not in Python.
Start the lesson project · 8 min

Open the lesson at Project: The Linked Store Explorer. Read the brief: a page where the reader picks a store, selects days in any chart and sees those days everywhere, with a one-line summary. Everyone types Step 1 (check: 2897 rows; ['index', 'date', 'day', 'store', 'visitors', 'revenue', 'promo']). Then on paper, three boxes: which three plots, which share a source, which share a range. Steps 2 to 5 are homework; tell them Step 4 holds the longest piece of JavaScript in the course and that it is a plain loop.

Checks for understanding

Workbook self-check, items Q1 to Q6.

Answers: Q1 B) Reads each marker's size from the visitors column of the source; Q2 4 2; Q3 D) Create the second plot with x_range=top.x_range; Q4 A) The selection is stored in a source, and the two plots have two separate sources; Q5 ['index', 'x', 'y'] 3; Q6 C) ("Revenue", "@revenue{$0,0}"). Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: give the complete left plot of lab 7.3-A and ask only for the right one; keep the lesson's tooltip table open (@col, @col{$0,0}, @col{0%}). Stretch: in lab 7.3-A color the markers by category with factor_cmap and legend_group; in 7.3-B add a second widget, a checkbox that keeps only products with at least 50 reviews (the lesson's bonus challenge shows the filter-combining idea); or lesson Exercise 4, the threshold counter.

7.4

Dashboards with Streamlit

65 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Write a Streamlit app as a plain Python script and run it locally with streamlit run
  • Explain the rerun model, and predict what a variable holds after a widget is used
  • Keep values across reruns with st.session_state and avoid repeated work with st.cache_data
  • Lay out a dashboard with a sidebar, columns and tabs, showing metrics, charts, a table and a download button
  • Test an app without a browser, and describe what it takes to put an app in front of other people
In the room / at home

Room (65 min): the frame, the nine-step demo, lab 7.4-B (the shortlist) and then 7.4-A (the catalog browser) as far as time allows, and Step 1 of the Pinecrest Sales Dashboard. Home: the rest of the project (dashboard.py with filters, four metrics, three tabs, a download and the AppTest check), Exercises 1 to 3 (4 is a stretch), quiz and journal. Deployment is two minutes of talk in the room and a careful read at home: the lesson's six conditions and its three checks before anyone else can open an app.

Mental model to say (10 min frame)

"Think of a spreadsheet with an input cell at the top and formulas below it. Change the input and every formula recalculates at once: you never tell the sheet which cells to update. A Streamlit app behaves the same way, except that the sheet is your script. Whenever a reader changes any widget, Streamlit runs the whole script again, from the first line to the last, with the widget's new value, and replaces what is on the page."

Bridge from before the break: "Your Bokeh dropdown ran two lines of JavaScript in the reader's browser. That was the ceiling. The moment someone asks to pick their own date range and download those rows, the controls must run pandas, and that means Python has to be running while they use the page." Show the lesson's comparison table (HTML file against app) and its rerun loop diagram. Board: the whole script reruns; under it, session_state remembers · cache_data does not repeat.

Live demo (you type, they follow) · 25 min

Editor and terminal, not a notebook: Streamlit runs .py scripts with its own server. Start from the course folder so data/ resolves. Each step shows the file to type, the terminal command, and a check with Streamlit's testing tool whose output is from a real run. Stop each app with Ctrl+C before starting the next (or pass --server.port 8502).

  1. An app is a script (3m). Work in an editor with a terminal open in the course folder, not in a notebook. Type the file, then start it. Say: "Not python hello.py. streamlit run." Change the store in the dropdown. "The metric, the chart and the table all changed. I wrote no code to connect them."

    File hello.py:

    import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

st.title("Pinecrest store sales")
sales = pd.read_csv("data/daily_sales.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
store = st.selectbox("Store", ["Boise", "Bend", "Flagstaff", "Asheville"])
one = sales[sales["store"] == store]
st.metric("Total revenue", f"${one['revenue'].sum():,.0f}")
st.line_chart(one, x="date", y="revenue")
st.write("The five best days:")
best = one.nlargest(5, "revenue")[["date", "visitors", "revenue"]]
st.dataframe(best, hide_index=True)

    Terminal:

    streamlit run hello.py

    Check without a browser (notebook or second terminal):

    from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest

at = AppTest.from_file("hello.py", default_timeout=30).run()
print("errors:", len(at.exception), "| title:", at.title[0].value)
print(at.selectbox[0].value, "->", at.metric[0].value)
at.selectbox[0].select("Asheville").run()
print(at.selectbox[0].value, "->", at.metric[0].value)
    errors: 0 | title: Pinecrest store sales
Boise -> $7,364,698
Asheville -> $4,140,977
    The check is Streamlit's own testing tool, AppTest: it runs the script in memory with no server and no browser. Keep a notebook or a second terminal open for these checks; you return to them in step 8.
  2. Edit while it runs, then stop it (2m). Change the title text and save the file. The page offers Rerun: choose Always rerun. Say: "Edit, save, look: that is how you build one of these." Then press Ctrl+C in the terminal and reload the browser tab. "Gone. The page exists only while the Python process runs. Remember that when we talk about sharing."
  3. Predict: two counters (4m). This is the heart of the lesson. Type the file. Before running, everyone writes down what both numbers say after three clicks. Then click three times. Say: "Trace one click. The script reruns. plain = 0. The button returns True, so plain becomes 1. Next click: back to 0, up to 1. It never survives the end of a run."

    File counter.py:

    import streamlit as st

st.title("Two counters")
plain = 0                                  # an ordinary variable
if st.button("Add one"):
    plain += 1
    st.session_state["kept"] = st.session_state.get("kept", 0) + 1
left, right = st.columns(2)
left.metric("Ordinary variable", plain)
right.metric("Session state", st.session_state.get("kept", 0))

    Terminal:

    streamlit run counter.py

    Check without a browser (notebook or second terminal):

    at = AppTest.from_file("counter.py", default_timeout=30).run()
print("start    plain:", at.metric[0].value, " kept:", at.metric[1].value)
for n in range(1, 4):
    at.button[0].click().run()
    print(f"click {n}  plain:", at.metric[0].value, " kept:", at.metric[1].value)
    start    plain: 0  kept: 0
click 1  plain: 1  kept: 1
click 2  plain: 1  kept: 2
click 3  plain: 1  kept: 3
    Write on the board: the whole script reruns. "That one sentence explains why apps are easy to write, why a plain variable forgets, and why caching matters."
  4. Keys and a reset callback (3m). Say: "Give a widget a key and its value lives in session state under that name. Starting values are set through session state. The reset happens in a callback, on_click=reset, which Streamlit runs before the rerun begins."

    File reset_demo.py:

    import streamlit as st

STORES = ["Boise", "Bend", "Flagstaff", "Asheville"]

def reset():
    st.session_state["stores"] = STORES
    st.session_state["min_revenue"] = 0

if "stores" not in st.session_state:        # first run of this session
    reset()
st.multiselect("Stores", STORES, key="stores")
st.slider("Minimum daily revenue ($)", 0, 20000, step=1000, key="min_revenue")
st.button("Reset filters", on_click=reset)
state = st.session_state
st.write("Showing", state["stores"], "at or above", state["min_revenue"])

    Terminal:

    streamlit run reset_demo.py

    Check without a browser (notebook or second terminal):

    at = AppTest.from_file("reset_demo.py", default_timeout=30).run()
at.multiselect[0].set_value(["Bend"])
at.slider[0].set_value(5000).run()
print("changed:", at.multiselect[0].value, at.slider[0].value)
at.button[0].click().run()
print("reset:  ", at.multiselect[0].value, at.slider[0].value)
    changed: ['Bend'] 5000
reset:   ['Boise', 'Bend', 'Flagstaff', 'Asheville'] 0
  5. Do not repeat slow work: st.cache_data (3m). Say: "Everything is recomputed on every rerun, including reading the file. Here is a load that takes two seconds." Run it and change the store three times: the first run waits two seconds (plus start-up), the rest are instant and the caption keeps saying 1.

    File cache_demo.py:

    import time
import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

@st.cache_data
def load_sales(path):
    time.sleep(2)                          # stand-in for a slow file or query
    st.session_state["loads"] = st.session_state.get("loads", 0) + 1
    return pd.read_csv(path, parse_dates=["date"])

sales = load_sales("data/daily_sales.csv")
store = st.selectbox("Store", ["Boise", "Bend", "Flagstaff", "Asheville"])
total = sales.loc[sales["store"] == store, "revenue"].sum()
st.metric("Total revenue", f"${total:,.0f}")
st.caption(f"The function body has run {st.session_state.get('loads', 0)} time(s).")

    Terminal:

    streamlit run cache_demo.py

    Check without a browser (notebook or second terminal):

    import time

at = AppTest.from_file("cache_demo.py", default_timeout=30)
for store in ["Boise", "Bend", "Flagstaff"]:
    started = time.perf_counter()
    at.run()
    if store != "Boise":
        at.selectbox[0].select(store).run()
    seconds = round(time.perf_counter() - started)
    print(f"{store:<10} {at.metric[0].value:>12}  about {seconds} s  body runs:",
          at.session_state["loads"])
    Boise        $7,364,698  about 3 s  body runs: 1
Bend         $5,045,467  about 0 s  body runs: 1
Flagstaff    $4,988,177  about 0 s  body runs: 1
    Cache the slow steps that do not depend on widgets. Leave the filtering uncached. The cache is shared by every user of the app; session state belongs to one browser tab.
  6. Layout: sidebar, columns, tabs (3m). Say: "By default elements stack down the page in script order. Four containers cover almost every dashboard: sidebar for filters, columns for things side by side, tabs for alternative views, an expander for details."

    File layout_demo.py:

    import pandas as pd
import streamlit as st

# set_page_config must be the first st call
st.set_page_config(page_title="Pinecrest Store Sales", layout="wide")

@st.cache_data
def load_sales(path):
    return pd.read_csv(path, parse_dates=["date"])

sales = load_sales("data/daily_sales.csv")
with st.sidebar:                                  # filters go in the sidebar
    store = st.selectbox("Store", ["Boise", "Bend", "Flagstaff", "Asheville"])
one = sales[sales["store"] == store]

st.title(f"{store} store")
left, right = st.columns(2)                       # side by side
left.metric("Revenue", f"${one['revenue'].sum():,.0f}")
right.metric("Visitors", f"{one['visitors'].sum():,}")
tab_trend, tab_data = st.tabs(["Trend", "Data"])  # alternative views
with tab_trend:
    st.line_chart(one, x="date", y="revenue")
with tab_data:
    st.dataframe(one[["date", "visitors", "revenue"]], hide_index=True)
    st.download_button("Download these rows as CSV", data=one.to_csv(index=False),
                       file_name="one_store.csv", mime="text/csv")

    Terminal:

    streamlit run layout_demo.py

    Check without a browser (notebook or second terminal):

    at = AppTest.from_file("layout_demo.py", default_timeout=30).run()
print("errors:", len(at.exception), "| sidebar widgets:", len(at.sidebar.selectbox))
print("metrics:", [(m.label, m.value) for m in at.metric], "| tabs:", len(at.tabs))
at.sidebar.selectbox[0].select("Flagstaff").run()
print(at.title[0].value, "|", at.metric[0].value)
    errors: 0 | sidebar widgets: 1
metrics: [('Revenue', '$7,364,698'), ('Visitors', '352,716')] | tabs: 2
Flagstaff store | $4,988,177
    Tabs organize the page; they do not skip code. Every tab's content is computed on every rerun.
  7. Break it on purpose: a half-chosen date range (3m). Say: "When a reader picks a new range there is a moment after the first click when the widget holds one date, and the script reruns right then." Show the red box in the browser, then the fix: check the length, show a message, st.stop().

    File dates_good.py:

    import datetime as dt
import streamlit as st

dates = st.date_input("Range", value=(dt.date(2025, 1, 1), dt.date(2025, 12, 31)))
if len(dates) != 2:
    st.info("Pick an end date to complete the range.")
    st.stop()
start, end = dates
st.write(start, end)

    Terminal:

    streamlit run dates_good.py

    Check without a browser (notebook or second terminal):

    import datetime as dt

for name in ["dates_bad.py", "dates_good.py"]:
    at = AppTest.from_file(name, default_timeout=30).run()
    at.date_input[0].set_value((dt.date(2025, 3, 1),)).run()    # a start date only
    problem = at.exception[0].message if at.exception else "none"
    notes = [i.value for i in at.info]
    print(f"{name:<14} error: {problem} | info shown: {notes}")
    dates_bad.py   error: not enough values to unpack (expected 2, got 1) | info shown: []
dates_good.py  error: none | info shown: ['Pick an end date to complete the range.']
    dates_bad.py is the same file without the three-line if block. st.stop() ends the current run cleanly; the lesson project uses exactly this for the date range and for an empty store list.
  8. A five-line safety net (2m). Say: "The check I have been running is a test. Save it as a file and it guards the app after every edit." Run it from the terminal.

    File test_hello.py:

    from streamlit.testing.v1 import AppTest


def test_hello_runs_and_switches_store():
    at = AppTest.from_file("hello.py", default_timeout=30).run()
    assert not at.exception
    at.selectbox[0].select("Asheville").run()
    assert at.metric[0].value == "$4,140,977"

    Terminal:

    python -m pytest -q test_hello.py
    1 passed
  9. What sharing an app takes (2m, no code). Say: "A Plotly file you send. An app you run. For a colleague to use it while your laptop is closed, six things must be true: a machine that runs Python all the time, the same packages (requirements.txt), the code and the data, a start command (streamlit run dashboard.py --server.headless true), a way in with a decision about who may open it, and secrets kept out of the code. Start local. Deploy when people ask to use it without you."
Three mistakes to expect
  • `python app.py` in place of `streamlit run app.py`. The terminal fills with missing ScriptRunContext warnings and nothing opens. Coach: "Read the first word of your command." (The kit's two Streamlit labs are the one exception, by design: run with python they test themselves; see the lab notes.)
  • Expecting a variable to remember. A list, a counter or a flag assigned in the script body is assigned again on every rerun. There is no error, only a number that will not grow. Coach: "Put your finger on line 1 and trace one click to the last line. What is the list at the top?" Then: "Where must it live?"
  • Changing a widget's value after it was drawn (st.session_state["x"] = 0 inside if st.button(...)), and two identical widgets without keys. Both give a red box whose first sentence says exactly what happened. Coach: have the learner read the first sentence aloud, then ask "what runs before the script does?" (A callback.)
Guided lab · 22 min

Lab 7.4-B labs/module-20/l7_4-streamlit/gear_shortlist_starter.py first (everyone; reference: gear_shortlist_solution.py): a tent shortlist that forgets. It is the counter demo turned into a task, and it is the lab that makes the rerun model stick. Then Lab 7.4-A labs/module-20/l7_4-streamlit/catalog_browser_starter.py (reference: catalog_browser_solution.py, test file test_catalog_browser.py): sidebar filters with keys, a reset callback, st.stop() on an empty result, three metrics, a table and a download.

  • Each lab file is an app and its own test. streamlit run gear_shortlist_starter.py opens it in the browser; python gear_shortlist_starter.py runs a built-in check with AppTest and prints what the app shows, with no server and no browser. Learners keep the app open in a browser tab (Always rerun) and run the check in the terminal after each TODO.
  • Minutes 0 to 3: before fixing anything, everyone predicts what python gear_shortlist_starter.py prints. It prints 0, 1, 0, 1, 0 in the first column: the list forgets.
  • Minutes 3 to 12: TODO 1 to 5 in the shortlist. Stall to expect: keeping if left.button(...): and also adding on_click=, which adds the tent twice in one click. One or the other.
  • Expected (shortlist): 24 tents. The first metric reads 0 at the start, 1 after adding the first tent, still 1 after adding it again and after choosing a second tent, 2 after adding the second ($259.90 in total: $41.95 + $217.95), and 0 after Clear. The third metric, the ordinary counter, reads 1 on every line. The unfinished starter prints 0, 1, 0, 1, 0: the list forgets.
  • Minutes 12 to 22: the catalog browser, TODO 1 to 6. The starter's check counts progress: metrics: 3, widgets in the sidebar: 4, empty selection handled: True.
  • Expected (catalog): Start (Tents): Products 24, Median price $298.45, Mean rating 4.25. Tents and Sleeping under $100: 12 products, median $46.95, mean rating 4.07; with In stock only: 11. No category: the warning shows, 0 metrics, 0 errors. After Reset: ['Tents'], (0, 620), False, 24 products. test_catalog_browser.py: 3 tests pass.
  • A trap worth one sentence: text passed to st.caption, st.write and st.markdown is Markdown, and a pair of dollar signs is read as math. "$0 to $620" renders as *0 to 620* in italics. Write \$, or put the amount in words, as the lab's caption does. st.metric values are not Markdown, so $298.45 is safe there.
Start the lesson project · 8 min

Open the lesson at Project: The Pinecrest Sales Dashboard. Read the brief: choose stores and a date range, see the key numbers, look at the trend and the weekly pattern, download the rows. Everyone creates dashboard.py, types Step 1 (page setup, constants, the cached load_sales) plus one temporary line, st.write(sales.shape), and starts it with streamlit run dashboard.py. Check: the page shows (2903, 10). Leave the app running with Always rerun: Steps 2 to 7 are homework, built by saving and looking. The final AppTest check should print Revenue $21,539,320 for all stores.

Checks for understanding

Workbook self-check, items Q7 to Q12.

Answers: Q7 B) 11; Q8 `20`; Q9 A) In a function passed as on_click=, which Streamlit runs before the rerun starts; Q10 D) Loading and preparing the CSV file, which is slow and the same whatever the widgets say; Q11 1 0; Q12 C) True only during the one rerun caused by a click, otherwise False. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: for the shortlist, hand out a card with the three places state can live (a variable: one run; st.session_state: one browser tab; @st.cache_data: everyone, until restart) and let pairs trace one click on paper before typing. In the catalog browser give TODO 1 complete. Stretch: add a st.download_button to the shortlist; add a fourth filter to the catalog browser (brand) with its own key and include it in the reset; write one more test in test_catalog_browser.py; or lesson Exercise 2 (a delta against the previous period), reading its caution about seasonal comparisons.

Capstone Kickoff

2:30

Capstone Kickoff: Choose a Question, Write the Plan

20 min
Purpose

Every learner leaves with a chosen capstone question and a one-paragraph plan in the workbook. The plan is Milestone 1 of Lesson 8.1 started in the room; the homework is Milestones 1 to 4, up to a first finding. Session 21 is a studio: it only works if people arrive with a prepared table and something they have noticed.

Run it on a clock
QQuestion (Lesson 8.1)Main dataLeans on
AWhy is Asheville falling behind?daily_sales.csv (store_weather.csv, survey.csv, sales_2025.xlsx possibly useful)time series, ratios, comparison between stores, careful wording about cause
BDoes it matter how we found the customer?customers.csv, orders.csvmerging, more than two groups, skewed data, effect sizes
CDoes the welcome discount bring people back?orders.csv (customers.csv possibly useful)per-customer features, two proportions, spotting an unfair comparison
DWhat did the March 2025 price increase do to sales?order_items.csv, orders.csv, products.csvmulti-table merges, seasonality, reasoning about what would have happened otherwise (the most demanding)
  1. Minutes 0 to 4 · the brief. Put the lesson's memo on screen ("We have four questions that keep coming up in meetings, and opinions on all of them. We would like evidence."). Say what is handed in: a notebook that runs top to bottom, one or two figures, a one-page report.md; a dashboard is optional. Say the sentence from the lesson that matters most: "A well-supported no clear difference scores exactly as well on the rubric as a dramatic discovery."
  2. Minutes 4 to 8 · choose. Learners reread the four questions (they read them for homework) and write a letter on a sticky note. Tell them the lesson's advice: choose by curiosity, not by ease. D is the most demanding. A learner may propose their own question if it passes the lesson's three checks (a decision, the data exists in data/, no lesson project already answered it).
  3. Minutes 8 to 16 · write the paragraph. In the workbook, complete the plan frame: the question and the decision it informs, the tables and what one row of the analysis table will be, the comparison and the method, why the comparison might be unfair and how they will check, the chart they expect to make, and what result would change their mind. Circulate. Your only questions: "What is being compared with what?" and "What else differs between those two groups?"
  4. Minutes 16 to 20 · partner check. Pairs swap workbooks. The reader answers one thing in writing under the plan: "From this plan, I predict your notebook will contain ...". That is the lesson's own done-when test for Milestone 1. Collect the sticky notes: they tell you how to split your coaching time in Session 21.
What to say and what not to say
  • Do not hint at any answer. The lesson deliberately has no answer key. Your notes for each question (sound method, key numbers, traps, what an honest null or an over-claim looks like) are in final-assessment.html; read them before Session 21, not aloud tonight.
  • Do point at the lesson's own "Think about" lines. Each question's paragraph already names its trap in general terms (time behind each customer, what else changed in March, which factor of revenue moved). Ask the learner to read theirs to you and say how the plan handles it.
  • A plan that is a topic ("look at Asheville") is the Beginning level of the rubric's first row. Ask for the comparison. A plan with six comparisons will not finish: ask which one is the headline.
  • Spread is not required. If everyone chooses A, let them: the showcase is then a study in how the same data yields different, defensible reports. Note it for the gallery walk grouping.
  • Tools and help. The lesson allows AI assistants and web code on working-analyst terms: the learner is responsible for every line and every claim, checks outputs another way, and says in the README what help was used. Say it now so nobody is surprised by the disclosure line at submission.

Closing

Exit ticket · 4 min (answers)
  1. Two Bokeh plots on one page. What must they share for a box selection in one to highlight the same rows in the other? What must they share to pan together? Answer: The same ColumnDataSource object for linked selection (brushing). The same range object (x_range=first.x_range) for linked panning and zooming.
  2. A reader changes one widget in your Streamlit app. What runs? Name the place for a value that must survive, and the decorator for a slow step that must not repeat. Answer: The whole script reruns from the top with the widget's new value. st.session_state keeps values across reruns (per browser tab); @st.cache_data stores a function's result so the slow body runs once.
  3. Write your capstone question letter (A, B, C or D) and the one comparison your plan is built on. Answer: No single answer. Check that it is a comparison (two or more groups, or before and after against something), not a topic, and that the learner can say what would make it unfair. Use the cards to balance your coaching time in Session 21.
Homework before Session 21
  • Capstone first: Milestones 1 to 4 of Lesson 8.1, up to a first finding (M1 Question and plan 30 min, M2 Load and check 45 min, M3 Clean and prepare 45 min, M4 Explore 75 min; 195 minutes in all). Bring: the plan as the first Markdown cell of pinecrest_report.ipynb, the loaded and checked tables, one function that builds the analysis table, a "What I have noticed" list, and two sentences on what you expect the answer to be and what could still prove you wrong.
  • Finish The Linked Store Explorer (7.3): store_explorer.html. Finish The Pinecrest Sales Dashboard (7.4): dashboard.py and its AppTest check.
  • Lesson exercises (7.3: 1 to 3; 7.4: 1 to 3), both quizzes and journals; the kit lab you did not finish.
  • Read the rest of Lesson 8.1 before you start: the worked mini-example, the one-page report template, the rubric and the five common mistakes.
  • If the week is short: capstone milestones, then the two lesson projects, then exercises.
Bring list for Session 21 (Capstone Studio and Showcase)
  • Your capstone folder pinecrest-capstone/ with pinecrest_report.ipynb that runs from a fresh kernel as far as you have got (Restart and Run All before you leave home), and the course data/ folder beside it.
  • Your one-paragraph plan (workbook) and your "What I have noticed" list.
  • Lessons 4.5, 4.7 and 3.3 within reach, plus your own helpers: overview, cohens_d, your chart helpers.
  • A way to show one figure to others: your laptop screen is enough for a gallery walk; a single PNG on a shared drive or USB stick for lightning talks.
  • Nothing to install, no servers, no accounts, no API keys.

If You Run Long or Short

Long, in 7.3: cut demo step 2 (layers and legend: it is Matplotlib thinking again) and step 10 (file sizes: say the two modes in a sentence); shorten step 9 to running the finished cell. Never cut step 3 (the source) or step 8 (brushing). Long, in 7.4: cut step 6 (layout: the lesson project teaches it) and step 4 (keys and reset: lab 7.4-A covers it); never cut step 3 (two counters) or step 5 (caching). If you are ten minutes behind at 2:20, drop "start the project" for 7.4 (it becomes homework from Step 1) and keep the kickoff whole. Short: run the second lab of each lesson in the room; have pairs open each other's margin_brush.html and state one thing the brush showed; or take five extra minutes in the kickoff for a second partner check, where the reader names the weakest sentence of the plan.

Instructor Kit · Facilitator Guide

Session 21: Capstone Studio and Showcase

How to run the last session: a studio where learners take their own capstone from a first finding to a quantified, visualized answer, a timed showcase, and the close of the course. The instructor answer notes and the rubric with weighting are in final-assessment.html.

1 lesson 3 hrs session Lesson 8.1 Session 21 of 21 Studio + showcase

How to Use This Guide

  • One lesson, no new tools. Session 21 is a studio and a showcase. The lesson page is capstone_project.html (The Pinecrest Report, 420 minutes); learners arrive with Milestones 1 to 4 done, work Milestones 5 and 6 here, and finish 7 and 8 within a week.
  • Your instructor answer notes are in `../../final-assessment.html`: for each of the four questions the tables and steps of a sound analysis, the key numbers, the traps, what an honest null looks like (Questions B and C; for D, what an over-claim looks like), follow-up questions and what weak work gets wrong, plus the rubric with weighting and the submission rules. Read it before class. Nothing from it is said aloud as an answer or copied into a learner page: the lesson deliberately has no answer key.
  • Coach by asking. Every coaching move in this guide is a question. If a learner asks "is my answer right?", ask what would make it wrong and whether they checked.
  • The optional lab labs/module-21/l8_1-capstone/ holds a filled-in version of the lesson's notebook outline on a practice question that is not a capstone question. Point stuck learners at its structure, not its question.
The one risk of Session 21: a room of stuck people waiting for you

Twenty learners on four questions will want you all at once. The clock below rations your attention: a check-in every 15 minutes in which every learner reports a status in one word, then coaching for the reds first. Learners who are green help ambers at their table. Never sit with one learner for more than four minutes in a round.

Before the Session

  • ☐ Read final-assessment.html end to end, especially the notes for the questions your learners chose (the Session 20 sticky notes tell you the mix).
  • ☐ Run python3 labs/check_labs.py module-21: 2 passed, 0 failed.
  • ☐ Decide the showcase format from the size of the room (table below) and print the gallery-walk rotation cards or set up the second circle and its timekeeper.
  • ☐ Traffic-light cards (green, amber, red) or three colors of sticky note for each table; a visible countdown timer on the projector.
  • ☐ Projector: the rubric from the lesson page (The Rubric section) and the report template, both readable from the back.
  • ☐ No servers, no internet, no installs are needed today. Learners need their capstone folder with data/ beside the notebook.
  • ☐ Prepare the course-close slide content: what next (machine learning, open data, regression), the feedback link or form you use, the submission deadline (one week from today).

Warm-up

0:00

Warm-up: Retrieval from Session 20 and a Plan Check

10 min
Five questions (with answers)
  1. Two Bokeh plots on one page: what must they share for a box selection in one to highlight the same rows in the other? Answer: The same ColumnDataSource object. (Sharing a range object links panning and zooming instead.)
  2. A Bokeh file saved with output_file has a dropdown. Which kind of callback works for a reader who opens the file? Answer: JavaScript: CustomJS (or js_link). A Python on_change callback needs a running Bokeh server.
  3. A reader moves a Streamlit slider. What runs? Answer: The whole script, from the top, with the slider returning its new value.
  4. Where does a value live that must survive reruns? And what stops a slow CSV load repeating on every click? Answer: st.session_state (per browser tab); @st.cache_data on the loading function (shared by all users).
  5. Your capstone: say the question letter and the headline comparison in one sentence: "I am comparing ___ with ___ using ___." Answer: No single answer. Listen for a comparison rather than a topic, and note who has none yet: they get the first coaching round.
How to run it

Questions 1 to 4 on paper for four minutes, answers called out in two. Then question 5 around the room, ten seconds each: write the comparisons on the board under A, B, C, D. Anyone without a comparison is your first coaching visit in Studio 1.

Lesson Plan

8.1

The Pinecrest Report

175 min
Objectives (from the lesson page)
  • Turn a business question into a written analysis plan before touching the data
  • Carry an analysis from raw files to a tested, quantified answer, working independently
  • Report a result with its estimate, confidence interval, test, effect size and caveats
  • Present the answer in a one-page report with one or two figures that state their finding
  • Make the work reproducible, review it against a rubric, and share it responsibly
Frame · 10 min: the rubric and the strong sentence

Put the rubric on screen. Say: "Six rows. Proficient in all six is a successful capstone. Exemplary is what makes a reviewer remember your name. And a well-supported "no clear difference" scores exactly as well as a discovery." Then write the five-part sentence on the board, using the lesson's example: "On promotion days 25.8% of visitors bought, against 23.4% on comparable ordinary days: 2.4 points more (95% CI 1.9 to 2.9; Welch t-test p < 0.001; d = 0.93)." Label the five parts: two estimates, the difference, the interval, the test, the effect size. "By the break, your main result is a sentence like this one." Explain the clock: check-ins at fixed times, one word each, reds first.

Studio 1 · 45 min · Milestone 5, test and quantify
  • 0:00 stand-up check-in (3 min). Each learner holds up a card: green (the analysis table exists and I know my comparison), amber (table exists, method unclear), red (no table yet). Reds come to you first, ambers pair with a green at their table.
  • Coaching round 1 (12 min). Reds: "Show me one row of your analysis table and say what it is." If it does not exist, do Milestone 3 together in five minutes using the scaffold lab's build_table() pattern, then move on.
  • 0:15 check-in (2 min). One word each: "estimate", "interval", "test", "effect", "stuck". Coaching round 2 (13 min): stuck learners first; ask which method fits the data type (proportions, skewed amounts, several groups).
  • 0:30 check-in (2 min). Everyone tries to break their result: one robustness check (another definition, without the extremes, within each store or year). Coaching round 3 (10 min).
  • 0:42 (3 min). Everyone writes the main result as one five-part sentence in a Markdown cell. Spot-read four sentences aloud (with permission) and name the missing part, if any.
  • Done when: the main result is one sentence in the strong form, and at least one attempt to make it disappear is recorded (the lesson's own done-when).
Coaching notes by question (no answers aloud)

For each question: what strong work does, the traps to listen for, and three questions to ask. The numbers that go with these notes are in final-assessment.html.

Question A · Why is Asheville falling behind?
  • Strong work writes revenue as visitors × conversion × basket for each store and year, finds which factor moved, and shows whether the pattern is steady through the year (month by month against the same month a year earlier) and unusual against the other three stores.
  • Traps to listen for: reading the decline as "customers spend less" without checking; comparing seasons; treating 363 days as 363 independent customers; tying the October to November 2025 survey (one snapshot) to a two-year trend; using orders.csv (account holders only) as if it were the store total; ignoring the one missing Asheville revenue day.
  • Questions to ask: "Which factor moved, and by how much in each month?" "What do the other three stores' same factors do?" "What data would tell you why fewer people come in?"
Question B · Does it matter how we found the customer?
  • Strong work builds one row per customer (including those who never bought, with zero), defines "worth" before looking, compares five channels with a method that suits skewed spend, counts its pairwise comparisons, and makes the time window fair.
  • Traps to listen for: customers who signed up during 2024 and 2025 have had less time to spend; inner merges silently drop the 1,112 customers with no completed order (or keep the 739 orders of closed accounts with no channel); ten pairwise tests with no adjustment; "worth twice as much" answered from one ratio of means.
  • Questions to ask: "Does every customer in your comparison have the same amount of time?" "How many comparisons did you look at?" "How large a difference could your data have missed?"
Question C · Does the welcome discount bring people back?
  • Strong work defines a true first order (the data start on 2024-01-01, so a customer who signed up in 2019 has no first order in this file), uses a fixed follow-up window, compares two proportions with an interval and effect size, and words the result without "because".
  • Traps to listen for: the time-to-return trap (late first orders have had no time to come back); counting long-standing customers' first order in the data as a first order; customers chose to use the code (self-selection); counting cancelled first orders.
  • Questions to ask: "What is your follow-up window, and who is excluded by it?" "Whose first order is really a first order?" "What would a fair test of the code look like?"
Question D · What did the March 2025 price increase do to sales?
  • Strong work identifies the repriced products from order_items.unit_price (not today's products.price), compares units of repriced against unchanged products over the same months a year apart, checks the comparison before the change (a placebo period), reports the drop in units with its interval (about 14% fewer than trend), and states that the products were not chosen at random.
  • Traps to listen for: before-and-after across seasons (January and February are slow, so repriced products look busier afterward); company growth (repriced units flat year over year look like "no effect" until the unchanged products are beside them); valuing old orders at today's price; bulk lines and discontinued SKUs; category mix between the two groups. This question has a real effect, so also listen for over-claims: "sales fell 14%" for the whole company, or a price elasticity the data do not show.
  • Questions to ask: "How did you decide which products were repriced?" "What happened to the unchanged products over the same months, and before March?" "Is your number about units or revenue, and about which products?"
Studio 2 · 40 min · Milestone 6, then the Answer
  • 0:00 check-in (2 min). "Which one chart carries your answer?" Each learner names it in a sentence.
  • Work (18 min). Redraw that chart to the Module 3 standard: a title that states the finding, labeled axes with units, purposeful color, error bars identified in a caption, saved from code with savefig(..., dpi=150).
  • 0:20 check-in (3 min). Pairs swap screens for 60 seconds each: "Without reading anything but the figure, what is the answer?" If the partner cannot say, the title or the comparison needs work.
  • Work (12 min). Fix the figure; then draft the Answer paragraph of report.md: two or three sentences a manager could repeat, leading with the answer and the main number with its uncertainty.
  • 0:35 (5 min). Restart the kernel and Run All. Anyone whose notebook fails fixes it now with a neighbor; note their name for a follow-up message this week.
Showcase prep · 10 min

Each learner prepares the one figure and three sentences: the question, the answer with its uncertainty, one specific caveat. Lightning talk or gallery station, the content is the same. A learner with a null result (most often Question B or C) says so first and states what the interval rules out: model that sentence for the room once.

Showcase · 35 min
LearnersLightning talks (35 min)Gallery walk (35 min)
8One circle, everyone presents: 8 × (3 min talk + 1 min one question and changeover) = 32 min, 3 min spare. You keep time.Two halves of 4. Half A at their screens, half B visits: 4 rounds of 3 min + 30 s to move = 14 min; swap (2 min); half B presents for 14 min; 5 min debrief. Every visitor sees every presenter in the other half.
16Two circles of 8 in parallel (two corners or two rooms), the same 32-minute clock; you sit in one, a co-facilitator or a learner timekeeper runs the other. If you must keep one circle: 2-minute talks (one figure, one sentence) × 16 = 32 min.Two halves of 8. Each visitor makes 4 visits of 3.5 min (14 min) to 4 of the 8 stations, assigned so every station has a visitor every round; swap; 14 min; 5 min debrief. Each presenter gives the 3-minute version four times.
24Three circles of 8 in parallel, each with a timekeeper (the third can be a learner); 32 min. One circle of 24 does not fit in 35 minutes: use the gallery walk.Two halves of 12. Each visitor makes 4 visits of 3.5 min to 4 of the 12 stations (a printed rotation card per visitor); swap; 5 min debrief. Recommended at this size.

Audience job (both formats): each listener writes one question per presenter on a sticky note and gives it to them; the presenter keeps the notes for the Next questions section of the report. Your job: keep time and say nothing evaluative in public. Note one strength per learner for their written feedback.

Course close · 10 min
  • What the course built (2 min). Point at the list from the lesson's summary: from installing Python and loading a CSV to answering a business question nobody had answered for them, and knowing how sure they are.
  • The last journal entry (4 min, started here, finished at home). The lesson's end-of-course prompt: read the first entry from Lesson 0.1 and write to the person who wrote it. Three things you can do now; the hardest lesson and how it looks from here; what the capstone taught you about how you work; one question about data in your own life.
  • What next (2 min). Prediction (machine learning) builds directly on this course, starting from the customer_features.csv table of Lesson 2.9; regression is the bridge; a second capstone on public open data; deeper SQL. Repeat the lesson's rule about data: never practice on private or work data without written permission.
  • Feedback (2 min). Your usual form. Ask one spoken question: "Which session would you change first, and how?"
Checks for understanding

Workbook self-check, all twelve items, as homework with the submission (or as a five-minute pair activity if the showcase runs short).

Answers: Q1 C) Did products repriced on 2025-03-01 sell fewer units, March to December, than comparable products whose price did not change?; Q2 A) The difference in medians with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval, reported next to the means; Q3 4 350.0; Q4 B) We found no clear difference: the data are consistent with anything from 1.5 points lower to 4.0 points higher, so a gain larger than about 4 points is unlikely; Q5 D) Give everyone the same window (for example 180 days) and keep only customers whose first order was at least 180 days before the data end; Q6 10; Q7 A) The change in the affected products, against the change in unaffected products over the same months a year earlier (a difference in differences); Q8 0.034; Q9 C) Customers chose whether to use the code, so those who used it may differ from those who did not in ways the data do not record; Q10 B) The answer, with the main number and its uncertainty; Q11 [10, 40, 30]; Q12 D) The question, then the answer with its uncertainty, pointing at the one figure. Full set with explanations in the Answer Key.

Differentiation

Support: learners who arrive without Milestones 1 to 4 work from the scaffold lab's structure in Studio 1 and narrow their question to one comparison; they present a plan and a first finding in the showcase, and the rubric still applies at submission. Stretch: the Exemplary column: a pre-stated result that would change the reader's mind, a robustness check reported in the page, multiple comparisons or non-independence addressed, an alternative explanation tested; or the optional dashboard (adapt dashboard.py from Lesson 7.4) after the page is done.

Closing

Exit ticket · 5 min (answers)
  1. Write your main result as one sentence with all five parts. Answer: Estimate for each group, the difference, its 95% interval, the test and p-value, and the effect size, in words a manager can repeat. A null result also says how large a difference the data can rule out.
  2. Name one caveat that is specific to your question and data (not "more data is needed"). Answer: Check it is specific: who or what is missing, what could not be separated, or why "because" is too strong for this design.
  3. What will you do in the 75 minutes of capstone work left after today, in order? Answer: Finish the figure, write report.md (Answer first, then Caveats), then Restart and Run All and check every number in the report against the fresh output, score yourself on the rubric, submit.
Submission (within one week) and what goes home
  • After class: 75 minutes of required work. Finish the figure, write report.md from the template (Answer first, then Caveats), then Milestone 8: Restart and Run All, check every number in the report against the output, score yourself on the six rubric rows, work through the self-review checklist. Optional: a dashboard or interactive file (60 minutes), only after the page is done.
  • Hand in the project folder: pinecrest_report.ipynb (runs top to bottom with relative paths), one or two figures, report.md (one page), README.md (what this is, how to run it, where the data is from, and what help was used: AI assistants, web code, a classmate), and the self-scored rubric. Deadline: one week from today. The full rules, late options and how the two checkpoints are recorded are in final-assessment.html.
  • Bring list: there is no Session 22. For the submission: the course data/ folder is not handed in; link to it as the lesson's Sharing Your Work section says.

If You Run Long or Short

Long: shorten Showcase prep to five minutes and Course close to the journal prompt and the deadline; never cut the 0:42 strong-sentence write-up in Studio 1 or the Restart and Run All at the end of Studio 2. With 24 learners and lightning talks, switch to the gallery walk rather than cutting talks to one minute. Short: do the twelve self-check items in pairs; or run a second gallery round with the sticky-note questions answered in writing; or start Milestone 7 in the room (draft the Caveats section next, then Next questions).
